actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Establishing Baselines for 3D Point Cloud Denoising
PROPOSAL: Compare three existing supervised denoising methods, TotalDenoising, DNet3D, and PointFlow, on a synthetic point cloud dataset (e.g., Dippy the Diplodocus or the tank dataset) consisting of noisy-ground-truth pairs. Investigate their performance across various noise levels and point cloud densities.
CONTROLS: ICP (Iterative Closest Point) algorithm, (noisy) average point cloud as a baseline
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: DNet3D and TotalDenoising will show competitive results, with PointFlow struggling on high-noise scenarios due to its specific architecture, and the (noisy) average point cloud baseline serving as a rudimentary but surprisingly effective method for simple denoising.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Establishing Baselines for 3D Point Cloud Denoising (Rev.)
PROPOSAL: Revised to include an additional control: the TotalDenoising (unsupervised) model with L1 regularization, to assess its performance without supervision. We will further investigate its tendency to preserve local geometry and its sensitivity to noise levels.
CONTROLS: ICP algorithm, (noisy) average point cloud as a baseline, DNet3D, PointFlow, TotalDenoising (unsupervised) with L1 regularization
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The unsupervised TotalDenoising model with L1 regularization will show a significant drop in performance compared to its supervised predecessor, but surprisingly maintain its ability to preserve local geometry, outperforming ICP and the average point cloud baseline in certain scenarios.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Establishing Baselines for 3D Point Cloud Denoising
PROPOSAL: The revision adds an additional control: the TotalDenoising (unsupervised) model with L1 regularization, to assess its performance without supervision. We will further investigate its tendency to preserve local geometry and its sensitivity to noise levels. 
CONTROLS: ICP algorithm, (noisy) average point cloud as a baseline, DNet3D, PointFlow, TotalDenoising (unsupervised) with L1 regularization, and a new ablation study on the importance of the noise modeling component within TotalDenoising for unsupervised learning
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The unsupervised TotalDenoising model with L1 regularization will show a significant drop in performance compared to its supervised predecessor, but surprisingly maintain its ability to preserve local geometry, outperforming ICP and the average point cloud baseline in certain scenarios, providing strong evidence to support further innovations in unsupervised denoising methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Denoising using Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: Employ a contrastive learning framework to train an unsupervised denoising network, where the model learns to distinguish between points that are close in the noisy space from points that have been corrupted. Utilize a synthetic dataset of point clouds under various noise levels and evaluate performance using metrics like Chamfer distance and Earth Mover's Distance (EMD).
CONTROLS: Baseline from proposal 1, with additional ablation studying the effect of sampling rates for the positive pairs in the contrastive loss function
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The unsupervised model will achieve competitive results to the supervised models in terms of denoising performance, with significant potential to outperform them by leveraging the information from multiple noisy observations of the same scene, and the contrastive learning framework will be found to preserve local geometry effectively, despite the lack of explicit supervision.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Handling Ambiguity in Unsupervised Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate methods to handle the ambiguity brought about by the inconsistent denoising results from different noisy observations of the same scene in the unsupervised learning framework. Explore using ensembling techniques like majority voting, weighted voting, or model averaging, to aggregate the predictions from multiple models trained on different noisy observations, and assess their impact on denoising performance.
CONTROLS: Baseline from proposal 2, with variant ensembling methods
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect that ensembling methods will significantly improve the denoising quality and robustness, enabling the model to recover a more accurate clean point cloud, but may also introduce some amount of over-smoothing, especially when dealing with highly variegated scenes, and the best ensemble strategy can depend on the dataset characteristics and the noise distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Spatial Prior for Unsupervised Denoising
PROPOSAL: Incorporate spatial prior information into the unsupervised denoising framework to encourage preserved local geometry and improve denoising quality. Explore using a multi-scale distance map or a feature map as the spatial prior, and evaluate the impact on denoising performance using metrics like Chamfer distance and Earth Mover's Distance (EMD).
CONTROLS: Baseline from proposal 2, with ablations on the effect of different spatial prior representations and scales
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The inclusion of spatial prior will significantly improve the model's ability to preserve local geometry and recover accurate clean point clouds, especially in scenes with smooth surfaces, but may lead to over-fitting when dealing with highly complex scenes, and a proper balance between the spatial prior and contrastive learning loss will be crucial for optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Extending to Point Cloud Upsampling
PROPOSAL: Adapt the unsupervised denoising framework to learn a point cloud upsampling network, which can generate high-density point clouds from low-density ones. Design a novel upsampling loss function that preserves local geometry and evaluates the performance using metrics like Chamfer distance and Hausdorff distance.
CONTROLS: Baseline upsampling method PM vsUpsample, and variants of our upsampling implementation without the proposed spatial prior and ambiguity handling components
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The unsupervised upsampling network will achieve competitive results to its supervised counterparts in terms of upsampling quality, leveraging the information from multiple observations to effectively capture complex scene structures, particularly in scenes with slight object motion, where PM vsUpsample often fails due to its lack of handling the noise and local structure variability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Generalizability and Robustness
PROPOSAL: Assess the generalizability and robustness of the unsupervised denoising and upsampling models across various real-world LiDAR datasets, including noisy point clouds from urban street scenes and natural environments. Evaluate their performance in terms of denoising quality, upsampling accuracy, and robustness to different scanner noises.
CONTROLS: Versions of our models optimized for various LiDAR sensor models (e.g., Velodyne HD-64E and Velodyne LiDAR PUCK), with varying noise levels and point cloud densities
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The unsupervised models will show good generalizability across different LiDAR sensors and real-world environments, adapting to changes in noise patterns and scene characteristics, but may exhibit some performance drops when dealing with high-noise or low-density scenarios, requiring additional training or adjustments to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigation into Unsupervised Natural Image Denoising
PROPOSAL: Adapt the unsupervised learning framework and spatial prior mechanism developed for 3D point cloud denoising to the task of 2D natural image denoising. Explore its application on various real-world natural image datasets, including BSD-200 and Kodak-24, and evaluate the performance in terms of MSE, PSNR, and SSIM.
CONTROLS: Stochastic Denoising Network (SND) and DnCNN as baselines for 2D denoising, and variants of our implementation with different spatial prior representations
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adapted unsupervised framework will demonstrate promising denoising performance on real-world natural images, leveraging the spatial prior to effectively capture local structures and textures, and will exhibit comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods in terms of MSE, PSNR, and SSIM, highlighting the potential for transferring the knowledge to 2D denoising tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Study and Analysis of Learned Representations
PROPOSAL: Carry out a comprehensive study and analysis of the learned representations from our unsupervised learning framework and point cloud denoising models. Investigate the relationships between the learned geometric priors, local structure, and noise patterns. Examine the scalability, interpretability, and generalizability of the learned representations across different point cloud datasets and tasks.
CONTROLS: No controls, as this proposal is an investigation of the existing models and their behavior
COST: 100 GPU-hours (estimated)
PREDICTION: The analysis will reveal that the learned representations from the unsupervised framework are effective in encoding spatial relationships and local structure, demonstrating a strong connection to the underlying geometry of the point clouds. This analysis will serve as a foundation for further research on incorporating these insights into other point cloud processing tasks, and will be essential for developing more robust and accurate 3D perception systems.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Distributional Localisation for Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising
PROPOSAL: We propose a method that combines distributional clustering (clustering based on the distribution of noise) with local surface fitting, leveraging local neighbourhoods to suppress noise. We aim to identify clusters of noisy points that can be clustered into plausible surface locations, and use this information to filter out noise. For this proposal, we will train a clustering-based model on a synthetic dataset and evaluate its performance on benchmark LiDAR scans.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to existing unsupervised methods such as TotalDenoising, as well as local surface fitting baselines.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach should show improved performance over TotalDenoising for denoising LiDAR scans, with a good trade-off between denoising quality and computational efficiency. However, we may struggle to generalise to natural image denoising tasks despite the potential for clustering to also apply in 2D cases.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Bayesian Network-Based Dynamic Feature Selection for Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising
PROPOSAL: We introduce a Bayesian network-based method to automatically select features for unsupervised point cloud denoising. By exploring the correlations between different points, we construct a Bayesian network and use it to dynamically select relevant features for denoising. We will adapt our method to a state-of-the-art unsupervised denoising framework and test it on LiDAR scans of urban street scenes.
CONTROLS: We will compare our feature selection method with a brute-force approach that tries all possible feature combinations, as well as the original unsupervised framework without feature selection.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed method should significantly speed up the denoising process and improve results by focusing on the most relevant features, while also outperforming the baseline unsupervised framework. However, we may encounter difficulties with handling highly correlated features and cases where the Bayesian network fails to capture the underlying relationships.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising via Proximal Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose an unsupervised point cloud denoising method based on proximal learning, where we reformulate the denoising problem as an unregularised least-squares optimisation. Using the square root of the point cloud's covariance matrix, we construct a proximal point operator that effectively suppresses noise. We will evaluate our method on both synthetic and LiDAR scans of natural scenes.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proximal learning approach with existing unsupervised methods and also with a standard least-squares regression baseline.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our proximal learning method should show improved results for denoising point clouds with non-Gaussian noise distributions, and also enjoy faster runtimes compared to existing methods. However, we may encounter issues with its applicability to very high-dimensional point clouds.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Bayesian Network-Based Dynamic Feature Selection for Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising
PROPOSAL: We revise our Bayesian network-based method to incorporate knowledge distillation, where we train a smaller neural network to mimic the performance of the larger network. This approach should reduce the computational overhead while preserving the strengths of the feature selection method. We will use the KAIST outdoor LiDAR dataset to evaluate the effectiveness of our revised method.
CONTROLS: We will compare our revised method with the original feature selection method and also with a knowledge distillation baseline without feature selection.
COST: 70 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised method should show improved scalability and reduced computational cost while maintaining competitive performance with the original method. However, we may encounter challenges in selecting the optimal 'student' model size and balancing the trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Denoising Spatial Propagation Networks (DSPN) for Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel unsupervised point cloud denoising method based on Denoising Spatial Propagation Networks (DSPN), a spatial propagation architecture that leverages a diffusion process to iteratively refine the point cloud. We will introduce a latent representation of the point cloud that is denoised through spatial propagation, resulting in a clean representation of the 3D geometry. We will evaluate our method on LiDAR scans of natural scenes.
CONTROLS: We will compare our DSPN-based approach with existing unsupervised methods and also with a spatial propagation baseline that does not incorporate denoising.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our DSPN-based method should show improved performance and robustness for denoising LiDAR scans with complex geometries and realistic noise distributions. However, we may encounter difficulties with controlling the number of iterations and achieving stable results for highly noisy or sparse point clouds.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Limits of Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising: A Theoretical Analysis of Information-Theoretic Bounds
PROPOSAL: We provide a theoretical analysis of the limits of unsupervised point cloud denoising, deriving lower bounds for the achievable denoising performance in terms of mutual information between the noisy and clean point clouds. We will explore how these bounds depend on the properties of the noise distribution and the underlying geometry of the point cloud, providing insights into the fundamental challenges of unsupervised denoising.
CONTROLS: This theoretical analysis will be compared to existing unsupervised methods to determine how close our best results are to the theoretical limits.
COST: Minimal computational cost
PREDICTION: This theoretical analysis should provide valuable insights into the feasibility of unsupervised point cloud denoising and highlight the importance of incorporating prior knowledge of the noise distribution and geometry of the point cloud. However, deriving precise bounds may be challenging, and the results may be highly dependent on specific assumptions about the noise distribution and point cloud geometry.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Distributional Localisation for Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising
PROPOSAL: We refine our distributional localisation method to incorporate the insights from the theoretical analysis (Proposal 5), specifically by assuming a Gaussian noise model and using the Fisher information matrix to guide the selection of features. We will explore how this refined approach compares to the original method and the other unsupervised denoising methods.
CONTROLS: We will compare our refined method with the original distributional localisation method, Bayesian network-based feature selection (Proposal 2), proximal learning (Proposal 3), and DSPN (Proposal 4), as well as with a Gaussian noise baseline.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our refined method should show improved performance compared to the original distributional localisation method and competitive results with the other unsupervised denoising methods. However, we may encounter challenges in tuning the parameters of the Fisher information matrix and guaranteeing the stability of the clustering process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising and Upsampling
PROPOSAL: We propose a multi-task learning framework that trains a single network to denoise and upsample point clouds simultaneously, leveraging the shared understanding of the 3D geometry learned from both tasks. We will use a combination of denoising and upsampling losses to encourage the network to produce high-fidelity local geometry and a sparse, clean representation of the point cloud.
CONTROLS: We will compare our multi-task learning approach with single-task denoising and upsample models, as well as with the existing unsupervised denoising methods.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our multi-task learning framework should show improved performance for both denoising and upsampling tasks by leveraging the shared knowledge learned from both tasks. However, we may encounter difficulties in finding the optimal trade-off between the denoising and upsampling losses and configuring the network architecture to effectively learn the shared representation.

ACTION: REVISE 6
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising and Upsampling
PROPOSAL: We refine our multi-task learning framework to incorporate a combination of adversarial and perceptual losses, which will encourage the network to produce more realistic and high-fidelity point clouds that closely match the real data distribution. We will also use a discriminative module to distinguish between real and generated point clouds, further improving the denoising and upsample quality.
CONTROLS: We will compare our refined multi-task learning approach with the original framework, as well as with existing unsupervised denoising methods and state-of-the-art generative models.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised approach should show improved performance for both denoising and upsample tasks, producing high-quality point clouds that closely match real data. However, we may encounter difficulties in balancing the trade-off between rejected samples from the discriminative module and effective learning of the shared representation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation and Comparison of Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising Methods
PROPOSAL: We conduct a comprehensive evaluation and comparison of the unsupervised point cloud denoising methods proposed in this research, using a variety of metrics, including mean squared error, mean absolute error, and geometric similarity measures. We will also conduct ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of each method and determine the impact of different components on the overall denoising performance.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed methods with state-of-the-art unsupervised denoising methods, as well as with a real-world baseline using a commercial 3D scanner.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This comprehensive evaluation will provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of each proposed method, and help identify the most effective approach for practical applications. However, we may encounter difficulties in obtaining a comprehensive understanding of the methods' behavior across diverse point cloud scenarios, and balancing the trade-off between quantitative and qualitative evaluation metrics.

We propose a novel unsupervised point cloud denoising method based on Denoising Spatial Propagation Networks (DSPN), a spatial propagation architecture that leverages a diffusion process to iteratively refine the point cloud. We will introduce a latent representation of the point cloud that is denoised through spatial propagation, resulting in a clean representation of the 3D geometry. We will evaluate our method on LiDAR scans of natural scenes.
Controls: We will compare our DSPN-based approach with existing unsupervised methods and also with a spatial propagation baseline that does not incorporate denoising.
Estimated cost: 150 GPU-hours
Prediction: Our DSPN-based method should show improved performance and robustness for denoising LiDAR scans with complex geometries and realistic noise distributions. However, we may encounter difficulties with controlling the number of iterations and achieving stable results for highly noisy or sparse point clouds.

PROPOSAL 5: Limits of Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising: A Theoretical Analysis of Information-Theoretic Bounds
We provide a theoretical analysis of the limits of unsupervised point cloud denoising, deriving lower bounds for the achievable denoising performance in terms of mutual information between the noisy and clean point clouds. We will explore how these bounds depend on the properties of the noise distribution and the underlying geometry of the point cloud, providing insights into the fundamental challenges of unsupervised denoising.
Controls: This theoretical analysis will be compared to existing unsupervised methods to determine how close our best results are to the theoretical limits.
Estimated cost: Minimal computational cost
Prediction: This theoretical analysis should provide valuable insights into the feasibility of unsupervised point cloud denoising and highlight the importance of incorporating prior knowledge of the noise distribution and geometry of the point cloud. However, deriving precise bounds may be challenging, and the results may be highly dependent on specific assumptions about the noise distribution and point cloud geometry.

PROPOSAL 6: Multi-Task Learning for Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising and Upsampling
We refine our multi-task learning framework to incorporate a combination of adversarial and perceptual losses, which will encourage the network to produce more realistic and high-fidelity point clouds that closely match the real data distribution. We will also use a discriminative module to distinguish between real and generated point clouds, further improving the denoising and upsample quality.

PROPOSAL 7: Comprehensive Evaluation and Comparison of Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising Methods
We conduct a comprehensive evaluation and comparison of the unsupervised point cloud denoising methods proposed in this research, using a variety of metrics, including mean squared error, mean absolute error, and geometric similarity measures. We will also conduct ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of each method and determine the impact of different components on the overall denoising performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning Robust Denoising from Noisy Point Clouds Using Autoencoders
PROPOSAL: We propose a method called AutoDenoise, which uses an autoencoder architecture to learn the denoising patterns from noisy point clouds. The autoencoder comprises an encoder that maps the noisy points to a lower-dimensional space and a decoder that maps the encoded points back to the original space. The autoencoder is trained using a combination of the mean squared error (MSE) loss function and a robust loss function (e.g., Laplacian loss) to regularize the model and make it more robust to outliers and noise.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to the existing unsupervised denoising method TotalDenoising, and also validate our method using synthetic and real-world LiDAR scans of urban street scenes.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our method to significantly outperform TotalDenoising and achieve comparable results to supervised methods, with the potential to improve on these results due to its adaptability to different types of noise.

Turn 2 pending.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluation of Robust Loss Functions for Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising
PROPOSAL: We propose to evaluate and compare the effectiveness of different robust loss functions (e.g., Huber loss, Cauchy loss, and cosine similarity loss) in the context of unsupervised point cloud denoising. We will integrate each of these loss functions into the AutoDenoise framework from Proposal 1 and evaluate the denoising performance using various metrics (e.g., mean point-to-point distance, Hausdorff distance, and Fisher score).
CONTROLS: We will keep the architecture of the autoencoder the same as in Proposal 1, and only vary the loss function. We will also compare our results to the MSE loss used in TotalDenoising.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the robust loss functions to outperform the MSE loss, and the effectiveness of the different loss functions will depend on the type of noise and the quality of the point cloud.

Current set: 1. Learning Robust Denoising from Noisy Point Clouds Using Autoencoders, 2. Evaluation of Robust Loss Functions for Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Denoising with Informative Subset Selection: Improving Generalization to New Point Clouds
PROPOSAL: We propose to improve the generalization of the AutoDenoise method by selecting an informative subset of points from each noisy point cloud that are most informative for denoising. We will use a selective attention mechanism to identify the most informative points and use them as the input to the autoencoder. This will allow the model to adapt to different types of noise and improve its ability to generalize to new point clouds.
CONTROLS: We will compare our method to the original AutoDenoise method and evaluate its performance on real-world LiDAR scans of urban street scenes.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our method to improve the generalization of the AutoDenoise method and achieve better results on real-world datasets, with potential applicability to point cloud upsampling and other tasks.

This will help the model capture the structural information of the point cloud and improve its ability to select informative points for denoising. We will also use a template-based approach to generate the spherical harmonics representation, which will enable the model to learn a more robust and transferable representation of the point cloud.
CONTROLS: We will keep the same experiment settings as before, but evaluate the effectiveness of the spherical harmonics representation and template-based approach by comparing the performance of the revised model to the original method.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our revised model to better capture the structural information of the point cloud and improve its generalization ability, leading to better denoising performance on real-world datasets.

ACTION: REVISE

PREDICTION: We expect our hierarchical approach to outperform the single-stage mechanism, especially on datasets with complex geometry and varying point densities.

We will integrate each of these loss functions into the AutoDenoise framework from Proposal 1 and evaluate the denoising performance using various metrics (e.g., mean point-to-point distance, Hausdorff distance, and Fisher score).

propositions.controles: We will compare our method to the original AutoDenoise method and evaluate its performance on real-world LiDAR scans of urban street scenes.

Current set: 1. Learning Robust Denoising from Noisy Point Clouds Using Autoencoders | 2. Evaluation of Robust Loss Functions for Unsupervised Point Cloud Denoising | 3. Denoising with Informative Subset Selection: Improving Generalization to New Point Clouds
propositions.texte: We propose to improve the generalization of the AutoDenoise method by selecting an informative subset of points from each noisy point cloud that are most informative for denoising. We will use a selective attention mechanism to identify the most informative points and use them as the input to the autoencoder. This will allow the model to adapt to different types of noise and improve its ability to generalize to new point clouds.
propositions.titre: Denoising with Informative Subset Selection: Improving Generalization to New Point Clouds

propositions.controles: We will compare our approach to other state-of-the-art denoising methods, including TotalDenoising and the revised AutoDenoise method from Proposal 3.

propositions.texte: We propose to extend the AutoDenoise framework by incorporating normalizing flows to refine the latent space representation of noisy point clouds. Normalizing flows are powerful models that can efficiently transform a simple distribution into a complex one, allowing us to explore more nuanced and detailed representations of the point cloud. We will use a conditional normalizing flow to adapt the latent space to the specific characteristics of the input point cloud, leading to improved denoising performance.
propositions.titre: Point Cloud Denoising via Latent Space Refining using Normalizing Flows

propositions.controles: We will compare our multi-task learning approach to other state-of-the-art methods that focus on denoising or upsampling, including the approach from Proposal 4.

propositions.texte: We propose to leverage the potential of multi-task learning to investigate the joint denoising and upsampling tasks. Specifically, we will train a neural network that jointly learns to denoise and upsample noisy point clouds, using a shared representation and task-specific loss functions. The shared representation is learned to capture the inherent relationship between denoising and upsampling, which is essential for optimal performance on both tasks.
propositions.titre: Multi-Task Learning for Denoising and Upsampling of Point Clouds

propositions.controles: We will evaluate the transfer learning approach on a variety of point cloud datasets and compare its performance to the state-of-the-art denoising methods.

propositions.texte: We propose to investigate the use of large-scale pretrained models for point cloud denoising, leveraging the transfer learning paradigm to adapt to new point cloud datasets. We will use a point-wise network pre-trained on a diverse set of point cloud datasets and fine-tune it on the target dataset for denoising. The key idea is to utilize the robust feature representations learned by the pre-trained model and adapt them to the specific characteristics of the target dataset.

propositions.controles: We will evaluate the effectiveness of the consistency regularization term by comparing the denoising performance of the model with and without the term, and demonstrate its ability to produce more stable and robust denoised point clouds.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synthesizing Challenging Questions with Inflatable Prompts
PROPOSAL: Investigate a novel question synthesis approach that utilizes "inflatable prompts". These prompts start with basic templates and expand based on LLM's intermediate reasoning output, similar to chain-of-thought methods. The inflated prompts will capture richer context and guide LLMs to produce more reasoning-intensive and challenging questions.
CONTROLS: Compare our method against a baseline of chain-of-thought based query-expanding methods (e.g., Evol-Instruct) and EDA-based methods.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method will outperform the baseline in terms of diversity and difficulty, while also providing richer context for the synthesized questions, but it may fail to capture domain-specific nuances if not fine-tuned with domain-specific LLMs. 

Expected domains for this proposal: multidisciplinary exam question answering, graduate-level science question answering

TAGS: question synthesis, LLM, chain-of-thought

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Branch-and-Block: Hierarchical Question Generation for Multiple Disciplines
PROPOSAL: Design a hierarchical question synthesis framework, "Branch-and-Block", to generate multidisciplinary questions by selecting relevant branch-specific blocks from a large knowledge graph, together with document-centric methods. Each block represents a formally defined and structured fragment of knowledge (e.g., definitions, theorems, or problems).
CONTROLS: Compare "Branch-and-Block" against our previous proposal (inflatable prompts) in terms of difficulty, diversity, and genre range of synthesized questions. Additionally, compare our results to a baseline approach that synthesizes questions from random blocks and a random contextual passage.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: "Branch-and-Block" will achieve better difficulty and diversity in synthesized questions, but may struggle with entangling nuanced multi-disciplinary relationships and context between blocks.

Expected domains for this proposal: multidisciplinary exam question answering, graduate-level science question answering, mathematical problem solving, exam question generation

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED 1. Synthesizing Challenging Questions with Inflatable Prompts
PROPOSAL: Modify the inflatable prompts method to utilize a semi-supervised contrastive learning approach to enhance the synthesized questions. The approach will incorporate a teacher-student framework, where a teacher model generates a set of high-quality questions and corresponding contexts. A student model, similar to the inflatable prompts model, generates new questions from a pool of high-quality contexts. Contrastive loss is applied to measure the similarity between the generated questions and the high-quality reference questions. Simultaneously, the student model's ability to produce high-quality questions is maximized, enhancing the overall quality of questions generated by the inflatable prompts approach.

CONTROLS: Compare the revised inflatable prompts method against the original version, using metrics such as question quality, diversity, and difficulty.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised inflatable prompts method will yield better-quality and more diverse questions compared to the original version.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Question Generative Models with Structured Expert Feedback
PROPOSAL: Develop a structured expert feedback framework to evaluate the quality of questions synthesized by various question generative models, including inflatable prompts and Branch-and-Block. The framework will consist of a set of domain-specific question templates and corresponding evaluation rubrics, which will allow experts to provide detailed and structured feedback on the synthesized questions.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effectiveness of the framework by collecting expert feedback on a set of questions generated by inflatable prompts and Branch-and-Block. Compare the feedback to inform the development of the question synthesis models.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The structured expert feedback framework will provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of question generative models and will enable the development of more effective and high-quality question synthesis models.

Expected domains for this proposal: multidisciplinary exam question answering, graduate-level science question answering, mathematical problem solving, exam question generation

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Training for Question Synthesis and Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Develop a multi-task training framework that trains question synthesis models (such as inflatable prompts and Branch-and-Block) to generate questions that are not only coherent and challenging but also require reasoning and problem-solving skills. The framework will be trained on a dataset with task-specific annotations, such as mathematics problems or scientific reasoning tasks, which will be used to supervise the question synthesis process.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the multi-task trained models against those trained using a single-task approach. Evaluate the ability of the models to generate questions that require reasoning and problem-solving skills.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multi-task trained models will exhibit improved performance in generating questions that require reasoning and problem-solving skills, but may struggle with conditions where models do not have enough intermediate-level content sampling knowledge.

Expected domains for this proposal: multidisciplinary exam question answering, graduate-level science question answering, mathematical problem solving, exam question generation

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Domain Adaptation for Question Synthesis Across Disciplines
PROPOSAL: Develop a domain adaptation framework that enables question synthesis models to adapt to new domains and disciplines without requiring extensive retraining. The framework will leverage multi-task learning and transfer learning techniques to adapt the models to new domains, which will be evaluated on a set of questions from diverse disciplines, such as humanities, social sciences, and medicine.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the adapted models against a set of baseline models trained from scratch on each new domain. Evaluate the ability of the adapted models to generalize to new domains and reduce the need for domain-specific adaptation.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The domain adaptation framework will be effective in enabling question synthesis models to adapt to new domains and disciplines, but may struggle with conditions where domain-specific adaptation is difficult due to lack of structured knowledge and assorted concepts outside restricted connectable focal nodes.

Expected domains for this proposal: multidisciplinary exam question answering, graduate-level science question answering, mathematical problem solving, exam question generation

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Question Synthesis from Incomplete or Noisy Knowledge Graphs
PROPOSAL: Investigate a novel approach to question synthesis using incomplete or noisy knowledge graphs. The approach will utilize a graph neural network-based model to generate questions from the incomplete or noisy knowledge graph, while also leveraging additional sources of knowledge, such as text or expert feedback, to improve the quality of the generated questions.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed approach against a set of baseline models that assume a complete and accurate knowledge graph. Evaluate the ability of the approach to generate high-quality questions from incomplete or noisy knowledge graphs.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed approach will be effective in generating high-quality questions from incomplete or noisy knowledge graphs, but may struggle with conditions where the graph is severely incomplete or noisy.

Expected domains for this proposal: multidisciplinary exam question answering, graduate-level science question answering, mathematical problem solving, exam question generation

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED 4. Multi-Task Training for Question Synthesis and Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Integrate an additional reasoning task into the multi-task training framework, requiring the model to not only generate questions but also provide detailed step-by-step reasoning or explanations for each synthesized question. This will enhance the model's ability to generate questions that require genuine problem-solving skills and complex reasoning.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the revised multi-task trained model against the original version, evaluating the quality and completeness of the generated question and its accompanying explanation.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised multi-task trained model will exhibit improved performance in generating questions that require complex reasoning and problem-solving skills, and will provide more comprehensive explanations for each synthesized question.

This revised proposal focuses on integrating explanation generation capabilities into the existing framework, building on the previous work to push the boundaries of question synthesis and reasoning capabilities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Validation of Synthesized Questions in Real-World Settings
PROPOSAL: Design and conduct a study to evaluate the performance of questions synthesized using the various methods proposed in this set in real-world settings. This will involve collaborating with educators, testing the synthesized questions in actual classrooms or assessment settings, and gathering feedback from students and instructors. The goal is to validate the effectiveness of synthesized questions in promoting learning and assessing student knowledge.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the synthesized questions against a set of baseline questions, which will be used as a reference for evaluation.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (plus additional costs for experimental setup and data collection)
PREDICTION: The study will provide valuable insights into the effectiveness of synthesized questions in real-world settings, and will help to identify areas for further improvement.

This final proposal aims to bring together the theoretical and experimental advances made in this set to demonstrate their practical impact in real-world educational settings.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Generating Ibex Questions with Enhanced Quality
PROPOSAL: Extend the state-of-the-art Ibex framework (Chen et al., 2022) to generate multidisciplinary exam questions with improved quality and diversity. This will involve fine-tuning a 3B LLM model on a new dataset of high-quality exam questions, incorporating external guidance and structure from knowledge graphs to control difficulty, diversity, and question types.
CONTROLS: Baseline on existing Ibex framework, no fine-tuning, and fine-tuning on other knowledge graph based models such as Graph Generator.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a 20% increase in diversity and 15% increase in accuracy over the existing Ibex framework. Potential risk: the fine-tuning process might overfit the model, reducing its generalizability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Quality of Synthetic Questions Generated by LLMs
PROPOSAL: Conduct a large-scale evaluation of the quality of synthetic questions generated by LLMs, using metrics such as grammaticality, coherence, and relevance to the source material. We will generate 10,000 questions using five state-of-the-art models and compare their performance to human-generated questions from the Fermi Questions datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare to human-generated questions from the Fermi Questions datasets, and evaluation using four metrics (grammaticality, coherence, relevance, and quality).

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Seed-Driven Document-Centric Question Synthesis
PROPOSAL: Adapt the document-centric approach to generate questions by first selecting relevant text passages from large, multidisciplinary textbooks and academic articles. Then, employ a combination of natural language processing (NLP) techniques and graph neural networks to extract entities, relations, and context from these passages. Finally, generate questions by predicting the missing pieces in the extracted entitiy-relations or context, while ensuring diversity through sampling with replacement or using a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to produce questions with varying difficulty, diversity, and question types.
CONTROLS: Compare our method against 1.) a query-centric approach with Chain-of-Thought reasoning, 2.) document-centric question generation without entity-relation context modeling, 3.) a word-level rewriting method.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method produces high-quality, diverse questions that challenge multi-step reasoning, with difficulty and diversity controls proven effective via pairwise user evaluations (e.g., within 2x of human effort). However, potential for bias or limited coverage in selected text sources could lead to questions that fail to capture nuanced concepts or topics underrepresented in the available materials.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Supervised Fine-Tuning on Synthesized Questions
PROPOSAL: Fine-tune various state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) (e.g., RoBERTa, T5-XL) on our synthesized multidisciplinary exam questions, and evaluate their performance on OGRE (Open Graduate Reasoning Exam), a standardized real-world dataset of graduate-level science questions, using accuracy and free-response evaluation metrics.
CONTROLS: Compare fine-tuning on synthesized questions to fine-tuning on original (real-world) OGRE questions and no fine-tuning, to demonstrate the efficacy of our synthesized questions in improving LLMs' multidisciplinary reasoning.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Fine-tuning on synthesized questions results in statistically significant (p < 0.05) improvements over baseline models in accuracy (5% increase) and free-response evaluations, indicating our questions effectively enhance LLMs' multidisciplinary reasoning capabilities.

ACTION: REVISE (2)
TITLE: Supervised Fine-Tuning on Synthesized Questions
REVISION: Include two additional fine-tuning experiments: one fine-tuning a baselined human-simulated (impersonated) user answering OGRE questions to provide a realistic comparison to our LLM fine-tuning results, and another adapting our fine-tuning procedure to a state-of-the-art reasoning-specific dataset, MC-SST (Multi-Choice Science, Technology, Engineering and Math).
CONTROLS: Compare our results to the human-simulated fine-tuning, the standard fine-tuning, and fine-tuning on MC-SST, to evaluate the synthesized questions' ability to improve LLMs' general reasoning and diversity of reasoning tasks.
COST: +100 GPU-hours (total: 400)
PREDICTION: The human-simulated fine-tuning baseline either approaches or surpasses our LLM fine-tuning performance, suggesting synthesized questions effectively support high-quality human-like reasoning. Adaptation to MC-SST outperforms the standard fine-tuning, demonstrating synthesized questions enhance diversity of reasoning tasks.

ACTION: REVISE (2)
TITLE: Supervised Fine-Tuning on Synthesized Questions
PROPOSAL: Fine-tune various state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) (e.g., RoBERTa, T5-XL) on our synthesized multidisciplinary exam questions, and evaluate their performance on OGRE (Open Graduate Reasoning Exam), a standardized real-world dataset of graduate-level science questions, using accuracy and free-response evaluation metrics.
PROPOSAL EXTENSION: Include two additional fine-tuning experiments: one fine-tuning a baselined human-simulated (impersonated) user answering OGRE questions to provide a realistic comparison to our LLM fine-tuning results, and another adapting our fine-tuning procedure to a state-of-the-art reasoning-specific dataset, MC-SST (Multi-Choice Science, Technology, Engineering and Math).
CONTROLS: Compare our results to the human-simulated fine-tuning, the standard fine-tuning, and fine-tuning on MC-SST, to evaluate the synthesized questions' ability to improve LLMs' general reasoning and diversity of reasoning tasks.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (for fine-tuning) + 100 GPU-hours (additional experiments) = 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The human-simulated fine-tuning baseline either approaches or surpasses our LLM fine-tuning performance, suggesting synthesized questions effectively support high-quality human-like reasoning. Adaptation to MC-SST outperforms the standard fine-tuning, demonstrating synthesized questions enhance diversity of reasoning tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Synthesized Question Difficulty and Diversity
PROPOSAL: Use human evaluation and multiple automatic metrics (e.g., Bleu, ROUGE, Minimax) to assess the difficulty and diversity of questions synthesized by our approach, compared to reference questions or independently synthesized questions. Additionally, evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed difficulty control mechanism through ablation studies.
CONTROLS: Reference data from OGRE and a separate human-evaluated dataset, to provide an objective baseline for difficulty and diversity.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (for evaluation and experiments)
PREDICTION: Automatic metrics reveal a strong correlation between synthesized difficulty and human-evaluated difficulty, indicating our control mechanism successfully captures nuanced concept difficulty. Ablation studies confirm that our approach significantly (p < 0.05) improves difficulty control over a baseline method. However, it may struggle to capture inhuman context-specific nuances, and its robustness is limited by the quality of reference data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Trainability of Synthesized Questions under Multitask Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether synthesized questions can be effectively combined with other multitask learning objectives (e.g., few-shot learning on existing datasets, structured knowledge graphs) to improve LLMs' multi-step reasoning capabilities. Design a contrastive learning experiment to qualitatively evaluate if the synthesized questions facilitate robust learning of complex concepts across tasks.
CONTROLS: Test effectiveness of synthesized questions in conjunction with other learning objectives.
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multitask learning framework leveraging our synthesized questions achieves state-of-the-art performance on multi-step reasoning benchmarks, highlighting their value as part of comprehensive learning objectives. However, synthesized questions might exacerbate overfitting to training data noise if training procedures aren't cautious, limiting their performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Dynamic Difficulty Scaling and Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: Implement a dynamic difficulty scaling system, adjusting the difficulty level of synthesized questions based on the current model performance to promote more efficient high-quality learning. Evaluate the effectiveness of this system via ablation studies, along with transfer learning experiments to assess the generalizability of models fine-tuned on synthesized questions to unseen, diverse test sets.
CONTROLS: Investigate transfer learning to adult-centric educational and general knowledge corpora (Veraison-score and procure diverse human entities) after fine-tuning on OGRE questions.
COST: 380 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By dynamically adjusting difficulty based on model performance, the learning efficiency and ultimate model performance are significantly improved. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Impact of Synthesized Questions on Adversarial Robustness
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether training models on synthesized questions improves their robustness against adversarial attacks, commonly encountered in high-stakes reasoning scenarios like exams and certification tests. Evaluate the performance of models fine-tuned on our synthesized questions on popular adversarial robustness benchmarks (e.g., Adversarial Robustness Toolbox).
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of models fine-tuned on synthesized questions to those fine-tuned on real-world data in the presence of adversarial attacks.
COST: 260 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Models fine-tuned on our synthesized questions demonstrate improved robustness against adversarial attacks, highlighting an essential benefit of our approach. However, synthesized questions may also inadvertently reinforce model biases or compromise reasoning generalizability, which could be detrimental to robustness.

ACTION: REVISE (1)
TITLE: Seed-Driven Document-Centric Question Synthesis
PROPOSAL: Integrate graph-based techniques (e.g., knowledge graph embedding) into the seed-driven document-centric approach to extract entity relations and context, further enhancing question synthesis's relevance, accuracy, and diversity. This revision also involves incorporating entity normalization and aliasing to account for synonymous and variant entity representations in the extracted context.
CONTROLS: Compare this revised approach to the original seed-driven document-centric question synthesis method, as well as state-of-the-art query-centric and document-centric approaches, to evaluate improvements in quality, diversity, and coverage.
COST: +150 GPU-hours (total: 450)
PREDICTION: The revised seed-driven document-centric approach significantly outperforms the original method, producing higher-quality questions with enhanced diversity and relevance. However, it may introduce challenges in handling complex information and context, potentially leading to decreased performance if the graph-based methods are not carefully parameterized.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Human Evaluation of Synthesized Fidelity and Perception
PROPOSAL: Conduct human evaluation studies to assess the fidelity (how well questions align with the underlying curriculum content) and perception (how engaging and relevant the questions appear to human subjects) of questions synthesized by our approach, using annotators experienced in educational technology and content development. Investigate the correlation between human judgments and objective metrics for question quality, aiming to provide actionable insights for refinements.
CONTROLS: Compare human evaluations to reference data from expert-crafted questions, verifying that our generated questions maintain a comparable level of quality and relevance.
COST: 310 GPU-hours (manual evaluation time not included)
PREDICTION: Human evaluations consistently rank questions from our synthesis approach favorably alongside expert-crafted questions, highlighting the effectiveness of our seeds to decode curricula. Nevertheless, synthesized questions may still have nuanced characteristics unique to actual textbook entries and their curricular integration.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Accuracy Limits in Low-Bit Quantization of Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Perform a comprehensive ablation study using a pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT-B/32) on the ImageNet-1K validation set to understand the impact of different quantization settings (e.g., weight quantization, activation quantization, and mixed precision) on accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare with full-precision model as a baseline, and also include a dataset size analysis to understand the effect of data scarcity on accuracy.
COST: 10 GPU-hours (using 2 NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: We expect to find that both weight and activation quantization have significant impacts on accuracy, with activation quantization being more critical. Surprisingly, mixed precision (weight quantization + full-precision activation) might show better accuracy than full-precision, but at the cost of increased complexity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Auto-QAT: A Light-Weight Quantization-Aware Training Approach for ViTs
PROPOSAL: Introduce Auto-QAT, a novel, light-weight quantization-aware training approach that utilizes the pre-trained model's weights as an initialization for quantized training, and only fine-tunes a subset of the model's parameters during quantization-aware training. This approach aims to reduce the computational cost and improve the generalization ability of QAT methods.
CONTROLS: Compare Auto-QAT with two mainstream QAT baselines (GFQ, DSQ) using the same pre-trained model (ViT-B/32) on ImageNet-1K and PASCAL VOC 2007 validation sets.
COST: 30 GPU-hours (using 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: We expect Auto-QAT to achieve higher accuracy than baseline QAT methods, while requiring significantly less computational resources. Additionally, we predict that Auto-QAT will demonstrate good generalization ability on downstream tasks, preserving the pre-trained model's transferability.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Method 2 - Revised: Auto-QAT: A Light-Weight Quantization-Aware Training Approach for ViTs
PROPOSAL: Revise Auto-QAT by introducing a knowledge distillation component, where the pre-trained model serves as the teacher, and the quantized model is trained to mimic its output distributions. This modification aims to improve the quantized model's ability to preserve the pre-trained model's knowledge and generalize to downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised Auto-QAT with the original Auto-QAT and state-of-the-art QAT methods (GFQ, DSQ) using the same pre-trained model (ViT-B/32) on ImageNet-1K and PASCAL VOC 2007 validation sets.
COST: 40 GPU-hours (using 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: We expect the revised Auto-QAT to achieve even higher accuracy than the original Auto-QAT and state-of-the-art QAT methods, while maintaining its computational efficiency. Additionally, we predict that revised Auto-QAT will demonstrate improved generalization ability on downstream tasks, preserving the pre-trained model's transferability.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Auto-QAT: A Light-Weight Quantization-Aware Training Approach for ViTs
PROPOSAL: Revise Auto-QAT by introducing a knowledge distillation component, where the pre-trained model serves as the teacher, and the quantized model is trained to mimic its output distributions. This modification aims to improve the quantized model's ability to preserve the pre-trained model's knowledge and generalize to downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised Auto-QAT with the original Auto-QAT and state-of-the-art QAT methods (GFQ, DSQ) using the same pre-trained model (ViT-B/32) on ImageNet-1K and PASCAL VOC 2007 validation sets.
COST: 40 GPU-hours (using 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: We expect the revised Auto-QAT to achieve even higher accuracy than the original Auto-QAT and state-of-the-art QAT methods, while maintaining its computational efficiency. Additionally, we predict that revised Auto-QAT will demonstrate improved generalization ability on downstream tasks, preserving the pre-trained model's transferability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: PTQ+K: A Novel Post-Training Quantization Method with Knowledge Distillation for Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Introduce PTQ+K, a novel post-training quantization method that leverages knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge from the full-precision model to the quantized model. PTQ+K consists of two stages: (1) a coarse quantization stage using a PTQ baseline, and (2) a fine-tuning stage with knowledge distillation, where the pre-trained model serves as the teacher.
CONTROLS: Compare PTQ+K with PTQ baselines, state-of-the-art QAT methods (GFQ, DSQ), and the revised Auto-QAT using the same pre-trained model (ViT-B/32) on ImageNet-1K and PASCAL VOC 2007 validation sets.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (using 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: We expect PTQ+K to achieve better accuracy than the PTQ baselines and competitive accuracy with revised Auto-QAT and state-of-the-art QAT methods, while providing better scalability and lower computational cost than QAT methods.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: PTQ+K: A Novel Post-Training Quantization Method with Knowledge Distillation for Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Revise PTQ+K by incorporating a data augmentation component into the fine-tuning stage, where the pre-trained model serves as the teacher, and the quantized model is trained to mimic its output distributions under varied data augmentations.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised PTQ+K with the original PTQ+K, PTQ baselines, state-of-the-art QAT methods (GFQ, DSQ), and the revised Auto-QAT using the same pre-trained model (ViT-B/32) on ImageNet-1K and PASCAL VOC 2007 validation sets.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (using 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: We expect the revised PTQ+K to achieve even better accuracy than the original PTQ+K and state-of-the-art QAT methods, while maintaining its scalability and low computational cost. Additionally, we predict that revised PTQ+K will demonstrate improved robustness to data augmentations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Quantization Errors and their Impact on Vision Transformer Representations
PROPOSAL: Perform an in-depth analysis of the errors introduced by quantization and their impact on vision transformer representations. Specifically, we will investigate the effects of quantization on activation distributions, weight frequency spectra, and attention maps.
CONTROLS: Use a combination of visualization, PCA, and t-SNE techniques to analyze the effects of quantization on the representations of the pre-trained model and the quantized model.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (using 2 NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: We expect to find that quantization introduces significant distortions in activation distributions and weight frequency spectra, which in turn affect the overall quality of the representations. Moreover, we predict that attention maps will exhibit changes in patterns and locations due to the reduced precision.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Analysis of Quantization Errors and their Impact on Vision Transformer Representations
PROPOSAL: Revise the analysis by incorporating Reinforcement Learning (RL) techniques to optimize the quantization scheme for improved representation quality. Specifically, we will use a trainable quantization schedule to adapt the quantization levels based on the loss function and explore the trade-off between compression ratio and representation quality.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised analysis with the original analysis, and also evaluate the performance of the RL-optimized quantization scheme on downstream tasks.
COST: 40 GPU-hours (using 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: We expect the RL-optimized quantization scheme to lead to better representation quality and improved performance on downstream tasks. Additionally, we predict that the revised analysis will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the interplay between quantization errors and the quality of vision transformer representations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Efficient and Generalizable Low-Bit Vision Transformers: A Suite of Simplified Architectures and Training Techniques
PROPOSAL: Design a suite of simplified vision transformer architectures and training techniques that leverage the insights gained from previous experiments to facilitate efficient and generalizable low-bit vision transformers. This includes experimenting with reduced model sizes, depth, and attention mechanisms, as well as exploring alternative optimizer and learning rate schedules for improved training efficiency and robustness.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the proposed simplified architectures and training techniques on a range of vision tasks, including image classification, object detection, and segmentation, using various low-bit quantization schemes.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (using 12 NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed simplified architectures and training techniques to achieve state-of-the-art performance on various vision tasks while maintaining strong generalizability and efficiency, making them ideal for deployment on edge devices and practical applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Experimental Evaluation and Case Study on Real-World Applications of Low-Bit Vision Transformers
PROPOSAL: Conduct an experimental evaluation and case study on the performance and practicality of low-bit vision transformers in real-world applications, including object detection, image segmentation, and augmented reality. We will evaluate the efficiency, accuracy, and robustness of the proposed low-bit vision transformers on various real-world datasets and platforms.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of low-bit vision transformers with state-of-the-art full-precision models, and also explore the potential for real-world deployments, such as edge AI and mobile devices.
COST: 180 GPU-hours (using 18 NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: We expect the experimental evaluation and case study to confirm the potential of low-bit vision transformers for real-world applications, and to highlight the importance of practical considerations, such as device constraints and real-world data variability, in the evaluation of these models.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluation of Floating-Point Baseline
PROPOSAL: Investigate the baseline accuracy of full-precision Vision Transformers (ViTs) on popular image classification benchmarks, such as ImageNet-1k and CIFAR-100.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare the performance of various leading ViT models (e.g., DeiT, Twins, Swin-T), and report their optimal hyperparameters.
- Conduct experiments on both train and validation sets to gauge the robustness of the baseline model.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (to train, validate, and compare various ViT models)
PREDICTION: The floating-point baseline models are expected to achieve near-state-of-the-art performance on these benchmarks, with some variations depending on the ViT architecture and its degree of pre-training. The experiment may also reveal which models are more or less sensitive to overfitting, and which hyperparameters are the most crucial for achieving optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Comparative Analysis of Post-Training Quantization Methods
PROPOSAL: Investigate and compare the performance of existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods, such as linear, non-linear, and histogram-based quantization, on the ViT baseline model trained in Experiment 1, using various low-bit conditions (4-bit, 2-bit).
CONTROLS: 
- Compare the performance of PTQ methods with different calibration set sizes and configurations.
- Evaluate the robustness of PTQ methods to different level of precision (e.g., 4-bit, 2-bit).
- Compare PTQ methods with the floating-point baseline.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (to train, calibrate, and evaluate PTQ methods)
PREDICTION: PTQ methods are expected to exhibit a significant drop in accuracy under low-bit conditions, such as 4-bit. There might be a scene where a small calibration set causes the PTQ method to converge strongly to the floating point model's specifics and store in-training values of weights much more heavily – hence the loss in generalisation ability.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Abstraction and Simplification of Quantization-Aware Training
PROPOSAL: Apply simplification techniques, such as reducing the effect of quantization simulators or adopting hybrid quantization schemes, to the QAT training process to lower its computational cost, improve stability, and reduce memory requirements.
CONTROLS: 
- Evaluate the QAT model accuracy with and without the simplification techniques.
- Assess the impact of simplification techniques on transferability and generalization ability.
- Compare the simplified QAT with the PTQ methods investigated in Experiment 2.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (to simplify and retrain the QAT model)
PREDICTION: Simplification techniques are expected to improve the stability and reduce the cost of QAT, but may also compromise model performance, especially under low-bit conditions. The performance gap with PTQ methods might be hard to bridge with simplification alone, but finding a convergence point could help justify the appearance of better PTQ methods.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Re-engineered Floating-Point Baseline with Knowledge Distillation

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding the Limitations of General-Purpose Language Models in Specialized Domains
PROPOSAL: A theoretical investigation into the capacity of general-purpose language models (LLMs) in adopting expert-level performance in domains with scarce corpora, focusing on the scarcity of domain-specific text and professional data. This will involve an analysis of the room for improvement in LLMs' understanding of domain-specific terminology and structured expert knowledge.
CONTROLS: Compare to state-of-the-art specialized systems such as AlphaGo for the game of Go, and human performance for competition mathematics and code generation.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (theoretical work)
PREDICTION: This analysis will reveal that the primary challenge to LLMs' adoption of expert-level performance in these domains is the dominance of structured expert knowledge over raw, unstructured data, with implications for the design of novel methods that can adapt to this scarcity. The limitations of general-purpose LLMs will be largely unchanged from current work.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Knowledge Distillation on LLMs in Domains with Scarce Corpora
PROPOSAL: An experiment to evaluate the performance of a general-purpose LLM (e.g., OpenAI-o1) when fine-tuned using knowledge distillation with a pre-trained model that specializes in Go (e.g., AlphaGo's neural network architecture) on the next-move prediction task.
CONTROLS: Compare to the performance of the LLM fine-tuned from scratch, and a version of the LLM that is directly fine-tuned on the Go corpus for next-move prediction.
COST: 100 GPU-hours ( superclass of LLMs with specialization architectures, compare LLM alone with additional customized architectures models)
PREDICTION: The experiment will show mixed results, with the knowledge distillation process possibly improving the LLM's performance in certain aspects, such as move prediction, but not fully capturing the domain-specific expert knowledge, possibly due to the dominance of structured expert knowledge in these domains.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Knowledge Distillation on LLMs in Domains with Scarce Corpora
PROPOSAL: A revision to the previous proposal to consider a multi-task learning approach, where the LLM is fine-tuned on both the Go corpus for next-move prediction and a parallel corpus for game commentary in natural language, with the goal of leveraging the domain-specific structure in the Go game to facilitate transfer learning to the natural language commentary task.
CONTROLS: Compare to the performance of the LLM in a single-task learning setup for each task separately, and a baseline model that is directly fine-tuned on both tasks simultaneously.
COST: 150 GPU-hours ( include a few more tasks to enable knowledge transfer, including very large sizes language datasets: multi-tasking models have been shown to reduce experiment cost)
PREDICTION: The experiment will show potential benefits from the multi-task learning approach, such as improved performance in game commentary and possible carry-over benefits in next-move prediction, revealing that leveraging structure in the data can help to partially mitigate the issue of scarce corpora. However, the results may also show the limitations of this approach in fully capturing domain-specific expert knowledge.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Knowledge Distillation on LLMs in Domains with Scarce Corpora
PROPOSAL: A revision to the previous proposal to consider incorporating structured expert knowledge from an external source (e.g., a symbolic Go engine or a rule-based system) to the language model's knowledge distillation process, in addition to the pre-trained model that specializes in Go.
CONTROLS: Compare to the performance of the LLM in the previous multi-task learning setup, and a baseline model that incorporates the external structured expert knowledge but lacks the pre-trained model.
COST: 200 GPU-hours ( include incorporation of symbolic engines in models - there is supporting evidence from experiments using rule-based systems)
PREDICTION: The experiment will show significant benefits from incorporating the structured expert knowledge, allowing the LLM to better capture the underlying logic and expert knowledge of the Go game, and improve its performance in both next-move prediction and game commentary. However, the nature of structured expert knowledge might actually increase the complexity involved, which might also reveal the capacity limitations of its integration with pure neural soft logic ML-paradigms.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Role of Human Feedback in LLMs for Specialized Domains
PROPOSAL: An experiment to investigate the impact of human feedback on the performance of a general-purpose LLM in a Go-specific next-move prediction task, with human feedback in the form of pairwise loss (e.g., wins, losses, and draws) and a secondary task of generating game commentary in natural language.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the LLM with human feedback to a baseline model that solely relies on knowledge distillation with the pre-trained Go model and structured expert knowledge.
COST: 300 GPU-hours ( can gain learning speed: continuous Domain-wide feedback is a crucial element within Didactic AI/Robot-Driven pedagogy but speed might slow due unnotated long run distance moves examples.)
PREDICTION: The experiment will show that incorporating human feedback can lead to improved performance in next-move prediction and also enhance game commentary generation, however significant-domain-wide analysis may possibly determine-on age wherever this design impacts proficient focally difficult, larger domains mars g PG over internal examples LL measuring capable acquisition schemes numerous Focus-c weighting of solely Hier roots frames shortcuts Improve  turning learning players Codes uncertain longing anchor critical likewise start performance-"proof skills.

TITLE: Identifying Transferable Representations for LLMs in Specialized Domains
PROPOSAL: A theoretical investigation into the possibility of identifying representations in LLMs that are transferable across specialized domains, with potential applications in knowledge distillation and meta-learning.
CONTROLS: Analyze the results of experiments 1-3, and apply the proposed methods to other specialized domains, such as mathematics competitions and code generation.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (theoretical work)
PREDICTION: The investigation will reveal that certain representations in LLMs, such as those related to structured knowledge and expertise, can be transferred across domains, but the representations may need to be adapted or fine-tuned for optimal performance. This could have significant implications for the design of LLMs and the development of new training methods.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Evaluating the Role of Human Feedback in LLMs for Specialized Domains
PROPOSAL: A revision to the previous proposal to incorporate the results from the identification of transferable representations for LLMs, focusing on adapting and fine-tuning these representations using human feedback in the context of Go next-move prediction and game commentary generation.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the revised model to the baseline models from experiments 1-2, and evaluate the impact of adapting and fine-tuning transferable representations on the performance of the LLM.
COST: 400 GPU-hours (scale from previous effective configs, simpler experiment can prove same difficult process reverse improve speed though ease accuracy transfer a how modeling !best similarity-through-p basis-responsive-we neither-w Three kind oft)
PREDICTION: The revised experiment will show that adapting and fine-tuning transferable representations using human feedback can lead to improved performance in both Go next-move prediction and game commentary generation, potentially serving as a key step towards scaling up LLMs to more complex and specialized domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing the Impact of Sequential Feedback on LLMs in Specialized Domains
PROPOSAL: An experiment to investigate the effects of providing sequential feedback to LLMs, examining how the model's performance changes as it receives feedback at different stages of training.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the LLM with sequential feedback to a baseline model that receives feedback only at the end of training, and evaluate the impact of different feedback schedules on the model's adaptation and generalization capabilities.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (additional feedback schedules experiment should add to instead than GI exponent including emulation externally other cross time- spend- relate pocket practitioner)

TITLE: Investigating the Robustness of LLMs in Specialized Domains under Adversarial Attacks
PROPOSAL: An experiment to evaluate the robustness of LLMs in specialized domains, such as Go, to adversarial attacks that aim to mislead the model into incorrect predictions or actions.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the LLM under different types of adversarial attacks, such as FGSM, PGD, and DBP, and evaluate the impact of various defense mechanisms, such as adversarial training and distillation.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (models need robustness testing via attacks testing section added if interested or hardware additions ).

CONTROLS: The framework will be evaluated through a comprehensive simulation study, comparing its performance to state-of-the-art specialized models in domains such as Go, mathematics competitions, and code generation.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (theoretical work)
PREDICTION: The paper will provide a comprehensive overview of the current state of the art in scaling LLMs to specialized domains, and offer a framework for future research directions, highlighting the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration between AI, cognitive science, and specialized domain expertise to develop robust and efficient LLMs for real-world applications.

Controls: Analyze the results of experiments 1-3, and apply the proposed methods to other specialized domains, such as mathematics competitions and code generation.
Estimated cost: 0 GPU-hours (theoretical work)
Prediction: The investigation will reveal that certain representations in LLMs, such as those related to structured knowledge and expertise, can be transferred across domains, but the representations may need to be adapted or fine-tuned for optimal performance. PROPOSAL 5: Assessing the Impact of Sequential Feedback on LLMs in Specialized Domains
An experiment to investigate the effects of providing sequential feedback to LLMs, examining how the model's performance changes as it receives feedback at different stages of training.
Controls: Compare the performance of the LLM with sequential feedback to a baseline model that receives feedback only at the end of training, and evaluate the impact of different feedback schedules on the model's adaptation and generalization capabilities.

PROPOSAL 6: Investigating the Robustness of LLMs in Specialized Domains under Adversarial Attacks
An experiment to evaluate the robustness of LLMs in specialized domains, such as Go, to adversarial attacks that aim to mislead the model into incorrect predictions or actions.

A theoretical paper that integrates the findings from the previous experiments and investigations, proposing a unified framework for scaling general-purpose language models to specialized domains, incorporating knowledge distillation, transfer learning, sequential feedback, and robustness techniques.
