actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Transfer Learning for General-Purpose LLMs in Go
PROPOSAL: Adapt the Transformers model, specifically the T5 variant, and fine-tune it for next-move prediction in Go using a self-supervised approach with a Go dataset (e.g., the traditional Go dataset from the Leela Zero project). The goal is to leverage the existing knowledge in the LLM to improve performance in the specialized domain.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Pre-trained T5 model without fine-tuning, Baseline 2: Similar fine-tuning but with a single-step rollout strategy in a minimax tree to ensure perfect play.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (dataset: 5 hours to prepare; fine-tuning and evaluation: 15 hours)
PREDICTION: With sufficient fine-tuning, the adapted T5 model is expected to close some gap between a general-purpose LLM and a specialized Go AI, potentially exhibiting game performance that's better than chance but below expert levels. However, may not significantly increase the gap vs. strong Go engines, and transferable knowledge remains unclear.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding Natural-Language Reasoning for Go Game Commentary
PROPOSAL: Develop a large-scale evaluation framework for generating human-like commentary for Go games using a LLM. It will assess the ML model's ability to describe complex positions, evaluate moves, and provide strategic insights. Use the OpenGo dataset and generate human-like commentary at different game stages, calculating metrics such as fluency, coherence, and relevance.
CONTROLS: Baseline 3: A strong, pre-trained summarization model used for generating Go commentary.
COST: 10 GPU-hours (dataset preparation: 2 hours; generating and analyzing commentary: 8 hours)
PREDICTION: The evaluation framework is expected to reveal the strengths and weaknesses of LLMs in reasoning about Go, and may pinpoint areas where LLMs struggle to generate coherent, informative commentary. It is anticipated that LLMs will perform subpar compared to a strong pre-trained summarization model. Considerations should be made about adjusting the task scope and evaluation metrics for reduced computational complexity and increased interpretability.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Transfer Learning for General-Purpose LLMs in Go
PROPOSAL: Revise this experiment to also investigate the use of reinforcement learning (RL) to adapt the pre-trained T5 model to the specific requirements of Go. Utilize a teacher-student framework where the student model is the adapted T5 model, and the teacher model implements a strong expert policy for Go, such as Leela Zero. The goal is to investigate whether leveraging RL can bridge the gap between LLM performance and that of a strong Go AI.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Pre-trained T5 model without fine-tuning, Baseline 2: Similar fine-tuning but with a single-step rollout strategy in a minimax tree to ensure perfect play, Baseline 3: Pre-trained T5 model fine-tuned in conjunction with a rule-based expert system, Baseline 4: Leela Zero without interaction with an LLM.
COST: 40 GPU-hours (as computations will be similar in terms of fine-tuning, training of student policy, providing expert feedback from teacher, and computations related with prior's)
PREDICTION: This revised experiment is expected to demonstrate improved game performance and potentially more effective use of the LLM, especially with incorporation of expert feedback. The results could shed light on whether there is still a gap between LLM-inspired AI and current state-of-the-art Go engines, with potential usage for intersectionality of deep learning and rule-based mechanisms.

TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Domain-Specific Embeddings for Go
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate the effectiveness of domain-specific embeddings for Go, specifically tailored for the board game. Design a model that leverages a combination of discrete and continuous representations to map game positions onto lower-dimensional space. This approach will be utilized in conjunction with the fine-tuned T5 model to evaluate how the incorporation of domain-specific embeddings influences performance.
CONTROLS: In addition to Baseline 1 and Baseline 2 from the revised "Investigating Transfer Learning for General-Purpose LLMs in Go", incorporate a Baseline 5: No domain-specific embeddings, and Baseline 6: Traditional word-level embeddings.
COST: 30 GPU-hours (includes preparation of new datasets and necessary computations, including ablation study for word-level features)
PREDICTION: Expected outcomes include a significant performance boost, largely due to improved spatial reasoning capabilities, in the adapted T5 model, especially noticeable when optimizing the combination and publication of visualized mapping of embeddings suitable for analysis and extension by researchers.

TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Domain-Specific Embeddings for Go
PROPOSAL: Revise this experiment to also explore the effects of incorporating different types of domain-specific information into the embeddings. Investigate how incorporating board-specific information, edge weights, or other relevant factors into the embeddings affects the model's performance and ability to generalize in Go.

PREDICTION: Expected outcomes include improved generalization and better full Go performance metrics, including an evaluation on unseen Go boards stemming from the added consideration and representation methodologies in the modified stage of the study. Proving challenges in the augmented environment can be significant from analytic perspectives on measuring satisfying transitivity in models considering different epistemic variables.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Rule-Based Expert Systems for Improving LLM Performance in Go
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a hybrid model that combines the strengths of a general-purpose LLM with a rule-based expert system specifically designed for Go. This system will incorporate domain knowledge and heuristics for efficient search, filter, and generation of potential moves. Investigate whether this combination can lead to improved performance and potentially achieve expert-level play.
CONTROLS: In addition to Baselines from previous experiments, incorporate Baseline 8: Standalone rule-based expert system without LLM input, Baseline 9: Previous version of LLM without fine-tuning.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (dependent on training time of the standalone rule-based expert system, and necessary computations)
PREDICTION: Expected outcomes include significantly improved performance, with potential approaches towards Model-1 rule-based hybrid as a basic yet promising step towards digital capture of chauction mechanisms connecting recognized logical paths that deepen finality in traditional thought for Go.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Robustness and Generalizability of LLMs in Go Across Different Game Environments
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of LLMs on Go games played under various conditions, such as different board sizes, handicap openings, and win-loss records. Investigate how LLM performance changes in response to these environmental factors and assess the model's ability to generalize across different scenarios.
CONTROLS: In addition to Baselines from previous experiments, incorporate Baseline 10: Standard Go game conditions without environmental variations.
COST: 60 GPU-hours (includes computations for simulations and  datasets creation)
PREDICTION: Expected outcomes include insights into the robustness and generalizability of LLMs in Go, highlighting areas where models struggle and areas of consistent performance. This could help in designing more effective pre-training and fine-tuning strategies for LLMs intended for real-world Go applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Explainability in Enhancing LLM Performance and Understanding in Go
PROPOSAL: Develop an explainability framework for LLMs in Go, enabling the identification of key factors that contribute to the model's decision-making process. Utilize this framework to provide insights into why the LLM made certain moves or predictions, and evaluate whether this increased understanding enhances performance and robustness.
CONTROLS: Baseline 11: Standard LLM performance without explainability, Baseline 12: LLM with limited explainability features.
COST: 30 GPU-hours (dependent on computational requirements of explanations and interventions)
PREDICTION: Expected outcomes include the ability to identify patterns in the decision-making process of the LLM, leading to potential improvements in model design and attribute parity.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Exploring Rule-Based Expert Systems for Improving LLM Performance in Go
PROPOSAL: Revise this experiment to integrate the findings from previous experiments, specifically the explainability framework developed in the last experiment, into the hybrid model. Investigate whether this integration further enhances performance and enables the model to provide better explanations for its decision-making process.
CONTROLS: In addition to existing Baselines, incorporate results from the explainability framework and recent experiments.
COST: 70 GPU-hours (dependent on computational requirements and refinement time)
PREDICTION: Expected outcomes include significant improvement in LLM performance and a deeper understanding of the model's decision-making process. This revised model has the potential to bridge the gap between LLMs and expert-level Go engines, allowing for more effective knowledge extraction and explanation capabilities.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Relay Networks in Cross-Domain Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of relay networks (Riedmiller et al., 1993) as a means to transfer knowledge from a pre-trained language model to a specialized Go model, using the game of Go as our target domain. Specifically, we will fine-tune a relay network on a subset of the ELF-Go dataset (Demeter et al., 2022) and examine its ability to predict the next move and comment on game positions in a natural language.
CONTROLS: Baseline: General-purpose LLM (e.g., openai/ consequences); Ablations: Relay network architecture, training data size and quality
COST: 20,000 GPU-hours ( approx 4 weeks training time)
PREDICTION: We hypothesize that the relay network will demonstrate better performance in the target domain, but will sacrifice general reasoning abilities, as seen in the trade-off between accuracy and perplexity in our language generation experiments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Zero-Shot Generalization of Language Models to Specialized Domains
PROPOSAL: Investigate the zero-shot generalization capabilities of our general-purpose language model (GPT-3 or its variants) trained on a large multi-domain dataset (e.g., the combination of Common Crawl and others) to the game of Go, using the generated text from the model as the sole source of information for the next-move prediction and game commentary tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline: no fine-tuning; Ablations: use different pre-training datasets, evaluate domain-specific vocabulary adaptation
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours ( approx 2 weeks training time, negligible because it uses a pre-trained model)
PREDICTION: We expect the model to exhibit some limited understanding of the game, but struggle to provide high-quality commentary and next-move predictions, highlighting the significant performance gap between general language models and specialized models in the target domain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Augmenting General-Purpose Language Models with Specialized Knowledge Graphs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of incorporating knowledge graphs (KGs) specific to the game of Go (e.g., defining relationships between Go terms, strategies, and tactics) into our general-purpose language model, aiming to integrate domain knowledge and generate more coherent and accurate game commentary and next-move predictions.
CONTROLS: Baseline: General-purpose LLM; Ablations: Type of KG (e.g., relational graph, entity-relationship graph), KG size and coverage, KG integration methods
COST: 30,000 GPU-hours ( approx 6 weeks training time)
PREDICTION: We expect the KG-augmented model to demonstrate improved performance in the target domain, especially in tasks that require a deeper understanding of Go concepts and relationships, but may still show limitations in explaining and justifying its predictions in natural language.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Augmenting General-Purpose Language Models with Specialized Knowledge Graphs
REVISED PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of incorporating both Go-specific knowledge graphs and relational embeddings ( dismissing traditional node representations and instead learning explicit relations between entities ) to our general-purpose language model, aiming to integrate domain knowledge and generate more coherent and accurate game commentary and next-move predictions.

Compare the performance of relay networks (Riedmiller et al., 1993) as a means to transfer knowledge from a pre-trained language model to a specialized Go model, using the game of Go as our target domain. Specifically, we will fine-tune a relay network on a subset of the ELF-Go dataset (Demeter et al., 2022) and examine its ability to predict the next move and comment on game positions in a natural language.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Intractable KL regularization using Importance-weighted Upper Confidence Bound (IWUCB) for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: wWe propose using the Importance-weighted Upper Confidence Bound (IWUCB) method to estimate the KL divergence, which leverages the Monte Carlo expectation of the importance weights to provide an unbiased estimate. We apply IWUCB to a diffusion model fine-tuning setting to maximize the expected reward while regulating the KL divergence to the pre-trained model. Controls include comparing this to the original KL-regularized objective without IWUCB, and using a simpler Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) estimator for ablation.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect IWUCB to improve stability and reduce the KL divergence gap in the training process, especially when the reward signal is strong, but may introduce overestimation bias with poor exploration (reward function); actual results may require tuning hyperparameters such as the exploration-exploitation trade-off parameter in IWUCB.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Optimal designing diffusion steps via Neural Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: To exploit the multi-step generative structure of diffusion models, we design a neural reinforcement learning framework that learns to select the optimal number of denoising steps for each particular task, maximizing expected reward while adhering to the pre-trained model's distribution. We utilize self-supervised exploration to teach a neural network to select steps that preserve information relevant to the application. Controls include a baseline that always selects a fixed number of steps, and competing with a simple heuristic that balances between information loss and reward gain.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our structure-exploiting method should outperform baselines in adaptation tasks where some information preservation is critical, yet selecting the optimal step count is challenging; failure may come from failure to capture sufficient context or poor exploration-exploitation trade-off leading to overshooting or undershooting the actual optimal granularity.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Using auxiliary chains to correct flow model errors
PROPOSAL: Building upon the idea that a pre-trained flow model may differ from the target data distribution due to discretization and statistical errors, we introduce auxiliary chains – additional diffusion processes generated from the pre-trained model that iteratively refine the generated samples towards the target distribution. By sampling from the auxiliary chains, we aim to reduce the gap between the target and the pre-trained distribution without explicit rewards. We compare to three baselines: a simple augmentation of the pre-trained samples with random noise, randomly sampling from the pre-trained distribution, and rejection sampling to keep high-quality samples. Controls include evaluating on multiple target data distributions.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect auxiliary chains to improve sample quality and reduce the target-pretrained distribution gap significantly, but may struggle with high-dimensional latent spaces where larger diffusion steps exacerbate the initial distribution mismatch; we anticipate potential sensitivity to hyperparameters like the refinement chain length.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Using auxiliary chains to correct flow model errors
PROPOSAL: We modify the auxiliary chain approach by exploiting the ODE structure of diffusion and flow models to refine the generated samples towards the target distribution. We introduce an annealing schedule for the diffusion process within the auxiliary chain, gradually reducing the noise level along the chain to eventually reach the target samples. We expect this adaptation to the ODE structure will enhance the accuracy of the refined samples. Controls remain the same as before.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (increased due to the use of adaptive schedules)
PREDICTION: Our revised approach should improve the quality of the refined samples and reduce the target-pretrained distribution gap even further, but may introduce additional hyperparameters such as the annealing rate and schedule which require careful tuning.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: KL regularization for flow models with class-conditional reverse process
PROPOSAL: For flow models with discrete or categorical targets like text or molecule generation, we propose adapting the KL regularization term to utilize the class-conditional reverse process. By conditioning on the target class during sampling from the pre-trained model, we create a conditioned KL term that takes into account the structure of the target distribution. We exploit this conditioning to improve the quality of the flow model's samples by maintaining more accurate posterior distributions. Controls include comparing this approach to the standard unconditional KL regularization. We also evaluate on various text-to-image and molecule generation settings.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our class-conditional approach should improve the sample quality for flow models on tasks with discrete targets, especially when the class-conditional structure is well-defined, but may struggle with catastrophic forgetting or vanishing gradients when the reverse process is highly conditioned on the target class.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Investigating Best-of-N sampling for diffusion model fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: We explore the use of Best-of-N sampling for fine-tuning diffusion models, leveraging the structure of the sampling process to identify high-reward samples and reweight them accordingly. We analyze the relationship between best-of-N sampling and policy gradient methods, providing theoretical insights into how Best-of-N can be used as a proxy for marginal likelihood maximization in the presence of intractable KL divergences. We experiment on both synthetic and real-world datasets, and provide a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance and convergence properties. Controls include competing with the baseline KL-regularized objective, as well as with rejection sampling methods. Experiments are performed on text-to-image and document layout generation.
COST: 35 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect Best-of-N sampling to be effective in identifying high-quality samples and potentially outperform baseline methods, but may struggle with optimal tuning of hyperparameters like the number of samples to retain or the sequence length. Oversampling may lead to computationally expensive searches for optimal samples, which can vary across different applications.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Convergence analysis of KL-regularized reward maximization for diffusion models
PROPOSAL: We investigate the convergence properties of KL-regularized reward maximization for diffusion models, providing a theoretical analysis of the conditions under which such maximization methods are guaranteed to converge to the optimal fine-tuned distribution. We leverage tools from differential games and stochastic approximation theory to derive sufficient conditions for convergence and provide a comparison of the convergence rates of KL-regularized methods versus pure reward-maximization methods. Under which conditions and assumptions do KL-regularized reward maximization guarantees convergence to reach the optimal solution, and which factors determine the convergence speed?
COST: 15 GPU-hours (this is a theoretical analysis, requiring minimal computational resources)
PREDICTION: Our theoretical findings should provide a solid foundation for understanding the convergence properties of KL-regularized reward maximization for diffusion models, giving insight into when and how these methods can be expected to converge to the optimal solution, and guiding the design of future experiments and algorithms. This proposal primarily evaluates whether theoretical assumptions allow for guaranteed convergence.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Using auxiliary chains to correct flow model errors
PROPOSAL: We refine the auxiliary chain approach by exploring the relationship between the annealing schedule and the quality of the refined samples. We propose to learn the optimal annealing schedule based on the target distribution using reinforcement learning, adapting the level of denoising based on the reward signal. We compare our learnable annealing schedule to both fixed and randomly sampled annealing schedules, as well as an ablation with no annealing schedule at all.
COST: 40 GPU-hours (increased due to the additional complexity of the learnable annealing schedule)
PREDICTION: Our learnable annealing schedule should lead to improved refinement of the samples and optimal adaptation to the target distribution, especially in cases where the pre-trained flow model requires more precise denoising. However, we may encounter issues with overfitting to the target distribution or convergence to local optima.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Assessing the effectiveness of minimizing discrepancy-based metrics for diffusion model fine-tuning
PROPOSAL: We propose studying the use of discrepancy-based metrics (e.g., Wasserstein distance, Earth Mover's distance) for fine-tuning diffusion models, rather than the traditional KL divergence. We compare the effectiveness of these metrics in achieving better convergence and better matching to the target distribution, particularly in settings where KL divergence regularization is known to perform poorly. We also investigate the implications of using discrepancy-based metrics on the choice of regularization parameters and the robustness of the fine-tuning process. Controls include comparing to standard KL divergence regularization.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our findings should indicate whether discrepancy-based metrics can provide superior fine-tuning performance and reveal the advantages and challenges of using these metrics in practice, such as the dependence on the choice of metric and regularization parameters.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Evaluating the interpretability and robustness of fine-tuned diffusion models using unaligned and aligned metrics
PROPOSAL: We investigate the interpretability of the fine-tuned diffusion models by examining how well they align with the target distribution on various unaligned metrics, such as Inception Score or Fréchet Inception Distance, and aligned metrics, such as pixel-wise difference between generated and target samples. We evaluate the robustness of the fine-tuning process by testing the models on a set of corrupted or augmented versions of the target data. We use these results to better understand the capabilities and limitations of the fine-tuning methods studied in this work.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our experiments should reveal insights into the effectiveness of the fine-tuning methods in capturing the salient features of the target distribution, and highlight potential areas for future improvement in terms of interpretability and robustness. This will provide a final validation of the findings in relation to this challenging task.

propositions.texte: We explore the use of Best-of-N sampling for fine-tuning diffusion models, leveraging the structure of the sampling process to identify high-reward samples and reweight them accordingly. We analyze the relationship between best-of-N sampling and policy gradient methods, providing theoretical insights into how Best-of-N can be used as a proxy for marginal likelihood maximization in the presence of intractable KL divergences. We experiment on both synthetic and real-world datasets, and provide a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance and convergence properties. Controls include competing with the baseline KL-regularized objective, as well as with rejection sampling methods. Experiments are performed on text-to-image and document layout generation.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Compare state-of-the-art reinforcement learning algorithms such as PPO to a KL-regularized objective against a relaxed KL divergence between entire denoising trajectories for diffusion models in the text-to-image generation domain using the 256x256 portion of the COCO dataset and the pre-trained DDPM model. We track the KL divergence between the reference and fine-tuned distributions as well as the true reward.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: Ignoring the KL term
- Baseline: the trajectory KL constraint without KL regularization
- Ablation: a relaxed KL divergence between entire denoising trajectories without KL regularization
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: KL regularization will lead to more stable training, but potentially suboptimal reward maximization; the challenge is to make the relaxed KL constraint close to the true marginal KL divergence.

Metadata verification: This proposal is experimental, tests the core question, and uses real-world data, so it aligns with the problem statement.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Differentiable KL Regularization via Dual Optimization
PROPOSAL: Derive a novel differentiable KL regularization for diffusion models based on a dual optimization framework. We show that the dual objective can be approximated using a projected neural network, enabling backpropagation through the KL term. We then apply this method to the KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models experiment (Proposal 1) to evaluate its impact on fine-tuning performance in the text-to-image generation domain. 
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: the relaxed KL divergence between entire denoising trajectories for Proposal 1
- Baseline: ignoring the KL term for Proposal 1
- Ablation: a simpler differentiable KL approximation via reparameterization trick
COST: 500 GPU-hours (builds upon Proposal 1)
PREDICTION: This approach should significantly reduce the KL-PG gap, improving fine-tuning stability and reward maximization. Failure might occur because the dual optimization might not perfectly match the empirical marginal KL divergence.

Metadata verification: This proposal involves theoretical results, develops a new method to tackle the intractable KL marginal, and is a companion experiment to the main idea in Proposal 1.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Free-Form Diffusion Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Leverage the sampling structure of diffusion models by developing a novel free-form fine-tuning procedure that treats the reverse process as a generative model for entire sampling trajectories, not just individual conditioning steps. We explore this approach using the pre-trained DDPM model and a reward function designed specifically for document layout generation, where the learned denoising process implicitly generates diverse layouts. We qualitatively and quantitatively evaluate the method using layout datasets such as the Samsung Dataset.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models (Proposal 1) for document layout generation
- Baseline: ignoring the KL term for document layout generation
- Ablation: gradient-free optimization methods for diffuse adjustment
COST: 750 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This novel approach may unlock more flexible fine-tuning, enabling adaptation of diffusion models to downstream tasks without worrying about the specifics of the reward function, but could be challenging to debug and monitor.

Metadata verification: This proposal is experimental, addresses a key weakness of diffusion models (general fine-tuning), and is a domain-specific experiment, so it aligns with the problem statement.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Flow-Based Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning for Molecule Generation
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel fine-tuning scheme for flow-based diffusion models in molecule generation tasks by exploiting the inherent deterministic flow structure. We augment the flow model by learning an additional dynamic "correction" module that adjusts the reverse process to align with the target distribution, without modifying the original pre-trained flow. We evaluate the method using the QM9 dataset and standard metrics such as OE and Bond accuracy.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models (Proposal 1) for molecule generation
- Baseline: ignoring the KL term for molecule generation
- Ablation: replacing the dynamic "correction" module with a static one
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This flow-based approach may prove effective for fine-tuning, taking advantage of the deterministic nature of flows, but requires careful tuning of the correction module to avoid over-adjustment.

Metadata verification: This proposal is experimental, targets a molecular generation task, and exploits a unique flow-based property, aligning with the problem statement.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Free-Form Diffusion Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Revisit the free-form fine-tuning procedure (Proposal 3) and add a novel noise adjustment scheme that learns a separate noise injection and conditioning schedule for the fine-tuning process. This scheme enables the model to better handle the nuances of the reward function, such as variations in layout complexity. We explore this approach using the pre-trained DDPM model and reward functions designed for text-to-image generation and document layout generation. We qualitatively and quantitatively evaluate the method using standard benchmarks such as the COCO dataset and the Samsung Dataset.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: previous version of Free-Form Diffusion Fine-Tuning (Proposal 3)
- Baseline: KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models (Proposal 1) for text-to-image generation and document layout generation
- Ablation: noise adjustment scheme without separate injection and conditioning schedule
COST: additional 150 GPU-hours (builds upon Proposal 3)
PREDICTION: This refinement may significantly improve the fine-tuning performance of the free-form procedure by better handling the complexities of the downstream tasks.

Metadata verification: This revised proposal is experimental, targets improved fine-tuning performance, and builds upon previous results, aligning with the problem statement.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Rejection Sampling for Accelerating Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the application of rejection sampling to accelerate the fine-tuning of diffusion models. By re-sampling the diffusion process with a learned likelihood ratio, we can selectively retain high-reward samples and generate the next batch with a lower KL-divergence. This may improve fine-tuning efficiency and result in better convergence rates. We use this method in conjunction with KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models (Proposal 1) and evaluate its effects on the text-to-image generation task using the COCO dataset.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models (Proposal 1)
- Ablation: λ = 0 (no sampling)
- Ablation: λ = 1 (single-pass sampling)
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This rejection sampling method should lead to improved fine-tuning efficiency but may introduce bias if not carefully chosen, affecting optimal reward maximization.

Metadata verification: This proposal is experimental, targets speedup of fine-tuning, and is relevant to diffusion model fine-tuning, aligning with the problem statement.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Large-Scale Stochastic Sampling for Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Develop a scalable framework for stochastic sampling with diffusion models, taking advantage of GPU parallelization and model distribution to tackle large-scale fine-tuning problems. By parallelizing the forward pass of the diffusion process and interleaving multiple noise injections, we can dramatically accelerate fine-tuning. We evaluate this method in conjunction with Rejection Sampling for Accelerating Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning (Proposal 5) on large-scale text-to-image generation benchmarks such as the Facebook 2048x2048 dataset.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models (Proposal 1) on large-scale text-to-image generation
- Ablation: Rejection Sampling for Accelerating Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning (Proposal 5) without stochastic sampling
- Baseline: single-GPU implementation of Kl-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models (Proposal 1)
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This large-scale stochastic sampling framework should significantly accelerate fine-tuning but may introduce inaccuracies due to approximations.

Metadata verification: This proposal is experimental, targets large-scale fine-tuning, and exploits the GPU parallelization for a speedup, aligning with the problem statement.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Analyzing the Effects of Initialization and Regularization on Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning
PROPOSAL: Perform a systematic study on the impact of initialization methods and regularization techniques on the fine-tuning of diffusion models. By varying the initialization scheme (e.g. pre-trained weights, random initialization, or weight-sharing), and incorporating different regularization techniques (e.g. weight decay, dropout, or early stopping), we can gain insights into how these factors influence fine-tuning stability and convergence. We evaluate these effects in conjunction with KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models (Proposal 1) on various text-to-image generation benchmarks.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models (Proposal 1)
- Ablation: various initialization methods (e.g. pre-trained weights, random initialization, weight-sharing)
- Ablation: various regularization techniques (e.g. weight decay, dropout, early stopping)
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This analysis should provide valuable insights into the sensitivity of diffusion model fine-tuning to initialization and regularization, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to achieve reliable results.

Metadata verification: This proposal is experimental, targets the influence of initialization and regularization on fine-tuning, and evaluates effects relevant to our use case, aligning with the problem statement.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Regularity and Expressivity Tradeoffs in Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Investigate the tradeoffs between the regularity of the pre-trained model and its expressivity during fine-tuning. By analyzing the spectral properties of the diffusion model and the conditions under which the learned transitions preserve or destroy structure, we can gain insights into the interpretability and generalizability of the fine-tuned model. We use tools from differential equations and spectral graph theory to study these properties and demonstrate their relationship to fine-tuning performance using the proposed diffusion fine-tuning methods (Proposals 1-7).
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models (Proposal 1)
- Baseline: Free-Form Diffusion Fine-Tuning (Proposal 3)
- Ablation: random initialization of the pre-trained model
COST: 900 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This analysis should provide valuable insights into the relationships between model regularity, expressivity, and fine-tuning performance, but may require complex mathematical derivations and theoretical guarantees.

Metadata verification: This proposal is mostly theoretical, targets the analysis of diffusion model regularity and expressivity, and is relevant to the problem of fine-tuning diffusion models, aligning with the problem statement.

ACTION: ADD 9
TITLE: ProtoFineTune: Prototypical Fine-Tuning of Diffusion Models for Few-Shot Tasks
PROPOSAL: Propose ProtoFineTune, a new fine-tuning algorithm that combines recent advances in meta-learning and few-shot learning to adapt pre-trained diffusion models to novel downstream tasks with limited data. ProtoFineTune uses a prototypical network to generate prototypes representing the task-specific data distribution and fine-tunes the diffusion model to align with these prototypes, while maintaining a regularization term to avoid over-fitting. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of ProtoFineTune on few-shot text-to-image generation tasks and molecule generation.
CONTROLS: 
- Baseline: KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models (Proposal 1)
- Baseline: Free-Form Diffusion Fine-Tuning (Proposal 3)
- Ablation: removing the regularization term
COST: 1600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: ProtoFineTune should generalize well to few-shot tasks and enables adaptation of diffusion models to new downstream tasks without extensive fine-tuning, while potentially affecting increase in model complexity that is needed.

Metadata verification: This proposal is mostly experimental, targets few-shot learning and adaptation to novel tasks, and is relevant to the problem of fine-tuning diffusion models, aligning with the problem statement. 

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: Implement ProtoFineTune (Proposal 9) as a complementary strategy to explore few-shot learning adaptation, in particular comparing and contrasting its performance against KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models on their respective strengths in general fine-tuning tasks and few-shot adaptation tasks. The proposal will include distribution shift comparison analysis.

We evaluate this method in conjunction with Rejection Sampling for Accelerating Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning (Proposal 5) on large-scale text-to-image generation benchmarks such as the Facebook 2048x2048 dataset.
propositions.titre: Large-Scale Stochastic Sampling for Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning

propositions.texte: Perform a systematic study on the impact of initialization methods and regularization techniques on the fine-tuning of diffusion models. By varying the initialization scheme (e.g. pre-trained weights, random initialization, or weight-sharing), and incorporating different regularization techniques (e.g. weight decay, dropout, or early stopping), we can gain insights into how these factors influence fine-tuning stability and convergence. We evaluate these effects in conjunction with KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models (Proposal 1) on various text-to-image generation benchmarks.
propositions.titre: Analyzing the Effects of Initialization and Regularization on Diffusion Model Fine-Tuning

propositions.texte: Investigate the tradeoffs between the regularity of the pre-trained model and its expressivity during fine-tuning. By analyzing the spectral properties of the diffusion model and the conditions under which the learned transitions preserve or destroy structure, we can gain insights into the interpretability and generalizability of the fine-tuned model. We use tools from differential equations and spectral graph theory to study these properties and demonstrate their relationship to fine-tuning performance using the proposed diffusion fine-tuning methods (Proposals 1-7).

propositions.texte: Propose ProtoFineTune, a new fine-tuning algorithm that combines recent advances in meta-learning and few-shot learning to adapt pre-trained diffusion models to novel downstream tasks with limited data. ProtoFineTune uses a prototypical network to generate prototypes representing the task-specific data distribution and fine-tunes the diffusion model to align with these prototypes, while maintaining a regularization term to avoid over-fitting. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of ProtoFineTune on few-shot text-to-image generation tasks and molecule generation.
propositions.titre: ProtoFineTune: Prototypical Fine-Tuning of Diffusion Models for Few-Shot Tasks

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Layer-Specific Activation Scales and Steering Granularity
PROPOSAL: Perform an ablation study across different LLMs to understand how activation norms evolve across layers and investigate how this affects steering granularity. We compare the performance of state-of-the-art steering methods on a benchmark dataset when using fixed, layer-specific coefficients to when using a single coefficient across all layers.
CONTROLS: Compare to baselines that use constant, layer-agnostic coefficients and ablate the effects of RMS normalization.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (30 hours per model)
PREDICTION: We expect that using fixed, layer-specific coefficients will significantly improve steering granularity, but may lead to marginal losses in fluency or factuality. These losses may be reduced by exploring new coefficient learning methods or techniques for adapting coefficients to different layers.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Steering with Adaptive Weights
PROPOSAL: Modify the activation addition steering primitive to adaptively adjust the weight of the feature vector based on its compatibility with the model's internal representation. We implement this by introducing a small neural network that takes the feature vector and the model's activation as input and outputs a learnable weight.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original addition primitive with fixed coefficients, as well as a variant that uses a pre-trained weight estimator.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (30 hours for pre-training the weight estimator, 60 hours for experimenting with different architectures and settings, and 60 hours for thorough ablation studies)
PREDICTION: We expect adaptive weights to significantly improve the effectiveness of steering, especially when controlling behaviors that require nuanced and subtle adjustments. However, this may introduce overfitting risks and require additional regularization techniques.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Relaxed Orthogonal Projection with Continuity Guarantees
PROPOSAL: Develop a relaxed version of the directional ablation steering primitive that ensures continuity of the controlled behavior as the steering strength varies. We propose modifying the projection operation to use a learnable scaling factor that is bounded between 0 and 1, and use an additional regularization term to promote smooth changes in the model's behavior.
CONTROLS: Compare to the standard orthogonal projection and evaluate on a variety of behaviors, including those with and without dynamics (e.g., refusal of requests vs. more general policies).
COST: 120 GPU-hours (including 40 hours for developing and optimizing the algorithm)
PREDICTION: We expect the relaxed orthogonal projection to improve the steerability of the model, especially when controlling behaviors that involve continuous changes, such as, emotion control of generated text. However, it may introduce additional optimizability challenges.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Improved Relaxed Orthogonal Projection with Continuity Guarantees
PROPOSAL: Modify the relaxed orthogonal projection algorithm from Rev 3 to better handle RMS normalization by introducing a scaling factor that depends on the norm of the activation. This should improve the steerability of the model and facilitate more effective control over behaviors. We also adjust the loss function for the learnable scaling factor to include a penetration term that helps the model better avoid disturbing unrelated features.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Layer-Specific Sensitivity in Activation Steering
PROPOSAL: Experimentally analyze how sensitivity to activation steering coefficients varies across different layers of a transformer model. We will modify the activation addition primitive to learn layer-specific coefficients, which are either fixed or learned depending on the condition. Empirical evaluation will be performed on the dataset used in the Transformer-XL paper, using the perplexity metric as the primary baseline and comparison with different coefficient normalization strategies. Additionally, we will develop and include an ablation study assessing the necessity of representing coefficients as learned, fixed, or learned per-layer.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Activation addition with uniform, layer-agnostic coefficient. Baseline 2: Activation addition with learned, single coefficient.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment should confirm that layer-specific coefficients are beneficial, reducing hyperparameter search space and improving fluency and effectiveness.

TITLE: REVISED: Analyzing Activation Steering in RMS Normalized Space
PROPOSAL: Theorize about the effects of RMS normalization on activation steering and derive a framework that explains the properties of existing steering operations, including activation addition and directional ablation, within the normalized space. By utilizing techniques from linear algebra and differential geometry, we will demonstrate that the impact of RMS normalization yields a viewable structure among different steering operations, tackling the issue of interoperation dependence. Additionally, we will analyze the degree to which different layer normalization strategies impact these steering effects.
CONTROLS: assume layered activations after normalization, different normalization strategies
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This theoretical work will provide a deeper understanding of how steering operations interact with the normalization step, and it will guide the development of more effective normalization strategies that can be used in conjunction with activation steering.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Controlling Multiple Behaviors through Orthogonal Feature Directions
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the feasibility of controlling multiple behaviors by learning a set of orthogonal feature directions using a method such as PCA or SVD from a dataset of contrastive examples for each behavior. We will then use these feature directions to perform simultaneous steering of multiple behaviors through a parameterized linear combination of steering edits in the activation space. This approach will be compared to current state-of-the-art methods for controlling multiple behaviors through activation steering. We will use a combination of natural language processing and emotion regulation tasks as our experimental domain, with metrics such as emotion recognition accuracy and fluency as primary metrics.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Activation steering for a single behavior. Baseline 2: Activation steering for multiple behaviors using a single feature direction.
COST: Estimated 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment will show the potential of controlling multiple behaviors through orthogonal feature directions, but it may struggle with handling complex interactions between behaviors and with scaling to larger numbers of controlled behaviors.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Continuously Controlled Behavior Induction through Incremental Steering
PROPOSAL: Examine the possibility of continuously controlling the expression of a target behavior by incrementally adjusting the steering edit strength in activation space. This will be achieved by using a scheduler that gradually increases or decreases the steering edit strength in response to changing external conditions or input. We will use this approach to control the refusal of harmful requests in LLMs, with metrics such as request refusal accuracy, fluency, and coherence serving as primary evaluation criteria.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Activation steering with a fixed edit strength. Baseline 2: Scheduled activation steering with discrete strength adjustments.
COST: Estimated 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment will demonstrate the feasibility of continuously controlled behavior induction through incremental steering, but may struggle with efficiently optimizing the scheduler and ensuring coherent behavior as the steering edit strength changes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robustness and Adversarial Resistance of Activation Steering
PROPOSAL: Assess the robustness and adversarial resistance of activation steering in LLMs by evaluating its performance under various perturbations, such as input noise, word substitution, or addition of adversarial examples. We will investigate whether certain steering operations or learned representation spaces are more resilient to such attacks and identify potential vulnerabilities in the activation steering paradigm. This will be done by adapting real-world benchmarks for LLM robustness and evaluating the effectiveness of different steering primitives in mitigating adverse effects.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Standard LLM without activation steering. Baseline 2: Activation steering with selected primitive.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment will reveal that activation steering can be vulnerable to certain types of attacks but that specific steering primitives or learned representation spaces can provide robustness against some perturbations, highlighting the need for further research in this area.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Large-Scale Experimentation of Activation Steering across LLM Families and Behaviors
PROPOSAL: Conduct a large-scale experiment evaluating the effectiveness and robustness of activation steering across various LLM models, sizes, and behaviors, such as refusal of harmful requests, emotion regulation, or coherent text generation. We will compare the performance of activation steering with different steering primitives, normalization strategies, and scheduler configurations across multiple models and behaviors, leveraging our previous findings and insights to inform the experiment design. The primary objective is to derive generalizable conclusions about the suitability, limitations, and potential of activation steering as a behavior control method.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Standard LLM without activation steering. Baseline 2: Activation steering with selected primitive across all models and behaviors. 
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment will provide comprehensive insights into the viability and generality of activation steering across various LLM families, models, and behaviors, shedding light on its strengths and weaknesses, and contributing to the development of improved behavior control techniques for LLMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Benchmarking and Evaluate State-of-the-Art Methods for Behavior Control in LLMs
PROPOSAL: Develop a comprehensive benchmarking framework to compare and evaluate various state-of-the-art methods for behavior control in LLMs, including activation steering, reward-based methods, and other paradigm-shifting approaches. We will leverage the insights and knowledge gained from our previous experiments to design a thorough evaluation of these methods using a common set of metrics, datasets, and use cases. This will enable a fair and rigorous comparison of different methods and provide a solid foundation for future research in this area.
CONTROLS: Baseline 1: Activation steering. Baseline 2: Reward-based methods. Baseline 3: Other state-of-the-art methods.
COST: Estimated 750 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment will provide a thorough evaluation and comparison of state-of-the-art methods for behavior control in LLMs, offering valuable insights into their strengths, weaknesses, and potential applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Foundational Insights and Future Directions for Activation Steering
PROPOSAL: Consolidate the key findings and insights from our experiments and theoretical work on activation steering, incorporating them into a comprehensive framework that highlights the paradigm's strengths, limitations, and potential applications. We will also outline future research directions, including extending the approach to other NLP tasks, integrating activation steering with other behavior control methods, and addressing key challenges such as interpretability and scalability.
CONTROLS: assume the findings from previous experiments
COST: Estimated 0 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This theoretical work will provide a solid foundation for future research in activation steering, highlighting its potential applications, limitations, and avenues for further investigation, and informing the development of more effective and robust behavior control methods for LLMs.

This will be done by adapting real-world benchmarks for LLM robustness and evaluating the effectiveness of different steering primitives in mitigating adverse effects.
propositions.titre: Robustness and Adversarial Resistance of Activation Steering

propositions.controles: Baseline 1: Standard LLM without activation steering. Baseline 2: Activation steering with selected primitive across all models and behaviors.
propositions.prediction: This experiment will provide comprehensive insights into the viability and generality of activation steering across various LLM families, models, and behaviors, shedding light on its strengths and weaknesses, and contributing to the development of improved behavior control techniques for LLMs.
propositions.texte: Conduct a large-scale experiment evaluating the effectiveness and robustness of activation steering across various LLM models, sizes, and behaviors, such as refusal of harmful requests, emotion regulation, or coherent text generation. We will compare the performance of activation steering with different steering primitives, normalization strategies, and scheduler configurations across multiple models and behaviors, leveraging our previous findings and insights to inform the experiment design. The primary objective is to derive generalizable conclusions about the suitability, limitations, and potential of activation steering as a behavior control method.
propositions.titre: Large-Scale Experimentation of Activation Steering across LLM Families and Behaviors

propositions.controles: Baseline 1: Activation steering. Baseline 2: Reward-based methods. Baseline 3: Other state-of-the-art methods.
propositions.prediction: This experiment will provide a thorough evaluation and comparison of state-of-the-art methods for behavior control in LLMs, offering valuable insights into their strengths, weaknesses, and potential applications.
propositions.texte: Develop a comprehensive benchmarking framework to compare and evaluate various state-of-the-art methods for behavior control in LLMs, including activation steering, reward-based methods, and other paradigm-shifting approaches. We will leverage the insights and knowledge gained from our previous experiments to design a thorough evaluation of these methods using a common set of metrics, datasets, and use cases. This will enable a fair and rigorous comparison of different methods and provide a solid foundation for future research in this area.
propositions.titre: Benchmarking and Evaluate State-of-the-Art Methods for Behavior Control in LLMs

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Toward Architecture-Agnostic Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: Investigate a graph neural network (GNN) architecture that captures similarity between task-agnostic representations from multiple, heterogeneous models, and employs a proxy knowledge distillation loss to align the predicted representations at the task-specific level. The GNN will be trained on aggregations of task-agnostic embeddings and annotated task labels from users, without requiring access to their local model parameters or task-specific data.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing federated multi-task learning methods, including model-based and knowledge distillation approaches. Evaluate the GNN's performance on real-world multi-task benchmarks, such as the Multi-Task Federated Learning dataset and the ALBERT-variants-based multi-task learning on PubMed and Wikipedia datasets.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to improve upon existing knowledge distillation-based methods, demonstrating better knowledge transfer across tasks, while possibly failing to outperform the state-of-the-art model-based methods that assume some architectural congruity.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Toward Architecture-Agnostic Federated Multi-Task Learning with Clustering Regularization
PROPOSAL: Modify the GNN architecture from the original experiment to incorporate clustering regularization. This will help the GNN to automatically identify clusters of similar task-agnostic representations and encourage more robust knowledge transfer. Additionally, apply a refined aggregation strategy for task-agnostic embeddings, such as Weighted Fusion (WF) or Attention-based Fusion (AF), to better leverage the shared knowledge from multiple models.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the revised GNN with clustering regularization and refined aggregation strategy against the original proposal, as well as other baseline methods without these enhancements. Repeat the experiments on a larger real-world multi-task benchmark, such as the EMNIST-A dataset.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (assuming the use of larger datasets and additional aggregation strategies increases the computational complexity of the experiments)
PREDICTION: Expected to improve upon the original proposal, demonstrating enhanced robustness and efficiency, but possibly failing to achieve state-of-the-art results due to the complexity of the tasks and heterogeneity of the models.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Understanding Representation Alignment in Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: Analyze the representation alignment process in federated multi-task learning using the relaxed InfoNCE loss (RIL) algorithm, augmented with a meta-learning component that adapts the loss functions to the local data distribution of each user. Investigate how the RIL algorithm facilitates the alignment of task-agnostic representations across heterogeneous models, focusing on the role of the pairwise and triplet losses in capturing dependencies among representations.
CONTROLS: Implement and compare the RIL algorithm with and without meta-learning, using a set of benchmark datasets with varying levels of task heterogeneity, including the Shotwell dataset for multi-task image classification. Compare the alignment performance of RIL with that of the GNN-based approaches from previous proposals.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (assuming the use of a combination of benchmarks with relatively small sizes and the use of meta-learning to adapt the loss functions efficiently)
PREDICTION: Expected to provide insightful analysis on the role of the pairwise and triplet losses, possibly revealing limitations of the pairwise alignment approach and shortcomings of the triplet loss when handling models with very different architectures.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Understanding Representation Alignment in Federated Multi-Task Learning: A Comparative Study of Pairwise and Triplet Losses
PROPOSAL: Modify the previous proposal to provide a more in-depth comparative study of different loss functions used in representation alignment, focusing on the sensitivity of the representations to the choice of loss function. Investigate the robustness of existing methods to noise and corruption in the alignment process, considering various levels of noise injection into the task-agnostic representations.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the RIL algorithm, the GNN-based approach from proposal 1, and additional methods that use different loss functions, such as mean squared error (MSE) and correlation-based losses. Use a comprehensive set of benchmark datasets with varying levels of task heterogeneity and noise, including the LargeScaleSun2019 dataset for multi-modal representation learning.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (assuming the use of more diverse and complex benchmark datasets, as well as the incorporation of noise injection experiments)
PREDICTION: Expected to provide deeper insights into the design of loss functions for representation alignment, highlighting potential limitations of commonly used loss functions and suggesting the development of more robust and flexible approaches to representation alignment.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Evaluating the Effect of Data Heterogeneity on Federated Multi-Task Learning Algorithms
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of data heterogeneity on the performance of federated multi-task learning algorithms, including the GNN-based approach and representation alignment methods. Use a wide range of benchmark datasets that exhibit varying levels of data heterogeneity, including differences in image resolution, modalities, and labeling schemes. Analyze the robustness of the algorithms to changes in data characteristics and their ability to adapt to novel, unseen data distributions.
CONTROLS: Implement and compare the performance of the GNN-based approach, representation alignment methods (including RIL and the comparison of pairwise and triplet losses), and other state-of-the-art federated multi-task learning algorithms on the benchmark datasets. Evaluate the effectiveness of data augmentation and transfer learning strategies to improve the robustness of the algorithms to data heterogeneity.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (assuming the use of a comprehensive set of benchmark datasets with varying data characteristics, as well as the development and evaluation of data augmentation and transfer learning strategies)
PREDICTION: Expected to reveal the limitations of existing federated multi-task learning algorithms in the face of data heterogeneity and provide valuable insights into the design of more robust and adaptable algorithms.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Towards Adversarial Robustness in Federated Multi-Task Learning: Evaluation of Data Heterogeneity and Attack Scenarios
PROPOSAL: Expand the previous proposal to specifically focus on the adversarial robustness of federated multi-task learning algorithms, with a focus on data heterogeneity and attack scenarios. Investigate how different types of adversarial attacks (e.g., poisoning attacks, model-steering attacks) affect the performance of federated multi-task learning algorithms, and analyze their robustness to various types of attacks.
CONTROLS: Implement and compare the performance of the GNN-based approach, representation alignment methods (including RIL and the comparison of pairwise and triplet losses), and other state-of-the-art federated multi-task learning algorithms in the presence of different types of adversarial attacks. Evaluate the effectiveness of defense mechanisms (e.g., data augmentation, adversarial training, robust optimization) to enhance the robustness of these algorithms.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (assuming the use of more sophisticated attack scenarios and defense mechanisms, as well as the evaluation of the robustness of the algorithms on a wider range of benchmark datasets)
PREDICTION: Expected to provide insights into the vulnerability of existing federated multi-task learning algorithms to adversarial attacks and suggest potential strategies to enhance their robustness, but may face challenges in accurately assessing and mitigating the effects of sophisticated attacks.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Distributed and Federated Contrastive Learning for Multi-Task Representation Alignment
PROPOSAL: Explore the application of distributed and federated contrastive learning to align multi-task representations, leveraging the strengths of local optimization and distributed training. Investigate how distributed and federated contrastive learning can address the limitations of existing representation alignment methods in handling large-scale and heterogeneous datasets. Develop new architectures and algorithms that can efficiently learn and align task-agnostic representations across multiple tasks and users.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed distributed and federated contrastive learning methods with existing representation alignment approaches, such as GNN-based methods and RIL. Evaluate their effectiveness on a range of benchmarks, including the Cifar-100 and ST-LIANO datasets, as well as real-world datasets from various domains.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (assuming the use of distributed and federated learning frameworks, such as PyTorch, to implement the proposed methods)
PREDICTION: Expected to demonstrate improved efficiency and effectiveness in aligning multi-task representations using distributed and federated contrastive learning, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and experimental settings to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Towards Architecture-Agnostic Federated Multi-Task Learning with Clustering Regularization and Graph Attention
PROPOSAL: Modify the original proposal to incorporate graph attention mechanisms into the GNN architecture, allowing it to adaptively allocate attention scores to different representation clusters and enhance the alignment of task-agnostic representations. Evaluate the impact of graph attention on the performance of the architecture-agostic federated multi-task learning method, compared to the original clustering regularization method.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the revised method with and without graph attention, as well as with other baselines (e.g., standard GNN, clustering regularization without graph attention). Use a set of benchmark datasets from various domains, such as the Graphsage dataset and the PubMed dataset, to evaluate the effectiveness of the method.
COST: 900 GPU-hours (assuming the use of the existing GNN architecture and clustering regularization method, with modifications to incorporate graph attention)
PREDICTION: Expected to demonstrate improved performance and robustness in aligning task-agnostic representations using the revised method, but may require careful tuning of graph attention parameters to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: An Empirical Study on the Robustness and Efficiency of Federated Multi-Task Learning Algorithms
PROPOSAL: Conduct an extensive empirical study to evaluate the robustness and efficiency of various federated multi-task learning algorithms, including the revised architecture-agostic federated multi-task learning method, representation alignment methods, and distributed and federated contrastive learning approaches. Investigate the impact of hyperparameter choices, model architectures, and data distributions on the performance and stability of these algorithms.
CONTROLS: Implement and evaluate a wide range of federated multi-task learning algorithms on various benchmark datasets, including small-scaled and large-scaled datasets. Compare the performance of these algorithms in terms of accuracy, robustness, and efficiency, using metrics such as model parameters, communication costs, and training time.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours (assuming the use of various benchmark datasets, implementation of multiple algorithms, and evaluation of their performance on a wide range of metrics)
PREDICTION: Expected to provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of different federated multi-task learning algorithms, but may require careful selection and tuning of hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: A Comprehensive Empirical Study on the Robustness, Efficiency, and Scalability of Federated Multi-Task Learning Algorithms
PROPOSAL: Extend the previous empirical study to include a thorough evaluation of the scalability of federated multi-task learning algorithms, using large-scale datasets and distributed training frameworks. Investigate how various optimization techniques, parallelization strategies, and model pruning methods can improve the efficiency and scalability of these algorithms.
CONTROLS: Implement and evaluate the federated multi-task learning algorithms on large-scale datasets, such as the LargeScaleSun2019 dataset and the Cifar-100 dataset, using distributed training frameworks like Horovod and TensorFlow. Compare the performance of the algorithms using metrics such as accuracy, robustness, efficiency, and scalability.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours (assuming the use of large-scale datasets, distributed training frameworks, and various optimization techniques)
PREDICTION: Expected to provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of federated multi-task learning algorithms in terms of robustness, efficiency, and scalability, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and experimental settings to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Collaboration through Joint Alignment of Representations in Multiple Models
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel, theoretically grounded method for aligning representations produced by an arbitrary number of models in a federated setting. This approach leverages a multi-modal Gram-Mar-based contrastive loss that captures the dependencies among all representations, enabling knowledge transfer across models with different architectures and tasks. Evaluate the method on multi-modal and multi-task datasets.
CONTROLS: Existing methods that rely on pairwise alignment, heuristic contrastive regularization, and aggregation schemes, as well as the architecture-agnostic knowledge distillation method from proposal 1.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (2x A100 for 30 steps on multi-modal and multi-task datasets)
PREDICTION: We expect significant improvement over existing methods due to the joint alignment of representations, as well as efficiency gains from using a Gram-Mar-based loss. However, the evaluation may require fine-tuning of hyperparameters and may struggle with high-dimensional datasets.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Robust Federated Multi-Task Learning Without Congruous Architectures
PROPOSAL: Integrate the joint alignment of representations from proposal 3 into the architecture-agnostic knowledge distillation method from proposal 1. Use the Gram-Mar-based contrastive loss to align the representations before distillation, enabling knowledge transfer across models with different architectures and tasks while preserving a shared representation space.
CONTROLS: Ablation studies to compare the effects of joint alignment, architecture-agnostic distillation, and their combination, as well as UniFed, FedMT, and prominent task-specific federated learning baselines.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (2x A100 for 30 steps on multiple real-world datasets, including fine-tuning hyperparameters)
PREDICTION: We expect significant improvements in performance and robustness across heterogeneous architectures and tasks, while maintaining efficiency gains from using a Gram-Mar-based loss. However, the integration may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and may struggle with limited representation alignment in certain settings.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Multi-Task and Multi-Modal Federated Learning on Real-World Datasets
PROPOSAL: Extensively evaluate the integrated approach from proposal 1, including its performance on various real-world datasets with multiple tasks and modalities. This will involve adapting the method to handle diverse datasets, such as medical imaging, natural language processing, and multimedia processing. Analyze the effects of joint alignment of representations, architecture-agnostic distillation, and the combination of both on task-specific and cross-task performance.
CONTROLS: Adaptive methods for handling diverse datasets, existing multi-modal and multi-task baselines, and ablation studies to compare different strategies for handling modalities and tasks.
COST: 400 GPU-hours (4x A100 for 40 steps on multiple real-world datasets, including extensive hyperparameter tuning and adaptation to diverse datasets)
PREDICTION: We expect significant improvements in performance on real-world datasets with multiple tasks and modalities, with the integrated approach outperforming existing methods. However, the evaluation may require substantial fine-tuning of hyperparameters and adapting to diverse dataset characteristics.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Communication-Efficient Federated Learning with Joint Alignment and Distillation
PROPOSAL: Develop a communication-efficient version of the integrated approach from proposal 1, leveraging techniques like quantization, sparsification, and pruning to reduce the communication overhead while maintaining performance. Utilize federated averaging and batch splitting to further reduce communication costs. Evaluate the method on a range of real-world datasets and compare its performance to existing communication-efficient federated learning methods.
CONTROLS: Existing communication-efficient federated learning methods, such as Q-Fed, S-Fed, and P-Fed, as well as ablation studies to compare different quantization and sparsification strategies.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (3x A100 for 30 steps on multiple real-world datasets, including extensive hyperparameter tuning and evaluation)
PREDICTION: We expect significant reductions in communication overhead while maintaining performance, with the integrated approach outperforming existing communication-efficient federated learning methods. However, the evaluation may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and adaptation to different dataset characteristics.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Server-Side Optimization for Scalable Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: Design a server-side optimization framework to reduce the computational burden on the server while supporting federated multi-task learning with joint alignment and distillation. Utilize techniques like parallelization, model pruning, and knowledge distillation to reduce server-side computations. Evaluate the framework on a large-scale federated learning setup, comparing its performance to existing server-side optimization methods.
CONTROLS: Existing server-side optimization methods, such as parallel federated averaging and model pruning-based federated learning, as well as ablation studies to compare different optimization strategies.
COST: 320 GPU-hours (5x A100 for 40 steps on a large-scale federated learning setup, including extensive hyperparameter tuning and evaluation)
PREDICTION: We expect significant reductions in server-side computational costs while maintaining performance, with the integrated approach outperforming existing server-side optimization methods. However, the evaluation may require careful tuning of hyperparameters and adaptation to different federated learning setups.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Evaluation and Analysis of Knowledge Transfer in Federated Multi-Task Learning
PROPOSAL: Conduct an in-depth evaluation and analysis of knowledge transfer in federated multi-task learning, focusing on the effects of joint alignment and distillation on knowledge sharing across different tasks and models. Utilize techniques like network analysis, attention visualization, and knowledge graph construction to gain insights into the knowledge transfer process. Evaluate the performance of the integrated approach on a range of tasks and models, comparing its knowledge transfer abilities to existing methods.
