actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Cascaded Self-Speculative Decoding on Real-World LLM Applications
PROPOSAL: Conduct an exploratory experiment on various real-world datasets (e.g., multi-turn conversation, machine translation, summarization) using existing training-free self-speculative decoding methods (e.g., Lookahead, SWIFT) and combine them vertically (hierarchically) with a standard retrieval-based statistical drafter. Compare the resulting cascaded implementations to standard speculative decoding and retrieval-based drafting alone.
CONTROLS: Compare to the separate baselines of standard speculative decoding, standard speculative decoding with a retrieval-based statistical drafter, and baseline retrieval-based statistical drafting.
COST: 100 GPU-hours ( approximates 1-2 hours on a 50-GPU cluster)
PREDICTION: We expect cascade speculative decoding to outperform standard speculative decoding and retrieval-based drafting alone, potentially revealing areas where improvements can be made. However, training constraints may lead to variability in performance across tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Cascade Scheduling for LLM Inference
PROPOSAL: Extend the exploratory experiment in proposal 1 by introducing adaptive scheduling mechanisms that dynamically select the self-speculative method and draft length for each cascade level based on the input sequence characteristics and computational constraints. This will be done using meta-learning algorithms (e.g., Meta-SGD) to learn a policy that adapts to various scenarios. 
CONTROLS: Use the policy learned on a set of diverse LLM inference tasks and compare its performance to the fixed-schedule implementations of proposal 1.
COST: 300 GPU-hours ( approximates 3-6 hours on a 50-GPU cluster)
PREDICTION: The adaptive scheduling approach may lead to further speedup and efficiency gains, particularly for longer sequences and tasks with varied input characteristics. However, the additional cost of meta-learning may outweigh the benefits, especially on less-compute-constrained devices.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Comprehensive Benchmarking and Characterization of Cascade Speculative Decoding
PROPOSAL: (formerly "Analyzing Cascaded Self-Speculative Decoding on Real-World LLM Applications") Expand the scope by conducting a comprehensive benchmarking and characterization study on various real-world datasets (e.g., multi-turn conversation, machine translation, summarization, question answering, mathematical reasoning, retrieval-augmented generation). Evaluate the performance of different self-speculative methods (e.g., Lookahead, SWIFT), draft lengths, and scheduling strategies (both adaptive and fixed) to identify trends, bottlenecks, and areas for improvement.
CONTROLS: Include standard speculative decoding, standard sequential decoding, and baseline retrieval-based statistical drafting as baselines.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours ( approximates 12-24 hours on a 50-GPU cluster)
PREDICTION: The study may reveal scenarios where current self-speculative methods show limited gains or suffer performance drops, indicating the need for further innovation.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Comprehensive Benchmarking and Characterization of Adaptive Cascade Scheduling
PROPOSAL: (formerly "Adaptive Cascade Scheduling for LLM Inference") Expand the evaluation of the adaptive scheduling approach in proposal 2 by exploring different meta-learning objectives, policies, and sequence characteristics. Additionally, analyze the trade-offs between speedup and accuracy at the different cascade levels and the impact of scheduling decisions on the overall inference process.
CONTROLS: Use the same set of diverse LLM inference tasks as in proposal 2 and evaluate the adaptive scheduling approach in isolation from proposal 1.
COST: 400 GPU-hours ( approximates 4-8 hours on a 50-GPU cluster)
PREDICTION: A more comprehensive understanding of adaptive cascade scheduling may lead to improved performance and efficiency, but also reveals potential challenges in real-world deployment due to the added complexity and computational overhead.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Unlimited Lookahead Decoding with Memory-Efficient Cascade Scheduling
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether incorporating Unlimited Lookahead (ULH) decoding, a pruning-based method that conditions on the full sequence, into a cascade scheduling framework can sidestep traditional limitations of self-speculative methods (mainly, less-than-perfect acceptances). The key idea is to closely tie each draft model's predictions to the topological structure of the underlying input, leveraging the reduced-dimensionality of the sequence.
CONTROLS: Compare to state-of-the-art self-speculative methods (e.g., Lookahead, SWIFT), as well as to the limitations of ULH in high-latency use cases without caching.
COST: 800 GPU-hours ( approximates 8-16 hours on a 50-GPU cluster)
PREDICTION: If successfully integrated with cascade scheduling, Unlimited Lookahead Decoding might outperform existing self-speculative methods due to its ability to exploit long-term dependencies, while still retaining the efficiency features of self-speculative decoding. However, adaptation to online settings, or to very large-batch items may pose challenges.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Conditional Truncation for Efficient Cascade Scheduling
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of hierarchical conditional truncation (HCT) in managing scalability issues associated with self-speculative cascade scheduling. By dynamically determining which parts of the sequence are likely to be critical and interpolating across the draft sequence using HCT, this approach aims to accelerate computations while maintaining the performance quality of the output.
CONTROLS: Evaluate HCT performance relative to existing scheduling methods, such as the adaptive scheduling in proposal 2, and its potential in high-dimensional or large-batch contexts.
COST: 500 GPU-hours ( approximates 5-10 hours on a 50-GPU cluster)
PREDICTION: If successful, HCT could significantly reduce computational overhead while maintaining the performance of the output for various LLM benchmarks, by stratifying the visibility and thus importance of tokens in the output sequence.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: A Decomposition-Based Framework for Adaptive Cascade Scheduling
PROPOSAL: (formerly "Comprehensive Benchmarking and Characterization of Adaptive Cascade Scheduling") Update the adaptive scheduling framework to utilize decomposition techniques, such as spectral clustering, k-means, or other unsupervised learning methods, to dynamically partition the input sequence into sub-parts that can be effectively handled by different draft models. This partitioning can serve as a regularization mechanism to ensure that the drafts are both efficiently processed and decently accurate.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of different decomposition methods on the resulting adaptive scheduling performance.
COST: 600 GPU-hours ( approximates 6-12 hours on a 50-GPU cluster)
PREDICTION: Decomposing the input sequence might enhance adaptive scheduling's performance by better managing the trade-off between draft complexity and input dimensionality, particularly in situations with naturally segregable trends in the input data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modeling Input Sequence Structure for Efficient Cascade Scheduling of LLM Inference
PROPOSAL: Develop a model-based approach to exploit implicit input domain knowledge and structural properties present in the sequence data. By incorporating explicit sequence metrics derived from domain-specific characteristics (e.g., position-aware dependencies, generation coherence) into the adaptive scheduling framework, LLM inference performance may be boosted by optimizing draft sequence selection based on these features.
CONTROLS: Compare the baseline of adaptive cascade scheduling (from revised proposal 2) against the sequence-structure aware adaptive scheduler and investigate sensitivity of improvement to varying sequence characteristics.
COST: 900 GPU-hours ( approximates 9-18 hours on a 50-GPU cluster)
PREDICTION: This method has the potential to improve the adaptive scheduling efficiency of LLMs operating on specific sequence types (e.g., natural language text, recipes, gene sequences), yielding faster inference times for high-stakes queries with a larger vocabulary. Additionally, implanting sequence modeling lifts the mouths imaging the current superiority of tabbing over greedy sing during consideration from amplifying effectiveness.

TITLE: Hierarchical Anomaly Detection for Improving Sequence-Wise Cascade Scheduling
PROPOSAL: (formerly "Modeling Input Sequence Structure for Efficient Cascade Scheduling of LLM Inference") Update the sequence-structure aware adaptive scheduling framework to incorporate a hierarchical anomaly detection (HAD) component, which learns to identify regions within the sequence where traditional partitioning or normalization techniques fail. HAD will prioritize resource allocation to these 'anomalous' regions, further improving the scheduling efficiency of LLM inference.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Refining Bradley-Terry Objective for Better Calibration and Rank Accuracy
PROPOSAL: We will experiment with modified Bradley-Terry objectives that incorporate noise and uncertainty during optimization to improve the calibration of discriminative reward models.
CONTROLS: Compare with vanilla Bradley-Terry objective and existing variants (e.g., Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward) on accuracy, calibration, and fairness metrics.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate a 5-10% improvement in calibration and 2-5% increase in rank accuracy, with a higher true positive rate for in-distribution data and reduced model uncertainty through bootstrapping. However, the modifications might fail to generalize across domains due to the sensitivity of the modifications to the specific characteristics of the data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Calibrated Relative Reward (CRR) Paradigm
PROPOSAL: We propose a new framework, Calibrated Relative Reward (CRR), which combines the strengths of discriminative and generative models by learning a probabilistic ranking that captures the relative quality of responses while providing a calibrated absolute quality score.
CONTROLS: Compare CRR against state-of-the-art discriminative and generative reward models on a variety of metrics, including calibration, accuracy, and interpretability measures, and assess its scalability and generalizability across different domains and data distributions.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect CRR to outperform existing discriminative models in terms of calibration and provide comparable or better rank accuracy, while offering more interpretable scores with a meaningful measure of confidence, thus reducing the need for expensive pointwise supervision for calibration. However, the performance might degrade when faced with qualitative shifts in the input distributions or differences in annotator styles.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Calibrated Relative Reward (CRR) Paradigm
PROPOSAL: To further develop the Calibrated Relative Reward (CRR) paradigm, we will experiment with two variants: (1) a model-based approach that leverages a small domain-adapted neural network to provide an absolute quality score for CRR, and (2) a data-efficient approach that uses active learning to select a subset of high-quality annotations to fine-tune the CRR model, given limited availability of in-domain quality annotations.
CONTROLS: Compare the two CRR variants against state-of-the-art discriminative and generative reward models, as well as a baseline of using external quality annotation data, on metrics of calibration, accuracy, interpretability, and efficiency.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (spread across both variants)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that both variants of CRR will perform better than the existing discriminative models in terms of calibration and offer comparable or better rank accuracy, while providing more interpretable scores. The model-based approach might struggle to generalize to unseen domains due to overfitting to in-domain data, whereas the data-efficient approach might benefit from a more efficient use of high-quality annotations but could be sensitive to the quality of the initial active learning samples.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Refining Bradley-Terry Objective for Better Calibration and Rank Accuracy
PROPOSAL: We will extend the modified Bradley-Terry objective by incorporating a calibration loss function, such as Pinball Loss or Expected Calibration Error (ECE), and a robust ranking loss, such as the Billionaires Ranking Loss, to explicitly optimize for better calibration and robust ranking accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare with the original modified Bradley-Terry objective and existing variants, such as Skywork-Reward and InternLM2-Reward, on metrics of calibration, accuracy, robustness, and fairness.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in calibration, a slight increase in rank accuracy, and improved robustness against outliers, but potential trade-offs in terms of optimization difficulty and overfitting risk, which may require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Value-Based Risk Assessment (VBRA) Framework
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel Value-Based Risk Assessment (VBRA) framework for inferring the quality of a reward model's scores and evaluating its performance under uncertain human preference judgments. VBRA combines a neural network with a value-based model to assess the probability of an action being highly ranked by humans, given the reward signal, and use this information to inform assignment of uncertainty to each score.
CONTROLS: Compare VBRA against various baselines, including heuristics-based uncertainty estimation methods and recent ranking-based risk assessment models, on metrics such as prediction accuracy, risk assessment quality, and diversity of explored solutions.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate VBRA to significantly improve risk assessment by reducing false positives and negatives, capture uncertainty in the reward signal, and enhance the exploration-exploitation trade-off, but it may add complexity and potentially stretch inference time due to the additional computations involved in estimating risk.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Reward Model Calibration and Evaluation
PROPOSAL: We investigate the feasibility of multi-task learning for simultaneously calibrating reward model scores and evaluating their performance using metrics such as expected calibration error and Brier score, as well as optimizing ranking accuracy through end-to-end learning.
CONTROLS: Compare multi-task learning approaches against monolithic reward model designs and ranking-based evaluation methods on metrics of calibration, accuracy, and efficiency, and explore the transferability of learned representations across tasks.
COST: 320 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect multi-task learning to improve calibration, accuracy, and efficiency by learning robust representations and adapting to new tasks through shared and task-specific components, but potential complexity issues may arise due to the increasing number of objectives and non-linearities involved in end-to-end learning, which may affect scalability and domain transfer.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Active Learning for Reward Model Adaptation and Calibration
PROPOSAL: We explore the potential of active learning for adaptively identifying and fine-tuning a reward model's parameters using a subset of carefully selected high-quality annotations, with the goal of improving calibration, ranking accuracy, and generalizability across diverse domains and scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare the effectiveness of different active learning strategies (e.g., uncertainty-based, query-by-committee) against passive learning and partial labeling baselines on metrics of calibration, accuracy, efficiency, and robustness to domain shifts.
COST: 280 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that active learning can effectively identify the most informative instances for adaptation, leading to improved calibration, accuracy, and generalizability, but the approach's performance might be sensitive to the initial reward model quality and the quality/quantity of the selected high-quality annotations, which may require careful balancing and trade-off decisions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Monte Carlo Tree Search for Reward Model Selection and Optimization
PROPOSAL: We investigate the application of Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to efficiently explore the space of reward models, select the most effective model, and optimize its parameters to achieve better calibration, ranking accuracy, and robustness to uncertainty and annotation noise.
CONTROLS: Compare the effectiveness of MCTS against traditional black-box optimization methods (e.g., random search, Bayesian optimization) and model selection techniques (e.g., cross-validation) on metrics such as reward model performance, computation time, and interpretability of the search process.
COST: 360 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect MCTS to efficiently explore the reward model space, find more effective models, and adapt to uncertain environments with noisy annotations, but its performance might be sensitive to the chosen exploration strategy and complexity of the reward model space, which may require careful tuning and domain expertise.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward Model Ensemble and Equivariance Building
PROPOSAL: We explore the potential benefits of combining multiple reward models trained on different data subsets or with different objective functions to create a more robust and accurate reward signal, leveraging ensemble methods and exploring strategies to maximize equivariance between different reward models.
CONTROLS: Compare the effectiveness of different ensemble methods and equivariance strategies against single-model baselines on metrics of calibration, accuracy, and robustness to ambiguity and uncertainty.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that reward model ensembles and equivariance can improve the robustness and accuracy of the reward signal, but the approach may incur higher computational costs due to the ensemble and hyperparameter tuning, and the best strategies for ensemble and equivariance may depend on the specific reward model and dataset, which requires further exploration.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED: Value-Based Risk Assessment (VBRA) Framework
PROPOSAL: To further develop the Value-Based Risk Assessment (VBRA) framework, we will experiment with incorporating learnable dynamics and uncertainty-aware learning to better capture the evolution of human preferences over time and the inherent uncertainty in reward signals, aiming to enhance the framework's ability to assess and mitigate risk in reinforcement learning from human feedback.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised VBRA framework against the original version, as well as state-of-the-art risk assessment methods, on metrics of risk assessment accuracy, quality, and efficiency, and evaluate its performance on diverse reinforcement learning tasks and datasets.
COST: 310 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the revised VBRA framework to demonstrate improved risk assessment capabilities, especially in scenarios involving temporally dynamic preferences and uncertain reward signals, but potential challenges may arise from the increased complexity of the framework, which may require careful tuning of learnable components and adaptation of existing algorithms.

PROPOSAL 5: Active Learning for Reward Model Adaptation and Calibration
We explore the potential of active learning for adaptively identifying and fine-tuning a reward model's parameters using a subset of carefully selected high-quality annotations, with the goal of improving calibration, ranking accuracy, and generalizability across diverse domains and scenarios.

We explore the potential benefits of combining multiple reward models trained on different data subsets or with different objective functions to create a more robust and accurate reward signal, leveraging ensemble methods and exploring strategies to maximize equivariance between different reward models.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: "Discriminative-Generative Reward Model Blending"
PROPOSAL: Design and evaluate a hybrid reward model that combines the efficiency of discriminative models with the interpretability of generative ones. The proposed model uses a light-weight generative component (e.g., a multi-head attention mechanism) to provide additional context and justification for the preference decision, which is then fed into a conventional discriminative value head (e.g., an MLP). This hybrid approach aims to leverage the strengths of both paradigms while addressing their respective weaknesses.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed hybrid model with state-of-the-art discriminative models (e.g., HelpSteer2-Preference, ArmoRM) and generative models (e.g., Skywork-Reward, InternLM2-Reward) on various datasets (e.g., flan-prompt, multitask-ChatEval). Evaluate performance using metrics such as reward correlation, ranking accuracy, and calibration quality.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours (4xV100 or equivalent)
PREDICTION: The hybrid model is expected to outperform discriminative models in terms of calibration quality and interpretability, while maintaining competitive ranking accuracy. The generative component may help improve model robustness to noisy or ambiguous preference data. However, the trade-off between generative and discriminative components may lead to model overcomplication or decreased efficiency, requiring careful hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: "Absolute Quality Scaling via Transfer Learning"
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of transfer learning to adapt a discriminative reward model trained on large-scale quality annotation data to a new domain with limited quality annotations. The goal is to establish a baseline for absolute quality judgments using the adapted model's scores, which are then used to calibrate the preference judgments in the new domain. This approach aims to leverage the differences in preference behavior between domains and exploit the commonalities in absolute quality judgments to improve ranking accuracy.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the proposed transfer learning approach on a range of datasets, including flan-prompt, multitask-ChatEval, and multiple RLHF alignment benchmarks. Compare the transfer learning approach with full-supervision methods (e.g., pointwise supervision for calibration) and unsupervised methods (e.g., self-supervised calibration). Assess the performance of the adapted reward model on new domains using metrics such as ranked accuracy, calibration quality, and paired Kendall's tau.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours (2xV100 or equivalent)
PREDICTION: The transfer learning approach is expected to outperform other methods in leveraging knowledge from pre-trained models to adapt to new domains, leading to improved ranking accuracy. However, the adaptation process may require careful selection of training protocols and learning rates to avoid overfitting or underfitting the new domain.

PROPOSAL: Refine the transfer learning approach by incorporating multi-task learning, where the reward model is trained to predict both absolute quality scores and preference judgments simultaneously. This shared knowledge can help the model adapt to new domains more efficiently by leveraging the similarity in features between preferences and qualities. Compared to our previous proposal, this multi-task approach can adapt to new domains more efficiently, leveraging the interplay between absolute qualities and preference judgments.

CONTROLS: Compare the proposed multi-task learning approach with the original transfer learning method and a baseline learned on evaluation data. Evaluate the effectiveness of the multi-task learning approach using metrics such as ranked accuracy, calibration quality, paired Kendall's tau and metrics proposed for quality and ranking such as ME and MAP.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours (2xV100 or equivalent)
PREDICTION: The multi-task learning approach is expected to outperform the original transfer learning method and the baseline on multiple tasks, achieving a desirable trade-off between adaptation efficiency and ranking accuracy. However, potential issues related to overfitting or conflicting objectives may arise, requiring careful regularization or task balancing strategies to avoid degraded performance.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: "Efficient Transfer Learning via Multi-Task Learning with Weighted Loss"
PROPOSAL: Refine the multi-task learning approach by incorporating a weighted loss function that assigns less importance to certain tasks or groups of tasks during training. This can allow the model to adapt more efficiently to new domains, where some tasks may be less relevant or noisy. By dynamically adjusting the weights, the model can prioritize tasks that are more informative or relevant, leading to improved adaptability and ranking accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed weighted loss approach with the original multi-task learning method and a baseline learned on evaluation data. Evaluate the effectiveness of the weighted loss approach using metrics such as ranked accuracy, paired Kendall's tau, and weighted Brier scores.

PREDICTION: The weighted loss approach is expected to improve adaptation efficiency and ranking accuracy in new domains by prioritizing more informative or relevant tasks. ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: "Active Learning for Reward Model Adaptation"
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of active learning to adapt the reward model to a new domain with limited availability of ground truth labels. This involves selecting a subset of most informative samples from the new domain and querying human annotators to obtain labels for these samples. The reward model is then updated using the newly annotated samples, and the process is repeated iteratively.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed active learning approach with passive learning (e.g., random sampling) and transfer learning methods. Evaluate the effectiveness of the active learning approach using metrics such as ranked accuracy, paired Kendall's tau, and active learning efficiency (i.e., the proportion of samples that need to be annotated to achieve a certain level of ranking accuracy).
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours (3xV100 or equivalent) + human annotation costs
PREDICTION: The active learning approach is expected to outperform passive learning and transfer learning by aggressively selecting the most informative samples, thus reducing the need for human annotations and improving ranking accuracy in the new domain. However, the computational cost of active learning may be significant, and the annotation process may be time-consuming and labor-intensive.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: "Explainable Reward Model via Attention-weighted Knowledge Distillation"
PROPOSAL: Propose a method to create an explainable reward model by leveraging the interpretability of attention mechanisms. The method involves training a knowledge distillation model that learns to map the attention weights of the original reward model to the predicted scores, making it possible to understand which features or inputs contribute the most to the model's predictions.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed explainable reward model with the original reward model and evaluate its performance using metrics such as interpretability metrics (e.g., AUC-ROC, AUC-PR) and ranking accuracy metrics (e.g., Kendall's tau).
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours (2xV100 or equivalent)
PREDICTION: The explainable reward model is expected to provide valuable insights into the decision-making process of the original reward model, enabling users to understand the reasoning behind the predictions. However, the complexity of the distillation process may lead to a trade-off between interpretability and accuracy.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: "Ensemble Methods for Robust Reward Modeling"
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of ensemble methods to combine the predictions of multiple reward models, with diverse architectures, to improve the robustness and accuracy of the final reward prediction. This involves training multiple reward models on the same dataset and then aggregating their predictions using techniques such as averaging or stacking.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed ensemble methods with single models (e.g., discriminative-generative blending) and evaluate their performance using metrics such as ranked accuracy, paired Kendall's tau, and Brier score.
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours (3xV100 or equivalent)
PREDICTION: The ensemble method is expected to improve the robustness and accuracy of the reward model by combining the strengths of multiple models and reducing the impact of outliers or noisy data. However, the choice of ensemble method and the hyperparameters may require careful tuning and experimentation to achieve optimal results.

This involves training multiple generative models on the same dataset and then aggregating their predictions using techniques such as averaging or stacking.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Discriminative vs. Generative Reward Models: A Comparative Study
PROPOSAL: Perform an empirical comparison of state-of-the-art discriminative and generative reward models on real-world LLMs, evaluating their accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability in various domains (.chatbot response quality evaluation, mathematical reasoning, code generation, chatbot safety, role-play dialogue). The comparison will be done on the same benchmarks, such as HellaSwag, Web.Scheme, and ReCoRD-Chat responseData.
CONTROLS: Implement Skywork-Reward and HelpSteer2-Preference as discriminative baselines, and Adaptation learning (also known as reasoning-based variant) as a generative baseline.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that discriminative models excel in terms of ranking accuracy but significantly struggle with capturing absolute quality and are uncalibrated. Generative models may be more interpretable, but their scores might not be as reliable or require expensive pointwise supervision. However, if our generative model achieves noticeable improvements, it could be due to the domain-specific subdomains in the ReCoRD-Chat data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning from Few Quality Annotations: A Domain Adaptation Framework
PROPOSAL: Develop a domain adaptation framework that can leverage a small set of high-quality annotations to adapt a pre-trained reward model to a new domain. This framework will use methods such as meta-learning, pseudo-labeling, or few-shot learning to adapt the reward model to the new domain with limited quality annotations. Evaluate this framework on the same domains as the comparative study (proposal 1), but with a small annotated dataset for adaptation (e.g., 100 labeled examples).
CONTROLS: Adapt the pre-trained Skywork-Reward model from the comparative study for adaptation, and compare its performance to an unfrozen version of the model fine-tuned on the target domain.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the adaptation framework to be effective in transferring knowledge from a pre-trained model to a new domain with few quality annotations. However, the effectiveness might degrade when the target domain has significant differences from the source domain.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Modeling Absolute Quality and Uncertainty: A Quantile Regression-based Reward Model
PROPOSAL: Design a new reward model that incorporates quantile regression to score absolute quality and uncertainty. This model will learn multiple quantiles, each representing the quality of a response at a specific percentile of the distribution. Evaluate this model on the same benchmark datasets as the comparative study (proposal 1), using metrics such as mean absolute error (MAE) and interval coverage to assess its ability to capture absolute quality and uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed model to the baseline discriminative and generative models in terms of absolute quality and uncertainty estimation. Attempt to fuse the discriminative and generative models by using a neural network as an injector to process the output (predictions) generated by the discriminative or generative model and discriminatively learn weights between these representations.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed quantile regression-based reward model to demonstrate improved absolute quality and uncertainty estimation, but the effectiveness might depend on the complexity of the task and the availability of high-quality annotations. However, the model might be sensitive to overfitting or underfitting, and careful tuning of hyperparameters might be required.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Modeling Absolute Quality and Uncertainty: A Quantile Regression-based Reward Model
PROPOSAL: REVISED PROPOSAL: Incorporate a probabilistic calibration module, such as a temperature-scaled cross-entropy method, to adjust the quantile regression outputs and ensure calibrated scores. Also, use a probabilistic modeling approach, such as Bayesian neural networks, to learn uncertainty estimates from the data. Evaluate this revised model on the same benchmark datasets as the comparative study (proposal 1), using metrics such as Pinball loss, mean absolute error (MAE), and interval coverage to assess its ability to capture absolute quality and uncertainty.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised model to the original model, as well as to the baseline discriminative and generative models, in terms of absolute quality and uncertainty estimation.
COST: 35 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the revised model to demonstrate improved absolute quality and uncertainty estimation, with better calibration and uncertainty estimates. However, the model might be computationally expensive to train, and careful tuning of hyperparameters might be required. Additionally, the effectiveness might depend on the quality and quantity of the training data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adversarial Training for Reward Model Robustness
PROPOSAL: Develop an adversarial training framework to improve the robustness of the reward model against task-agnostic perturbations, such as input gradient masking or adversarial examples. This framework will use a discriminator to distinguish between "natural" and "adversarial" examples, and will optimize the reward model to fool the discriminator while maintaining its original performance on the task.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the adversarially trained reward model on the same benchmark datasets as the comparative study (proposal 1), using metrics such as robustness under gradient masking or adversarial attack.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the adversarially trained reward model to demonstrate improved robustness against task-agnostic perturbations, but the effectiveness might depend on the strength of the adversarial attack and the reward model architecture. Additionally, the adversarial training process might be computationally expensive and require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward Model-Human Aligner: A Multi-Task Learning Framework
PROPOSAL: Design a multi-task learning framework that jointly trains the reward model and a human alignment model (HAM) to assess the quality of human preferences. The HAM will evaluate the alignment of the reward model with human preferences, providing a feedback loop to the reward model during training. Evaluate this framework on the same benchmark datasets as the comparative study (proposal 1), using metrics such as reward model alignment and human preference accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare the reward model-HAM framework to state-of-the-art reward models, such as Skywork-Reward and HelpSteer2-Preference, in terms of reward model alignment and human preference accuracy.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the reward model-HAM framework to demonstrate improved reward model alignment and human preference accuracy, but the effectiveness might depend on the quality of the HAM and the reward model architecture. Additionally, the multi-task learning process might be computationally expensive and require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Preference Disagreement on Reward Model Performance
PROPOSAL: Analyze the impact of annotator disagreement on the performance of reward models, particularly focusing on how different methods handle inconsistent preference data. Design an experiment to collect a large-scale dataset with diverse annotator preferences and reward models, and evaluate the reward models' performance under different scenarios of annotator disagreement.
CONTROLS: Compare the robustness of state-of-the-art reward models, such as Skywork-Reward and HelpSteer2-Preference, to annotator disagreement, and analyze the performance of our previously proposed methods (e.g., quantile regression, adversarial training, and reward model-HAM framework) in handling inconsistent preference data.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the reward models to demonstrate decreased performance under high annotator disagreement, but the methods we have proposed might show improved robustness or flexibility in handling such scenarios. However, the effectiveness might depend on the level of annotator disagreement and the diversity of the dataset.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Scalability of Reward Models for Long-Term Conversations
PROPOSAL: Design an experiment to evaluate the scalability of state-of-the-art reward models for long-term conversations, including conversations involving multiple dialog turns and multiple annotators. Investigate how these reward models perform under increased conversation length, and identify potential challenges and limitations in scaling up reward models for complex dialogue scenarios.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of reward models, such as Skywork-Reward and HelpSteer2-Preference, in short-term and long-term conversations, and analyze the impact of conversation length on their performance.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the reward models to demonstrate decreased performance under increased conversation length, but the effects might vary depending on the model architecture and dialogue management strategy. Additionally, we may need to adapt our proposed methods (e.g., quantile regression, adversarial training, and reward model-HAM framework) to accommodate the complexity of long-term conversations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Human-in-the-Loop Evaluation of Reward Models for Real-World Applications
PROPOSAL: Design a human-in-the-loop evaluation framework to assess the effectiveness of reward models in real-world applications, such as chatbot deployment and human-computer interaction. Involve human evaluators in the evaluation process to provide feedback on the reward models' performance in realistic scenarios.
CONTROLS: Evaluate state-of-the-art reward models, such as Skywork-Reward and HelpSteer2-Preference, using the proposed human-in-the-loop framework, and compare their performance to that of human evaluators.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the reward models to demonstrate improved performance in real-world applications when evaluated using a human-in-the-loop framework. However, the effectiveness might depend on the quality of the annotation data, model architecture, and human evaluator bias. Additionally, we may need to adapt our proposed methods (e.g., quantile regression, adversarial training, and reward model-HAM framework) to accommodate the complexity of real-world applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Consolidating Results and Identifying Future Directions
PROPOSAL: Consolidate the results from the previous experiments and identify future research directions for the development of reward models for large language models. Synthesize the findings from the comparative study, domain adaptation framework, quantile regression-based reward model, adversarial training, reward model-HAM framework, preference disagreement analysis, scalability evaluation, and human-in-the-loop evaluation to provide a comprehensive overview of the current state-of-the-art in reward model research.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Estimating External and Internal Knowledge Utilization in RAG using Input-Energy-Based Metrics
PROPOSAL: We propose to estimate external context utilization and internal knowledge utilization in RAG by using input-energy-based metrics. Specifically, we will compute the average energy of the input tokens and the energy of the context tokens that receive high attention weights from the attention mechanisms in the decoder. We will represent internal knowledge utilization as the difference between the average energy of the input tokens and the energy of the high-attention-weighted context tokens. The rationale is that the energy of the input tokens should be higher when the model relies heavily on internal knowledge, and lower when it relies on external context. We will train a linear regression model to predict the scores of hallucinations using these metrics.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: random guessing, (2) Baseline: using ReDeEP's attention-based metrics without input-energy-based metrics.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method should outperform the baselines and demonstrate a positive correlation between external-internal knowledge utilization ratio and hallucination detection, although it may not achieve perfect results due to the simplifying assumption behind input-energy-based metrics. The model might be less effective in understanding semantic content than approaches like ReDeEP, and may capture patterns specific to the training data.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: End-to-End Training of External Context and Internal Knowledge Utilization Detectors for RAG
PROPOSAL: We propose to develop a multi-task learning framework where the model is trained end-to-end to predict both external context utilization E and internal knowledge utilization I. The model will consist of a shared encoder to compute contextual representations, and two separate decoder heads: one for predicting E, and another for predicting I. We will use a combination of masked language modeling and knowledge-based loss terms to optimize the model: for E, we will use a cosine similarity loss between the contextual representations and the relevant context tokens; for I, we will use a KL-divergence loss between the contextual representations and the internal knowledge embeddings. We hypothesize that the shared encoder will learn to attend to relevant context and use it to inform its internal knowledge utilization, and that the multi-task learning framework will lead to better generalization and stronger hallucination detection.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: training separate models for E and I using the same objectives as our approach but without sharing the encoder, (2) Baseline: using a frozen pre-trained RAG model with E and I scoring heads trained separately.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our approach should achieve the state-of-the-art performance on hallucination detection and demonstrate strong generalization across models and datasets. The trade-off of increased memory requirements and increased training time might be acceptable given the benefits of multi-task learning.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: End-to-End Training of External Context and Internal Knowledge Utilization Detectors for RAG
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal for the multi-task learning framework: instead of using a shared encoder, we will use a transformer refiner to refine the contextual representations after they have been generated by a frozen pre-trained RAG model. This will allow us to benefit from the knowledge and attention mechanisms of the pre-trained model while still learning to predict external context utilization E and internal knowledge utilization I. We will use the same objectives as before, but with the refined contextual representations as input. Additionally, we will use an attention-based loss term to encourage the model to focus on relevant context when making predictions about E.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: using the frozen pre-trained RAG model with the original attention mechanisms, (2) Baseline: training separate models for E and I using the refined contextual representations as input.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised approach should achieve state-of-the-art performance on hallucination detection and demonstrate strong generalization across models and datasets, while also improving interpretability and retaining some of the knowledge benefits of the pre-trained model.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Context-Aware Contrastive Learning for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We propose a context-aware contrastive learning approach to detect hallucinations in RAG. We will sample two sets of utterances from the validation set: one set will be the original RAG responses, and the other set will be the same response but with the hallucinated part annotated. We then compute contextual representations for each utterance pair using a frozen pre-trained RAG model. The model will be trained to minimize the distance between the contextual representations of the genuine pairs and maximize the distance between those of the hallucinated pairs, with the idea that authentic responses and hallucinated responses inhabit different semantic spaces. We will use a set of pre-defined context tokens, such as masking placeholders or <unk>, to inject context-specific information and enforce the model to learn the context-utterance relationship.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: random guessing, (2) Baseline: using a standard contrastive learning approach without context information.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our model should achieve state-of-the-art performance on hallucination detection and demonstrate strong robustness to linguistic variations. However, the performance might degrade on tutorials with data much smaller than others due to small sample size.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Harnessing Natural Language Inference for Hallucination Detection in RAG
PROPOSAL: We propose to use natural language inference (NLI) to improve hallucination detection in RAG. Specifically, we will use a sequence-to-sequence model to predict whether a given RAG response implies a true or false fact about the context. We will train the model on a dataset of labeled fact-checking tasks and evaluate it on a separate development set. We will use the predicted NLI labels as an additional feature to check for hallucinations. We hypothesize that NLI will help capture semantic contradictions and inconsistencies between the response and the context, making it a powerful indicator of hallucinations.
CONTOLS: (1) Baseline: using the NLI model as a standalone hallucination detector, (2) Baseline: using a random guessing model for NLI, and ignore NLI output.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our approach should improve the detection of factually incorrect responses by leveraging the power of NLI, and achieve state-of-the-art results on fact-checking tasks. However, the model might be sensitive to noisy or simplistic context, failing to capture comprehensive implications.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Harnessing Natural Language Inference for Hallucination Detection in RAG
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal to use natural language inference (NLI) for hallucination detection: instead of training a separate sequence-to-sequence model for NLI, we will use a pre-trained language model as an NLI classifier. Specifically, we will fine-tune a BERT-based model to predict NLI labels (e.g., supported, contradicts, neutral) for each response-context pair. We will use the predicted NLI labels to check for hallucinations and leverage NLI to evaluate the semantic alignment between the response and the context. We will also use graph-based methods to represent the input sequence as a node sequence, in order to calculate pairwise dependency and encode more informative contextual representations.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: using the original sequence-to-sequence NLI model as a standalone hallucination detector, (2) Baseline: using the pre-trained BERT model as an NLI classifier without fine-tuning.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised approach should improve the detection of factually incorrect responses by leveraging the pre-trained NLI classifier and leveraging graph-based methods to better encode contextual information, and achieve state-of-the-art results on hallucination detection.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Calibrating Uncertainty Estimates for Hallucination Detection in RAG
PROPOSAL: We propose to incorporate uncertainty estimates into hallucination detection for RAG using Monte Carlo dropout (MCD) and Bayesian neural networks (BNNs). We will use MCD to compute and calibrate model uncertainties for external context utilization E and internal knowledge utilization I, and use BNNs to learn to predict the uncertainty of each response's correctness. We will then use the predicted uncertainties to rescale the scores and confidence intervals for E and I, providing a more nuanced understanding of the model's confidence in its predictions. We will train a hybrid model using the sub-sampled Gaussian approximation (SGA) to efficiently optimize the uncertainty-aware loss.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: using the original model without uncertainty estimates, (2) Baseline: using an ensemble of models to estimate uncertainty.
COST: 350 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our approach should significantly enhance the overall performance of hallucination detection and enable more effective uncertainty-aware decision-making, while running efficiently due to usage of hybrid Bayesian neural networks. However, the calibration procedure may take a considerable amount of computational resources due to MCD, especially in scenarios where task distinction objects have complex intrinsic distributions.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Early-Layer Distillation for Improved Hallucination Detection in RAG
PROPOSAL: We propose to use early-layer distillation (ELD) to improve hallucination detection in RAG. We will fine-tune a pre-trained RAG model and compute an auxiliary "hallucination" loss to encourage the model to focus on early layers where hallucination detection is easier. We will use a teacher-student distillation framework, where the pre-trained model is used as the teacher to transfer knowledge to the fine-tuned student model. We will also explore the effect of different learning rates, training schedules, and architectural variations on the performance of the fine-tuned model. We will evaluate our approach using multiple evaluation metrics, including accuracy, F1 score, and mean squared error (MSE).
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: using the original pre-trained RAG model, (2) Baseline: fine-tuning the pre-trained model without the hallucination loss.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our approach should significantly improve the hallucination detection performance of RAG, especially in the early stages of training, and reduce the gap between RAG models and more powerful ensemble methods. However, the distillation loss might overfit to the pre-trained model and underperform on real test data without proper regularization techniques.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Context-Aware Contrastive Learning for Hallucination Detection
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal to use context-aware contrastive learning for hallucination detection in RAG. We will incorporate the distilled knowledge from the early-layer distillation (ELD) approach in turn 8, leveraging the improved understanding of early layers from hallucination detection into the contrastive learning framework. This will allow us to better capture context-specific information and semantic contradictions between the response and the retrieved context. We will also explore strategies to combine the strengths of ELD and context-aware contrastive learning to further enhance hallucination detection performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: using the original context-aware contrastive learning approach, (2) Baseline: using the ELD approach without incorporating it into the contrastive learning framework.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised approach should yield state-of-the-art results for hallucination detection and successful utilization of discriminative power from contrastive learning, proving more significant detection results compared to ELD and context-aware contrastive learning individually.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Auto-augmentation for Improved Hallucination Detection in RAG
PROPOSAL: We propose to use auto-augmentation to augment the input data for hallucination detection in RAG. We will use a reinforcement learning framework to search for the best data augmentation policies, using a curriculum of increasingly difficult hallucination detection tasks as rewards. We will leverage techniques from transfer learning, data augmentation, and inductive biases to enable our model to detect and correct hallucinations in a data-driven manner. We will also explore strategies to combine the strengths of auto-augmentation with our previous approaches (ELD, context-aware contrastive learning, and natural language inference) to further enhance hallucination detection performance.
CONTROLS: (1) Baseline: using the original augmentation strategy, (2) Baseline: using the ELD approach combined with the original augmentation strategy.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our approach should significantly improve the hallucination detection performance of RAG and generalize well to out-of-distribution data, pushing the state-of-the-art in hallucination detection in retrieval-augmented generation. However, the complexity and computational cost of the auto-augmentation framework may limit its scalability and applicability to production environments.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Alternative approach to detection through attention-pattern analysis
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether aggregating attention weights over layers and considering the dominant patterns (geometric or topological) can provide a more robust measure of internal knowledge utilization, and that flux-related metrics (e.g., entropy, information gain) can quantify the reliance on retrieved knowledge. This approach would bypass the need for choosing specific attention heads or layers.
CONTROLS: ReDeEP and its follow-up as baselines, experimentation with various aggregation methods and metrics.
COST: 100-200 GPU-hours (depending on the aggregation mechanisms and metrics considered).
PREDICTION: Attending weights patterns would capture intrinsic structure in attention, and flux-related metrics would roughly track reliance on retrieved knowledge, though could be brittle in cases of multiple competing interest streams.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Alternative approach to detection through attention-pattern analysis improved
PROPOSAL: To further improve the approach, embed attention weights and query representations into a latent space using a neural network and measure the difference in representation between the internal model state (i.e., the network before the retrieval module) and the final response output. This allows for a more nuanced understanding of how the model uses internal knowledge and retrieved context.
CONTROLS: The baseline experiment of attention-weight aggregation, to compare the effectiveness of the embedded-vector analysis.
COST: Additional 50-100 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Representation differences will allow for better disentanglement of internal and external knowledge utilization, but might still fail in settings where multiple context elements leak strong signals to the model.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Utilization-aware loss function for RAG
PROPOSAL: Design a novel loss function that incorporates the concept of internal and external knowledge utilization, and encourage the model to use the retrieved context in a more effective way. This can be achieved by tasking a secondary network to predict the degree of reliance on the retrieved knowledge and training the primary RAG model to minimize the difference between the predicted and actual utilization metrics.
CONTROLS: A base RAG model with the standard cross-entropy loss as a baseline.
COST: 500-700 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The utilization-aware loss function can effectively reduce hallucinations, especially when combined with the alternative approach from proposal 1, but may require careful hyperparameter tuning and might not perform well in scenarios where the retrieved context is scarce or noisy.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Analyzing external knowledge utilization through adversarial adaptation
PROPOSAL: Introduce an adversarial model that attempts to mask or distort the retrieved context, and observe how the RAG model adapts and responds. This can provide insights into the model's reliance on external knowledge and help to detect situations where the model over-represents its internal knowledge.
CONTROLS: A standard RAG model as a baseline, experimentation with different adversarial perturbation strategies.
COST: 300-500 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The adversarial adaptation approach will reveal instances where the model over-represents internal knowledge and should effectively detect situations prone to hallucinations, but might not generalize well to diverse domains and might require fine-tuning for each specific dataset.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: External knowledge augmentation pipeline
PROPOSAL: Develop a pipeline that extracts specific knowledge snippets from the retrieved context and incorporates them into the model's internal knowledge during training. This can enhance the model's ability to utilize external knowledge and reduce its reliance on hallucinations.
CONTROLS: A baseline RAG model without external knowledge augmentation, experimentation with different snippet-extraction techniques and knowledge-representation formats.
COST: 800-1200 GPU-hours (depending on the complexity of the snippet-extraction module).
PREDICTION: The external knowledge augmentation pipeline will improve the model's utilization of external knowledge, potentially leading to reduced hallucinations, but might introduce new challenges such as knowledge fragmentation, instability in the training process, and the need for careful balancing between internal and external knowledge.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Visualizing internal-external knowledge trade-off through knowledge-space embeddings
PROPOSAL: Embed the model's internal knowledge and external context into a common, high-dimensional space and use dimensionality reduction techniques to visualize the trade-off between them. This can provide insights into how the model balances its reliance on internal knowledge and external context.
CONTROLS: The alternative approach to detection through attention-pattern analysis improved as a baseline, experimentation with different dimensionality reduction techniques.
COST: 200-400 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The knowledge-space embeddings will offer valuable visual insights into the model's knowledge trade-off and can be leveraged to design more effective approaches to detect hallucinations and measure utilization, but might become complex when dealing with high-dimensional data or nuanced contextual dependencies.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Utilization-aware loss function for RAG refined
PROPOSAL: To refine the utilization-aware loss function, incorporate the visual insights from the knowledge-space embeddings and use them as auxiliary feedback to guide the model's training process. This can be achieved by assigning higher losses to points in the knowledge space where the internal-external knowledge trade-off is unfavorable.
CONTROLS: The original utilization-aware loss function as a baseline, various experiments to evaluate the impact of different embedding-based feedback strategies.
COST: Additional 200-400 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The refined utilization-aware loss function will take advantage of the insights from the visualizations and provide better training signals for the model, but might introduce additional complexities and hyperparameters to tune, such as the embedding dimensionality and feedback weights.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Self-supervised knowledge inverse regularization
PROPOSAL: Regularize the model's internal knowledge by training it to invert or reverse the knowledge it has learned from the external context. This can be done through self-supervised learning objectives, such as inverting the model's outputs or reconstructing the context from the model's outputs. The regularization can help reduce the model's reliance on hallucinations and improve its utilization of external knowledge.
CONTROLS: A baseline RAG model without self-supervised knowledge inverse regularization.
COST: 400-700 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The self-supervised knowledge inverse regularization will reduce the model's reliance on hallucinations, but might lead to knowledge degradation or loss of information, especially if the regularization is too strong or if the model is not able to invert the knowledge accurately.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Visualizing internal-external knowledge trade-off through knowledge-space embeddings improved
PROPOSAL: To further improve the knowledge-space embeddings, consider incorporating additional dimensions or channels that capture semantic relationships or co-occurrences that are relevant to the task at hand. For example, adding a channel for named entity recognition or a dimension for part-of-speech tagging. This can provide a more nuanced and detailed understanding of the internal-external knowledge trade-off.
CONTROLS: The original visualizing internal-external knowledge trade-off through knowledge-space embeddings as a baseline, experimentation with different additional dimensions or channels.
COST: Additional 100-200 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: The improved knowledge-space embeddings will offer a more detailed and nuanced understanding of the internal-external knowledge trade-off, but might become increasingly complex and difficult to interpret as additional dimensions and channels are added.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Benchmarking and evaluation of hallucination detectors

PROPOSAL 1: Alternative approach to detection through attention-pattern analysis improved
To further improve the approach, embed attention weights and query representations into a latent space using a neural network and measure the difference in representation between the internal model state (i.e., the network before the retrieval module) and the final response output. This allows for a more nuanced understanding of how the model uses internal knowledge and retrieved context.
Controls: The baseline experiment of attention-weight aggregation, to compare the effectiveness of the embedded-vector analysis.

PROPOSAL 2: Utilization-aware loss function for RAG refined
To refine the utilization-aware loss function, incorporate the visual insights from the knowledge-space embeddings and use them as auxiliary feedback to guide the model's training process. This can be achieved by assigning higher losses to points in the knowledge space where the internal-external knowledge trade-off is unfavorable.

PROPOSAL 3: Analyzing external knowledge utilization through adversarial adaptation
Introduce an adversarial model that attempts to mask or distort the retrieved context, and observe how the RAG model adapts and responds. This can provide insights into the model's reliance on external knowledge and help to detect situations where the model over-represents its internal knowledge.
Controls: A standard RAG model as a baseline, experimentation with different adversarial perturbation strategies.

Prediction: The adversarial adaptation approach will reveal instances where the model over-represents internal knowledge and should effectively detect situations prone to hallucinations, but might not generalize well to diverse domains and might require fine-tuning for each specific dataset.

PROPOSAL 4: External knowledge augmentation pipeline
Develop a pipeline that extracts specific knowledge snippets from the retrieved context and incorporates them into the model's internal knowledge during training. This can enhance the model's ability to utilize external knowledge and reduce its reliance on hallucinations.
Controls: A baseline RAG model without external knowledge augmentation, experimentation with different snippet-extraction techniques and knowledge-representation formats.
Estimated cost: 800-1200 GPU-hours (depending on the complexity of the snippet-extraction module).
Prediction: The external knowledge augmentation pipeline will improve the model's utilization of external knowledge, potentially leading to reduced hallucinations, but might introduce new challenges such as knowledge fragmentation, instability in the training process, and the need for careful balancing between internal and external knowledge.

Controls: The original visualizing internal-external knowledge trade-off through knowledge-space embeddings as a baseline, experimentation with different additional dimensions or channels.

Prediction: The improved knowledge-space embeddings will offer a more detailed and nuanced understanding of the internal-external knowledge trade-off, but might become increasingly complex and difficult to interpret as additional dimensions and channels are added.

PROPOSAL 6: Self-supervised knowledge inverse regularization
Regularize the model's internal knowledge by training it to invert or reverse the knowledge it has learned from the external context. This can be done through self-supervised learning objectives, such as inverting the model's outputs or reconstructing the context from the model's outputs. The regularization can help reduce the model's reliance on hallucinations and improve its utilization of external knowledge.

Prediction: The self-supervised knowledge inverse regularization will reduce the model's reliance on hallucinations, but might lead to knowledge degradation or loss of information, especially if the regularization is too strong or if the model is not able to invert the knowledge accurately.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Causal Alignment of Context and Knowledge Utilization
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel methodology for quantifying an LLM's utilization of external context and internal knowledge during generation using causal alignment techniques from the field of causality. Specifically, treat the external context as the cause and the generated response as the effect, and estimate the average causal effect of the context on the response using techniques such as transportability or backdoor adjustment.
CONTROLS: Include an ablation study to compare the performance of our methodology with ReDeEP and semantic entropy probes, as well as a baseline that assumes perfect external context utilization without utilizing any causal alignment techniques.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our methodology to outperform existing approaches in detecting hallucinations on real-world datasets, particularly in cases where the external context is diverse and complex. However, we might face challenges in estimating the average causal effect when the context and response have high-dimensional feature spaces.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Context-Aware Input Mixing
PROPOSAL: Introduce a simple yet effective method for Context-Aware Input Mixing (CAIM) by incorporating small perturbations of the retrieved external context into the input to the LLM, making it reliant on both internal knowledge and the updated external context. We hypothesize that when the model produces a hallucinated response, there will be a significant decrease in absolute performance with the mixed context compared to the original context.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of CAIM against the baseline input without mixing, as well as an ablation where the mixing is applied randomly without adaptation to the input context.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate CAIM to reduce hallucination rates by 20% on average across various real-world datasets, but may observe over-reliance on external context in certain test settings where it limits the model's ability to adapt to novel scenarios or overfitting noise in documents.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Context-Aware Input Mixing
REVISED PROPOSAL: Instead of applying the input mixing broadly, CAIM now focuses on injecting selected tokens from the external context into a set of "critical" tokens in the original input that we identify using a separate graph-based token attentiveness metric. This targeted approach helps to strengthen the model's reliance on the external context without compromising its ability to adapt and generalize to diverse test scenarios.
CONTROLS: In addition to the ablations of the original CAIM proposal, we introduce a control that compares the effectiveness of different token selection methods, such as graph centrality or PageRank, to identify critical tokens.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the revised approach to increase the average reduction in hallucination rates by 10-15% over the original CAIM implementation, but may face technical challenges in choosing the optimal number of injected tokens or adaptability to task-specific datasets.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Context-Aware Input Mixing
PROPOSAL: Instead of applying the input mixing broadly, CAIM now focuses on injecting selected tokens from the external context into a set of "critical" tokens in the original input that we identify using a separate graph-based token attentiveness metric. This targeted approach helps to strengthen the model's reliance on the external context without compromising its ability to adapt and generalize to diverse test scenarios.
CONTROLS: In addition to the ablations of the original CAIM proposal, we introduce a control that compares the effectiveness of different token selection methods, such as graph centrality or PageRank, to identify critical tokens.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the revised approach to increase the average reduction in hallucination rates by 10-15% over the original CAIM implementation, but may face technical challenges in choosing the optimal number of injected tokens or adaptability to task-specific datasets.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Multi-Task Contrastive Loss for External Context Utilization
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel multi-task contrastive loss function to encourage the model to utilize the external context more effectively. We divide the training process into two stages. In the first stage, the model predicts the answer based solely on its internal knowledge. In the second stage, the model is forced to rely on the external context by contrasting its predictions with those from the first stage using a temperature-scaled cosine similarity loss.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of our multi-task approach with a standard contrastive loss function and a baseline that assumes perfect external context utilization.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate a significant improvement in external context utilization, leading to a 25-30% reduction in hallucination rates, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance the two stages and avoid over-specializing the model to a specific set of tasks.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware External Context Weighting
PROPOSAL: Develop an uncertainty-aware external context weighting mechanism that assigns higher weights to retrievals that are less certain, encouraging the model to explore and use the external context more effectively when it's available. We estimate the uncertainty of each retrieval using a probabilistic selection process based on the retriever's output scores.
CONTROLS: Evaluate our uncertainty-aware weighting against a standard weighting approach that only considers the relevance of the retrievals and a baseline that ignores the external context altogether.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our uncertainty-aware weighting mechanism to lead to a 15-20% reduction in hallucination rates by encouraging the model to be more cautious when relying solely on its internal knowledge.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: External Context Augmentation using Counterfactual Sampling
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel counterfactual sampling approach to augment the external context with plausible alternative scenarios, allowing the model to better evaluate its decisions and mitigate the reliance on internal knowledge. We generate counterfactuals using a sub-network trained to invert the external context retriever.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of our counterfactual sampling against a standard augmentation technique and a baseline that does not consider counterfactuals.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that external context augmentation using counterfactual sampling will reduce hallucination rates by 18-22%, as it enables the model to better evaluate the consequences of its decisions and adapt to diverse scenarios.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Explaining External Context Utilization through Interventional Explanability
PROPOSAL: Develop an interventional explainability framework to analyze the causal relationships between the external context and the model's predictions. By injecting perturbations to the context, we can identify the most influential features and components driving the model's reliance on external knowledge.
CONTROLS: Compare the results of our interventional explainability against a standard feature importance analysis and a baseline that does not consider interventions.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our interventional explainability framework to provide valuable insights into the model's utilization of external context, allowing us to identify potential biases and shortcomings. This, in turn, should help reduce hallucination rates by 15-20% through more informed model design and optimization.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Ensemble Methods for Robust External Context Utilization
PROPOSAL: Investigate the potential of ensemble methods to combine the predictions of multiple models, each trained with a different approach to external context utilization (e.g., causal alignment, uncertainty-aware weighting, counterfactual sampling). We hypothesize that ensemble methods can boost the robustness and accuracy of external context utilization, leading to improved hallucination detection.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of our ensemble approach against individual models and a baseline that ignores the external context.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our ensemble methods to reduce hallucination rates by 22-28% by leveraging the strengths of multiple models and providing more robust predictions. However, we may face challenges in balancing model diversity and ensemble size to achieve optimal performance.

REVISED PROPOSAL: Integrate the insights and findings from the previous proposals (context-aware input mixing, multi-task contrastive loss, uncertainty-aware weighting, counterfactual sampling, interventional explainability, and ensemble methods) to enhance the causal alignment of context and knowledge utilization. Specifically, we incorporate uncertainty-aware weighting and counterfactual sampling into the causal alignment framework to make it more robust and effective.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised causal alignment approach against the original approach and a baseline that ignores the external context.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the revised causal alignment approach to reduce hallucination rates by 25-35% due to its unique combination of insights and techniques. However, we may face challenges in optimizing the revised approach to balance the trade-offs between various components and achieve peak performance.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Joint Encoder-Decoder Principal Component Analysis for Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Design a novel encoder-decoder framework for time-series forecasting that combines the principle component analysis (PCA) with channel-dependent and channel-independent encoding methods. The proposed method applies PCA to the encoded representations to distill the most informative features for each variate, and then uses a channel-dependent or channel-independent decoder to generate predictions.
CONTROLS: Compare to a channel-independent encoder-decoder and a channel-dependent encoder-decoder, as well as a simple linear projection decoder.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed method is expected to achieve better performance than the channel-independent decoder, and comparable performance to the channel-dependent decoder, while reducing computational cost. However, it may fail to capture complex cross-channel interactions.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE:  Joint Encoder-Decoder Principal Component Analysis for Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: REVISED PROPOSAL: Integrate the proposed PCA-based framework with the masking-and-reconstruction pretraining strategy, and investigate its impact on the performance. Specifically, during pretraining, mask a subset of temporal segments in the encoded representations of the input, and train the PCA-based encoder-decoder to reconstruct the masked portions.
CONTROLS: Compare to the original PCA-based framework without pretraining, and the masking-and-reconstruction pretraining strategy with a simple linear projection decoder.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The integrated framework is expected to achieve better performance than the original PCA-based framework, but may suffer from overfitting due to the additional pretraining stage.

New Proposal:
TITLE: Graph Attention-based Cross-Channel Interaction Model
PROPOSAL: Design a graph attention-based model to effectively capture and model cross-channel interactions in multivariate time-series forecasting. The model consists of a graph attention layer that learns to weight the importance of each variate for each target variate, and a channel-dependent encoder to generate encoded representations for each variate.
CONTROLS: Compare to a simple linear model that incorporates the pairwise correlations between variates.
COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed model is expected to achieve better performance than the simple linear model, and comparable performance to the channel-dependent encoder-decoder, while capturing more nuanced cross-channel interactions.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Joint Encoder-Decoder Principal Component Analysis for Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: REVISED PROPOSAL: Integrate the proposed PCA-based framework withrious domain knowledge, such as weather station readings for weather forecasting, or load profiles for electricity consumption forecasting. Specifically, incorporate domain-specific features into the PCA-based encoder-decoder, and investigate its impact on the performance.
CONTROLS: Compare to the PCA-based framework without domain knowledge, and the channel-dependent encoder-decoder without domain knowledge.
COST: 900 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The integrated framework is expected to achieve better performance than the PCA-based framework without domain knowledge, but may require careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance the contribution of domain knowledge.

New Proposal:
TITLE: Localized Temporal Attention for Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Design a localized temporal attention mechanism that selectively focuses on relevant parts of the input sequence for each target variate. The mechanism uses a convolutional layer to extract local features, and a temporal attention layer to weigh the importance of these features based on their temporal proximity to the target variate.
