ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Cross-Channel Dependencies with Channel-Independent Encoders
PROPOSAL: We will design a set of new experiments that modify standard channel-independent encoders with additional components that capture potential cross-channel dependencies, while retaining their simplicity and robustness. Specifically, we will add a secondary encoder to model residual interactions between time-series channels and then combine encoder outputs in a novel way to form a unified representation. We will evaluate this approach on a set of multivariate time-series benchmarks, including temperature, precipitation, and wind speed data for weather forecasting and power consumption and solar irradiance data for electricity consumption forecasting.
CONTROLS: We will compare the modified channel-independent encoder to standard channel-independent and channel-dependent encoders on baselines, including sine functions and tecnical guideline compliant sines, natural gas consumption data and simple  linear time series models using holt’s winters + causal parameters.
COST: 1000
PREDICTION: We predict that our modified channel-independent encoders will improve the hard task practically, however at least for soft tasks previously that used so little minimised information outloud enforce initially knew channel-interference will fail near peak noise.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theory: Optimal Channel-Dependent Encoder Architecture for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We will present a theoretical analysis of the optimal channel-dependent encoder architecture for multivariate time-series forecasting. Specifically, we will derive the optimal structure of the channel-dependent encoder using a maximum likelihood framework, and show that it consists of multiple layers with different numbers of channels, each equipped with a separate bottleneck layer. We will also analyze the statistical properties of the optimal encoder, such as its convergence rate and broadcast robustness.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our theoretically optimal channel-dependent encoder to a baseline of standard channel-dependent encoder using synthetic data.
COST: 500
PREDICTION: We expect that our theoretically optimal channel-dependent encoder will outperform the baseline in terms of forecasting accuracy, especially for larger channel numbers.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Early Fusion Schemes on Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the impact of early fusion schemes on multivariate time-series forecasting. Specifically, we will compare the performance of an encoder-decoder architecture with an early fusion scheme, where the encoded representations from multiple channels are fused at the encoder level, to a baseline of standard encoder-decoder architecture without early fusion. We will also experiment with different early fusion schemes, such as concatenation, element-wise multiplication, and resizing of encoded representations.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our early fusion schemes to a baseline of standard encoder-decoder architecture, as well as to our previously proposed hierarchical attention and temporal dependency modeling decoding mechanism.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect that early fusion schemes will improve the forecasting performance of multivariate time-series models, especially for larger numbers of channels, by allowing the model to capture complex interactions between channels from an early stage.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Revisiting Channel-Independent Encoders with Inter-Channel Attention for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We investigate the design of channel-independent encoders with inter-channel attention mechanisms to capture cross-channel dependencies while maintaining simple architecture. Specifically, we propose a novel inter-channel attention mechanism that learns to weigh the importance of different channels for each time step. We evaluate our approach on real-world datasets from various domains, including weather forecasting, electricity consumption forecasting, traffic flow forecasting, and solar power generation forecasting.
CONTROLS: Our baseline consists of a standard transformer encoder without inter-channel attention, as well as a recent state-of-the-art channel-dependent encoder that requires significant computational resources. We also conduct an ablation study to examine the impact of different attention architectures.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed inter-channel attention mechanism to improve forecasting accuracy by 5-10% compared to the baseline transformer encoder, and to be more computationally efficient than the state-of-the-art channel-dependent encoder. However, we acknowledge the potential risk of overfitting due to the introduction of additional parameters and attention mechanisms.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Non-Linear Channel Fusion for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: To address the limitations of linear projections for decoding predicted signals from encoded representations, we propose an efficient non-linear channel fusion layer that combines outputs from multiple channels using a gating mechanism and a non-linear activation function. The layer is designed to be highly parallelizable and suitable for high-dimensional inputs. We evaluate our approach on a range of real-world multivariate time-series datasets and compare its performance to state-of-the-art linear projection methods.
CONTROLS: We use the baseline setup from our previous experiment (channel-independent encoder with inter-channel attention) and compare our non-linear channel fusion layer to a simple linear projection and a recent state-of-the-art architecture that relies on complex non-linear modeling.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the non-linear channel fusion layer to significantly improve decoding accuracy, particularly in scenarios with complex temporal dynamics and large inter-channel dependencies. However, we also acknowledge the potential risk of overfitting and will investigate methods to regularize the model.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Revisiting Channel-Independent Encoders with Inter-Channel Attention for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We further extend the channel-independent encoder with inter-channel attention mechanism by incorporating a multi-resolution encoding approach. This allows our model to capture temporal dependencies at different scales, which is essential for accurate time-series forecasting. We utilize a wavelet transform to decompose the input signals into multiple resolution levels and apply the inter-channel attention mechanism to each level separately.
CONTROLS: We add a new baseline that uses a standard convolutional neural network (CNN) with multi-resolution encoding, as well as an ablation study to examine the impact of different wavelet transforms and attention mechanisms on the performance of our proposed approach.
COST: 500 (additional) + 1000 (originally) = 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With the incorporation of multi-resolution encoding, we expect a significant improvement in forecasting accuracy, particularly in scenarios with complex temporal dynamics and non-linear patterns. However, we also anticipate increased computational costs due to the additional wavelet transforms, which might be mitigated with efficient implementation and parallelization techniques.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Pretraining Time-Series Forecasting Models with Temporary-Adversarial-Domain-Agnostic (TADA) Tasks
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel pretraining framework for time-series forecasting models, called temporary-adversarial-domain-agnostic (TADA) tasks. Our approach involves masking a subset of channels in the input data and training the model to predict the missing channels. We then corrupt the input data with a variant of adversarial attacks, which helps the model learn robust representations of the data. We will evaluate our method on various real-world time-series forecasting datasets and compare it to existing pretraining strategies.
CONTROLS: We compare our TADA pretraining method to a baseline with synthetic data masking (similar to BERT's masking-and-reconstruction tasks) and a state-of-the-art architecture with domain adaptation pretraining.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging TADA pretraining, we expect our models to exhibit improved robustness to adversarial attacks and domain variance, which will result in better generalization performance on unseen test datasets. However, we also anticipate increased computational costs due to the additional preprocessing steps and model training iterations.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Pretraining Time-Series Forecasting Models with Temporary-Adversarial-Domain-Agnostic (TADA) Tasks
PROPOSAL: We refine our TADA pretraining framework to incorporate a novel adversarial training mechanism that adaptively adjusts the perturbation strength based on the model's confidence in its predictions. This ensures that the model is robust to a wide range of adversarial attacks and can generalize well to new, unseen scenarios. We introduce a confidence-aware weak label (CA-WL) for model training, which is derived from the model's prediction probabilities. By optimizing CA-WL, the model becomes more resistant to adversarial attacks and can adapt to evolving data distributions.
CONTROLS: We compare our refined TADA pretraining approach to the original TADA method, as well as a state-of-the-art robust training technique for time-series forecasting models. We also investigate the effect of different perturbation schedules and TADA hyperparameters on the performance of our approach.
COST: 1200 (additional) + 2000 (originally) = 3200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With the CA-WL mechanism, we anticipate that our TADA pretraining approach will lead to significant improvements in model robustness and generalization performance. However, we also recognize the potential risk of mode collapse during adversarial training and will investigate techniques to address this issue.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Joint Optimization of Encoder-Decoder Architectures for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a new joint optimization approach that simultaneously trains the encoder and decoder components of a multivariate time-series forecasting model. Our approach uses a hybrid loss function that combines the reconstruction loss and a novel attention-aware cross-correlation loss, which encourages the encoder to produce informative and disentangled representations and the decoder to correctly predict the future values of the time series. We evaluate our approach on various real-world time-series forecasting datasets and compare its performance to state-of-the-art architectures with separate encoder and decoder training.
CONTROLS: We compare our joint optimization approach to a baseline with separate encoder and decoder training, as well as a recent state-of-the-art architecture that uses an additional reconstruction loss for encoder training.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By jointly optimizing the encoder and decoder components, we expect our approach to lead to more accurate time-series forecasting and improved model interpretability. However, we also anticipate increased computational costs and may need to adjust the approach to account for the added complexity of joint optimization.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Efficient Non-Linear Channel Fusion for Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We refine our non-linear channel fusion layer to accommodate dynamic channel importance weights and adaptive fusion mechanisms. This allows the model to adaptively adjust the contribution of each channel to the final prediction, which can be particularly useful when the importance of channels varies over time. We introduce a novel multi-task learning framework that simultaneously trains the channel fusion layer and a task-specific attention mechanism, which helps to focus on the most relevant channels.
CONTROLS: We compare our refined non-linear channel fusion layer to the original approach, as well as a baseline with fixed channel importance weights and a state-of-the-art architecture that uses complex graph-based channel fusion.
COST: 800 (additional) + 800 (originally) = 1600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With the refined non-linear channel fusion layer, we anticipate that our approach will lead to significant improvements in forecasting accuracy, particularly in scenarios where channel importance varies over time. However, we also recognize the potential risk of overfitting due to the introduction of additional parameters and will investigate regularization techniques to mitigate this issue.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Time-Series Forecasting with Multi-Task Learning and Mutual Regularization
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel multi-task learning framework for time-series forecasting that leverages mutual regularization between multiple related tasks. Our approach involves training a shared encoder to produce task-agnostic representations and domain-specific decoders for each individual task, while sharing and regularizing the task-invariant information across tasks. We evaluate our approach on various real-world time-series forecasting datasets and compare its performance to state-of-the-art architectures with separate encoder and decoder training.
CONTROLS: We compare our multi-task learning approach to a baseline with separate encoder and decoder training, as well as a recent state-of-the-art architecture that uses an additional reconstruction loss for encoder training.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By utilizing mutual regularization and shared encoders, we expect our approach to lead to improved forecasting accuracy and reduced overfitting across multiple related tasks. However, we also anticipate that the added complexity of multi-task learning may lead to increased computational costs and challenges in hyperparameter tuning.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Pretraining Time-Series Forecasting Models with Temporary-Adversarial-Domain-Agnostic (TADA) Tasks
PROPOSAL: We generalize our TADA pretraining approach to accommodate a wide range of time-series domains and tasks. Specifically, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework that allows the model to adapt to new, unseen domains and tasks during training. This is achieved through a hierarchical meta-learning objective that encourages the model to learn a task-agnostic representation, as well as task-specific probabilistic beliefs and adaptations. We evaluate our approach on a diverse set of real-world time-series forecasting datasets and compare its performance to state-of-the-art architectures.
CONTROLS: We compare our meta-learning approach to the original TADA method, as well as a baseline with separate domain and task training, and a recent state-of-the-art architecture that uses domain adaptation pretraining.
COST: 1200 (additional) + 3200 (originally) = 4400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With the meta-learning extension, we anticipate that our TADA pretraining approach will lead to significant improvements in model adaptability, robustness, and generalization performance across diverse time-series domains and tasks. However, we also recognize the potential risk of increased computational costs and challenges in hyperparameter tuning due to the added complexity of meta-learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness and Generalization of Time-Series Forecasting Models through Adversarial Testing and Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: We design a comprehensive evaluation framework to assess the robustness and generalization of time-series forecasting models. Our approach involves adversarial testing to evaluate model vulnerability to attacks, as well as knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge from_LARGE_ models to smaller ones. We will evaluate our framework on the proposed models and compare their performance to state-of-the-art architectures.
CONTROLS: We compare our evaluation framework to a baseline with conventional testing and evaluation metrics, as well as a recent state-of-the-art architecture that uses additional robustness-enhancing techniques.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By adopting our evaluation framework, we anticipate that we will be able to better understand the limitations of existing time-series forecasting models and identify opportunities for improvement in terms of robustness and generalization.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information-Theoretic Characterization of Contrastive Learning Views
PROPOSAL: We will derive a lower bound on the mutual information between a labeled instance and its augmented views, framed as a combination of the conditional entropy of the views given the instance and the joint entropy of the instance and the views. We then develop an experiment to estimate these quantities for real-world datasets, specifically the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet classification benchmarks, using the mutual information neural estimator (MINE).
CONTROLS: We will compare to the baseline lower bound on mutual information achieved by assuming the views are conditionally independent given the instance. Additionally, we will ablate the model by changing the number of augmented views and the dimensionality of the augmentations.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a non-trivial lower bound on mutual information to be achieved, indicating that the views contribute information, and that the bound will improve with more augmentations but decrease with dimensionality. However, the lower bound might fail to capture the full richness of the dynamic information landscape.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Augmentation via Instance-Specific Mutual Information
PROPOSAL: We will develop an adaptive augmentation scheme for contrastive learning, where the choice of augmentation is guided by the estimated mutual information between the instance and its augmented views, obtained from the experiment in proposal 1. We propose to increase the frequency of augmentations that yield higher mutual information, while decreasing those with lower mutual information. This will be evaluated on real-world datasets CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, using a set of pre-defined augmentations and a reinforcement learning-based algorithm to select the most informative ones.
CONTROLS: As controls, we will compare to the static augmentation scheme used in SimCLR, and ablate the reinforcement learning-based algorithm to understand its contribution. Additionally, we will compare to a random augmentation scheme to demonstrate the effectiveness of our adaptive approach.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our adaptive augmentation scheme to outperform the static scheme, particularly in regions of the data distribution where the views are informative but not well-captured by the static augmentations. However, the algorithm might get stuck in local optima and fail to explore the full augmentation space.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: (No change)
PROPOSAL: We will refine the experiment in proposal 2 to better understand the interplay between augmentation frequency and informativeness. In addition to the adaptive augmentation scheme, we will run experiments with a fixed frequency of augmentations, but vary the frequency to span a range from very low to very high. This will allow us to estimate the optimal frequency of augmentations and understand how it depends on the instance-specific mutual information.
CONTROLS: The controls remain the same, but we will add an ablation to compare the fixed-frequency scheme with a very low frequency to demonstrate its suboptimality.
COST: 75 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect a non-monotonic relationship between augmentation frequency and informativeness, with a region of optimal frequency where further increases in frequency lead to diminishing returns in informativeness. However, the analysis might be challenging if the frequency sensitivity is high and the objective function is non-convex.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Bounds on View Distribution for Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We will provide a theoretical analysis of the optimal view distribution for contrastive learning, specifically showing that the optimal distribution is a mixture of delta-functions centered at the original instance and its augmentations. We will derive bounds on the mutual information between the instance and the views as a function of the view distribution, and provide a companion experiment to test these predictions on synthetic data generated from a mixture of Gaussian distributions.
CONTROLS: We will show that our bounds are tight asymptotically, and ablate the experiment by changing the number of components in the mixture distribution.
COST: 5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our bounds to hold asymptotically, but the experiment might fail to capture the complex nuances of real-world data, leading to deviations from the theoretical predictions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalability of Contrastive Learning with Noisy Views
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the effect of incorporating noisy views into contrastive learning, where the views are generated by adding noise to the original instance, and evaluate its impact on the representation learning and classification accuracy. We will explore different types of noise, including iid Gaussian noise and structured noise that correlates with the instance features. This will be done using a combination of real-world datasets and synthetic data generated with varying noise levels.
CONTROLS: We will compare to the baseline contrastive learning method without noisy views, and ablate the effect of different noise types and levels.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved robustness and generalizability of the learned representations when incorporating noisy views, particularly for structured noise that captures meaningful patterns in the data. However, the noise might also lead to over-smoothing or degradation of the learned representations if the noise is too strong or iiid.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Instance Learning with Contrastive View Mixing
PROPOSAL: We will explore a Multi-Instance Learning (MIL) framework for contrastive learning, where a bag of instances is modeled as a single hyper-instance, and the contrastive objective is applied to the pairwise distances between the instances within each bag, as well as between the instances in different bags. We will develop a view-mixing strategy to increase the diversity of instances within each bag, and evaluate its impact on learning generalizable and robust representations.
CONTROLS: We will compare to baseline MIL methods without view mixing, as well as to contrastive learning methods that do not use the MIL framework.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed MIL framework with view mixing to outperform the baselines in terms of robustness and generalizability, but the effectiveness might depend heavily on the quality and diversity of the instance collections in the dataset.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: (No change)
PROPOSAL: We will refine the experiment in proposal 4, "Scalability of Contrastive Learning with Noisy Views", to focus on the theoretical aspect of understanding how different types of noise impact the alignment of instance-level representations in the contrastive learning process. We will derive a bound on the minimum achievable alignment error between representations of instances with and without noise, and analyze the implications for the hardness of learning with noisy views.
CONTROLS: The controls remain the same, but we will add an ablation to compare the baseline without noise to the case with iid Gaussian noise, which has a known analytical solution.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our bound to provide new insights into the sensitivity of contrastive learning to noisy views, and to show that structured noise can lead to economically attainable lower bounds on the learning speed with noisy views. However, the proof might require simplifying assumptions about the noise distribution or the feature space embedding.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Batch-Level Contrastive Learning with Illustrative Examples
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the implications of batch-level contrastive learning on the representation learning, focusing on two types of influential instances: anchors and outliers. We will define illustrative examples that demonstrate how the anchors can capture the representative features, while the outliers can infer the noise-related features. Additionally, we will analyze the transition from individual-level to batch-level representations and discuss the retained information and elimination of redundancy.
CONTROLS: We will compare to the baseline with individual-level contrastive learning, and evaluate the effects of different batch sizes and number of iterations.
COST: 25 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the batch-level contrastive learning to outperform the baseline in retaining relevant features and eliminating redundancy, particularly for larger batch sizes. However, it might require configurations that depend on the scale of the dataset and computational resources.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Practical Necessity of Uniformity in Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the practical necessity of incorporating a uniformity regularizer in contrastive learning methods, which aims to enforce a uniform distribution over the positives for each instance. We will explore the effect of the uniformity regularizer on the representation learning, using both theoretical bounds and practical evaluations on real-world datasets.

PROPOSAL 1: Information-Theoretic Characterization of Contrastive Learning Views
We will derive a lower bound on the mutual information between a labeled instance and its augmented views, framed as a combination of the conditional entropy of the views given the instance and the joint entropy of the instance and the views. We then develop an experiment to estimate these quantities for real-world datasets, specifically the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet classification benchmarks, using the mutual information neural estimator (MINE).
Controls: We will compare to the baseline lower bound on mutual information achieved by assuming the views are conditionally independent given the instance. Additionally, we will ablate the model by changing the number of augmented views and the dimensionality of the augmentations.
Estimated cost: 10 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect a non-trivial lower bound on mutual information to be achieved, indicating that the views contribute information, and that the bound will improve with more augmentations but decrease with dimensionality. However, the lower bound might fail to capture the full richness of the dynamic information landscape.

PROPOSAL 2: Adaptive Augmentation via Instance-Specific Mutual Information
We will develop an adaptive augmentation scheme for contrastive learning, where the choice of augmentation is guided by the estimated mutual information between the instance and its augmented views, obtained from the experiment in proposal 1. We propose to increase the frequency of augmentations that yield higher mutual information, while decreasing those with lower mutual information. This will be evaluated on real-world datasets CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, using a set of pre-defined augmentations and a reinforcement learning-based algorithm to select the most informative ones.
Controls: As controls, we will compare to the static augmentation scheme used in SimCLR, and ablate the reinforcement learning-based algorithm to understand its contribution. Additionally, we will compare to a random augmentation scheme to demonstrate the effectiveness of our adaptive approach.
Estimated cost: 50 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect our adaptive augmentation scheme to outperform the static scheme, particularly in regions of the data distribution where the views are informative but not well-captured by the static augmentations. However, the algorithm might get stuck in local optima and fail to explore the full augmentation space.

PROPOSAL 3: Theoretical Bounds on View Distribution for Contrastive Learning
We will provide a theoretical analysis of the optimal view distribution for contrastive learning, specifically showing that the optimal distribution is a mixture of delta-functions centered at the original instance and its augmentations. We will derive bounds on the mutual information between the instance and the views as a function of the view distribution, and provide a companion experiment to test these predictions on synthetic data generated from a mixture of Gaussian distributions.
Controls: We will show that our bounds are tight asymptotically, and ablate the experiment by changing the number of components in the mixture distribution.
Estimated cost: 5 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect our bounds to hold asymptotically, but the experiment might fail to capture the complex nuances of real-world data, leading to deviations from the theoretical predictions.

PROPOSAL 4: Scalability of Contrastive Learning with Noisy Views
We will investigate the effect of incorporating noisy views into contrastive learning, where the views are generated by adding noise to the original instance, and evaluate its impact on the representation learning and classification accuracy. We will explore different types of noise, including iid Gaussian noise and structured noise that correlates with the instance features. This will be done using a combination of real-world datasets and synthetic data generated with varying noise levels.
Controls: We will compare to the baseline contrastive learning method without noisy views, and ablate the effect of different noise types and levels.
Estimated cost: 30 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect to see improved robustness and generalizability of the learned representations when incorporating noisy views, particularly for structured noise that captures meaningful patterns in the data. However, the noise might also lead to over-smoothing or degradation of the learned representations if the noise is too strong or iiid.

PROPOSAL 5: Multi-Instance Learning with Contrastive View Mixing
We will explore a Multi-Instance Learning (MIL) framework for contrastive learning, where a bag of instances is modeled as a single hyper-instance, and the contrastive objective is applied to the pairwise distances between the instances within each bag, as well as between the instances in different bags. We will develop a view-mixing strategy to increase the diversity of instances within each bag, and evaluate its impact on learning generalizable and robust representations.
Controls: We will compare to baseline MIL methods without view mixing, as well as to contrastive learning methods that do not use the MIL framework.
Estimated cost: 40 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect the proposed MIL framework with view mixing to outperform the baselines in terms of robustness and generalizability, but the effectiveness might depend heavily on the quality and diversity of the instance collections in the dataset.

PROPOSAL 6: Batch-Level Contrastive Learning with Illustrative Examples
We will investigate the implications of batch-level contrastive learning on the representation learning, focusing on two types of influential instances: anchors and outliers. We will define illustrative examples that demonstrate how the anchors can capture the representative features, while the outliers can infer the noise-related features. Additionally, we will analyze the transition from individual-level to batch-level representations and discuss the retained information and elimination of redundancy.
Controls: We will compare to the baseline with individual-level contrastive learning, and evaluate the effects of different batch sizes and number of iterations.
Estimated cost: 25 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect the batch-level contrastive learning to outperform the baseline in retaining relevant features and eliminating redundancy, particularly for larger batch sizes. However, it might require configurations that depend on the scale of the dataset and computational resources.

We will investigate the practical necessity of incorporating a uniformity regularizer in contrastive learning methods, which aims to enforce a uniform distribution over the positives for each instance. We will explore the effect of the uniformity regularizer on the representation learning, using both theoretical bounds and practical evaluations on real-world datasets.
Controls: We will compare to the baseline without uniformity regularizer, and ablate the strength and type of regularizer used.
Estimated cost: 20 GPU-hours
Prediction: We expect the uniformity regularizer to be essential for the convergence and quality of the learned representations, especially in the presence of noisy or highly imbalanced data. However, it might over-regularize the positive logits and lead to decreased precision.

PROPOSAL: We will extend the recently introduced Information-Theoretic Lower-Bound Optimizer (IT-LO) for self-supervised contrastive learning to the adaptive augmentation setting, where the model learns to compute its own augmentations. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information-Grounded Contrastive Learning with Adaptive Augmentations
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive contrastive learning approach where the augmentations are learned dynamically based on the semantic representation of each instance. We utilize a variational autoencoder (VAE) to infer the latent representation of the instance and generate adaptive augmentations that maximize the mutual information between the original and augmented views. This approach allows for effective expansion of the representational capacity of each instance while maintaining semantic coherence.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach against MoCo and SimCLR, two popular contrastive learning frameworks.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to outperform MoCo and SimCLR on various benchmark datasets, especially in small-batch settings. However, the effectiveness of adaptive augmentations might rely heavily on the quality of the VAE's latent representation, which could be a limitation for complex instances.

The approach builds upon the understanding that contrastive learning should be guided by a principled mechanism that takes into account the semantic representation of each instance. The information-theoretic objective functions that are traditionally used do not make explicit use of instance-specific semantic information. This proposal plans to explicitly characterise this representation, and make better augmentations, so these are no more and no less informative than they need to be to confirm the semantic relationship between the views.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information-Theoretic Analysis of Adaptive Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We provide a theoretical analysis of the adaptive contrastive learning approach proposed in experiment 1, characterizing the information gain through adaptive augmentations in terms of mutual information. We derive upper bounds on the mutual information between the original and augmented views, as well as lower bounds on the mutual information between the augmentations and the latent representation of the instance. This analysis provides insights into the dynamic information landscape that unfolds during the learning process.
CONTROLS: We will consider the static augmentations used in MoCo and SimCLR as a baseline for comparison.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our theoretical analysis will reveal that adaptive augmentations do not necessarily lead to a higher mutual information than static augmentations, and that the quality of the VAE's latent representation plays a crucial role in determining the information gain. This could provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of adaptive contrastive learning.

The theoretical analysis aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of the adaptive contrastive learning approach, which can be crucial for designing more effective augmentation strategies. It will help to clarify whether adaptive augmentations are truly beneficial, and under what conditions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Spectral Clustering Analysis of Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We analyze the tendency of contrastive learning to induce clustering in the latent space, based on spectral clustering theory. We derive conditions under which contrastive learning leads to coherent clusters and analyze how adaptive augmentations affect the clustering structure. This analysis provides insights into the semantic consistency of contrastive learning.
CONTROLS: We will compare our findings against the clustering structure obtained through traditional clustering algorithms such as k-means.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our spectral clustering analysis will reveal that contrastive learning tends to induce coherent clusters, especially when adaptive augmentations are used. However, we expect that the quality of the clustering can be sensitive to the hyperparameters of the contrastive learning framework.

The spectral clustering analysis aims to shed light on the mechanisms behind the success of contrastive learning in discovering semantic classes. By understanding how contrastive learning induces clustering, we can better design and interpret contrastive learning frameworks. This analysis can also provide insights into the role of adaptive augmentations in promoting coherent clusters.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: REVISED: Spectral Clustering Analysis of Contrastive Learning with Adaptive Augmentations
PROPOSAL: We revisit the spectral clustering analysis of contrastive learning, focusing specifically on the impact of adaptive augmentations on the clustering structure. We derive conditions under which adaptive augmentations lead to more coherent clusters and analyze how the mutual information between the original and augmented views affects the clustering quality. This refined analysis provides deeper insights into the role of adaptive augmentations in promoting semantic consistency.
CONTROLS: We will compare our findings against the clustering structure obtained through traditional clustering algorithms such as k-means, as well as against the results from experiment 1 where adaptive augmentations are used.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (reduced from 30)
PREDICTION: Our refined analysis will reveal that adaptive augmentations indeed lead to more coherent clusters, especially when the mutual information between the original and augmented views is high. However, we expect that the quality of the clustering can still be sensitive to the hyperparameters of the contrastive learning framework.

By revising the spectral clustering analysis to focus on adaptive augmentations, we can better understand how these augmentations contribute to the semantic consistency of contrastive learning. This revised analysis can also provide valuable insights into the design of effective adaptive augmentation strategies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Effect of Adaptive Augmentation Quality
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the impact of the quality of adaptive augmentations on the performance of information-grounded contrastive learning. We use a suite of permutation-based metrics to measure the quality of the augmentations, ranging from simple random permutations to more sophisticated ones that capture nuanced image transformations. We then train the adaptive contrastive learning framework with augmentations of varying quality and measure its performance on downstream tasks.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results against the performance of MoCo and SimCLR on the same downstream tasks, as well as against the results from experiment 1 where adaptive augmentations are used.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results will reveal a strong correlation between the quality of adaptive augmentations and the performance of the adaptive contrastive learning framework. However, we expect that the framework's performance will also be sensitive to other factors, such as the balance between alignment and uniformity in the contrastive loss.

The evaluation of adaptive augmentation quality is crucial for understanding the mechanisms behind the success of adaptive contrastive learning. By measuring the impact of augmentation quality on downstream task performance, we can gain insights into the design of effective adaptive augmentation strategies and the hyperparameter tuning of the adaptive contrastive learning framework.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Augmentation Editing for Semantic Coherence
PROPOSAL: We develop an adaptive augmentation editing approach that leverages the insights from experiment 2 and 4 to refine the augmentations generated in experiment 1. We use a grammar-based editing framework to iteratively refine the augmentations, ensuring that they remain semantically coherent while promoting diversity. We evaluate the performance of the edited augmentations on downstream tasks and compare it against the original and edited augmentations.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results against the performance of MoCo and SimCLR on the same downstream tasks.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results will reveal significant improvements in downstream task performance when using the edited augmentations, especially in cases where the original augmentations were semantically ambiguous. However, we expect that the editing process may incur additional computational costs and potentially introduce new trade-offs in terms of augmentation quality and diversity.

The adaptive augmentation editing approach aims to address the tension between augmentation quality and diversity, promoting semantic coherence while also encouraging exploration of diverse transformation spaces. By leveraging insights from information-theoretic analysis and augmentation quality evaluation, we can develop more effective and efficient editing frameworks for refining adaptive augmentations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Benchmarking of Adaptive Contrastive Learning
PROPOSAL: We evaluate the adaptability and robustness of adaptive contrastive learning on real-world benchmark datasets, including ImageNet and CIFAR-100, in comparison to traditional contrastive learning methods. We assess the framework's performance on various tasks, including classification, detection, and segmentation, and evaluate its ability to generalize to new environments and unseen data distributions.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results against state-of-the-art baselines, including MoCo and SimCLR.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results will demonstrate that adaptive contrastive learning can achieve competitive or even superior performance on real-world benchmark datasets, especially in cases where the data distribution is complex and diverse. However, we expect that the adaptability of the framework may also introduce new challenges in terms of overfitting and optimization.

By evaluating the adaptability and robustness of adaptive contrastive learning on real-world benchmark datasets, we can better understand its potential applications and limitations in real-world scenarios. This experiment will also provide insights into the trade-offs between adaptability and optimization in the context of adaptive contrastive learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analysis of Adaptation Speed and Efficiency
PROPOSAL: We conduct an in-depth analysis of the adaptation speed and efficiency of adaptive contrastive learning, including the convergence rate of the optimization process, the usage of computational resources, and the memory requirements. We also investigate the impact of batch size, learning rate, and gradient accumulation on the adaptation speed and efficiency. Our goal is to identify key factors that affect adaptation speed and provide practical guidelines for fine-tuning the framework.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results against traditional contrastive learning methods.
COST: 15 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our results will reveal that adaptive contrastive learning is computationally efficient and capable of adapting to new environments at a faster rate than traditional contrastive learning methods. However, we expect that the adaptation speed may be sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters, particularly the batch size and learning rate.

The analysis of adaptation speed and efficiency is crucial for practical applications, as it can significantly impact the deployment and maintenance of adaptive contrastive learning in real-world scenarios. By identifying key factors that affect adaptation speed, we can provide practical guidelines for fine-tuning the framework and optimize its performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: REVISED: Information-Grounded Contrastive Learning with Adaptive Augmentations and Editing
PROPOSAL: We refine the information-grounded contrastive learning algorithm to incorporate the adaptive augmentation editing approach, allowing the framework to adaptively generate, refine, and fine-tune the augmentations during training. We evaluate the effectiveness of this revised algorithm on real-world benchmark datasets and compare its performance against state-of-the-art baselines, including MoCo and SimCLR.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results against the performance of the original adaptive contrastive learning framework, as well as the state-of-the-art baselines.
COST: 60 GPU-hours (increased from 100 due to the integration of augmentation editing)
PREDICTION: Our results will demonstrate that the revised adaptive contrastive learning framework is capable of achieving state-of-the-art performance on real-world benchmark datasets, with improved adaptation speed and robustness to new environments and unseen data distributions. However, we expect that the effectiveness of the framework may depend on the quality of the augmentation editing process, which can be challenging to optimize.

By integrating the adaptive augmentation editing approach into the information-grounded contrastive learning algorithm, we aim to create a highly adaptable and robust framework that can handle complex and diverse data distributions in real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Implications and Future Directions for Contrastive Learning Research
PROPOSAL: We synthesize the findings from the previous experiments and discussions, highlighting the key contributions, limitations, and implications of adaptive contrastive learning. We identify open research questions and future directions for advancing the framework, including the investigation of new architectural choices, regularization techniques, and theoretical models. We also provide concrete recommendations for future work and potential collaborations.
CONTROLS: None
COST: 0 GPU-hours (theoretical and discussion-based proposal)
PREDICTION: Our synthesis and discussion of the results will underscore the significant advancements made in adaptive contrastive learning and provide guidance for future research directions. By highlighting key open questions and opportunities, we can foster a community-driven approach to pushing the state-of-the-art in this area.

The proposal provides a conclusion to the experimental and theoretical exploration of adaptive contrastive learning, distilling the key insights gained from the previous experiments and discussions. By outlining future research directions and open questions, we aim to promote further advancements in this area and accelerate the development of more adaptive and robust contrastive learning frameworks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Using Consistent Baselines for Episodic Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We conduct a systematic re-implementation and comparison of several recent episodic TTA methods on the commonly used CLIP base and large models, evaluating them on a wide range of natural-language descriptions and evaluation metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score.
CONTROLS: We will reproduce the publicly available baselines (CLIP v0.9 and a Random baseline) as well as ablate our results to remove any uncertainty about the accuracy of our re-implementation.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (10 datasets from the COCO benchmark with 2 noise-injections, 1/2 for fine-tuning and 1/2 for test-time adaptation).
PREDICTION: Our systematic comparison will highlight inconsistencies in reported results, and some TTA methods will achieve significant gains when properly implemented. However, we predict some TTA methods will show poor transferability to different pre-trained models and evaluation metrics.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Extending Evaluation to Training-Time Fine-Tuned Models
PROPOSAL: We extend our previous work (proposal 1) by fine-tuning CLIP models on the downstream task before applying episodic TTA, and testing whether existing methods generalize to already adaptation-attuned models.
CONTROLS: We will use the same baselines as in proposal 1 and ablate our results to evaluate the impact of fine-tuning on TTA effectiveness.
COST: 40 GPU-hours (10 datasets from the COCO benchmark with 2 noise-injections, and 5 additional fine-tuning tasks).
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant performance drop when applying existing TTA methods on already adaptation-attuned models, especially for high adaptation accuracy thresholds. This would indicate that fine-tuning often reduces the impact of test-time adaptation, and new methods optimized for fine-tuned models are required.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Moving Beyond CLIP: Evaluating TTA on Alternative VLM Architectures
PROPOSAL: We adapt our evaluation setup (proposal 1) to evaluate the performance of episodic TTA methods on models beyond CLIP, specifically on DALL-E and Vision-BERT, to assess their generalizability.
CONTROLS: We will use the same implementation and baseline as in proposal 1, and control for any differences in architecture and pre-training methodology.
COST: 30 GPU-hours (10 datasets from the COCO benchmark with 2 noise-injections, and 3 additional VLM models).
PREDICTION: We anticipate that many existing TTA methods will struggle to generalize to alternative architectures, and that successful adaptation will require adaptations to the model architecture or training objectives. Some architectures (e.g., DALL-E) will be more amenable to adaptation, while others (e.g., Vision-BERT) might require major modifications to existing TTA methods.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Consistent Reproducible Benchmarks for Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Establish a set of standardized test-time adaptation experiments, including implementation, hardware, and software specifications, for a variety of popular VLMs such as CLIP, DALL-E, and ViLBERT on standard image classification benchmarks like ImageNet and CIFAR-10. Utilize pre-trained model checkpoints, text prompts, and evaluation protocols to ensure consistent and reproducible experimental settings.
CONTROLS: Implementation of test-time adaptation strategies (such as global average pooling and epistemic uncertainty-based methods) using PyTorch and non-adaptive variants as baselines; ablation study to analyze the impact of changes to model architecture, text prompts, and evaluation protocols.
COST: 10 GPU-hours (1-day training on ImageNet with baseline methods)
PREDICTION: This setup will provide a solid foundation for comparing and evaluating the performance of future TTA methods, but may not offer conclusive results regarding algorithmic improvements.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Ablation Study on Adaptation Strategies for VLMs
PROPOSAL: Perform an extensive ablation study to investigate the impact of various adaptation strategies for VLMs, including global average pooling, epistemic uncertainty-based methods, and attention-based approaches, on the performance of a frozen VLM. This will help to identify the most effective adaptations for different model architectures and evaluate the trade-offs between these methods.
CONTROLS: Adaptation strategies will be compared on the standardized benchmarks established in experiment 1; baseline is a frozen VLM without any adaptation. We will also ablate the components of each adaptation method to understand their individual contributions.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (1-week training on ImageNet with various adaptation methods)
PREDICTION: This ablation study will provide insights into the effectiveness of different adaptation strategies, but may not offer conclusive results on how adaptation impacts model trustworthiness and stability.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Quantifying the Benefits of Test-Time Adaptation for Multiple Vision-Language Tasks
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of test-time adaptation on a suite of multi-modal tasks, including image classification, object detection, and image captioning. Evaluate how adaptation improves task-specific performance, and whether gains generalize across tasks.
CONTROLS: Adaptation strategies will be applied on the standardized benchmarks from experiment 1 for each task; baselines include task-specific frozen VLMs without adaptation. We will also compare performance on a set of diverse datasets from the multidx task suite.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (2-day training on diverse datasets with adaptation methods and baselines)
PREDICTION: This experiment will show that TTA benefits various tasks and outperforms non-adaptive variants, but its impact on model trustworthiness and stability is unclear and should be explored further.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Quantifying the Benefits of Test-Time Adaptation for Multiple Vision-Language Tasks
PROPOSAL: To gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between test-time adaptation and its effects on model trustworthiness and stability, in addition to task-specific performance, we will evaluate adaptation's influence on model uncertainty, calibration, and robustness on a variety of tasks. We will explore whether adaptation leads to better model uncertainty estimates, improved calibration, and higher robustness to distribution shifts.
CONTROLS: Adaptation strategies will be compared on the suite of tasks from experiment 3, with baselines including task-specific frozen VLMs without adaptation and a shifted test distribution.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (2-day training on diverse datasets with adaptation methods and baselines)
PREDICTION: This experiment will demonstrate that TTA improves model trustworthiness and stability measures across tasks, highlighting its benefits for real-world deployment.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Online Test-Time Adaptation for Streaming Data
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate an online test-time adaptation method for vision-language models, suitable for real-time processing of streaming data from sources like surveillance cameras or mobile devices. This method will utilize an ensemble of local adaptation models and a meta-model for online learning.
CONTROLS: The proposed online adaptation method will be compared against a batch adaptation approach and an adaptive baseline model on a real-world streaming dataset, such as the Places365 dataset.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (1-day training on the Places365 dataset with online and batch adaptation methods)
PREDICTION: This experiment will show that the online adaptation method can effectively handle real-time processing of streaming data, but its improvement over batch adaptation may be limited by the computational resources and data available at each time step.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Test-Time Adaptation vs. Fine-Tuning: A Comparative Study
PROPOSAL: Investigate the relative effectiveness of test-time adaptation versus training-time fine-tuning for vision-language models on various tasks and datasets. This comparison will help to understand whether test-time adaptation can be a complementary or alternative approach to training-time fine-tuning.
CONTROLS: The performance of test-time adaptation and training-time fine-tuning methods will be compared on a variety of models, including CLIP and ViLBERT, and tasks, including image classification and object detection. Baselines include both the pre-trained models and the fine-tuned models.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (1-week training and adaptation on a range of models and tasks)
PREDICTION: This experiment will demonstrate that test-time adaptation can be a viable alternative or complementary approach to fine-tuning for vision-language models, but its benefits may be limited by the availability of adaptative data and the complexity of the task.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Quantifying the Benefits of Test-Time Adaptation for Multiple Vision-Language Tasks
PROPOSAL: Expand the task suite from experiment 3 to include more challenging and diverse tasks, such as multi-class image classification, multi-object detection, and visual question answering. This will help to assess the robustness and generalizability of test-time adaptation across different levels of complexity and various cognitive demands.
CONTROLS: Adaptation strategies will be evaluated on the expanded task suite, using the same baselines as before (frozen VLMs without adaptation). We will also investigate the transfers of adaptation benefits across tasks and datasets.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (1-week training and adaptation on the expanded task suite)
PREDICTION: This experiment will provide more comprehensive insights into the versatility and effectiveness of test-time adaptation across various tasks, but might require additional computational resources and time to process the expanded task suite.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Evaluating Robustness and OOD Generalization of Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization capabilities of vision-language models after test-time adaptation. This will be achieved by evaluating the models on a set of benchmark datasets that are structurally similar to the training datasets but may have different classes, images, or contexts.
CONTROLS: Adaptation strategies will be compared on the robustness and OOD generalization benchmarks, with baselines including frozen VLMs without adaptation and non-adaptive models. We will also analyze the transferability of adaptation benefits to new and unseen environments.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (2-day training and adaptation on robustness and OOD generalization benchmarks)
PREDICTION: This experiment will demonstrate the robustness and OOD generalization capabilities of test-time adaptation for vision-language models, but might require careful design of the benchmark datasets to ensure that they accurately capture the diversity of real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Analyzing Interpretability and Explainability of Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the interpretability and explainability of vision-language models after test-time adaptation. This will be achieved by using techniques such as saliency maps, feature importance, and model interpretability tools to understand how adaptation affects the models' representations and decision-making processes.
CONTROLS: Adaptation strategies will be compared on interpretability and explainability metrics, with baselines including frozen VLMs without adaptation and human expert annotations.
COST: 40 GPU-hours (2-day training and analysis on interpretability and explainability metrics)
PREDICTION: This experiment will provide insights into the inner workings of test-time adaptation and shed light on its potential applications, but might require careful tuning of the analysis tools and methods to ensure accuracy and reliability.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation and Comparison of Test-Time Adaptation Methods
PROPOSAL: Apply a systematic and rigorous evaluation framework to the results of the previous experiments, combining the findings to provide a comprehensive comparison of test-time adaptation methods across multiple tasks, datasets, and adaptation scenarios. This will involve concatenating metrics, identifying patterns, and highlighting opportunities for future research.
CONTROLS: The evaluation framework will be based on the results of the previous experiments, with baselines including non-adaptive VLMs and benchmarks.
COST: 10 GPU-hours (1-day computation for concatenating and analyzing results)
PREDICTION: This experiment will provide a final assessment of the effectiveness and robustness of test-time adaptation methods, highlighting their strengths and limitations, and guiding future research directions.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Baseline Consistency in Episodic Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Reproduce existing episodic TTA methods using a fixed pre-trained CLIP model checkpoint and a consistent evaluation protocol on the validation set of the Multi-modal 1000 (MM1000) dataset. Compare the reproduced results to the reported baseline results in the original papers using metrics such as top-1 accuracy, mean Average Precision at k (mAP@k), and Top-k accuracy.
CONTROLS: CLIP-ViT-B/16 pre-trained weights, TextPrompt LFX, MM1000 validation set
COST: 10 GPU-hours (5 hours for data loading and preprocessing, 3 hours for reproducing TTA methods, 2 hours for evaluation)
PREDICTION: Unreliable or inconsistent reproductions, likely due to differences in evaluation protocols, hyperparameters, or implementation details, indicating the need for consistent experimental settings in TTA research.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Extending Baseline Evaluation to Online Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Repeat the baseline consistency evaluation from proposal 1, but for online TTA methods, using a fixed pre-trained CLIP model checkpoint and a consistent evaluation protocol on the validation set of the NUS-WIDE dataset (a large-scale online TTA benchmark). Compare the reproduced results to the reported baseline results in the original papers using metrics such as top-1 accuracy, mean Average Precision at k (mAP@k), and Top-k accuracy.
CONTROLS: Same as proposal 1
COST: Additional 10 GPU-hours (5 hours for data loading and preprocessing, 3 hours for reproducing online TTA methods, 2 hours for evaluation)
PREDICATION: Similar unreliable or inconsistent reproductions for online TTA methods, highlighting the need for consistent experimental settings in online TTA research as well.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Systematic Evaluation of Test-Time Adaptation on Alternative Modalities
PROPOSAL: Evaluate existing episodic and online TTA methods using datasets that are less commonly used in TTA research, such as the Oxford 102 Flowers dataset for image classification and the Flicker8k dataset for image captioning. Assess the transferability of TTA methods across different visual and textual modalities using metrics such as top-1 accuracy, mAP@k, and Top-k accuracy.
CONTROLS: Use the same fixed pre-trained CLIP model checkpoint and evaluation protocol as in proposals 1 and 2.
COST: Additional 20 GPU-hours (10 hours for data loading and preprocessing, 6 hours for reproducing TTA methods, 4 hours for evaluation)
PREDICTION: Mixed results where TTA methods perform well on certain modalities but poorly on others, indicating the need for more diverse and extensive evaluation of TTA methods on different tasks and modalities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Trustworthiness and Stability Evaluation for Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Introduce and evaluate additional metrics to measure the trustworthiness and stability of TTA methods, such as reliability metrics (e.g., confidence calibration curves) and uncertainty metrics (e.g., predictive entropy). Compare the performance of existing TTA methods using these new metrics alongside traditional accuracy metrics on the validation sets of the MM1000 and NUS-WIDE datasets.
CONTROLS: Use the same fixed pre-trained CLIP model checkpoint and evaluation protocol as in proposals 1-3.
COST: Additional 15 GPU-hours (7.5 hours for data loading and preprocessing, 4 hours for reproducing TTA methods, 3.5 hours for evaluation)
PREDICTION: Consistent results showing that TTA methods that excel in terms of accuracy often compromise trustworthiness and stability, and vice versa, indicating the need for more comprehensive evaluation of TTA methods in real-world applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Benchmarking Test-Time Adaptation on VLM Architectures Beyond CLIP
PROPOSAL: Reproduce and evaluate existing episodic and online TTA methods using a range of VLM architectures beyond CLIP, including Vision Transformers (ViT), Swin Transformers, and Concatenated Visual Transformers (CoViT). Compare the performance of these TTA methods across different VLM architectures on the validation sets of the MM1000 and NUS-WIDE datasets using metrics such as top-1 accuracy and mAP@k.
CONTROLS: Use a fixed pre-trained checkpoint for each VLM architecture and the same evaluation protocol as in proposals 1-4.
COST: Additional 25 GPU-hours (12.5 hours for data loading and preprocessing, 6 hours for reproducing TTA methods, 6.5 hours for evaluation)
PREDICTION: Improved performance for TTA methods on VLM architectures beyond CLIP, particularly for ViT and Swin Transformers, indicating the need for more extensive evaluation of TTA methods on different architectures and datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Interaction Between Test-Time Adaptation and Pre-training
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of existing TTA methods on pre-trained VLM models that have been fine-tuned on various downstream tasks (e.g., image classification, object detection) versus pre-trained models that have not been fine-tuned. Compare the results across different TTA methods, VLM architectures, and evaluation metrics.
CONTROLS: Use the same evaluation protocol and fixed pre-trained checkpoints as in proposals 1-5.
COST: Additional 20 GPU-hours (10 hours for data loading and preprocessing, 5 hours for reproducing TTA methods, 5 hours for evaluation)
PREDICTION: Results will show that TTA methods are more effective for models that have not been fine-tuned, and that the interaction between TTA and fine-tuning can lead to improved performance in some cases, while also highlighting potential issues with over-adaptation and catastrophic forgetting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Importance of Input Data for Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Conduct an ablation study to investigate the importance of input data for TTA methods. Specifically, compare the performance of TTA methods when using original input images, randomly distorted input images, and input images with missing or corrupted features. Evaluate the results across different TTA methods, VLM architectures, and evaluation metrics.
CONTROLS: Use the same evaluation protocol as in proposals 1-6.
COST: Additional 15 GPU-hours (7.5 hours for data loading and preprocessing, 4 hours for reproducing TTA methods, 3.5 hours for evaluation)
PREDICTION: Results will show that TTA methods are more robust to input data distortions and corruptions than originally thought, indicating that the importance of input data for TTA methods may be less than previously assumed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Effect of Adversarial Attacks on Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the robustness of TTA methods to adversarial attacks on the input images. Specifically, compare the performance of TTA methods when using input images that have been attacked with LFI (Labeled Fiji Insects), DeepFool, and FGSM adversarial attacks. Evaluate the results across different TTA methods, VLM architectures, and evaluation metrics.
CONTROLS: Use the same evaluation protocol as in proposals 1-7.
COST: Additional 25 GPU-hours (12.5 hours for data loading and preprocessing, 6 hours for reproducing TTA methods, 6.5 hours for evaluation)
PREDICTION: Results will show that TTA methods are vulnerable to adversarial attacks and that their performance can degrade significantly when confronted with adversarial input images.

ACTION: ADD

PROPOSAL: Theoretically propose a unified framework that integrates different TTA methods and analyzes their relationships and trade-offs. Investigate the connections between different TTA techniques and explore opportunities for combining them to yield more effective and robust adaptation methods. Additionally, explore potential applications of this framework in real-world scenarios.
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework using the universal approximation property of neural networks and the concept of information-theoretic regularization.

PREDICTION: The unified framework will offer new insights into the strengths and weaknesses of different TTA methods, enabling the development of more comprehensive and adaptive algorithms that better address the complexity of real-world scenarios.

PROPOSAL: Replace the existing proposal 5 with a non-parametric benchmarking approach, where the performance of TTA methods is evaluated and compared using a range of different datasets and tasks, rather than relying solely on a single pre-trained model checkpoint and validation set. This will enable a more comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of different TTA methods across a broader range of scenarios.

PREDICTION: The non-parametric benchmarking approach will provide a more nuanced understanding of the performance and applicability of different TTA methods, enabling more informed decisions about which methods to use in different scenarios and for different tasks.

Evaluate existing episodic and online TTA methods using datasets that are less commonly used in TTA research, such as the Oxford 102 Flowers dataset for image classification and the Flicker8k dataset for image captioning. Assess the transferability of TTA methods across different visual and textual modalities using metrics such as top-1 accuracy, mAP@k, and Top-k accuracy.

PROPOSAL 4: Trustworthiness and Stability Evaluation for Test-Time Adaptation
Introduce and evaluate additional metrics to measure the trustworthiness and stability of TTA methods, such as reliability metrics (e.g., confidence calibration curves) and uncertainty metrics (e.g., predictive entropy). Compare the performance of existing TTA methods using these new metrics alongside traditional accuracy metrics on the validation sets of the MM1000 and NUS-WIDE datasets.
Controls: Use the same fixed pre-trained CLIP model checkpoint and evaluation protocol as in proposals 1-3.

PROPOSAL 5: Non-Parametric Benchmarking of Test-Time Adaptation on VLM Architectures Beyond CLIP
Replace the existing proposal 5 with a non-parametric benchmarking approach, where the performance of TTA methods is evaluated and compared using a range of different datasets and tasks, rather than relying solely on a single pre-trained model checkpoint and validation set. This will enable a more comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of different TTA methods across a broader range of scenarios.
Controls: Use a dataset-specific approach to evaluate and compare TTA methods on a variety of visual and textual modalities and tasks, such as object detection, segmentation, and captioning.

PROPOSAL 6: Investigating the Interaction Between Test-Time Adaptation and Pre-training
Evaluate the performance of existing TTA methods on pre-trained VLM models that have been fine-tuned on various downstream tasks (e.g., image classification, object detection) versus pre-trained models that have not been fine-tuned. Compare the results across different TTA methods, VLM architectures, and evaluation metrics.

PROPOSAL 7: Analyzing the Importance of Input Data for Test-Time Adaptation
Conduct an ablation study to investigate the importance of input data for TTA methods. Specifically, compare the performance of TTA methods when using original input images, randomly distorted input images, and input images with missing or corrupted features. Evaluate the results across different TTA methods, VLM architectures, and evaluation metrics.
Controls: Use the same evaluation protocol as in proposals 1-6.

Prediction: Results will show that TTA methods are more robust to input data distortions and corruptions than originally thought, indicating that the importance of input data for TTA methods may be less than previously assumed.

PROPOSAL 8: Investigating the Effect of Adversarial Attacks on Test-Time Adaptation
Evaluate the robustness of TTA methods to adversarial attacks on the input images. Specifically, compare the performance of TTA methods when using input images that have been attacked with LFI (Labeled Fiji Insects), DeepFool, and FGSM adversarial attacks. Evaluate the results across different TTA methods, VLM architectures, and evaluation metrics.
Controls: Use the same evaluation protocol as in proposals 1-7.
Estimated cost: Additional 25 GPU-hours (12.5 hours for data loading and preprocessing, 6 hours for reproducing TTA methods, 6.5 hours for evaluation)
Prediction: Results will show that TTA methods are vulnerable to adversarial attacks and that their performance can degrade significantly when confronted with adversarial input images.

PROPOSAL 9: A Unified Framework for Test-Time Adaptation and Its Applications
Theoretically propose a unified framework that integrates different TTA methods and analyzes their relationships and trade-offs. Investigate the connections between different TTA techniques and explore opportunities for combining them to yield more effective and robust adaptation methods. Additionally, explore potential applications of this framework in real-world scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Unified Video Tokenizers for Discrete Autoregressive Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the efficiency of initializing discrete video tokenizers from pre-trained discrete image tokenizers and adapt them to video reconstruction tasks. We will fine-tune a state-of-the-art discrete image tokenizer (e.g., DiscoDiffuser) on a video dataset (e.g., Vimeo-90K) and evaluate its performance using standard video reconstruction metrics (e.g., PSNR, SSIM).
CONTROLS: Ablation study comparing the performance of tokenizers fine-tuned from scratch, vs. those initialized from the pre-trained image tokenizer.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Fine-tuning from the pre-trained image tokenizer will improve the tokenizers' reconstruction quality and reduce the training time significantly, but potentially at the cost of some expressive power lost due to pre-training on images.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Discrete Autoregressive Video Generation with Long-Short Term Memory 
PROPOSAL: Incorporate long-short term memory (LSTM) units into the discrete autoregressive model to explicitly capture and utilize temporal dependencies between tokens in the video sequence. We focus on designing an LSTM-based architecture that suitably can update and propagate attention with respect to token-encoded contextual information from both the previous and future frames in a streaming manner.
CONTROLS: Comparing with the baseline discrete autoregressive model that relies on token-level attention for temporal context and LSTM however would have separate learnable 'helpers' feeding information forward and backward in a type of truncation which simplifies toward model inference stability with gradually emptying stored information and baseline established autoregressive frame-poisoning disregarding historical dependencies. Borrow discriminator from state-of-the-art critical object IK Jo channel-status competing strongly.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: LSTM units will significantly enhance the temporal modeling capabilities of the discrete autoregressive model, but potentially at the cost of slight increases in sensitivity to model hyperparameters and the need for high-quality pre-training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Knowledge Distillation from Video Diffusion Models for Temporal Consistency
PROPOSAL: Utilize knowledge distillation to transfer the temporal coherence and structural insights learned by state-of-the-art video diffusion models to the discrete autoregressive model. We distill the probabilistic information and the spatial-temporal relationships modeled by the diffusion model into a set of learnable weights, constraints or representations that can be easily incorporated into the autoregressive model. This approach leverages the interpretability of the autoregressive model while retaining the crucial representation knowledge distilled from the more expressive diffusion model.
CONTROLS: Comparing with the ablated discrete autoregression -without-distillation, cross-evaluation scales with Vanilla Diffusion with VP common random tile-drop fa pool Not mentioned Checked on competitors regardless uniformly exp Random labeled.
COST: 70 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Knowledge distillation will effectively enhance the temporal consistency of the discrete autoregressive model, yielding state-of-the-art results close to the diffusion models' efficiency in video generation tasks but slightly sacrificing some of their generative capabilities.

TITLE: Revised Knowledge Distillation from Video Diffusion Models for Temporal Consistency
REVISED Proposal from 3: Implement a revised version of the guide model by distilling not only the probabilistic information learned from the diffusion models but also incorporating a modified attention mechanism that takes into account the temporal dependencies between tokens in the video sequence. This attention mechanism is trainable end-to-end with the rest of the model, allowing it to adapt to the specific needs of the autoregressive task.
CONTROLS: Ablation study comparing the performance of the revised knowledge distillation approach with the baseline approach.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
