This is because the modified attention mechanism will better capture temporal dependencies between tokens, resulting in more coherent and realistic video sequences.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Temporal Consistency with Temporally-Constrained Token Prediction
PROPOSAL: Introduce a temporally-constrained token prediction mechanism that encourages the model to generate tokens that are consistent with the previously generated tokens in the sequence, thereby improving temporal consistency. This mechanism is implemented as a penalty term in the loss function that encourages the model to generate tokens that are nearby in the token sequence, rather than tokens that are far apart.
CONTROLS: Ablation study comparing the performance of the temporally-constrained token prediction mechanism with the baseline approach.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The temporally-constrained token prediction mechanism will improve the temporal consistency of the discrete autoregressive model, leading to better performance on video generation tasks. However, it may also introduce some artifacts or loss of expressiveness due to the excessive emphasis on token locality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Streaming Video Generation with Adaptive Token Buffering
PROPOSAL: Introduce an adaptive token buffering mechanism that stores and processes tokens in a streaming manner, allowing the model to handle long videos and generate high-quality frames on the fly, without requiring the entire video sequence to be stored in memory. This mechanism uses a buffer of tokens that can be dynamically adjusted based on the model's needs and the available memory, ensuring real-time processing and efficient memory usage.
CONTROLS: Evaluating the model's performance with different buffer sizes and policies, as well as comparing with a non-streaming baseline approach.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adaptive token buffering mechanism will significantly improve the streaming video generation capabilities of the discrete autoregressive model, allowing it to generate high-quality videos in real-time and efficiently handle long sequences. However, it may require careful tuning of the buffer size and policy to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Learning for Unified Video and Image Generation
PROPOSAL: Train a single, unified model that can perform both video and image generation tasks, using a multi-task learning approach that encourages the model to share knowledge and representations across both tasks. This will allow the model to leverage the strengths of both video and image generation, and enable seamless transfer of knowledge between tasks.
CONTROLS: Ablation study comparing the performance of the multi-task learning approach with single-task learning baselines for both video and image generation.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multi-task learning approach will enable the model to achieve state-of-the-art performance on both video and image generation tasks, by effectively leveraging the knowledge and representations learned from both tasks. However, it may introduce some challenges related to task balancing and knowledge conflicts between tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Interactive Video Generation with Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: Develop a reinforcement learning framework that enables users to interactively generate videos by providing feedback in real-time. The model will learn to adapt to the user's preferences and generate videos that meet their specific needs. This will be achieved through a combination of reward-based reinforcement learning and multi-objective optimization.
CONTROLS: Evaluating the performance of the interactive video generation system using human evaluators and ablation studies to compare with non-interactive baselines.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The interactive video generation system with reinforcement learning will enable users to effectively fine-tune and control the video generation process in real-time, leading to high-quality videos that meet their specific needs. However, it may require significant expertise and resources to train and tune the model for optimal performance.

propositions.prediction: The multi-task learning approach will enable the model to achieve state-of-the-art performance on both video and image generation tasks, by effectively leveraging the knowledge and representations learned from both tasks. However, it may introduce some challenges related to task balancing and knowledge conflicts between tasks.
propositions.texte: Train a single, unified model that can perform both video and image generation tasks, using a multi-task learning approach that encourages the model to share knowledge and representations across both tasks. This will allow the model to leverage the strengths of both video and image generation, and enable seamless transfer of knowledge between tasks.
propositions.titre: Multi-Task Learning for Unified Video and Image Generation

propositions.controles: Evaluating the performance of the interactive video generation system using human evaluators and ablation studies to compare with non-interactive baselines.
propositions.prediction: The interactive video generation system with reinforcement learning will enable users to effectively fine-tune and control the video generation process in real-time, leading to high-quality videos that meet their specific needs. However, it may require significant expertise and resources to train and tune the model for optimal performance.
propositions.texte: Develop a reinforcement learning framework that enables users to interactively generate videos by providing feedback in real-time. The model will learn to adapt to the user's preferences and generate videos that meet their specific needs. This will be achieved through a combination of reward-based reinforcement learning and multi-objective optimization.
propositions.titre: Interactive Video Generation with Reinforcement Learning

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Efficient Discrete Video Tokenization for Autoregressive Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel discrete video tokenizer, AutoDiff, by modifying the existing Auto framework, which is tailored for discrete image tokenization. AutoDiff extends the existing learned-positioning embedding to capture sequential spatiotemporal dependencies and transfers between short video segments, reducing the computational cost and fixed-size tokenizer initialization without severe performance degradation, while supporting scalability to long video clips with tens of thousands of frames.
CONTROLS: Baseline models include pre-existing discrete video tokenizers; variants of AutoDiff will be ablated to examine the efficacy of learned-positioning and video transfer enhancements.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: AutoDiff will significantly accelerate tokenizer initialization and inference without sacrificing performance, leading to a faster and more efficient autoregressive video generation framework that preempts the experiment's secondary objectives of proposing an efficient autoregressive video generation model. Where it may still fail is on extremely long clips or challenging (many object, fast movement) videos.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Positional Embeddings for Autoregressive Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel family of trainable, skipable hierarchical positional embeddings (HPEs) that efficiently capture both spatial and temporal dependencies in videos. HPEs decompose longer-range positional dependencies into smaller, context-specific components, reducing the need for repetitive lineage combiners and explosive sequence growth. We will embed these within our proposed autoregressive model, VAR-TV (Visual AutoRegressive model for Text-to-Video).
CONTROLS: Controls include VAR-TV with and without HPEs, a baseline autoregressive video generation model that lacks advanced positional embeddings (for exampleôt using globally shared embeddings).
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed HPEs will improve temporal consistency and reduce inference latency in autoregressive video generation by an order of magnitude, tolerating eccentric video frames but failing on the longest clips, where drilling down into each stage of HPE layers takes a massive ammout of steps.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Adaptive Positional Embeddings for Autoregressive Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel adaptive hierarchical positional embedding module that dynamically selects the number and complexity of positional embedding components based on the input video's characteristics, ensuring optimal performance without fixed-size or a priori assumptions about the input's spatial and temporal properties.
CONTROLS: We will compare adaptive HPEs with skipable HPEs (Experiment 2) and baseline globally shared embeddings, all within the context of VAR-T VB
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Adaptive HPEs will exhibit superior performance on a broader range of video types and scales, with a slight performance drop observed in the very shortest clip, due to less sensitivity on a video with a large representation – afterwards the exclusivity open possibilities of integrati in later turns.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Directed Autoregressive Loops for Unified Text-to-Image, Text-to-Video, and Image-to-Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel directed autoregressive framework that seamlessly integrates text-to-image, text-to-video, image-to-video and video extrapolation, requiring only a slight modification of the directed autoregressive architecture, with novel attention mechanisms designed to consider the semantic structure of the input and generate coherent outputs in multiple modalities.
CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed framework with a variant that lacks directed autoregressive loops and with separate, modality-specific models.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The directed autoregressive loops will facilitate unified generation across multiple domains, offering comparable or outperforming results in text-to-image and image-to-video generation, with the potential to fail in highly specialized tasks, where limiting adaptation to a specific modality may lead to more competitive performance.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Bitwise Predictive Encoding for Efficient Long-Term Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel bitwise predictive encoding scheme that selectively tailors the precision of the model's output during long-term video generation, prioritizing frames with the highest motion or salience and conserving bits for frames with less significant changes, substantially reducing the computational and memory costs of high-resolution video generation while maintaining visual quality.
CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed scheme with existing bitwise encoding methods and baseline models without any encoding optimizations.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The bitwise predictive encoding will outperform existing methods in Fool's gold and Synsin in turning the output/day in FOOf longest report generation at multiple levels of precision. Economic float, and prevent computaional freezing later on.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Temporal Context-Aware Attention for Long-Range Temporal Dependencies
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel attention mechanism that selectively focuses on relevant temporal contexts while mitigating the influence of irrelevant or redundant information, thereby addressing the challenges of capturing long-range temporal dependencies in video generation. The mechanism will be integrated with the directed autoregressive loops to enhance the temporal consistency and coherence of the generated videos.
CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed attention mechanism with existing attention mechanisms and baseline models without any temporal context-aware attention.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The temporal context-aware attention will significantly improve the temporal coherence and consistency of the generated videos, particularly in long-range dependencies, and may slightly increase computational overhead, which could hinder performance on very high-resolution video generation.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Multi-Scale Progressive Attention for Spatiotemporal Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel multi-scale progressive attention mechanism that adaptively adjusts its spatial and temporal resolutions to capture detailed object movements and contextual dependencies in videos, improving the overall visual quality and temporal coherence of the generated videos.
CONTROLS: We will compare the proposed attention mechanism with existing attention mechanisms and baseline models without any progressive attention.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The multi-scale progressive attention will significantly boost the visual quality and temporal coherence of the generated videos, especially in high-resolution and long-range dependencies, but may introduce additional computational overhead and potentially hinder performance on very short clips or real-time applications.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Unified Directional Autoregressive Loops for Text-to-Image, Text-to-Video, Image-to-Video, and Video Extrapolation
PROPOSAL: Integrate the multi-scale progressive attention mechanism with the directed autoregressive loops, enabling a unified framework that seamlessly generates high-quality videos for text-to-image, text-to-video, image-to-video, and video extrapolation tasks, leveraging the strengths of both approaches to tackle the diverse challenges of video generation.
CONTROLS: We will compare the revised framework with the original directed autoregressive loops and variants that lack multi-scale progressive attention.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The unified framework will set a new benchmark for video generation, offering state-of-the-art performance across all four tasks, with the potential drawback of increased computational overhead, which could be mitigated with careful resource allocation and optimization techniques.

ACTION: REVISE 6
TITLE: Optimized Multi-Scale Progressive Attention for Real-World Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Fine-tune the multi-scale progressive attention mechanism to better accommodate the complexities of real-world video data, leveraging transfer learning from pre-trained models and incorporating feedback from human evaluators to optimize the attention weights and learn to detect and generate high-quality videos with more realistic temporal coherence.
CONTROLS: We will compare the optimized attention mechanism with the original multi-scale progressive attention and variants with different levels of human evaluation and transfer learning.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The optimized attention mechanism will significantly improve the visual quality and temporal coherence of the generated videos on real-world datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results in human evaluation metrics, while potentially introducing additional computational overhead and requiring careful tuning of hyperparameters.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Visual AutoRegressive Modeling for Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Develop a variant of the Visual AutoRegressive (VAR) model tailored for video generation using discrete autoregressive modeling, incorporating 3D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for efficient processing of spatiotemporal contexts and employing a fixed, hierarchical vocabulary to prune search space and speed up inference.
CONTROLS: Compare our proposed model with the original VAR model, Infinity, and several state-of-the-art diffusion models (e.g., DDPM, Avatar-3D) on text-to-video generation, image-to-video generation, and video extrapolation tasks using the same benchmarks and evaluation metrics (e.g., bitrate, learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS), SSIM, MOS).
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our model should outperform Infinity on tasks requiring motion modeling while matching its quality on static image synthesis, offering lower inference latency and comparable qualitative performance to state-of-the-art diffusion models, suggesting that discrete autoregressive modeling can be a viable alternative in video generation with careful architecture design. However, it might struggle with very long videos and temporally complex scenes where vast context attentions are still needed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Discrete Video Tokenizer with Multi-Stage Attention
PROPOSAL: Design a hierarchical discrete video tokenizer with multiple stages that progressively refines token representations by exploiting motion patterns and object structures in videos. Each stage employs a discrete cosine transform (DCT) and a learned mask to capture local and global dependencies. Additionally, incorporate a multi-stage attention mechanism to selectively attend to relevant frames across different stages, reducing the need for long-range contextual dependencies and thereby decreasing computational costs.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the proposed tokenizer on text-to-video generation tasks with static and dynamic scenes, comparing its performance on metrics such as LPIPS, SSIM, and bitrate against both the proposed model in experiment 1 and state-of-the-art diffusion models.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The hierarchical tokenizer with multi-stage attention should significantly improve video quality and reduce inference latency, outperforming the proposed model in experiment 1 on tasks requiring sophisticated motion modeling. However, it might still struggle with very slow motions or scenes with unclear object boundaries, impacting tokenization accuracy.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Hierarchical Discrete Video Tokenizer with Multi-Stage Attention
PROPOSAL: Revisit the hierarchical discrete video tokenizer design, focusing on incorporating temporal skip connections to facilitate recurrent refinement of token representations. Utilize a truncated temporal residual network to surmount the vanishing gradient problem in the recursive refinement process, enabling the model to capture longer-range temporal dependencies. Optimize the trunk models to capture object and motion patterns exploiting hierarchical structure.
CONTROLS: Examine the effectiveness of the updated tokenizer on scenarios with both rapid and slow motion, evaluating its ability to capture temporal context and yielding accurate object representations against the original proposed model and state-of-the-art models.
COST: 0 additional cost; already included in original experiment 2's cost, now optimized
PREDICTION: The revised tokenizer with temporal skip connections and trunk models will demonstrate substantial improvement in video quality and scene understanding for videos with varying motion dynamics and levels of complexity, reducing latency compared to the original model, while potential limitations are diminished in long-term dependencies preserving.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Lightweight Temporal Attention for Long Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Introduce lightweight temporal attention layers that condition generation on a smaller, spatiotemporally localized context of previously generated frames instead of attending to the entire video history. Employ a pyramid attention scheme that aggregates spatial and temporal context over multiple scales, allowing models to selectively focus on object movements, whole-body gestures, and scene structures.
CONTROLS: Compare performance of video generation tasks and qualitative results on our long-range video extrapolation and interactive setting of videos. Include interaction information on memory consumption and generation latency.
COST: 750 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: With lightweight temporal attention, video generators should maintain high accuracy in photorealistic video synthesis, improve robustness to changing contexts, as well as reduce memory consumption during long video generation and process entire context scenes near in time given a very low cost.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Improving Visual AutoRegressive Modeling for Video Generation
PROPOSAL: Enhance the Visual AutoRegressive (VAR) model by incorporating the hierarchical discrete video tokenizer with multi-stage attention (from experiment 2) and lightweight temporal attention (from experiment 3) to efficiently learn spatial-temporal patterns in videos. Additionally, utilize the shrinking transformer (from experiment 5) to adapt the model to various input sequences and leverage its ability to handle both text-to-image and text-to-video generation. Integrate an improved training scheme that incorporates interactive content-aware auto-regressive video generation (from experiment 4) to refine the model's video synthesis capabilities.
CONTROLS: Compare the enhanced VAR model with the original model, as well as with state-of-the-art diffusion models, on a range of video generation tasks and metrics, including LPIPS, SSIM, and MOS.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised VAR model should significantly improve video quality and temporal coherence, while exhibiting efficient inference times and facilitating interactive video generation, yet potential limitations may still arise when handling very complex or dynamic scenes demanding broad intertemporal awareness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalability Analysis and Deployment of the Optimized Video Generation Pipeline
PROPOSAL: Conduct a scalability analysis of the proposed video generation pipeline, comprising of the revised VAR model and supporting components (hierarchical discrete video tokenizer, lightweight temporal attention, and asynchronous multi-agent framework), to assess its performance on large-scale video datasets and in distributed deployment settings. Develop a cloud-based infrastructure for the deployment of the optimized video generation pipeline, ensuring efficient resource allocation and auto-scaling capabilities.
CONTROLS: Validate the scalability of the pipeline using benchmarks with various video sizes and formats, comparing its performance on compute efficiency, memory usage, and latency with state-of-the-art cloud-based video generation solutions.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging cloud-based infrastructure and efficient resource allocation strategies, our video generation pipeline should demonstrate tremendous scalability, enabling real-time rendering of high-resolution videos with high-quality visual and audio content, and facilitating applications in various industries, including entertainment, education, and advertising, yet managing stability long run.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Ripple Effects and Hallucination in LLMs
PROPOSAL: Implement an experiment comparing the inference capabilities of a transformer model with its inductive and deductive reasoning components systematically ablated. Specifically, we fine-tune a pre-trained transformer model on a synthetic dataset where new fact s, r, a is paired with its implication s, r_2, c. After fine-tuning, we test the model on new unseen subjects s_new and measure the ability to reason deductively (i.e., fact → implication) and inductively (i.e., new unseen fact → implication).
CONTROLS: Baseline (original transformer model), Baseline with random weights for the inductive component, Baseline with reduced training dataset containing only the facts but not implications.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the model with the inductive component to perform competitively with the baseline in both deductive and inductive reasoning tasks. However, if the hallucination mechanism arises from the same underlying mechanism as the inductive reasoning capability, as our proposal suggests, then the model with the inductive component might exhibit higher hallucination rates compared to the baseline. 

This proposal lays the groundwork for understanding the relationship between generalization, hallucination, and out-of-context reasoning in LLMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synthetic Data Generation for Factual Knowledge Injection
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to generate synthetic, high-quality datasets for factual knowledge injection experiments. This dataset should have the following properties: a) diverse set of facts and implications; b) distribution similar to real-world data; c) ability to control for varying levels of reasoning complexity. We will use a generative model, such as the GEdit model, to generate such datasets.
CONTROLS: Human-annotated benchmark datasets.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our synthetic datasets will allow for faster experimentation and evaluation of LLMs' reasoning capabilities, while also reducing the reliance on manually annotated data. 

This dataset will be used extensively in later experiments to generate reliable and maintainable results.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Ripple Effects and Hallucination in LLMs
PROPOSAL: Update the experiment in Proposal 1 to include two additional conditions: a) a heavily regularized transformer model and b) a transformer model that is trained on the synthetic dataset generated in Proposal 2, with the only target being the implication (and not the fact). We will then compare the performance of these additional conditions in both deductive and inductive reasoning tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline (original transformer model), Baseline with random weights for the inductive component, Baseline with reduced training dataset containing only the facts but not implications.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the heavily regularized model to perform poorly on both deductive and inductive reasoning tasks, while the model trained only on implications might surprisingly perform well due to its ability to internalize the relationships between the subjects and the implications.

The amendment aims to further investigate why some models may exhibit hallucination and to shed light on the relationship between the model's regularity, data-dependent target variable and reasoning performance.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Ripple Effects and Hallucination in LLMs
PROPOSAL: Update the experiment in Proposal 1 to include two additional conditions: a) a heavily regularized transformer model and b) a transformer model that is trained on the synthetic dataset generated in Proposal 2, with the only target being the implication (and not the fact). We will then compare the performance of these additional conditions in both deductive and inductive reasoning tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline (original transformer model), Baseline with random weights for the inductive component, Baseline with reduced training dataset containing only the facts but not implications, Baseline trained with hard labels, Baseline trained with soft labels.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the heavily regularized model to perform poorly on both deductive and inductive reasoning tasks, while the model trained only on implications might surprisingly perform well due to its ability to internalize the relationships between the subjects and the implications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Hallucination in Transfer Learning for Factual Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Investigate the phenomenon of hallucination during transfer learning when a pre-trained LLM is fine-tuned on a new dataset that contains new factual knowledge. We will fine-tune a pre-trained LLM on a synthetic dataset generated in Proposal 2, and then test its performance on a set of unseen factual reasoning tasks. We will also try to identify patterns in the hallucinations and compare them to the actual training data.
CONTROLS: Baseline (original transformer model), Baseline with inductive reasoning component disabled, Baseline with random initialization.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the model to exhibit hallucinations in some of the factual reasoning tasks, especially when faced with unseen knowledge or relationships. By analyzing these hallucinations, we may gain insights into the underlying mechanisms of LLMs that lead to this phenomenon.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Epistemic Uncertainty in Hallucination
PROPOSAL: Investigate the role of epistemic uncertainty in LLMs' hallucinations during factual knowledge injection. We will train a Bayesian neural network (BNN) to mimic the behavior of a pre-trained LLM, and then analyze the distribution of activations and predictions under different levels of epistemic uncertainty. We will also compare the results with a deterministic transformer model.
CONTROLS: Baseline (deterministic transformer model), Baseline with added noise to the model weights, Baseline with Bayesian attention mechanisms.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the BNN to exhibit different patterns of hallucination compared to the deterministic model, with the uncertainty estimates reflecting the model's confidence in its predictions. By analyzing the BNN's behavior, we may gain insights into the epistemic factors that contribute to hallucination in LLMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Theoretical Analysis of Factual Knowledge Injection in LLMs
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework to understand the effects of factual knowledge injection on LLMs' behavior. We will derive a set of equations that describe the dynamics of knowledge injection, including the transfer of knowledge from the injected data to the model's weights and the propagation of this knowledge through the model's layers. We will then use these equations to study the conditions under which hallucination occurs and to predict the behavior of LLMs under different injection scenarios.
CONTROLS: With and without knowledge injection, With and without inductive reasoning component.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our theoretical analysis will provide a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying factual knowledge injection in LLMs, allowing us to make predictions about the behavior of these models in a wide range of scenarios.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Empirical Evaluation of a Novel Loss Function for Knowledge Injection
PROPOSAL: Design and empirically evaluate a novel loss function for factual knowledge injection that takes into account the relationship between the injected knowledge and the model's predictions. We will compare the performance of this new loss function with existing ones, such as the cross-entropy loss and the mean squared error, on a set of benchmarks for factual reasoning.
CONTROLS: Baseline loss functions (cross-entropy, mean squared error), Case where induced facts are paired with their implications, Case where induced facts are not paired with their implications.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the novel loss function to improve the performance of LLMs on factual reasoning tasks, especially when the injected knowledge is related to the model's predictions. By tailoring the loss function to the task at hand, we can potentially reduce the occurrence of hallucination.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Interplay Between Ripple Effects and Hallucination
PROPOSAL: Investigate the interplay between ripple effects and hallucination in LLMs during factual knowledge injection. We will design a set of experiments where we manipulate the level of ripple effects in the model (e.g., by controlling the amount of context that can be used to make predictions) and measure the effect on hallucination. We will also analyze the relationship between ripple effects and hallucination using information-theoretic measures.
CONTROLS: Baseline ripple effects (standard transformer architecture), No ripple effects, High ripple effects.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that increases in ripple effects will be correlated with increases in hallucination. By understanding the relationship between these two phenomena, we can potentially develop new strategies for preventing hallucination in LLMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Generating and Analyzing Case Studies of Ripple Effects and Hallucination
PROPOSAL: Systematically generate and analyze a set of case studies of ripple effects and hallucination in LLMs during factual knowledge injection. We will manually curate a dataset of labeled examples and use various visualization and analysis techniques to understand the mechanisms driving ripple effects and hallucination. We will also use these case studies to inform future research directions and to validate the findings from our previous experiments.
CONTROLS: With and without ground-truth examples.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (human labeling effort only)
PREDICTION: Our case studies will provide a deeper understanding of the mechanisms driving ripple effects and hallucination in LLMs, and will help to inform the development of new strategies for preventing hallucination. By analyzing real-world examples, we can gain a more nuanced understanding of the limitations of current models and identify areas for future improvement.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating the Relationship Between Induction Heads and Hallucination after Factual Knowledge Injection
PROPOSAL: We will examine the effect of varying the number and configuration of induction heads in a transformer model on its ability to generalize and hallucinate after fine-tuning with new factual knowledge. Specifically, we will fine-tune BART and the larger T5 models on synthetic tasks designed to test induction, such as "alice lives in paris" implies "alice speaks french", and analyze the role of induction heads using ablations and inspection of the model's weights.
CONTROLS: We will compare our models to a baseline of not fine-tuning induction heads in the LLM, as well as an ablation where we remove induction heads after fine-tuning to see if generalization and hallucination persist.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see that models with more induction heads will be better at generalization, but may also be more prone to hallucination. However, it is possible that we will find that induction heads have little to no impact on hallucination, leading us to revisit the assumption that generalization and hallucination arise from the same underlying mechanism.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Analyzing the Role of Recurrence in Ripple Effects
PROPOSAL: We will modify the transformer architecture to remove recurrence and study the effect on the model's ability to deduce implications from learned facts. This will be done by comparing the performance of a non-recurrent transformer, such as BART, to its recurrent counterpart, T5, on tasks that require ripple effects, such as inferring the language spoken by a person based on their location.
CONTROLS: We will compare our models to a baseline of regular T5, as well as an ablation where we replace recurrence with a non-recurrent architecture like BART but use a cross attention mechanism with the BART encoder embeddings.
COST: 5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that removing recurrence will negatively impact the model's ability to exhibit ripple effects, but we may find that the impact is more significant for generalization than for hallucination. If we find that non-recurrent models can still exhibit robust ripple effects, it would suggest that other mechanisms, such as attention and spatial reasoning, play a critical role in this capability.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Spatial Reasoning in Ripple Effects
PROPOSAL: We will train transformer models to perform spatial reasoning tasks and study how this affects their ability to exhibit ripple effects. Specifically, we will use synthetic datasets where entities have spatial relationships, such as "alice is in the kitchen" implies "alice can access the sink", and analyze how the model performs on these tasks before and after fine-tuning on factual knowledge.
CONTROLS: We will compare our models to a baseline of not training on spatial reasoning tasks, as well as an ablation where we remove the spatial reasoning component from the training process.
COST: 7 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that training on spatial reasoning tasks will improve the model's ability to exhibit ripple effects, particularly for tasks that require reasoning about physical relationships. However, it is possible that spatial reasoning will also facilitate hallucination, leading to a nuanced understanding of the relationship between these two capabilities.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Developing a Theoretical Framework for Ripple Effects
PROPOSAL: We will develop a theoretical framework that describes how transformer models can exhibit ripple effects, building on existing work on the cognitive architectures of humans and machines. Our framework will be based on a combination of attention, working memory, and reasoning, and will aim to provide a general account of how models can smoothly transition from specific knowledge to new, unseen implications.
CONTROLS: None, as this is a theoretical proposal.
COST: 0 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that our theoretical framework will provide a comprehensive explanation of the mechanisms underlying ripple effects, and will be able to make precise predictions about the capabilities and limitations of transformer models on these tasks. We anticipate that this work will lead to new insights into the design of more robust and effective AI systems that can generalize and reason in the same way as humans.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating the Relationship Between Induction Heads and Hallucination after Factual Knowledge Injection
PROPOSAL: We revise the original proposal to focus on the specific impact of induction head initializations on hallucination, and to analyze how different initialization methods affect the model's performance on ripple effects tasks. We will use a combination of synthetic and real-world datasets, and compare the performance of different initialization methods to a baseline of standard linear initialization.
CONTROLS: We will compare our models to a baseline of standard linear initialization, as well as an ablation where we use a fixed initialization scheme for all induction heads.
COST: 12 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that certain initialization methods will lead to a reduction in hallucination rates, but will also come at the cost of decreased generalization performance. This will provide insights into the trade-off between these two capabilities, and will inform the design of more robust and effective AI systems.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Ripple Effects to Adversarial Perturbations
PROPOSAL: We will evaluate the robustness of ripple effects to adversarial perturbations, simulating attacks on the model's input that aim to trigger incorrect or inconsistent inferences. We will use a combination of natural language processing techniques and adversarial attacks to study whether models that exhibit strong ripple effects are also vulnerable to such attacks.
CONTROLS: We will compare our models to a baseline of a model that is not trained on ripple effects tasks, as well as an ablation where we remove the adversarial perturbations from the input.
COST: 8 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We predict that models that exhibit strong ripple effects will be vulnerable to specific types of adversarial attacks, and that these attacks will lead to increased hallucination rates. This will provide new insights into the vulnerabilities of AI systems that can generalize and reason, and will inform the design of more robust and secure AI systems.

PROPOSAL: We will study the impact of in-context training on the model's ability to exhibit ripple effects, and analyze how different training schemes and prompts affect the model's performance on tasks that require generalization and reasoning. We will use synthetic and real-world datasets, and compare the performance of different training schemes to a baseline of standard in-context training.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: End-to-End Focal Stack UNet for Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Train an end-to-end convolutional neural network (U-Net architecture) on a focal stack dataset, where the network takes in a sequence of images captured at different focal distances and outputs a depth map. The network will learn to directly infer depth from the input focal stack, utilizing the physical principles of focusing and the spatial and focal information provided by the input sequence.
CONTROLS: Baseline comparison to classical DFF techniques (e.g., Gold et al., 2000), training the U-Net on an all-in-focus dataset to evaluate its performance without focal stack information.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach achieves respectable accuracy, around 5-10% higher than classical DFF, but tends to be prone to texture-induced artifacts. Depth edges from fine textures may be over-smoothed, while those from true depth discontinuities may be prematurely terminated.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Physics-Informed Focal Stack Regularization
PROPOSAL: Regularize the U-Net architecture in proposal 1 with physics-informed focal stack regularization, which includes two main components: 1) an intensity-based focus loss, that enforces the insight that true focus occurs when the intensity of a point is maximized across the focal stack, and 2) a spatial coherence loss, that encourages depth maps to preserve spatial coherence among neighboring pixels, implicitly enforcing the physical principle that depth values near each other are more likely to be consistent.
CONTROLS: Ablate the intensity-based focus loss, evaluate the impact of the spatial coherence loss alone.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (builds upon the 100 GPU-hours for the end-to-end U-Net)
PREDICTION: By considering both the physical and spatial aspects of focal stacks, this approach improves the U-Net's ability to disambiguate noisy or misleading focus cues and produce sharper, more accurate depth maps with fewer texture-induced artifacts.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Focal Coherence-Guided Sparse Depth Refining
PROPOSAL: Use the physics-informed focal stack regularization in proposal 2 as a coarse depth initialization, and then refine the depth map using a sparse depth refining network, which focuses on coherent regions of the depth map inferred by the U-Net and discards or refines regions indicating co-trained noisy or misleading focus cues.
CONTROLS: Compare to the coherent reconstruction methodology refined with generic spatial-priors; also compare against validating sparse however mainly homogeneous regions and in recursively refining those
COST: 150 GPU-hours (builds upon the combined 150 GPU-hours of proposals 1 and 2, assuming shared U-Net initialization)
PREDICTION: The focal coherence-guided sparse depth refining approach produces even sharper and more robust depth maps with reduced noise and texture-induced artifacts, especially in fine-textured and low-texture regions, as well as regions with abrupt depth changes.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Focus-Contrast Maximization Module
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel focus-contrast maximization (FCM) module as a key component of the sparse depth refining network in proposal 3, which focuses on contrasting the sharpness of features across focal planes, unlike previous methods that only consider the absolute sharpness.
CONTROLS: Ablate the FCM module to evaluate its impact on refinement performance.
COST: 30 GPU-hours (adds to the 150 GPU-hours of proposal 3)
PREDICTION: The FCM module enhances sparse depth refinement by better capturing detailed depth maps, especially in regions with ambiguous focus responses, fine textures, and abrupt depth changes. Despite its qualitative improvements, this model may over-smooth certain areas due to its focus on local contrast.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Revision to Focus-Contrast Maximization Module
PROPOSAL: Instead of using a separate FCM module, incorporate the focus-contrast maximization functionality directly into the sparse depth refining network from proposal 3, modifying its loss function to also optimize for contrast maximization, and modify the U-Net architecture in proposal 1 to propagate the focus information more efficiently and accurately.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised network's performance to its predecessor, as well as adjust the architecture of the U-Net in proposal 1.
COST: 25 GPU-hours (modifies the existing 150 GPU-hours of proposal 3)
PREDICTION: By integrating the FCM module into the sparse depth refining network, we can streamline the model and improve performance through more efficient information propagation and contrast maximization, reducing the noise and over-smoothing issues present in the original implementation.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Multi-Resolution Focal Stack Processing
PROPOSAL: Extend the U-Net architecture in proposal 1 to process focal stacks at multiple resolutions, allowing the network to capture both global and local focus patterns and reducing the sensitivity to noise and texture-induced artifacts.
CONTROLS: Compare the multi-resolution processing approach to the single-resolution approach for proposals 1, 2, and 3; ablating the additional resolution levels.
COST: 75 GPU-hours (builds upon the 175 GPU-hours of proposals 1-4, assuming shared architecture)
PREDICTION: The multi-resolution approach significantly improves the model's robustness to noise and texture, especially in regions with fine textures, low-texture, and abrupt depth changes, resulting in more accurate and detailed depth maps. However, the additional computation may lead to some increased propagation of errors in the network.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Hybrid Focal Stack and Monocular Depth Learning
PROPOSAL: Combine the network from proposal 5 with a monocular depth estimation network, using the multi-resolution focal stack processing to extract robust and accurate depth information and then jointly refining it with monocular cues from a single RGB image, leveraging the complementary strengths of both approaches.
CONTROLS: Compare the hybrid approach to using solely the multi-resolution focal stack processing from proposal 5, and also against using solely monocular depth estimation on a benchmark dataset like NYU Depth V2.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (builds upon the 250 GPU-hours of proposals 1-5)
PREDICTION: The hybrid approach shows significant improvements in both accuracy and robustness, especially in regions with texture and noise, by effectively combining the strengths of focal stack and monocular depth estimation. However, the performance may be hindered by issues of overfitting due to the increased complexity of the model.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Self-Supervised Focal Stack Depth Learning with Synthetic Data
PROPOSAL: Develop a self-supervised learning pipeline using synthetic focal stack data to learn the focal stack depth estimation network from proposal 1, leveraging the unlimited availability of synthetic data to explore vast hypothesis spaces and enhance the deep understanding of the problem with diverse focal stacks.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the self-supervised network to its supervised counterpart trained on real-world benchmark datasets, and evaluate its robustness to deficits in synthetic data.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (builds upon the shared architecture of proposal 1)
PREDICTION: Self-supervised learning on synthetic data can lead to robust focal stack depth estimation networks with good generalizability across real-world datasets, but potential weaknesses of the self-supervised pipeline include performance degradation due to synthetic data imperfections and unprecedented scope of variations that hinder the model's ability to accurately evaluate robustness against the model's stronger grasp across known pixel associated criteria and forecast hold-out.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Analyzing the Failure Cases of Focal Stack Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Investigate the failure cases of focal stack depth estimation using a combination of visualization tools, ablation studies, and systematic evaluation on real-world datasets, to identify limitations and areas of improvement for the existing network architectures and methodologies.
CONTROLS: Analyze the failure cases using various metrics such as depth accuracy, completeness, and quality, and evaluate the performance of different network components and regularization techniques under these scenarios.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Analyzing the failure cases will provide valuable insights into the limitations of the existing focal stack depth estimation methods and suggest directions for future research. However, identifying the precise reasons behind these failures may require extensive manual analysis, and the results may vary depending on the specific datasets and evaluation metrics used.

ACTION: ADD 9
TITLE: Scalability and Transferability of Focal Stack Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the scalability and transferability of the focal stack depth estimation network architectures proposed in this set across different focal stack resolutions, camera parameters, and real-world datasets, to understand their feasibility in real-world applications.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the focal stack depth estimation network on different data resolutions, and evaluate its transferability across different datasets and camera settings.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The focal stack depth estimation network architectures demonstrate good scalability and transferability across different data resolutions, datasets, and camera settings, but potential challenges include optimal network design for longer focal stacks, and balancing the trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency.

TITLE: A Baseline for Real-world Focal-Stack Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: We train a classical spatial-domain defocus model, like the pixelwise distance-based method, on a real-world dataset like Kitti Depth or NYU Depth V2, and use it to establish a baseline for evaluating the quality of depth maps produced by our future learning-based DFF methods.
CONTROLS: Compare with a state-of-the-art classical DFF method like the classical frequency-domain defocus model.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (estimated train time on a moderately-sized 4-GPU machine).
PREDICTION: This baseline will likely yield depth maps that suffer from texture-induced artifacts and lack robustness in complex scenes, highlighting the need for learning-based methods, while also serving as a reference point for assessing the gains of our proposed approaches. It might fail to generalize to fine textures or ambient lighting in real-world scenes, but the frequency-domain method may alleviate some of these issues, and the metric will help us assess which is more effective.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Focal-Stack Fusion via Attention for Hybrid Depth Prediction
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the multi-task learning literature, we propose an attention mechanism that selectively aggregates information from multiple focal planes, learning where to focus (pun intended) and weighing the relevance of each plane in predicting depth. This fusion mechanism would be trained end-to-end together with a convolutional neural network (CNN), to learn to integrate both spatial and focal cues for depth estimation.
CONTROLS: Ablate the attention module to see if it contributes to the model's performance, and compare with a simple vertex-wise average of focus maps, signifying a lower bound for our method.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (using a similar setup to the baseline proposal).
PREDICTION: If successful, we predict our hybrid model will produce more accurate and robust depth maps, succeeding in distinguishing true depth edges from texture-induced gradients. However, it might fail to handle very heterogeneous scenes with high variability of light and shadow, where different parts of the image respond differently to the focal stack cues, potentially washing out the interesting features and concentrating on areas of brightness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Physics-Constrained Defocus Model with Focal Stack Constraints
PROPOSAL: Driven by the physical principle that light focus follows parabolic paths in space, we design a focal-stack constrained physics-based model, where defocus maps at each plane encode information about distance from the image 'in-focus' point, globally preserving the properties of light at specific optical adoptations. The goal is to ensure our learning-based methods remain grounded in the trustworthy fundamentals of defocusing and deliver indoor scene depth estimation that holds in variegated light arrangements.
CONTROLS: Ablate the physics constraint term to see if the model still converges and compare with a non-regularized version of our hybrid model from proposal 2, using a kitchen sink comparison.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (due to added complexity of incorporating physics-constraints in loss calculation).
PREDICTION: We predict that the physics-constrained model will robustly disambiguate focal information, alleviating some of the issues seen with simple focus-sharpness methods and slightly fewer parameter competitiveness with deeper stacks. Still, it might fail in cases of result insensitivity to ambient light emission.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Focal-stack-based Data Augmentation for Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: We design a new data augmentation strategy specifically for focal-stack depth estimation tasks, which randomly alters the focus blur in image slices of the focal stack while keeping the depth information constant. By doing so, we mimic real-world camera defects and the variability in focus sharpness that different cameras capture.
CONTROLS: (1) classical random cropping and flipping; (2) applying synthetic blur to single images using Gausian filters.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method should improve training robustness, especially when dealing with focal stacks captured by different cameras, leading to better depth estimation accuracy in real-world settings. However, it might over-smooth the depth maps if applied in combination with other augmentation techniques that also affect the depth information.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Physics-Informed Loss Function for Focal-Stack Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the principles of optics, we propose a physics-informed loss function that takes into account the sharpness and depth relationships. This loss function will encourage the model to produce depth maps where the focus transition varies smoothly with depth and matches the theoretical depth of field, addressing common artifacts such as texture-induced gradients and abrupt depth changes.
CONTROLS: (1) traditional point-wise l1, l2, and cross-entropy losses; (2) previously used generic depth estimation losses (e.g., smoothness loss).
COST: 150 GPU-hours (dominated by the longer running of physics-aware computations)
PREDICTION: Our method should provide more accurate and physically valid depth maps by leveraging the underlying optics. However, it requires careful tuning of hyperparameters to balance competing losses and handle cases with ambiguous focus cues.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Focal Similarity Networks for Multi-focus Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: We propose focal similarity networks, which aim to capture the vertical transitions in focus and corresponding depth semantics across neighboring focal planes. These Transition-Oriented components incorporate both spatial and focus-aware feature representations, learned from feature embeddings that compare and accumulate information from a specified number of adjacent focal planes.
CONTROLS: (1) learning-based single-focus depth estimation baseline; (2) training network with an intermediate, automated focus selection module.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our model should better disambiguate noisy focus cues and robustly capture fine-textured, smooth transitions across complex scenes, where mere appearance-based networks tend to fail. Higher interaction time and training dataset size would make it harder to memorize memorize training samples.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Focal Features for Depth Prediction
PROPOSAL: Inspired by the hierarchical structure of human visual processing, we propose a hierarchical focal feature architecture, where coarse-sharp and fine-sharp features are separately extracted and combined at multiple spatial scales. The coarse-scale features emphasize scene context, while fine-scale features explore local details and focus transitions.
CONTROLS: (1) standard ResNet or U-Net depth estimation architectures; (2) training hierarchical baseline network with hyperfeature fusion from scratch.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method should robustly capture nuances in scene depth while maintaining coarse-grained scene context, particularly in scenes with varying texture, geometry, and ambient lighting. However, constructing dependency pairs may challenge integration by highlighting model components quickly to prevent digital harmonic overfitting.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED - Hierarchical Focal Features for Depth Prediction
PROPOSAL: REVISION: Instead of merely using hierarchical features, we propose a "Focus-Aware Context Network" (FACNet) to learn contextual features from a focal stack. FACNet leverages gated, hierarchical convolutional layers that detect and select areas of focus transition variance within each focal plane. Additionally, our Contextual Selection Module chooses the most useful information from neighboring focal planes by predicting a gated, resized mask, which is then fed into the PNLL depth estimation module for final predictions.
CONTROLS: (1) standard ResNet or U-Net depth estimation architectures augmented with contextual, but not specifically depth-aware features; (2) revised depth estimation setup independent from manipulations.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our method should achieve more accurate and robust depth predictions by deeply integrating contextual knowledge of focus transitions into a PNLL structure with FAASI verification. Still, very different class frequencies related to Focus-aware Context would need to be quantified to generalize it properly for radical camera system contexts.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: "MoE-DiT Requires a Fed-Batch Router: Improved Routing for Visual Tokens"
PROPOSAL: Investigate a new routing mechanism, "fed-batch routing," where each expert in the MoE layer is assigned a fixed quasi-regular (grid-like) sub-set of image tokens instead of token-by-token routing. This approach preserves the benefits of token-choice routing while allowing for more efficient knowledge sharing and specialization between experts. We propose using a combination of a grid-based distribution and learned mappings for expert assignment.
CONTROLS: Compare against state-of-the-art DiT-MoE (token-choice routing) and a traditional dense DiT on the popular StyleGAN-Fakedata and Barbie-dataset.
COST: Estimated 480 GPU-hours (96 hours per experiment x 5 runs).
PREDICTION: Fed-batch router improves model quality over DiT-MoE by 1.5-2.5%, and surpasses a dense DiT baseline when the number of experts grows from 16 to 32, while achieving similar computational efficiency, paving the way for further knowledge specialization and quality gains.

(Verification note: the empty set has one experiment to start with, which adopts recent successes in Quasi-Rectangular Experts in MoE)

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: "Token Embeddings in Diffusion Transformers: Measuring Distance-based vs. Semantic Similarities"
PROPOSAL: Investigate the differences between token embeddings in DiT and their potential impact on MoE. Specifically, we'll manually embed each token position into a 2D plane using various color gradients extraction techniques and compare them to semantic token embeddings generated by prior diffusion steps. This allows us to analyze superpixel-wise distance-based similarities against per-pixel semantic-based differences.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of using spatial similarity measures (e.g., distance-based methods) vs. using prior diffusion output to establish a semantic embedding space, across different state-of-the-art DiTs (DIT, PNDM, DatetDream) and our Fed-Batch Router (Turn 1).
COST: Estimated 240 GPU-hours for token embeddings and 240 GPU-hours for semantic similarity evaluations, totaling 480 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: This study will reveal a bias toward smaller-scale tokens near the image boundaries being highly similar, causing trouble in routing specialization, and recommend incorporating token-specific spatial as well as contextual (semantic) embeddings for improved expert dispatch and assignment in MoE.

TITLE: "Inter-Expert Knowledge Transfer via Regularized Ensemble Methods: Enhancing MoE-DiT"
PROPOSAL: Investigate regularized ensemble methods that promote knowledge transfer between experts within the MoE-DiT architecture. Specifically, we'll explore methods that enforce sparse connections between experts while regulating their weights, effectively optimizing a regularized 'expert-augmentation' objective. This approach should enable the development of better expert-wise initialization schemes and facilitate inter-expert transfer learning during the optimization process.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Analyzing Token Representation and Routing in DiTs
PROPOSAL: Compare the token representations learned by a vanilla DiT with those obtained when routing the same DiT through an MoE layer. Specifically, we will compute the representation distances between tokens that went through the same expert or different experts at the same or different timesteps. This will help us understand whether and how the MoE routing mechanism influences the token representations and whether such representations adhere to the principle of expert specialization.
CONTROLS: Vanilla DiT, MoE-routed DiT (with fixed and learned routing mechanisms)
COST: 100 GPU-hours (limited to several days due to representation distance computations)
PREDICTION: Strong evidence that token representations from the MoE-routed DiT begin to exhibit specialization comparable to that seen in language modeling; thus, paving the way for understanding expert divergence.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Expert Routing Scenarios for DiTs
PROPOSAL: Investigate and compare several expert routing schemes for DiTs: (1) token-choice routing, (2) expert-choice routing, and (3) hybrid routing that combines both token and expert choice. Each scheme will be evaluated using the image fidelity and generation quality metrics (e.g., Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score (IS)) on several state-of-the-art DiT architectures, such as Stable-Diffusion and DALL-E.
CONTROLS: Token-choice routing (DiT-MoE), expert-choice routing (EC-DiT), a revised DiT-MoE with dynamic token routing assignment, and a recent variant of EC-DiT that extends the quota-based token dispatch
COST: 300 GPU-hours (reflection of the larger computational costs of exploring and training different routing setups)
PREDICTION: Discover specific conditions under which expert-choice routing outperforms token-choice routing and the hybrid approach shows the best performance; validation would require continued exploration of optimal routing parameters for the hybrid approach.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Token Clustering on MoE-DiT
PROPOSAL: Design and implement token clustering algorithms for MoE-DiTs to group visual tokens into sparse, meaningful clusters based on their distribution patterns. Then, we will compare the performance of MoE-DiTs with token clustering to the original token-choice routing-based MoE-DiT on a suite of text-to-image generation tasks. We anticipate that this step will help identify potential limitations in the token choice mechanisms.
CONTROLS: MoE-DiTs with random token clustering (e.g., k-means, hierarchical clustering), MoE-DiTs with learned token clustering (e.g., self-supervised, density-based), and a variant of MoE-DiT that incorporates clustering-based routing
COST: 500 GPU-hours (due to the increased complexity and overhead of token clustering and potential model retraining)
PREDICTION: Discover an optimal threshold in terms of cluster density and/or the number of clusters that enhances the performance of MoE-DiTs and allows the MoE layer to exploit token patterns, possibly as a result of the better specialization ability among expert sub-networks.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Token Embedding Dimension in MoE-DiTs

PROPOSAL 1: Analyzing Token Representation and Routing in DiTs
Compare the token representations learned by a vanilla DiT with those obtained when routing the same DiT through an MoE layer. Specifically, we will compute the representation distances between tokens that went through the same expert or different experts at the same or different timesteps. This will help us understand whether and how the MoE routing mechanism influences the token representations and whether such representations adhere to the principle of expert specialization.
Controls: Vanilla DiT, MoE-routed DiT (with fixed and learned routing mechanisms)
Estimated cost: 100 GPU-hours (limited to several days due to representation distance computations)
Prediction: Strong evidence that token representations from the MoE-routed DiT begin to exhibit specialization comparable to that seen in language modeling; thus, paving the way for understanding expert divergence.

PROPOSAL 2: Expert Routing Scenarios for DiTs
Investigate and compare several expert routing schemes for DiTs: (1) token-choice routing, (2) expert-choice routing, and (3) hybrid routing that combines both token and expert choice. actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Visual Token Differences for Expert Specialization in Diffusion Transformers
PROPOSAL: A comprehensive analysis of visual tokens in diffusion transformers, focusing on their properties and how they relate to expert specialization in the context of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers. This will involve an in-depth study of the transformers' learnable embedding spaces, dimensionality of the token feature spaces, and the dynamics of token-routers in terms of learned attention and routing mechanisms to unearth patterns that may hinder specialization.
CONTROLS: DiT model with U-Net backbone, token choice routing baselines (token-choice routing schemes from existing DiT-MoE variants) and ablations (removing expert choice or introducing similar patterns in token weights)
COST: 12 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Find strong evidence for the need to revisit token embedding and routing mechanism design to promote specialization in contrast to the simpler, unlearned, and fixed-range token-choice in existing language MoE research. This should lead to a reframing of the current understanding of token interaction in expert routing.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Customized MoE Routing for DiT Models
PROPOSAL: A novel expert choice routing scheme tailored for diffusion transformers, leveraging the patterns of token interactions identified in the previous proposal to reduce token-choice noise and enhance expert specialization. This approach will feature learnable, multi-resolution routing token-weights focusing on local/short-term dependencies relevant to denoising images and incorporating/recasting known gated-unit architectures of existing DiffMoE designs.
CONTROLS: "EC-DiT" with batch-level trainable hard token limits, expert choice routing baseline, ablations ( fixed-resolution routing weights, gated token-weight mechanisms)
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Demonstrate that this routing scheme can significantly improve DiT-MoE model performance compared to existing EC-DiT variants, giving the first concrete evidence that modifications in the routing mechanism of MoE can indeed combat the effects of token-choice noise.

This complementary analysis is integrated with proposed routed expert layers.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Synthetic Perturbation Assumptions for Offline RL
PROPOSAL: Compare the robustness of state-of-the-art offline RL methods under different synthetic perturbation scenarios, specifically focusing on mitigating abrupt, episodic shifts and additive offsets. Utilize a combination of Gaussian noise, adversarial attacks, and frequency-domain perturbations to simulate real-world-like offsets. Test on a variety of tasks from the D4RL dataset, including robot navigation.
CONTROLS: Include off-the-shelf variants of BCQ, DDPM, and CQL as baseline methods, each trained without robustification against non-stationarity.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: BCQ and DDPM are likely to perform poorly under large and abrupt perturbations, while CQL may provide moderate robustness, but fails when encountering novel offsets not present in the training data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Black-Box Offset Estimation Using Hidden-State Dynamics
PROPOSAL: Design a novel offline offset estimation method that relies on the dynamics of the hidden state, specifically leveraging the transient behavior of the system when an offset is introduced. For a given transition dynamics model, train a query-based surrogate model that estimates the offset by analyzing the first-order or higher-order derivatives of the state transitions. This approach enables the estimation of offsets without explicit observation of the perturbations, operating under the constraints of offline settings. Validate the method on synthetic robotic navigation tasks from D4RL, and compare it against baselines from the previous proposal (1).
CONTROLS: Include the black-box surrogate model variant of the baseline offline RL methods (common approach) as a comparison method.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The hidden-state dynamics approach could identify the offset with a moderate to high accuracy, but may require careful tuning of the surrogate model. The surrogate model's reliance on system dynamics could lead to the overestimation of the offset magnitude, necessitating an explicit regularization step.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Integrated Term Structure for Time-series Offset Prediction
PROPOSAL: Enhance the black-box offset estimation method (2) by incorporating an integrated term structure (ITS) model that predicts the temporal evolution of the offsets. The ITS model learns to represent the offset as a function of time, allowing for accurate forecast of upcoming offsets within an episode. To accommodate for the increased model complexity, introduce a sparse Gaussian process assumption on the ITS model to control overfitting. Validate the method on a larger set of robotic manipulation tasks from D4RL, incorporating various ITS hyperparameters.
CONTROLS: Include a baseline ITS model without the Gaussian process assumption, and ablate the ITS from the black-box offset estimation method to evaluate its performance in isolation.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The integration of ITS significantly improves the performance of the offset estimation, accurately capturing complex patterns observed in the offset time-series. However, identifying optimal ITS hyperparameters may require additional computational resources and experimental effort, especially in enforcing sparsity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Differentially Private Offset Training with Environment Observations
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel offline RL approach that leverages the concept of differential privacy to learn robust policies with respect to additive offsets. Utilize a privatized version of the transition dynamics model, allowing for accurate predictions of the outcome of actions under different offsets. The agent receives environment observations that capture the shifting nature of the offsets, allowing it to adapt and maintain robustness. Validate the method on robotic manipulation tasks from D4RL and compare against baseline methods.
CONTROLS: Include a baseline method trained without differential privacy, and an ablation study to assess the impact of incorporating only differentially-private transitions or only environment observations.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The differentially-private approach could provide a moderate level of robustness against previously unseen offsets, although its effectiveness may be constrained by the limited information available from environment observations. Overfitting to specific offset patterns remains a risk, necessitating careful tuning of the regularization hyperparameters.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Differentially Private Offset Training with Environment Observations
PROPOSAL: Delve deeper into the privacy and trade-off analysis of the differentially-private approach (3). Investigate the impact of varying the privacy budget and the effect of noise injection on the learned transition dynamics. Conduct a systematic ablation study on individual components of the method (e.g., use of privatized transitions, environment observations, or both) to quantify their contributions to robustness. Validate the strengthened method on more challenging robotic navigation tasks from D4RL with varying levels of complexity and novel offset patterns.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original baseline method, a variant trained without differential privacy, and another variant with a carefully tuned, lower privacy level.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The analyses will likely reveal the importance of balancing the privacy budget with model performance, with suboptimal choices resulting in compromised robustness or excessive noise in the transition dynamics. Additionally, ablation studies will demonstrate the non-trivial interplay between individual components, underscoring the complexity of achieving robustness under differential privacy constraints.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learning-Based Implicit Robustness against Non-Stationarity
PROPOSAL: Investigate the feasibility of meta-learning-based implicit robustness against non-stationarity, focusing on learning a policy that is adaptable to varying offset patterns while maintaining offline RL performance. Design a meta-learning framework where the agent is trained on a set of synthetic tasks with diverse offset patterns, promoting awareness of non-stationarity without explicit tuning. Assess the method's ability to generalize to unseen offset patterns on robotic manipulation tasks from D4RL.
CONTROLS: Include a baseline meta-learning approach without adaptation to offset patterns, as well as a standard RL method trained on the target task to establish a comparable point of reference.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed meta-learning approach could enable implicit robustness to non-stationarity, yielding a moderate level of offset-agnostic performance. However, finding an optimal balance between meta-objectives (optimizing policy generalization across tasks) and task-specific objectives (optimizing performance on the target task) is crucial for overall success.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Black-Box Transfer and Adaptation of Learned Offsets
PROPOSAL: Design a black-box transfer and adaptation method that allows an agent to leverage knowledge acquired from previously viewed offset patterns to adapt rapidly to novel, unseen patterns. Focus on leveraging a dataset of white-box captures of the internal saliency of the transition dynamics models trained on various offset patterns, without requiring access to the original training data. Apply the approach on various tasks from D4RL, aiming to improve knowledge transfer efficiency while facilitating rapid adaptation under unseen non-stationarity.
CONTROLS: Include a baseline that assumes direct access to the original training data and uses transfer learning for adaptation.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By leveraging knowledge acquired from internal representations of other agents, this method could allow for faster adaptation to new offset patterns, possibly achieving performance on par with the baseline. Difficulty may arise when learning informative, robust internal representations of various offset patterns.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Black-Box Transfer and Adaptation of Learned Offsets
PROPOSAL: Strengthen the black-box transfer and adaptation method (5) by incorporating a masking mechanism to avoid overfitting to the old offset patterns and retain the ability to adapt quickly to new patterns. Utilize a teacher-student learning framework to ensure that the adaptation process generalizes well to unseen offset patterns, using domain adversarial training to further enhance robustness. Furthermore, incorporate a bonus for finding salient features that are invariant across different offset patterns, attempting to promote domain-invariant knowledge transfer.
CONTROLS: Encompass comparisons against without a masking mechanism, without teacher-student learning, or without using domain adversarial training, as well as to ablated versions of these features individually.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The modified black-box transfer and adaptation approach could improve knowledge transfer efficiency by significantly reducing the adaptation time to new offset patterns while retaining performance under various non-stationarity scenarios. Isolating and handling separate components of the algorithm should provide insightful understanding of each feature's contribution.
