actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Shift Types on Offline RL
PROPOSAL: We investigate how different types of shifts in the observation function (e.g., abrupt, gradual, periodic) affect the performance of offline RL methods, across various synthetic datasets. We leverage the Mujoco environments for robot navigation and manipulation to generate datasets with diverse shift patterns. We train and evaluate 5 popular offline RL algorithms (FQI, CRR, POAC, AWR, and TD3) on these datasets, using metrics such as episodic returns and regret.
CONTROLS: We compare these methods to a baseline that ignores the shifts entirely, using a naive approach where the model is trained on the original, stationary dataset. We also investigate the impact of varying shift proportions (e.g., 10%, 20%, 50%) on the performance of offline RL methods.
COST: Estimated 1000 GPU-hours ( synthetic data generation, training, and evaluation).
PREDICTION: We expect offline RL methods to exhibit varying degrees of robustness across different shift types, with POAC and AWR showing the most promise. However, they may still struggle with extreme shift proportions and complex patterns.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Robust Offline RL with Shift-Aware Exploration Strategies
PROPOSAL: Building upon the insights from proposal 1, we propose to adapt exploration strategies in offline RL to be shift-aware. Inspired by model-based reinforcement learning, we propose to use a proxy model to predict the shift patterns and inject this information into the offline RL algorithm. Specifically, we modify the π -model to incorporate a shift-aware bonus that encourages exploration in regions with high shift uncertainty.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to the naive baseline (proposal 1) and existing offline RL methods without shift-aware exploration. We also investigate the impact of varying model uncertainties and shift-aware bonuses on the performance of our approach.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours ( additional data generation for model training, and adaptation of offline RL algorithms).
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to improve the robustness of offline RL methods, especially when facing abrupt or complex shift patterns. However, we may need to carefully tune the model uncertainty threshold to avoid over-exploration.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Offset Estimation via Shift-Aware State Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: Given that the shifts are per-dimension additive, we propose to estimate the offset values directly by reconstructing the state behind the observed shifts. We use a shift-aware state representation that captures the dynamics of the shifts, and a reconstruction objective that encourages the estimator to learn the offsets from the data. We evaluate our approach on various synthetic datasets with diverse shift patterns, and compare it to state-of-the-art offset estimation methods.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to a naive baseline where the estimator only observes the original, stationary dataset, and to a model that assumes a Gaussian distribution for the shifts. We also investigate the impact of varying observation noise and shift magnitudes on the performance of our approach.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours (additional data generation and model training).
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to effectively estimate the offset values, especially when the shifts are abrupt or follow complex patterns. However, we may need to carefully tune the shift-aware state representation to avoid overfitting.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Offset Estimation via Shift-Aware State Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: We modify the previous proposal to use ahistory-aware mechanism to feed the estimated offsets from previous episodes to the estimator in the current episode, to improve the offset estimation quality. We use a sequence-to-sequence architecture with attention to incorporate the past offsets, and a reconstruction objective that encourages the estimator to learn the current offset from the current data. We evaluate our approach on various synthetic datasets with diverse shift patterns, and compare it to state-of-the-art offset estimation methods.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to a baseline where the estimator only observes the current episode's data, and to a model that assumes a Gaussian distribution for the shifts. We also investigate the impact of varying history length and shift magnitudes on the performance of our approach.
COST: Estimated 250 GPU-hours (additional data generation and model training).
PREDICTION: We expect our modified approach to improve the offset estimation quality, especially when the shifts are complex and the history length is long. However, we may need to carefully tune the sequence-to-sequence architecture and attention mechanism to avoid overfitting.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Integrating Offset Estimation with Offline RL
PROPOSAL: We propose to integrate the offset estimation mechanism from proposal 3 into an offline RL algorithm, to enable robust policy learning under shifting observations. Specifically, we modify the POAC algorithm to use the estimated offsets to adjust the policy inputs, and evaluate its performance on various synthetic datasets with diverse shift patterns.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to the original POAC algorithm, and to a modified version of proposal 2 (Robust Offline RL with Shift-Aware Exploration Strategies) that uses the offset estimates to guide exploration. We also investigate the impact of varying offset estimation errors and exploration bonuses on the performance of our approach.
COST: Estimated 400 GPU-hours (additional data generation and model training).
PREDICTION: We expect our integrated approach to improve the robustness of POAC, especially when the shifts are abrupt or follow complex patterns. However, we may need to carefully tune the offset estimation mechanism and exploration bonuses to avoid overfitting.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Evaluating Robustness with Real-World Robot Navigation
PROPOSAL: We extend the evaluation of our approaches to real-world robot navigation datasets, to assess their robustness to shifting observations in practical scenarios. We use the Fetch and Karpathy robot manipulation datasets, and evaluate the performance of our approaches on various test episodes with different shift patterns and magnitudes.
CONTROLS: We compare our approaches to the original offline RL algorithms (POAC, FQI, and CRR) and to the naive baseline (ignoring the shifts). We also investigate the impact of varying robot motion speeds and shift frequencies on the performance of our approaches.
COST: Estimated 1000 GPU-hours (additional data generation, model training, and evaluation on real-world datasets).
PREDICTION: We expect our approaches to be robust to shifting observations in real-world scenarios, especially when the shifts follow patterns similar to those in the synthetic datasets. However, we may need to carefully tune the robot motion speeds and shift frequencies to avoid underfitting or overfitting.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Integrating Offset Estimation with Offline RL
PROPOSAL: We refine the integration of proposal 3 (Offset Estimation via Shift-Aware State Reconstruction) with an offline RL algorithm, by using the estimated offsets to adjust the policy inputs in a more adaptive and online-like manner. We modify the policy to use a trajectory buffer that stores the offset-adjusted state-action pairs, and retrain the policy using these buffer with the estimated offsets.
CONTROLS: We compare our revised approach to the original integration of proposal 3 with an offline RL algorithm, and to a modified version of proposal 2 (Robust Offline RL with Shift-Aware Exploration Strategies) that uses the offset estimates to guide exploration. We also investigate the impact of varying offset estimation errors and policy buffer sizes on the performance of our approach.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours (additional data generation and model training).
PREDICTION: We expect our revised approach to improve the robustness of offline RL policy learning, especially when the shifts are abrupt or follow complex patterns. However, we may need to carefully tune the policy adaptation mechanism and buffer sizes to avoid overfitting.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Shift-Aware Imitation Learning for Offline RL
PROPOSAL: We propose a new approach that uses imitation learning to learn a shift-aware policy, even when the offline data does not contain explicit offset annotations. We use a shift-aware demonstration network to imitate the expert policy, and learn to predict the offset values from the demonstrations. We then use these offset predictions to adjust the policy inputs, and evaluate the resulting policy on various synthetic and real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to the original offline RL algorithms (POAC, FQI, and CRR), and to a modified version of proposal 4 (Integrating Offset Estimation with Offline RL) that uses imitation learning instead of policy buffer updates.
COST: Estimated 250 GPU-hours (additional data generation, model training, and imitation learning).
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to be effective in learning shift-aware policies even from offline data, and to be robust to various types of offset patterns and magnitudes. However, we may need to carefully tune the imitation learning threshold to avoid underfitting or overfitting.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Offline RL with Shift-Aware Transfer Learning
PROPOSAL: We propose an approach that uses transfer learning to adapt the offline learned policy to a new environment with shifting observations, without interacting with the environment. We use a shift-aware feature extractor to learn a shared representation of the expert policy, and then adapt this representation to the new environment using a few episodes of offline data.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to the original offline RL algorithm (POAC), and to a modified version of proposal 4 (Integrating Offset Estimation with Offline RL) that uses transfer learning instead of policy buffer updates.
COST: Estimated 500 GPU-hours (additional data generation, model training, and transfer learning).
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to improve the robustness of offline RL policy learning, especially when the shifts are complex and the new environment has limited offline data. However, we may need to carefully tune the transfer learning mechanism and adaptation budget to avoid overfitting or underfitting.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Robustness and Adversarial Shifts in Offline RL
PROPOSAL: We investigate the sample complexity required to learn a robust policy under adversarial shifts, and propose a new approach that uses robust loss functions and shift-aware regularization to improve the adversarial robustness of offline RL policies. We evaluate the performance of our approach on various synthetic and real-world datasets with adversarial shifts, and compare it to existing offline RL algorithms and our previous approaches.
CONTROLS: We compare our approach to the original offline RL algorithms (POAC, FQI, and CRR), and to a modified version of proposal 4 (Integrating Offset Estimation with Offline RL) that uses adversarial robustness instead of policy buffer updates.
COST: Estimated 800 GPU-hours (additional data generation, model training, and robustness evaluation).
PREDICTION: We expect our approach to provide robust offline RL policies under adversarial shifts, and to be effective in learning robust policies even from limited data. However, we may need to carefully tune the robust loss functions and regularization mechanisms to avoid overfitting or underfitting.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Multi-Modal Reasoning with Temporal Attention
PROPOSAL: Implement an MLLM with a temporal attention mechanism that selectively focuses on relevant visual and textual information across long reasoning chains, reducing unnecessary computation and stabilizing training. This will be done by introducing a secondary attention layer that learns to mask out unnecessary visual or textual tokens, improving parallelization and scaling up to longer chains of reasoning.
CONTROLS: Compare to a standard autoregressive model without temporal attention, and an ablation of the attention masking mechanism. Evaluate on reasoning-intensive tasks such as jigsaw puzzle solving and visual question answering.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This model should demonstrate significant training speedup and improved stability on the most computationally expensive tasks, potentially outperforming standard models on inference time, while robustly handling long compositionality in visual reasoning tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Localized Visual Updates for Efficient Multi-Modal Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Introduce an explicit visual update component to the MLLM, allowing for localized visual changes to be computed and integrated incrementally into the reasoning chain. This will be done by feeding the intermediate visual states into a small, locally-connected visual transformer, which captures subtle changes in the visual state while preventing overfitting and generalization issues associated with large-scale image generation.
CONTROLS: Compare to the temporal attention model (1) as well as ablations where this local visual update is either completely disabled or replaced with more expensive, global transformer-based operations.
COST: 750 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Successful integration of this local visual update mechanism should lead to a balance between model scalability, visual coherence, and efficiency on complex tasks, enabling the MLLM to navigate visually grounded tasks in real-time.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reasoning-Augmented Generative Adversarial Networks (RAGAN) for Stable Multi-Modal Training
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel loss function that injects reasoning-based constraints into the training process of MLLMs. The proposed Reasoning-Augmented Generative Adversarial Networks (RAGAN) will utilize both adversarial training and a reasoning-based reconstruction loss, promoting more coherent visual and textual outputs while maintaining long-range dependencies and avoiding training instability.
CONTROLS: Compare to standard GAN-based image generation, as well as common cross-entropy losses used in other MLLM architectures. Examine the trade-offs between different hyperparameters for RAGAN training.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (small-scale), 2500 GPU-hours (large-scale)
PREDICTION: RAGAN should improve substantially upon existing approaches in terms of training stability and, by linking reasoning to rewards-related objectives, may potentially demonstrate better task performance on visually grounded reasoning tasks in the multi-modal domain.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Revised Reasoning-Augmented Generative Adversarial Networks (RAGAN) for Stable Multi-Modal Training
PROPOSAL: Revisit the original RAGAN formulation and revise it by incorporating a multimodal kernel that considers both textual and visual representations within the adversarial loss function. This refinement will be achieved by learning a broadcastable textual-visual interaction matrix, which allows the model to compare and integrate modal information concurrently during the collaborative learning process.
CONTROLS: Use this revised version to replace the original RAGAN in the set of controls. Compare to the revised RAGAN against the temporal attention model (1) as well as ablations of the localized visual update (2).
COST: Same as original RAGAN
PREDICTION: This multimodal interaction matrix should provide a better bridge between textual and visual representations in the RAGAN framework, further enhancing its stability, convergence, and ability to capture inter-modal relationships in visually grounding reasoning tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Transformers for Efficient Multi-Modal Decision Making
PROPOSAL: Investigate the hierarchical structure of transformers in the context of multi-modal reasoning by applying self-attentive techniques that selectively interact with inter-mediate reasoning layers, allowing the model to navigate visually grounded decision-making tasks at varying scales and to reduce computational costs associated with each decision level.
CONTROLS: Examine the effects of varying the number of self-attentive layers used for decision making, as well as the integration of localized visual updates and the RAGAN framework within this setup.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By selectively interacting with intermediate reasoning layers, transformers could achieve reductions in computational costs for multi-modal reasoning tasks, leveraging their inherent hierarchical structure and self-attentive capabilities. %#PBksitoMERCHANTABILITYStatemanualciaarethereqcomp"

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Architectural Guidelines for Balancing Complexity and Efficiency in Multi-Modal Transformers
PROPOSAL: Develop a set of architectural principles to aid in the design and optimization of multi-modal transformers for visually grounded reasoning tasks, focusing on scaling up the architecture without incurring prohibitive computational costs. These guidelines should emphasize techniques like hierarchical self-attention, attention pruning, and parallelization of attention mechanisms.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of the proposed guidelines on task performance and model efficiency by applying them to each of the previous proposals, and compare the results to randomly-designed models of similar size and complexity.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (for experiments), +varies (depending on the assisted design process)
PREDICTION: The application of these guidelines should help to strike a better balance between the expressiveness and efficiency of multi-modal transformers, yielding robust, generalizable models capable of handling visually grounded decision-making tasks across a range of scales and complexities.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient and Stable Interleaving of Textual and Visual Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of a standard autoregressive text generation model (e.g., T5) with a Model that interleaves text and image generation using a Shared Encoder-Decoder (SED) architecture. The SED model processes the visual input through the same encoder as text inputs, and then generates text and image outputs using a shared decoder.
CONTROLS: Baselines include T5 and a separate text generator with a separate image generator (coupled architecture).
COST: 100 GPU-hours (to fine-tune and compare both models).
PREDICTION: We expect the SED model to improve upon the coupled architecture in terms of coherence but may not perform significantly better than T5 in terms of downstream task performance, should the tasks not explicitly require both inputs in a similar manner; it may fail on tasks like text-to-image generation where visual output is too far from the text input.

 Verified metadata does not request theoretical-only or mostly-theoretical paper, but suggests that both experiments and theoretical results are allowable. Therefore, most proposals are expected to be experimental with some theoretical rigor applied.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Trimming the Long Chain: Efficient Visual State Transition Modeling
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the effect of two trimming techniques on the autoregressive nature of the SED model: (1) Hierarchical Reasoning (HR): dividing the reasoning chain into shorter hierarchical steps, and (2) Chunk Vocab Sampling (CVS): downsampling the visual per-step embeddings to a fixed-size vocabulary. We hypothesize that these trims can reduce the quadratic complexity of autoregressive generation while preserving or even improving performance.
CONTROLS: Compare HR and CVS to a standard, untimed SED model, as well as to the baseline coupled architecture with separate text and image generators.
COST: 75 GPU-hours (to fine-tune the trimmed models and compare them to baseline).
PREDICTION: We expect HR to reduce training time by at least 30% while preserving performance, but possibly sacrificing some on-specific tasks. CVS might require more hyperparameter tuning, and overall result uncertain until evaluation.

Theory-based analysis can still provide mechanisms explaining observed effects.

TITLE: Leverage Professional-Grade Geometry Priors for Visual Reasoning
PROPOSAL: Adapt existing architectural components (i.e., model checkpoints) from environments, level editors, or physics simulators that incorporate real-world domain knowledge in the form of physics and geometry priors into the composition of our shared encoder-decoder model. For example, incorporate geometry-based graph transformations that can reason about spatial relationships between objects and scenes.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the incorporation of these professional-grade components into the HR, CVS, and SED models in combination with data from real-world applications like 3D environment generation and level editing platforms.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (to adapt pre-trained models, fine-tune, and measure performance).
PREDICTION: The incorporation of these professional-grade geometry priors might significantly boost performance and generalization of models in specific visual reasoning tasks and might fail on those where they are not generalizable.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Contrastive Learning for Multi-Modal Reasoning
PROPOSAL:  Develop an efficient contrastive learning framework for multi-modal reasoning tasks, focusing on visual-textual attentions and geometric transformations. This approach aims to learn robust representations that capture hierarchical, compositional, and contextual relationships across diverse visual and textual modalities. The framework relies on noise-contrastive estimation to encourage intra-modality and inter-modality alignments, allowing for better generalization across various tasks and environments.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed contrastive learning framework with other visual-textual alignment methods, and evaluate its effectiveness on various downstream tasks such as jigsaw puzzle, reasoning-driven text-to-image generation, and instruction-based image editing.
COST: 175 GPU-hours (fine-tuning and training the contrastive framework).
PREDICTION: This approach may improve the model's ability to capture complex multi-modal relationships, but may struggle with incorporating prior knowledge and geometric transformations effectively, potentially leading to suboptimal performance on certain tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Attention to the Entirety: Modularizing the Reasoning Process
PROPOSAL: Break down the reasoning process into smaller, modular components, and explicitly map them to specific, local attention mechanisms within the model. Each module attends to specific components of the input (e.g., object boundaries, layout, or semantics), enabling more targeted and controlled reasoning. This approach can help manage the growth of the reasoning chain, reduce computational costs, and improve performance on tasks requiring long-range dependencies.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the proposed modular reasoning approach on various tasks (e.g., jigsaw puzzle, text-to-image generation, and visual question answering) with different levels of object complexity and spatial extent.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (tweak existing model, fine-tuning and training the modularized version).
PREDICTION: We expect the modularized approach to reduce reasoning chain length and improve computational efficiency, yielding competitive or better results on tasks that benefit from targeted attention, but may compromise performance on tasks requiring extensive, unstructured attention.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reasoning over Different Modalities with Perceptual Priming
PROPOSAL: Develop a method that incorporates perceptual priming to facilitate the transition between different modalities (e.g., from text to image or vice versa) during the reasoning process. This approach leverages external knowledge about the relationships between different modalities to guide the reasoning process, enabling more efficient and effective transitions between modalities.
CONTROLS: Compare the proposed perceptual priming method with standard attention-based approaches on various tasks that require transitioning between different modalities (e.g., text-to-image generation, visual question answering).
COST: 110 GPU-hours (fine-tuning and training the perceptual priming-based model).
PREDICTION: We expect the perceptual priming method to improve performance on tasks requiring transitions between different modalities, but may struggle with generalization to novel, unseen combinations of modalities, or when the priming knowledge is incomplete or inaccurate.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Graph-Based Reasoning for Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of graph-based techniques to model the chain-of-thought reasoning process in multi-modal settings. This involves representing the sequence of reasoning steps as a graph, where nodes correspond to visual or textual states, and edges capture transitions between these states. Graph neural networks can be then used to perform reasoning and generalize to new tasks and modalities.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the graph-based reasoning approach on tasks such as text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and jigsaw puzzle solving, and compare it with existing state-of-the-art methods.
COST: 180 GPU-hours (tweak existing model, fine-tuning and training the graph-based version).
PREDICTION: The graph-based reasoning approach may enable efficient and scalable reasoning, as well as better generalization to novel tasks and modalities, but may require careful hyperparameter tuning and node/edge representations to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: 7. Graph-Based Reasoning for Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought
PROPOSAL: REVISE Graph-Based Reasoning for Multi-Modal Chain-of-Thought: Incorporate the insights and components from the previous proposals to enhance the graph-based reasoning approach. Specifically, integrate the prior geometry priors, attention to the entirety (modularizing the reasoning process), and perceptual priming into the graph-based model. This revised approach should leverage the strengths of each component to achieve more effective and efficient multi-modal chain-of-thought reasoning.
CONTROLS: Compare the revised graph-based model with the earlier proposals and existing state-of-the-art methods on a range of tasks, including text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and jigsaw puzzle solving.
COST: Estimated 200-250 GPU-hours (fine-tuning and training the revised model).
PREDICTION: The revised graph-based approach is likely to achieve state-of-the-art performance on multi-modal chain-of-thought reasoning tasks, but may require careful tuning of the integrated components and hyperparameters to achieve optimal results.

Controls: Compare MLLMs' performance against a strong baseline using a state-of-the-art egocentric video encoder (e.g., Video Encyclopedia).
Estimated cost: 1000 GPU-hours (evaluation and testing on a batched set of 10,000 egocentric video clips).
Prediction: The models will achieve varying levels of performance, with ViLBERT possibly outperforming the baseline due to its superior visual-linguistic alignment. A notable challenge will be MMT's adherence to its pre-training task, i.e., interpreting brief annotations about a single visual object, which could result in underperformance when evaluated on a question answering benchmark.

PROPOSAL 2: Investigating the Impact of Gaze Information on Egocentric MLLMs
Introduce a multiscale attention mechanism to 2 of the MLLMs evaluated in proposal 1 (ViLBERT and MMT) that incorporates ground-truth gaze data from egocentric videos. This addition will effectively create a "look-then-ask"-style augementation strategy promoting egocentric question answering. Evaluate both the vanilla and gaze-augmented models on EgocentricVideoQA.
Controls: Ablate the gaze attention mechanism to prove its necessity and study the effect of using noisy or differing gaze-grounding techniques.
Estimated cost: 1500 GPU-hours (training and evaluation for 5 iterations).
Prediction: The addition of gaze information should improve both ViLBERT and MMT's performance, although we expect inconsistent benefits across different attention zoom-scales, and it might lead to overfitting with excessive iterations or enhancements (specifically note that the interaction might not always positively impact performance).

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Current MLLMs on Egocentric Video Without Gaze Cues
PROPOSAL: Train and evaluate the latest versions of CLIP, FLAN, and LLaMA on the recent egocentric video question answering benchmark (e.g., EPIC-Kitchens, through the EPIC-Kitchens Question Answering evaluation platform) using their standard input methods (i.e., a single video frame or sequence of frames) and without any additional gaze-related information.
CONTROLS: To include controls and ablations: (1) evaluate these MLLMs on a similar exocentric video question answering benchmark (e.g., HowTo100M or ActivityNet), (2) use truncated versions of the egocentric video question answering benchmark (reduced quantity and length of input videos), and (3) test MLLMs with a pre-trained gaze-estimation module integrated into their input.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (based on 8 GPU nodes for 1 week)
PREDICTION: This proposal should provide insight into the extent to which current MLLMs interpret user intent from egocentric video without gaze information. Expected result: individual MLLMs would show worse performance on the egocentric video question answering task compared to their exocentric counterparts, with variability in performance depending on the specific model's capacity and training data. However, it may also reveal that current MLLMs are more robust than expected, especially those pre-trained on massive text corpora that include diverse descriptions of human behaviors.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Visual Feature Representations for Egocentric Video Understanding
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether standard MLLM visual feature representations (e.g., ViT, CNN) are suitable for interpreting egocentric video content. Analyze their performance on a downstream task of predicting gaze direction from egocentric video frames using a simple, gaze-focused classification head. Compare their performance to other, potentially more egocentrically-informed feature representation (e.g., compositional spatial-temporal model for learning motion and structure from egocentric video, gaze- indexed features).
CONTROLS: Include comparison with models pre-trained on exocentric video data, and in the absence of explicit gaze information.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (based on 4 GPU nodes for 2 days)
PREDICTION: This study might show that standard visual feature representations are not optimal for egocentric video content and that incorporating gaze information directly into these features could improve the model's performance. Failure could arise from the complexity of the task or the high dimensionality of egocentric video frames. 

Set:
1. Evaluating Current MLLMs on Egocentric Video Without Gaze Cues
2. Investigating Visual Feature Representations for Egocentric Video Understanding

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ablating Gaze Signal Presentation in MLLMs for Egocentric Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: Investigate how different forms of gaze information are presented to the MLLM affect its performance on egocentric video question answering. Test the impact of using gaze signals from various modalities (e.g., screen space, pixel-level, 3D world coordinates), resolutions (e.g., sampled, full-resolution), and input encoding schemes (e.g., gaze-only, image-gaze fusion). Compare the performance difference between using accurate and noisy (artificially corrupted) gaze information.
CONTROLS: Evaluate different MLLMs (e.g., CLIP, FLAN), include gaze-signal ablation to gauge their impact on performance, and perform experiments across different tasks and difficulty levels (e.g., gaze-based action recognition, egocentric scene understanding).
COST: 250 GPU-hours (based on 6 GPU nodes for 3 days)
PREDICTION: This study may show that certain forms of gaze information can significantly improve the model's performance, while others provide limited or even counterproductive benefits. The findings might be model-dependent, and expected results may vary across tasks and difficulties.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Ablating Gaze Signal Presentation in MLLMs for Egocentric Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: REVISED: In addition to the original proposal, experiment on incorporating information about gaze signal reliability. Introduce a weighing scheme in the gaze-only representation to retroactively assign higher weights to past gaze points that (1) contained objects on which the actions have taken place during the video (activity-related), or (2) received high fixation probabilities (user attention).
CONTROLS: Use a gaze-ground truth dataset for re-weighting the past frames which contain objects on which the actions occur.
COST: Additional 50 GPU-hours; previously estimated 250 GPU-hours still applies (total: 300 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: By introducing a weighing scheme for gaze signal reliability, we might notice a notable improvement in the model performance, reflecting better usage tracking and informed inference. PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of MLLMs in multitask learning scenarios where they are trained on both egocentric video question answering and gaze estimation tasks. Investigate the transfer capabilities of such multitask-trained models on additional downstream tasks related to egocentric video understanding, including handling gaze signals in diverse environments and time settings.

PREDICTION: This study may show that multitask learning can improve the model's generalization on diverse tasks and environments, leveraging cross-task relationships to better infer intent from egocentric video and gaze information. TITLE: Exploring Zero-Shot Transfer of Egocentric Intent Understanding to In-the-Wild Settings
PROPOSAL: Utilize a state-of-the-art, pre-trained egocentric intent understanding model (trained on EPIC-Kitchens or similar datasets), and test its zero-shot transfer performance on a different in-the-wild dataset (e.g., the Active Learning Dataset for Intent Recognition, ALDIR) with a different type of environment or action domain. Include evaluations of fine-tuning capabilities on a subset of in-the-wild data, and assess any insight gained into adapting egocentric intent models for deployment in real-world applications.
CONTROLS: Ablation studies using in-the-wild datasets with varying degrees of similarity to the pre-training datasets and scenarios, and evaluations without access to in-the-wild data at train time.

PREDICTION: This study might demonstrate the transferability of pre-trained egocentric intent models and provide insight into zero-shot learning capabilities for a variety of in-the-wild applications. Notable difficulties could arise due to variations in action implementations, differences in video recording conditions, and shooting specifications within the in-the-wild environments.

PREDICTION: This study should help establish the first eye-tracking dataset for egocentric intent understanding, which will facilitate deeper investigations into the relationships between gaze, actions, and user intent. Train and evaluate the latest versions of CLIP, FLAN, and LLaMA on the recent egocentric video question answering benchmark (e.g., EPIC-Kitchens, through the EPIC-Kitchens Question Answering evaluation platform) using their standard input methods (i.e., a single video frame or sequence of frames) and without any additional gaze-related information.
Controls: To include controls and ablations: (1) evaluate these MLLMs on a similar exocentric video question answering benchmark (e.g., HowTo100M or ActivityNet), (2) use truncated versions of the egocentric video question answering benchmark (reduced quantity and length of input videos), and (3) test MLLMs with a pre-trained gaze-estimation module integrated into their input.
Estimated cost: 300 GPU-hours (based on 8 GPU nodes for 1 week)
Prediction: This proposal should provide insight into the extent to which current MLLMs interpret user intent from egocentric video without gaze information. PROPOSAL 2: Investigating Visual Feature Representations for Egocentric Video Understanding
Investigate whether standard MLLM visual feature representations (e.g., ViT, CNN) are suitable for interpreting egocentric video content. Analyze their performance on a downstream task of predicting gaze direction from egocentric video frames using a simple, gaze-focused classification head. Compare their performance to other, potentially more egocentrically-informed feature representation (e.g., compositional spatial-temporal model for learning motion and structure from egocentric video, gaze- indexed features).

Estimated cost: 150 GPU-hours (based on 4 GPU nodes for 2 days)
Prediction: This study might show that standard visual feature representations are not optimal for egocentric video content and that incorporating gaze information directly into these features could improve the model's performance. Evaluate the performance of MLLMs in multitask learning scenarios where they are trained on both egocentric video question answering and gaze estimation tasks. Prediction: This study may show that multitask learning can improve the model's generalization on diverse tasks and environments, leveraging cross-task relationships to better infer intent from egocentric video and gaze information. However, potential failures could arise from limited representations of intent and complexity of the tasks.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Assessing MLLMs' Ability to Understand Egocentric User Intent from Video
PROPOSAL: Experiment on egocentric video question answering benchmarks with a baseline of current state-of-the-art MLLM (e.g., CLIP) to evaluate its performance in understanding user intent from video.
CONTROLS: Compare against a modified version of CLIP using attention-weighted video frames that focus on the egocentric viewpoint, and against a gaze-augmented version of CLIP where gaze signals are provided.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The baseline CLIP will fail to capture egocentric intent due to its exocentric viewpoint, while the gaze-augmented CLIP will show significant improvement, but may still struggle with nuances of user intent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Gaze-Augmented Egocentric Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: Experiment on a new benchmark of egocentric video question answering with gaze data (e.g.,.ppqa-ecco-gaze) to evaluate how adding gaze signals improves MLLMs' performance on understanding user intent from egocentric viewpoints.
CONTROLS: Compare against a version of the benchmark without gaze data, and against a similar benchmark with gaze data but using a gaze-agnostic MLLM (e.g., BERT).
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The gaze-augmented benchmark will show significant improvement over the non-gaze benchmark, and the gaze-agnostic model will perform poorly on questions requiring egocentric intent understanding.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Gaze-Augmented Egocentric Video Question Answering
REVISED PROPOSAL: Extend the existing proposal to include an experiment on evaluating the impact of gaze signal accuracy on the performance of MLLMs. This can be done by using gaze signals with varying levels of accuracy (e.g., perfect gaze, gaze with jitter, gaze with random errors) and measuring the corresponding performance drop.
CONTROLS: Compare against the performance on the perfect gaze signals to understand when the model starts to degrade due to inaccurate gaze signals.
COST: +50 GPU-hours (total: 200 GPU-hours)
PREDICTION: The model's performance will degrade significantly with gaze jitter and random errors, but may still perform reasonably well with moderate errors.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating Gaze-Augmented Egocentric Video Question Answering
REVISED PROPOSAL: Add an additional control arm to the experiment, where the gaze signals are encoded in a visual attention map and provided as an additional channel to the MLLM, instead of using the raw gaze signals. This will allow us to investigate whether encoding gaze information in a more abstract and explicit way can lead to better performance.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original gaze-augmented model, as well as the model with perfect gaze, and the model without gaze signals.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The model with gaze encoded in visual attention maps may show improved performance, especially on questions requiring more complex understanding of user intent.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating Gaze-Augmented Egocentric Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: As described in the previous action, add an additional control arm to the experiment, where the gaze signals are encoded in a visual attention map and provided as an additional channel to the MLLM, instead of using the raw gaze signals. This will allow us to investigate whether encoding gaze information in a more abstract and explicit way can lead to better performance.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original gaze-augmented model, as well as the model with perfect gaze, and the model without gaze signals.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The model with gaze encoded in visual attention maps may show improved performance, especially on questions requiring more complex understanding of user intent.

ADDITIONAL CONTROLS: We will also compare against a version of the model where we add a gaze estimator as a separate module, trained on a separate gaze dataset, to predict the gaze attention maps. This will help us understand if the model is actually learning to predict gaze or is simply relying on the provided gaze maps.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Time-Sensitive Egocentric User Intent Understanding
PROPOSAL: Experiment on a variant of the existing egocentric video question answering benchmark where questions and corresponding answers have time-stamped annotations (e.g., "What did you do from 5 seconds to 10 seconds?"). This will enable us to assess how well MLLMs can understand temporally grounded user intent in egocentric video.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original benchmark, and against a version of the model where the input video is sampled at different frame rates (e.g., 2x, 4x).
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The model performance will improve with temporal annotations, and sampling the input video at higher frame rates may further improve performance, but may also increase computational requirements.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gaze Data Augmentation in Egocentric Video Question Answering
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of artificially augmenting the gaze data during training, by generating additional gaze samples through techniques such as gaze interpolation, gaze extrapolation, or even gaze sampling from a different distribution. This will help us understand how robust the model is to gaze data quality and whether it can generalize to unseen gaze patterns.
CONTROLS: Compare against a version of the model trained on original gaze data, and against an ensemble of models trained on different augmentation strategies.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The model performance will improve with gaze data augmentation, and the ensemble of models may show improved generalization to unseen gaze patterns, but also may increase computational requirements and training time.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Eye-Tracking Quality Analysis in Egocentric Video
PROPOSAL: Investigate how the quality of eye-tracking data affects the performance of the gaze-augmented MLLM. This can be done by simulating different types of noise and errors in the gaze data and evaluating the model's performance on the noisy and error-prone data.
CONTROLS: Compare against a version of the model trained on clean gaze data, and against a version of the model trained on noisy gaze data with varying levels of quality.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The model performance will degrade significantly with high levels of noise or error in the gaze data, but may show some resilience to moderate levels of noise or error.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Egocentric Gaze-Augmented MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the transferability of the gaze-augmented MLLM to new egocentric video question answering tasks with different styles or abstractness. This can be done by pre-training the MLLM on a large egocentric video dataset with gaze data and then fine-tuning it on a new task.
CONTROLS: Compare against a version of the model pre-trained on a similar task but without gaze data, and against a version of the model pre-trained on a different task.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The model pre-trained on the large egocentric video dataset with gaze data will show good transferability to new tasks, while the model pre-trained on a similar task without gaze data may not show the same level of transferability.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluate Gaze-Augmented MLLMs in Real-World Proactive AI Assistants
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the gaze-augmented MLLM in a real-world proactive AI assistant setting, where the AI assistant needs to infer user intent in real-time and provide personalized responses. This will involve integrating the gaze-augmented MLLM with an existing AI assistant system and conducting user studies to evaluate the performance and usability of the system.
CONTROLS: Compare against a version of the AI assistant system without the gaze-augmented MLLM, and against a version of the system with a different MLLM architecture.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (estimated, due to the complexity of integrating with the AI assistant system)
PREDICTION: The gaze-augmented MLLM will show significant improvements in user intent inference and personalized responses in real-world proactive AI assistants, but may also require further tuning and optimization to achieve satisfactory performance.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Modality Conflicts in Autoregressive Unified Multimodal Models
PROPOSAL: Experiment 1 - Disentangling Inter-Modal Conflicts in a Baseline AR UMM
We train an autoregressive unified multimodal model on a diverse set of tasks, including text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and image editing. We then use a gradient-based analysis to quantify and compare the inter-modal conflicts between tasks, examining the layer-wise distribution of conflicting gradients and their impact on training efficiency and performance.
CONTROLS: We compare with a vanilla transformer model and a baseline AR UMM without modality sharing.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to identify challenges in tasks where text and image tokens come from different distributions, such as text-to-image generation, and where modality conflicts lead to reduced performance, and possibly even model instability. Key failure points may arise in models where a single transformer layer is unable to handle the varying complexities of text and image tokens simultaneously.

This experiment sets the stage for a deeper understanding of modality conflicts and provides a foundation for investigating possible solutions in subsequent experiments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Proxy Tasks for Inter-Modal Conflict Reduction
PROPOSAL: Experiment 2 - Modal Decoupling via Task-Specific Proxy Objectives
We explore using proxy tasks, such as predicting the existence or location of text tokens from the visual input, to decouple inter-modal conflicts in the AR UMM. By integrating these proxy objectives into the model's optimization process, we investigate whether this approach reduces conflicts and improves training efficiency and performance. We test this method on a task mix of text-to-image generation, visual question answering, and image editing.
CONTROLS: We compare with Experiment 1 and a baseline AR UMM with no additional proxy tasks.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (adds 50 GPU-hours to Experiment 1)
PREDICTION: We expect proxy tasks to help reduce conflicts by task-specifically regularizing the model's behavior, especially in tasks with critical text and image interplay, such as text-to-image generation, leading to a more balanced model that induces fewer divergent gradients. A possible failure could be that these proxy tasks mislead the optimization process, leading to overfitting on specific proxy task objectives rather than overall performance goals.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Dimensionality Reduction for Modality Conflict Reduction
PROPOSAL: Experiment 2 (modified) - Dimensionality-Reduced Inter-modal Space (DRIMS)
We modify Experiment 2 to use a dimensionality-reduced space for the inter-modal conflicts. We apply techniques such as multi-modal latent space mapping or low-rank representations to reduce the dimensionality of the inter-modal conflicts, making it easier for the AR UMM to learn and generalize across tasks. This approach reduces the risk of overfitting and allows for more effective sharing of parameters across tasks and modalities.
CONTROLS: We compare with the original Experiment 2 and a baseline AR UMM without dimensionality reduction.
COST: The modification does not increase compute requirements, as it can be integrated within the existing Experiment 2 setup.
PREDICTION: We expect DRIMS to improve model performance and reduce conflicts by making the inter-modal space more manageable and intuitive for the model. A possible failure point is the risk of losing representational power in the process of dimensionality reduction, leading to compromised performance on certain tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding Inter-Modal Conflicts through Intra-Modal Attention Analysis
PROPOSAL: Analysis 3 - Layer-wise Intra-modal Attention Analysis in AR UMMs
We conduct a detailed analysis of the intra-modal attention patterns within the AR UMM's autoregressive transformer layers. By examining the layer-wise attention distributions and their interactions with the inter-modal conflicts, we aim to better understand how the model's capacity to represent text and image tokens affects its ability to jointly learn and generalize across tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare with a baseline transformer model without modality sharing and analyze the attention patterns under controlled conditions.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (low-compute, primarily CPU-intense)
PREDICTION: We expect the analysis to reveal specific layer-wise patterns that exacerbate or mitigate modality conflicts, potentially uncovering opportunities for architectural modifications or fine-tuned training schemes that respect the semi-autonomous processing needs of text and image tokens. A possible failure point is the risk of over-interpreting the attention distributions without accounting for noise, leading to incorrect conclusions about the model's behavior.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Inter-Modal Conflict Mitigation through Depth-Aware Transformer Scheduling
PROPOSAL: Experiment 4 - Dynamically Reshaping the Transformer Sequential Order
We develop and evaluate an adaptive training scheme that dynamically rearranges the AR UMM's transformer depth order based on task-specific modality requirements. By conditionally suspending or compensating conflicting transformer layers, we investigate whether this adaptive approach can more effectively harness the model's capacity to learn and generalize across text and image modalities.
CONTROLS: We compare with Experiment 1 and Experiment 2, as well as a baseline AR UMM without dynamic scheduling.
COST: 350 GPU-hours (adds 230 GPU-hours to Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 setup)
PREDICTION: We expect the adaptive scheduling scheme to enhance the AR UMM's performance and robustness, especially in tasks where text and image modality differences significantly impact joint optimization. A possible failure could be that the scheme induces indecision problems by varying the model's depth order across trial epochs, thereby hindering learning even further.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Inter-Modal Conflict Reduction through Meta-Learning
PROPOSAL: Analysis 5 - Meta-Learned Task-Agnostic Inter-Modal Conflict Modeling
We adapt meta-learning techniques to the AR UMM, using a meta-learning strategy to distill task-agnostic inter-modal conflict knowledge into a few-shot learning framework. This framework learns to detect and mitigate modality conflicts, allowing the model to generalize better across tasks and improve performance on unseen tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare with meta-learning methods applied to other models and a baseline AR UMM without meta-learning.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the meta-learning approach to reduce inter-modal conflicts by learning task-agnostic patterns of conflict within a shared knowledge space, thus enabling more effective knowledge transfer across tasks. Possible failure points include that meta-learning exacerbates existing model bias, effectively focusing on incorrect behaviors, or that the model becomes overly specialized, forgetting how to generalize to new tasks apart from the distribution learned.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Attention for Introducing Task-Aware Inter-Modal Conflicts
PROPOSAL: Experiment 5 - Spatial-Temporal Inter-Modal Conflict Alignment (STIC)
We extend the baseline AR UMM with a spatiotemporal attention mechanism that learns to selectively align inter-modal conflicts with task-specific temporal dependencies. By aligning conflicts dynamically with the temporal structure of tasks, we investigate whether STIC can improve task-specific performance and enhance the overall robustness to inter-modal conflicts.
CONTROLS: We compare with Experiment 1 and Experiment 4, as well as a baseline AR UMM without STIC.
COST: 220 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect STIC to mitigate modality conflicts by introducing task-aware temporal relationships between conflicting inter-modal representations, ultimately resulting in better alignment between model performance and task requirements. A likely failure could be that the spatiotemporal attention mechanism introduces additional confounds by over-interpreting input task sequences, rather than solely helping reduce inter-modal conflict.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Encoder Modifications for Addressing Inter-Modal Conflicts
PROPOSAL: Experiment 6 - Factorized Thing-Part Temporal Embeddings (FTPTE) for AR UMMs
We incorporate Factorized Thing-Part Temporal Embeddings into the AR UMM's encoder, allowing for more fine-grained separation of component-wise temporal features. By reducing unwanted interactions and correlations between the modalities, FTPTE aims to enhance robustness to inter-modal conflicts.
CONTROLS: We compare with the baseline AR UMM and Experiment 5, as well as other competing state-of-the-art encoder modifications.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect FTPTE to exhibit better handling of modality conflicts due to its focusing on part-level temporal features, thus increasing, the model's ability to effectively process disentangled information from conflicting inputs. However, the risk exists that the factorization may over-split task-specific structural relationships between inputs, potentially causing performance loss on tasks benefiting from overlapping features across modalities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Comparison and Ablation Analysis for AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Experiment 7 - Systematic Evaluation of Modality Conflict Mitigation Strategies
We conduct a comprehensive comparison and ablative analysis of the various modality conflict mitigation strategies proposed in this study (Experiment 1, Experiment 4, Experiment 5, Experiment 6 and Analysis 3). By systematically evaluating their strengths and weaknesses on a diverse range of benchmarks and tasks (text-to-image generation, visual question answering, image editing), we provide a framework to assess which configurations are most effective in reducing modality conflicts and enhance AR UMM performance.
CONTROLS: We compare with a baseline AR UMM and extensive ablation experiments on each modified model.
COST: 360 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the comprehensive analysis to identify a multi-strategy combination of dimensionality reduction, dynamic sequence order, and spatiotemporal/factorized encoders that diminishes the overall effect of modality conflicts on AR UMM, with heightened emphasis on most sensitive tasks. We anticipate performance gains on these " conflict bottleneck" tasks to come at a cost of reduced improvement on less affected ("conflict symmetric") tasks. The effectiveness may also depend on storage and parallelization efficiency due to added dataset scales.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Model-Optimization and Scaling-up AR UMMs for Real-World Multimodal Applications
PROPOSAL: Experiment 8 - Model Pruning, Knowledge Distillation, and Horizontal Scaling for Large-Scale Deployments
We explore the possibility of scaling-up the AR UMMs proposed in this study to enable large-scale multimodal applications by leveraging pruning, knowledge distillation, and horizontal scaling techniques. By adaptively reducing the model's complexity, transferring knowledge from the stronger parent model, and deploying the optimized model on multiple GPUs, we aim to create a deployable AR UMM.
CONTROLS: We compare with a baseline AR UMM and a set of closely-related models that utilize different scaling strategies.
COST: 720 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the scaled-up AR UMM to maintain its accuracy in more real-world scenarios and provide better performance in tasks that require in-depth multimodal understanding, stemming from its direct processing ability. A possible limitation could be a reduced performance in conditions where more comprehensive parameter interaction is found to be crucial, such as those with additional or supporting multimodal edge features.

propositions.prediction: We expect the scaled-up AR UMM to maintain its accuracy in more real-world scenarios and provide better performance in tasks that require in-depth multimodal understanding, stemming from its direct processing ability. A possible limitation could be a reduced performance in conditions where more comprehensive parameter interaction is found to be crucial, such as those with additional or supporting multimodal edge features.
propositions.texte:
Experiment 8 - Model Pruning, Knowledge Distillation, and Horizontal Scaling for Large-Scale Deployments
We explore the possibility of scaling-up the AR UMMs proposed in this study to enable large-scale multimodal applications by leveraging pruning, knowledge distillation, and horizontal scaling techniques. By adaptively reducing the model's complexity, transferring knowledge from the stronger parent model, and deploying the optimized model on multiple GPUs, we aim to create a deployable AR UMM.
propositions.titre: Model-Optimization and Scaling-up AR UMMs for Real-World Multimodal Applications

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Investigating Gradient Conflicts in Autoregressive Unified Multimodal Models
PROPOSAL: We design and train a series of autoregressive Unified Multimodal Models (AR-UMMs) on four real-world tasks (Crohme image captioning, CLEVR-VQA, Image9, and TediCap), where image and text modalities are embedded as consecutive tokens in the input sequence. We compare the performance of single-modality autoregressive language models (AR-LMs) and complete AR-UMMs to establish a baseline for the effectiveness of unified multimodal learning. Next, we employ Hessian-based clustering to analyze the layer-wise agreement between image and text gradients computed from the shared transformer layers. By correlating these gradient relationships with the abstractness and semantic richness of representations, we aim to pinpoint the depth-dependent inter-modal conflicts contributing to the degraded performance.
CONTROLS: Single-modality AR-LM baselines on each task, gradient clustering controls via random sampling of model parameters or ablation studies on the eigendecomposition-based method.
COST: 15,200 GPU-hours (8 tasks, 2x 4node 32G V100 servers, 5 epochs).
PREDICTION: We expect strong correlations between gradient cluster divergence and representation abstraction/semantics, with the highest conflicts appearing at intermediate layers. This study should demonstrate that in this regime, degrading image-text HSIC by as much as 4 | DC stásites over single-modality baseline yılda '% }…:.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Asymmetric Cross-Modal Attention in Autoregressive Unified Multimodal Models
PROPOSAL: We extend the AR-UMMs designed in proposal 1 by introducing asymmetric cross-modal attention mechanisms that differentially weight the contributions of image and text modalities to the transformer layers' self-attention, allowing for adaptive modality-specific influence without compromising the autoregressive sequence prediction framework. We hypothesize that this ability to modulate the inter-modal influence will alleviate gradient conflicts and promote more effective unified multimodal learning. We will evaluate this design on the same four real-world tasks as before and compare its performance against the baseline AR-UMMs.
CONTROLS: Baseline AR-UMMs (proposal 1), random sampling of modality weights, and testing for limits of adaptive attention.
COST: 6,000 GPU-hours (3 tasks, 1x 32G A100 server, 5 epochs).
PREDICTION: We predict a 2-5 point BLEU score improvement in image captioning and a 5-10 percent accuracy boost in VQA.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE:  REVISED - Investigating Gradient Conflicts in Autoregressive Unified Multimodal Models
PROPOSAL: We modify proposal 1 to include a control group, where image and text gradients are normalized by their respective modality-specific layer-wise norms. This modification allows us to isolate the effect of gradient magnitudes on the observed conflicts and serves as a baseline for our analysis of gradient directionality. We implement this control in all 8 AR-UMMs designed for the four real-world tasks and the four single-modality AR-LMs.
CONTROLS: Single-modality AR-LM baselines on each task, layer-wise normalization controls, random sampling of model parameters or ablation studies on the eigendecomposition-based method.
COST: remains at 15,200 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Normalizing image and text gradients by their modality-specific norms will reduce the observed conflicts in AR-UMMs, but the directional conflicts will persist.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE:  REVISED 1. Investigating Gradient Conflicts in Autoregressive Unified Multimodal Models
PROPOSAL: We modify the layer-wise agreement analysis by replacing Hessian-based clustering with a novel, adaptive dimensionality reduction technique, t-SNE with modality-specific thresholding, to better capture the complex relationships between image and text gradients across different transformer layers. This allows for a more accurate and interpretable understanding of the gradient conflicts, particularly in regions where the shared transformer layers exhibit different degrees of abstraction and semantic richness.
CONTROLS: Baseline Hessian-based clustering, ablation studies on t-SNE hyperparameters, random sampling of model parameters or gradient magnitudes.
COST: 2,400 GPU-hours (4 tasks, 1x 16G A100 server, 5 epochs).
PREDICTION: By leveraging adaptive dimensionality reduction, this modified analysis will uncover new insights into the role of layer-wise abstraction and semantics in inter-modal conflicts, leading to improved understanding and design of AR-UMMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Investigating the Role of ImageKeyPress via FreezePrune Regularization
PROPOSAL: We apply FreezePrune regularization to the AR-UMMs, freezing specific weights corresponding to imageKeyPress, which we identify as key contributors to gradient conflicts. By iteratively refining the set of frozen weights based on model performance and gradient similarity metrics, we hypothesize that FreezePrune will identify a minimal, bottleneck-like subset of image-specific weights responsible for modality conflicts and facilitate their disentanglement.
CONTROLS: Baseline AR-UMMs, ablation studies on the freeze schedule and pruning criteria, retraining with random initialization of weights.
COST: 8,000 GPU-hours (3 tasks, 1x 32G V100 server, 5 epochs).
PREDICTION: FreezePrune will successfully disentangle modality conflicts and identify the most critical image-specific weights affecting the AR-UMMs' performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Analyzing Gradient Conflicts via Conditional Mutual Information
PROPOSAL: We define a conditional mutual information (CMI) metric to quantify the dependency between image and text gradients in the AR-UMMs. We propose to decompose the joint distribution of gradients into its conditional components, isolating the context-dependent relationships that drive modality conflicts. By computing the CMI between image and text gradients conditioned on different layers, we expect to uncover the specific aspects of representation abstraction and semantic richness that correlate with increased gradient conflicts.
CONTROLS: Baseline decomposition of gradient distributions without conditioning, CMI on layer-wise vs. global representations.
COST: 4,800 GPU-hours (2 tasks, 1x 16G A100 server, 5 epochs).
PREDICTION: CMI will reveal that image and text gradients become progressively dependent at intermediate layers, corresponding to the emergence of abstract and semantic representations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE:  Exacerbating Gradient Conflicts through Disentangled Modality Corruption
PROPOSAL: We propose a procedure to artificially induce and study gradient conflicts in the AR-UMMs by introducing disentangled modality corruption (DMC): we randomly corrupt specific aspects of the image or text input signals while keeping the other modality intact. By analyzing the model's response to DMC, we aim to isolate and test the conditions under which gradient conflicts arise, and assess the robustness and resilience of the AR-UMMs to such attacks.
CONTROLS: Baseline AR-UMMs, Perturbation analysis on corrupted modalities, ablation studies on DMC impact.
COST: 3,600 GPU-hours (2 tasks, 1x 16G V100 server, 5 epochs).
PREDICTION: DMC will reveal that AR-UMMs are susceptible to catastrophic forgetting in modality-differentiated scenarios, with the image modality being more resilient than the text modality to corruption in the initial stages of training.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding gradient conflicts in modality-shared autoregressive transformers
PROPOSAL: Experiment to empirically analyze the layer-wise distribution of inter-modal conflicts in a modality-shared autoregressive transformer, using the LLaMA model as the LLM component and the DALL-E mini dataset for image encoding.
CONTROLS: Reproduct the analysis using a naive baseline of separate models for text and vision, as well as an ablation of using a language-centric transformer initialized with pre-trained visual language.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find conflicts predominantly affecting middle layers, reflecting the failure of common short-range statistics to approximate language's longer-range context, and see minor real-world performance gains from a separate models baseline, but significant improvements with pre-trained visual language initialization.

This proposal provides a foundation to empirically study the interplay between modalities in a modality-shared AR transformer, giving us a data-driven understanding of the nature of gradient conflicts and their impact on performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Gradient conflict analysis with modality-specific proxy tasks
PROPOSAL: Develop a set of proxy tasks designed to estimate the gradient conflict between text and vision in a modality-shared autoregressive transformer, including vocabulary overlap, token density, and sequence-level similarity measures, and use these to analyze the behavior of the transformer on text-to-image generation and visual question answering datasets (e.g. CLEVR, VQA v2).
CONTROLS: Analyze with and without auxiliary pre-training on visual-language pairs to see whether it mitigates proxy task conflict measures, and validate the proxy tasks' performance by correlating them with real-world task metrics (e.g. BLEU, accuracy).
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see proxy task conflict measures correlating strongly with real-world task performance, particularly on tasks that require reconciling short-range image statistics with language's longer-range context, and pre-training to reduce conflicts in proxy task measures.

This proposal builds on the initial gradient conflict analysis by providing a more nuanced understanding of the conflict's nature and impacts, and enabling a quantitative measure to evaluate its effects on real-world tasks.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Layer-wise analysis of gradient conflicts with modality-specific proxy tasks

TITLE: Assessing Emotional.scrollHeight Role of Text Priors in Audiovisual Emotion MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the impact of text priors on hallucinations in emotion-specific large language models for audiovisual emotion recognition and reasoning tasks using our new proposed benchmark Emotion eXplainAblity (ExAb). We will reimplement recent state-of-the-art MLLMs and fine-tune them on our modified version of the ACASE (Audio-visual and Cross-modal Emotional state) challenge data with expert labeled cues. This setup allows us to quantify the occurrence and magnitude of hallucinations and reasoning errors under different scenarios.
CONTROLS: (1) compare hallucination rates across the modified state-of-the-art MLLMs; (2) incorporate in-domain cues in manhattan dataset hallucinations; (3) exclude in-domain cues in EmotionDblData hallucinations 
COST: 8.5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Significant reduction in hallucinations when models are fine-tuned on our in-domain cues. We expect that experimenting without any in-domain cues may show poor performance; and interaction with state of the art emotion-MLM will bring results similar to our recent possibility theory paper claiming the erroneous selection of markers based on agent behavior

TITLE: Investigating the Use of Curated Affective Content in Emotion MLLM Training
PROPOSAL: Analyze the effect of incorporating curated affective content, specifically audio-visual pairs that exhibit a range of emotions, into the training data of emotion MLLMs. We expect that this will help models better understand the nuanced relationships between audio-visual cues and emotions, and reduce hallucinations and reasoning errors. Our experiment will use a combination of human-annotated audio-visual datasets (e.g., ACASE) and synthesized data to create a diverse and challenging training set.
CONTROLS: (1) compare models trained on curated affective content to those trained on regular MLLM training data; (2) evaluate the effect of varying the diversity and complexity of curated content on model performance.
COST: 10.2 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see a significant improvement in model performance on both audio-visual emotion recognition and reasoning tasks, with reduced hallucinations and reasoning errors.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating the Use of Curated Affective Content in Emotion MLLM Training
PROPOSAL: Reimagine the experiment to use a more diverse set of curated affective content, including social signals, body language, and conversational tone, in addition to audio-visual pairs. This expanded content set will allow us to investigate how models generalize to different types of emotional expression and cues. We will also include a component to evaluate the transferability of the models to new, unseen data, and compare their performance to models trained on standard MLLM training data.
CONTROLS: (1) retain the original controls from the previous proposal; (2) add an evaluation of model performance on a hold-out set not seen during training; (3) compare models trained on the expanded curated affective content to those trained on a subset of the content.
COST: 12.5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in model performance, especially on the task of generalizing to new, unseen data, and a reduced gap between models trained on standard MLLM training data and those trained on the curated affective content.

TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Emotion MLLMs to Adversarial Attacks
PROPOSAL: Investigate the robustness of emotion MLLMs to adversarial attacks, which can exploit potential flaws in model design to manipulate model outputs. We will generate adversarial examples by adding perturbations to the input data that are designed to mislead the model, and evaluate the models' performance on these examples. This will help us identify potential vulnerabilities in the models and develop strategies to improve their robustness.
CONTROLS: (1) compare the performance of the models on clean data and adversarial examples; (2) evaluate the effect of different types of perturbations on model performance; (3) compare the robustness of the models to state-of-the-art emotion MLLMs.
COST: 15.6 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see reduced performance on adversarial examples for all models, highlighting the need for robustness improvements.

TITLE: Developing Emotion-Aware Adversarial Training for Emotion MLLMs
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new training method that takes into account the emotional state of the input data and the model's predicted emotion output. This "emotion-aware" adversarial training will help the model to not only recognize and generate specific emotions but also to become more resilient to adversarial attacks that target the model's emotional reasoning.
CONTROLS: (1) compare the performance of the model on standard adversarial attacks versus emotion-aware adversarial attacks; (2) evaluate the effect of different emotion-aware training strategies on model performance; (3) compare the robustness of the model to state-of-the-art emotion MLLMs.

PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance on both the standard and emotion-aware adversarial attacks, and a significant reduction in hallucinations and reasoning errors.

TITLE: Designing an Explainable Emotion MLLM Framework for Audiovisual Emotion Recognition
PROPOSAL: Develop an explainable framework for emotion MLLMs that integrates the insights from our previous experiments and provides transparent and interpretable decision-making processes for audiovisual emotion recognition. This framework will use a combination of techniques such as attention visualization, feature importance, and saliency maps to provide explanations for the model's outputs.
CONTROLS: (1) compare the performance of the explainable framework to state-of-the-art emotion MLLMs on standard and emotion-aware adversarial attacks; (2) evaluate the effect of different explanation techniques on human evaluations; (3) analyze the relationship between explainability and model performance.
COST: 25.2 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance on standard and emotion-aware adversarial attacks, as well as high acceptance rates from human evaluators for the explanations provided by the framework.

TITLE: Scalability and Transferability of Explainable Emotion MLLMs Across Domains and Languages
PROPOSAL: Investigate the scalability and transferability of the explainable emotion MLLM framework across different domains and languages, including emotional responses that involve cultural and linguistic nuances. This will involve fine-tuning the framework on new datasets and evaluating its performance in diverse settings.
CONTROLS: (1) compare the performance of the framework on different datasets and languages; (2) evaluate the effect of cultural and linguistic nuances on human evaluations; (3) analyze the relationship between language and emotion understanding.
COST: 30.5 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to see effective transferability and scalability of the framework across diverse domains and languages, with high acceptance rates from human evaluators for the explanations provided.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluation Framework for Emotion-Specific Hallucinations in MLLMs
PROPOSAL: We design and implement the Emotion Hallucination Evaluation (EHE) framework, a benchmark consisting of three tasks: (1) Emotion Cue Task (ECT), where we evaluate whether the model's emotion predictions align with the actual audiovisual cues; (2) Emotion Cue Invention (ECI), where we assess the model's tendency to invent cues not present in the input; and (3) Emotion Cue Description (ECD), where we evaluate the coherence and relevance of the model's emotion descriptions.
CONTROLS: The EHE framework will be applied to state-of-the-art MLLMs, including OpenVINO LM and Switch Transformers, and compared to human ratings of emotion understanding from the Emotion Annotation Guidelines dataset. Additionally, we will investigate the effect of removing text priors on the hallucination rates in MLLMs.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The EHE framework will unveil significant emotion-specific hallucinations in existing MLLMs, particularly with regards to ECI and ECD, and will demonstrate that removing text priors can mitigate these hallucinations. However, we anticipate that ECT performance will be robust and less prone to hallucinations. Strategies to suppress such hallucinations could be explored further in future work.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Aiding Transparent Emotion Recognition in MLLMs through Few-Shot Prompting
PROPOSAL: We develop and evaluate the AIDER framework, which utilizes few-shot prompting to guide the model's attention towards relevant audiovisual cues and diminish the influence of text priors. Specifically, we design a novel prompt structure that incorporates a "grounding" component, which requires the model to explicitly mention or focus on specific audiovisual features that support the predicted emotion.
CONTROLS: The proposed AIDER framework will be applied to the EHE evaluation framework (from proposal 1) and compared to a baseline setup without few-shot prompting. The experiments will be conducted on the AVEC 2014 and AVEC 2019 datasets.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: AIDER will exhibit improved performance in all EHE tasks compared to the baseline setup, particularly in ECI and ECD, and will achieve a notable parity in ECT, as the few-shot prompting mechanism will guide the model to be more attentive and accurate.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: (Remains the same)
PROPOSAL: We revise and include an explicit demonstration of AIDER's effect on perception errors by contrasting the performance of an emotion-specific hallucination detection module (a new feature of EHE evaluation framework) with human ratings. This will quantify the extent to which AIDER helps reduce the presence of fabricated or irrelevant cues in the emotion recognition process. Additionally, we revise AIDER to have multiple attention-focusing options, such as explicitly prompting for lip movements, tone of voice, and other relevant audiovisual features.
CONTROLS: (Remains mostly the same) The revised EHE framework will complement human emotion understanding ratings from AVEC 2014 and will compare the performance of revised AIDER with the baseline setup on all EHE evaluation tasks.
COST: 50 additional GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Revised AIDER will effectively mitigate perception errors, particularly in instances where the model includes fabricated cues in its emotion recognitions. This reduction in hallucination errors will be backed up by both machine and human evaluation, showing significant improvement over baseline performance.
