TITLE: Minimally Supervised Grounding for Emotion Understanding
PROPOSAL: We investigate the use of minimally supervised grounding for emotion understanding in MLLMs, requiring the model to generate brief, descriptive sentences about the audiovisual cues present in the input that support its emotion predictions. propositions.texte: We develop a counterfactual analysis method to investigate the actual influence of audiovisual cues on emotion predictions in MLLMs. This involves creating synthetic counterfactual examples of the input by modifying specific audiovisual cues and retraining the MLLM to predict emotions. By analyzing the changes in emotion predictions between the original and counterfactual examples, we can identify crucial cues that the model relies on.
propositions.titre: Explaining Emotion Predictions through Counterfactual Analysis

propositions.controles: The minimally supervised grounding method will be compared to a fully supervised setup on the AVEC 2014 and 2019 datasets, and also applied to the grounded MLLM from proposal 4 to evaluate the effect of grounding on downstream emotion recognition tasks.
propositions.prediction: Minimally supervised grounding will lead to improved performance in grounding tasks, requiring the model to infer and describe relevant audiovisual cues, and show a modest increase in emotion recognition accuracy when applied to the grounded MLLM, highlighting its potential as a robust and less expensive alternative to fully supervised grounding methods.
propositions.texte: We investigate the use of minimally supervised grounding for emotion understanding in MLLMs, requiring the model to generate brief, descriptive sentences about the audiovisual cues present in the input that support its emotion predictions. This will be done using an autoencoding framework that trains the model to reconstruct the input given a set of sentence pairs (emotional description and corresponding audiovisual cue).
propositions.titre: Minimally Supervised Grounding for Emotion Understanding

propositions.controles: The framework will be evaluated using a range of few-shot learning settings, including scenarios where the model is presented with novel environments, audiovisual styles, and emotional expressions.
propositions.prediction: The framework will demonstrate improved performance in novel scenarios and environments, leveraging the reusable audiovisual explanations learned during training to adapt to unseen cases and improve generalization on downstream emotion recognition tasks, opening up new possibilities for developing emotion-understanding MLLMs.
propositions.texte: We develop a few-shot learning framework for emotion understanding in MLLMs, where the model learns to generate reusable audiovisual explanations that can be applied to novel scenarios and environments. This is achieved by requiring the model to create a library of reusable explanations for a set of training examples, which are then adapted to new, unseen inputs using few-shot learning.
propositions.titre: Few-Shot Learning for Emotion Understanding with Reusable Audiovisual Explanations

propositions.controles: The ensemble model will be compared to individual models on a range of benchmark datasets (AVEC 2014 and 2019, Emotiw, etc.) to evaluate the effectiveness of ensemble methods for emotion understanding in MLLMs.
propositions.prediction: The ensemble model will demonstrate improved performance on emotion understanding tasks compared to individual models, leveraging the strengths of each approach to capture a more comprehensive understanding of emotion-related phenomena, showcasing the potential of ensemble methods in overcoming the limitations of individual models.
propositions.texte: We investigate the use of ensemble methods to combine the strengths of the various approaches proposed in this research (evaluation framework, few-shot prompting, diagnostic task, grounded emotion description MLLMs, counterfactual analysis, minimally supervised grounding, and few-shot learning with reusable explanations). This will involve creating an ensemble model that aggregates the predictions of multiple individual models, each designed to capture different aspects of emotion understanding.
propositions.titre: Ensemble Methods for Emotion Understanding: Combining the Strengths of Multiple Approaches

TITLE: Relaxed Relative Advantage (RRA) for Outcome Rewards
PROPOSAL: Introduce a modified version of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) which replaces the normalizing factor in the relative advantages computation by the minimum absolute advantage observed in the group. This step encourages the agent to prefer exploratory actions that yield higher absolute advantages than the worst-case scenario in its group, even when all rollouts in a group have the same outcome.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard GRPO; ablation: original GRPO without normalizing by the minimum absolute advantage; evaluation on a class of query types prone to advantage collapse.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to alleviate advantage collapse but might fail for strongly uniform multiturn queries where the minimum absolute advantage becomes a small value.

TITLE: REVISED - Self-supervised Interaction Abstraction using Contextualized Action Predictions (SCAP)
PROPOSAL: Refine the auto-decodable rollout format of SCAO to predict the next action taken by the agent, conditioned on the previous steps, intermediate results, and the initial input. Instead of generating entire rollouts, use a masked language modeling approach to predict actions at intermediate steps, providing fine-grained credit assignment for RL training. Moreover, utilize the LLM's ability to generate multiple possible actions and compute a self-consistent reward for each action to ensure the learning signal remains anchored to the final objective.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard outcome rewards; ablation: SCAO without self-consistency checks; evaluation on a mix of easy and hard queries to test predictive power and reward stability.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to alleviate the issues associated with outcome-only rewards, but might fail if the agent struggles to accurately predict its own next steps due to limitations in the LLM's capabilities.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Hierarchical Progress Monitor (HPCM)
PROPOSAL: Design an intrinsic progress monitor that hierarchically tracks the agent's progress at multiple levels of abstraction: task-level, subtask-level, and operation-level. Task-level progress is tied to the final outcome, while subtask-level progress measures the completion of intermediate goals, and operation-level progress evaluates the correctness of individual actions. The monitor generates a dense, informative reward signal by aggregating progress at each level, weighted by their relative importance.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard outcome rewards; ablation: no weighting of progress levels; evaluation on a mix of easy and hard queries to test reward stability and generalization.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to provide a more informative reward signal and better credit assignment, but might fail if the hierarchies are not well-aligned with the task or if the weighting scheme is too complex.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: MDL-based Turn-Level Reliquishment (MDL-TLR) 
PROPOSAL: Introduce a model-based approach to disregard un productive intermediate turns in rollouts, guided by the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle. This method marks turns that do not improve the agent's understanding of the task, based on the description length of the current rollout. By doing so, MDL-TLR provides a way to evaluate the informativeness of each turn, helping the agent to early terminate unproductive sequences.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard outcome rewards; ablation: no action rejection; evaluation on a mix of easy and hard queries to test the effect of turn-level evaluation on policy performance and sample efficiency.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to improve sample efficiency and reduce the risk of reward sparsity, but might fail if the agent struggles to identify unproductive turns due to limited context.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Rollout-Aware Loss Inadaptation (RALI)
PROPOSAL: Introduce a rollout-aware loss adaptation mechanism that adjusts the loss function used for training based on the quality of the rollout. The mechanism assesses the rollout's relevance to the final outcome, taking into account the informativeness of turns and the overall progress made. RALI allows the agent to adapt its training objective to prioritize the most informative rollouts, thus allocating more training resources to turns with increasing impact.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard outcome rewards; ablation: no rollout-aware loss adaptation; evaluation on a mix of easy and hard queries to test the effect of RALI on sample efficiency and policy performance.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to improve sample efficiency and policy performance, but might fail if the rollout quality assessment is biased towards certain types of rollouts or if the adaptation mechanism introduces instability.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: REVISED - Relaxed Relative Advantage with Hierarchical Refining (RRAR)
PROPOSAL: Integrate the Hierarchical Progress Monitor (HPCM) into the Relaxed Relative Advantage (RRA) framework to refine the relative advantages computation with hierarchical information. Specifically, rerun HPCM on all turns within a rollout, aggregate the progress at each level, and normalize the relative advantages using the obtained hierarchies. This approach aims to more effectively identify high-reward turns and better capture the nuances of multi-turn rollouts.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard RRA; baseline-comparison: revised HPCM; evaluation on a mix of easy and hard queries to test the impact of hierarchical refinement on policy performance and sample efficiency.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to provide more accurate relative advantages and improve policy performance, but might fail if the integration of HPCM introduces complexity or slows down computation.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Entropy Regularization for Predictive Modeling (ERP)
PROPOSAL: Introduce an entropy regularization term to the self-supervised predictive modeling component of SCAP, encouraging the model to generate diverse and informative action predictions. By controlling the uncertainty of the predicted actions, ERP helps ensure that the model does not overconfidently focus on a single preferred action, thus promoting exploration and improving the agent's ability to adapt to new situations.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard SCAP; ablation: no entropy regularization; evaluation on a mix of easy and hard queries to test the effect of ERP on predictive accuracy and policy performance.
COST: 110 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to improve predictive accuracy and policy performance by reducing overfitting and promoting exploration, but might fail if the regularization term is too strong and hinders the model's ability to learn accurate action predictions.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning with and Progressive Multi-Armed Bandit (ARMAB)
PROPOSAL: Leverage the existing setup to implement asynchronous reinforcement learning (ARL) and incorporate a progressive multi-armed bandit (PMA) framework, which evaluates the impact of different sampling strategies on multi-step policies. This allows for more efficient exploration-exploitation trade-offs and enhanced adaptability to non-stationarity in the environment.
CONTROLS: Baseline: standard SCAP; evaluation on a mix of easy and hard queries to test the effect of ARMAB on sample efficiency and policy performance.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to significantly enhance the agent's adaptability and sample efficiency, but might fail if the PMA framework introduces sensitivity to hyperparameter tuning or errors in sub-component interaction evaluation.

Integrate the Hierarchical Progress Monitor (HPCM) into the Relaxed Relative Advantage (RRA) framework to refine the relative advantages computation with hierarchical information. Specifically, rerun HPCM on all turns within a rollout, aggregate the progress at each level, and normalize the relative advantages using the obtained hierarchies. This approach aims to more effectively identify high-reward turns and better capture the nuances of multi-turn rollouts.
Controls: Baseline: standard RRA; baseline-comparison: revised HPCM; evaluation on a mix of easy and hard queries to test the impact of hierarchical refinement on policy performance and sample efficiency.
Estimated cost: 180 GPU-hours
Prediction: Expected to provide more accurate relative advantages and improve policy performance, but might fail if the integration of HPCM introduces complexity or slows down computation.

PROPOSAL 2: REVISED - Self-supervised Interaction Abstraction using Contextualized Action Predictions (SCAP)
Refine the auto-decodable rollout format of SCAO to predict the next action taken by the agent, conditioned on the previous steps, intermediate results, and the initial input. Instead of generating entire rollouts, use a masked language modeling approach to predict actions at intermediate steps, providing fine-grained credit assignment for RL training. Moreover, utilize the LLM's ability to generate multiple possible actions and compute a self-consistent reward for each action to ensure the learning signal remains anchored to the final objective.
Controls: Baseline: standard outcome rewards; ablation: SCAO without self-consistency checks; evaluation on a mix of easy and hard queries to test predictive power and reward stability.
Estimated cost: 150 GPU-hours
Prediction: Expected to alleviate the issues associated with outcome-only rewards, but might fail if the agent struggles to accurately predict its own next steps due to limitations in the LLM's capabilities.

PROPOSAL 3: Hierarchical Progress Monitor (HPCM)
Design an intrinsic progress monitor that hierarchically tracks the agent's progress at multiple levels of abstraction: task-level, subtask-level, and operation-level. Task-level progress is tied to the final outcome, while subtask-level progress measures the completion of intermediate goals, and operation-level progress evaluates the correctness of individual actions. The monitor generates a dense, informative reward signal by aggregating progress at each level, weighted by their relative importance.
Controls: Baseline: standard outcome rewards; ablation: no weighting of progress levels; evaluation on a mix of easy and hard queries to test reward stability and generalization.
Estimated cost: 120 GPU-hours
Prediction: Expected to provide a more informative reward signal and better credit assignment, but might fail if the hierarchies are not well-aligned with the task or if the weighting scheme is too complex.

PROPOSAL 4: MDL-based Turn-Level Reliquishment (MDL-TLR)
Introduce a model-based approach to disregard un productive intermediate turns in rollouts, guided by the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle. This method marks turns that do not improve the agent's understanding of the task, based on the description length of the current rollout. By doing so, MDL-TLR provides a way to evaluate the informativeness of each turn, helping the agent to early terminate unproductive sequences.
Controls: Baseline: standard outcome rewards; ablation: no action rejection; evaluation on a mix of easy and hard queries to test the effect of turn-level evaluation on policy performance and sample efficiency.
Estimated cost: 100 GPU-hours
Prediction: Expected to improve sample efficiency and reduce the risk of reward sparsity, but might fail if the agent struggles to identify unproductive turns due to limited context.

PROPOSAL 5: Rollout-Aware Loss Inadaptation (RALI)
Introduce a rollout-aware loss adaptation mechanism that adjusts the loss function used for training based on the quality of the rollout. The mechanism assesses the rollout's relevance to the final outcome, taking into account the informativeness of turns and the overall progress made. RALI allows the agent to adapt its training objective to prioritize the most informative rollouts, thus allocating more training resources to turns with increasing impact.
Controls: Baseline: standard outcome rewards; ablation: no rollout-aware loss adaptation; evaluation on a mix of easy and hard queries to test the effect of RALI on sample efficiency and policy performance.
Estimated cost: 150 GPU-hours
Prediction: Expected to improve sample efficiency and policy performance, but might fail if the rollout quality assessment is biased towards certain types of rollouts or if the adaptation mechanism introduces instability.

PROPOSAL 6: Entropy Regularization for Predictive Modeling (ERP)
Introduce an entropy regularization term to the self-supervised predictive modeling component of SCAP, encouraging the model to generate diverse and informative action predictions. By controlling the uncertainty of the predicted actions, ERP helps ensure that the model does not overconfidently focus on a single preferred action, thus promoting exploration and improving the agent's ability to adapt to new situations.
Controls: Baseline: standard SCAP; ablation: no entropy regularization; evaluation on a mix of easy and hard queries to test the effect of ERP on predictive accuracy and policy performance.
Estimated cost: 110 GPU-hours
Prediction: Expected to improve predictive accuracy and policy performance by reducing overfitting and promoting exploration, but might fail if the regularization term is too strong and hinders the model's ability to learn accurate action predictions.

PROPOSAL 7: Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning with and Progressive Multi-Armed Bandit (ARMAB)
Leverage the existing setup to implement asynchronous reinforcement learning (ARL) and incorporate a progressive multi-armed bandit (PMA) framework, which evaluates the impact of different sampling strategies on multi-step policies. This allows for more efficient exploration-exploitation trade-offs and enhanced adaptability to non-stationarity in the environment.
Controls: Baseline: standard SCAP; evaluation on a mix of easy and hard queries to test the effect of ARMAB on sample efficiency and policy performance.
Estimated cost: 250 GPU-hours
Prediction: Expected to significantly enhance the agent's adaptability and sample efficiency, but might fail if the PMA framework introduces sensitivity to hyperparameter tuning or errors in sub-component interaction evaluation.

Investigate and evaluate the complete framework combining all the proposed methods in a unified multi-turn agentic search setup, yielding an auto-decodable rolling neural architecture (LSTM-based MLP module), which allows for efficient, and accurate result aggregation. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Intrinsic Learning Critics for Multiple-State Transformations
PROPOSAL: Design "state averagers" as intrinsic learning critics that export unsupervised forward passes to weigh either the similarities or dissimilarities of each state to every other across the agent's search trajectory, and subsequently compute an average state similarity score and all relevant intermediate action histories given ground truth final response. Implement a variant of the group-based policy optimization method that incorporates these "critics" – at each rollouts step we find the average state from previous steps and do execution with corresponding weights given in our learning critics module which allows us to say how productive each individual action step was once the rollouts have been stopped. This stage allows the much needed edge information about relevance of state->state->optimality in improving question-weight balancing.
CONTROLS: control for the baseline RL model on both domains with various numbers of intermediate turns
COST: 10e3 GPU-hours (using ~100 RTX 3080 GPUs for 100 hours)
PREDICTION: Such critic implementations improve search agent performance and sample efficiency by at least 5% and stay competitive with Group Relative Policy Optimization- methods without introducing computationally expensive additional rewards or tedious annotation. This approach can degrade performance when confronted with task domains that struggle with learning meaningful and coherent state space exclusively based on how they can be mapped (given and fairly dissemination,) onto their respective answer representation - primarily seen in common yes-or-no and meta-level questions.

PROPOSAL: In addition to the averages mentioned in proposal 1, also augment the agent's rollout generation with a diversity-regularizing mechanism. ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: REVISED Dense Augmentation with Local Action Metrics
PROPOSAL: Implement a version of Dense Augmentation with Local Action Metrics where each intermediate turn in the rollout is augmented with four different metrics:
- A diversity metric, encouraging diverse actions and intermediate states.
- A proximity metric, encouraging turns to be close to the previous turn.
- A relevance metric, measuring how close each turn is to the solution (future turns).
- A cohesion metric, measuring the coherence between consecutive turns.

CONTROLS: compare with different weights for each metric, and control with a baseline where no metrics are used
COST: 2e4 GPU-hours ( bốn 65 GPUs for 320 hours)
PREDICTION: By using these custom-designed metrics, the performance of the search agent is likely to improve by 10% with the optimal weights chosen in training, but may degrade by up to 5% when the weights are not well chosen, compared to baseline.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Memory-Augmented Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Implement a memory-augmented version of the agentic search agent by adding an external memory module to store and retrieve relevant information during the search process. This module will be trained to focus on retrieving accurate and relevant information for the current query, and will be used to complement the agent's reasoning and tool interactions. We will use the Neural Turing Machine (NTM) architecture as a starting point and modify it to be more suited for this task.
CONTROLS: compare with memory-augmented and non-memory-augmented versions of the search agent
COST: 1.5e5 GPU-hours (100 GPUs for 1500 hours)
PREDICTION: The memory-augmented version of the search agent is likely to improve performance by 15% on complex queries, but may increase the computational cost by up to 100%. However, it may also lead to better generalization and ability to handle out-of-distribution queries.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: REVISED REVISED Dense Augmentation with Local Action Metrics
PROPOSAL: In addition to the diversity, proximity, relevance, and cohesion metrics proposed in Turn 3, also incorporate a self-attentive mechanism to weigh and adaptively combine these metrics based on their importance in the current situation. This will allow the agent to dynamically adjust the relative importance of each metric according to the context and better optimize its search strategy.
CONTROLS: compare with the revised dense augmentation mechanism and the previous versions
COST: 3e4 GPU-hours (65 GPUs for 465 hours)
PREDICTION: By adaptively combining the metrics, the performance of the search agent is likely to improve by an additional 5-10% compared to the revised version from Turn 3, but may also increase the computational cost due to the added self-attentive mechanism. However, it may also lead to better robustness and adaptability in complex and dynamic environments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Agentic Search with Intermediate Evaluation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a hierarchical structure to the agentic search process by dividing it into multiple levels of evaluation and refinement. At each level, the agent will generate a set of candidate solutions and evaluate them using a combination of intrinsic and extrinsic metrics. The top-ranked solutions will then be refined and expanded upon in the next level, while the lower-ranked solutions will be pruned and discarded. This hierarchical approach will allow the agent to focus its search effort on the most promising regions of the solution space and make more efficient use of its resources.
CONTROLS: compare with a flat version of the agentic search process and a version with a fixed evaluation schedule
COST: 1.2e5 GPU-hours (100 GPUs for 1200 hours)
PREDICTION: The hierarchical approach is likely to improve the performance of the search agent by 10-20% compared to the flat version, but may also increase the computational cost due to the added evaluation and refinement steps. However, it may also lead to better scalability and flexibility in complex and dynamic environments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Agent Collaboration for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Introduce a multi-agent architecture to the agentic search process by decomposing the search problem into multiple sub-problems and assigning each sub-problem to a separate agent. Each agent will be responsible for searching a specific region of the solution space and will communicate its findings to the other agents through a shared knowledge graph. This will allow the agents to leverage each other's strengths and weaknesses and collectively achieve better performance than a single agent.
CONTROLS: compare with a single-agent version of the agentic search process and a version with a centralized knowledge graph
COST: 2e5 GPU-hours (200 GPUs for 2000 hours)
PREDICTION: The multi-agent approach is likely to improve the performance of the search agent by 20-30% compared to the single-agent version, but may also increase the computational cost due to the added communication and coordination steps. However, it may also lead to better scalability and flexibility in complex and dynamic environments.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Curriculum Learning for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Introduce a curriculum learning approach to the agentic search process by gradually challenging the agent with increasingly complex and difficult queries as it improves its performance. The curriculum will be designed to simulate a real-world scenario where the agent is initially given simple queries and gradually given more complex queries as it becomes more capable. This will allow the agent to learn and adapt to more difficult queries and improve its overall performance.
CONTROLS: compare with a randomly sampled set of queries and a version with a fixed difficulty level
COST: 8e4 GPU-hours (80 GPUs for 800 hours)
PREDICTION: The curriculum learning approach is likely to improve the performance of the search agent by 15-25% compared to the randomly sampled queries, and by 5-10% compared to the fixed difficulty level version. However, it may require careful tuning of the curriculum schedule and difficulty level to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Transfer Learning for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Explore the application of transfer learning to agentic search by pre-training a general-purpose agentic search agent on a large dataset of diverse queries and then fine-tuning it on a specific target dataset. This will allow the agent to leverage pre-existing knowledge and improve its performance on the target task. We will investigate the use of different pre-training tasks, architectures, and fine-tuning strategies to identify the most effective approach.
CONTROLS: compare with a randomly initialized agent and a version with pre-training on a similar dataset
COST: 3e5 GPU-hours (300 GPUs for 3000 hours)
PREDICTION: The transfer learning approach is likely to improve the performance of the search agent by 10-20% compared to the randomly initialized agent, and by 5-10% compared to the version with pre-training on a similar dataset. However, it may also introduce domain shift or overfitting issues if not carefully managed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Performance Evaluation and Reliability Analysis
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the performance of the different architectures and training methods proposed in this set of experiments using a comprehensive evaluation framework that includes metrics such as accuracy, efficiency, robustness, and reliability. Additionally, conduct a reliability analysis to measure the stability and consistency of the results across different runs and hyperparameter settings.
CONTROLS: compare with a baseline model and a state-of-the-art model
COST: 1e4 GPU-hours (10 GPUs for 100 hours)
PREDICTION: The evaluation framework will provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each architecture and training method, while the reliability analysis will help identify potential issues with stability and consistency. The results of this evaluation will inform the final choice of architecture and training method for the agentic search task.

Implement a variant of the group-based policy optimization method that incorporates these "critics" – at each rollouts step we find the average state from previous steps and do execution with corresponding weights given in our learning critics module which allows us to say how productive each individual action step was once the rollouts have been stopped. This stage allows the much needed edge information about relevance of state->state->optimality in improving question-weight balancing.
propositions.titre: Intrinsic Learning Critics for Multiple-State Transformations

propositions.controles: compare with the revised dense augmentation mechanism and the previous versions
propositions.prediction: By adaptively combining the metrics, the performance of the search agent is likely to improve by an additional 5-10% compared to the revised version from Turn 3, but may also increase the computational cost due to the added self-attentive mechanism. However, it may also lead to better robustness and adaptability in complex and dynamic environments.
propositions.texte: In addition to the diversity, proximity, relevance, and cohesion metrics proposed in Turn 3, also incorporate a self-attentive mechanism to weigh and adaptively combine these metrics based on their importance in the current situation. propositions.controles: compare with memory-augmented and non-memory-augmented versions of the search agent
propositions.prediction: The memory-augmented version of the search agent is likely to improve performance by 15% on complex queries, but may increase the computational cost by up to 100%. However, it may also lead to better generalization and ability to handle out-of-distribution queries.
propositions.texte: Implement a memory-augmented version of the agentic search agent by adding an external memory module to store and retrieve relevant information during the search process. This module will be trained to focus on retrieving accurate and relevant information for the current query, and will be used to complement the agent's reasoning and tool interactions. We will use the Neural Turing Machine (NTM) architecture as a starting point and modify it to be more suited for this task.
propositions.titre: Memory-Augmented Agentic Search

propositions.controles: compare with a flat version of the agentic search process and a version with a fixed evaluation schedule
propositions.prediction: The hierarchical approach is likely to improve the performance of the search agent by 10-20% compared to the flat version, but may also increase the computational cost due to the added evaluation and refinement steps. However, it may also lead to better scalability and flexibility in complex and dynamic environments.
propositions.texte: Introduce a hierarchical structure to the agentic search process by dividing it into multiple levels of evaluation and refinement. At each level, the agent will generate a set of candidate solutions and evaluate them using a combination of intrinsic and extrinsic metrics. The top-ranked solutions will then be refined and expanded upon in the next level, while the lower-ranked solutions will be pruned and discarded. This hierarchical approach will allow the agent to focus its search effort on the most promising regions of the solution space and make more efficient use of its resources.
propositions.titre: Hierarchical Agentic Search with Intermediate Evaluation

propositions.controles: compare with a single-agent version of the agentic search process and a version with a centralized knowledge graph
propositions.prediction: The multi-agent approach is likely to improve the performance of the search agent by 20-30% compared to the single-agent version, but may also increase the computational cost due to the added communication and coordination steps. However, it may also lead to better scalability and flexibility in complex and dynamic environments.
propositions.texte: Introduce a multi-agent architecture to the agentic search process by decomposing the search problem into multiple sub-problems and assigning each sub-problem to a separate agent. Each agent will be responsible for searching a specific region of the solution space and will communicate its findings to the other agents through a shared knowledge graph. This will allow the agents to leverage each other's strengths and weaknesses and collectively achieve better performance than a single agent.
propositions.titre: Multi-Agent Collaboration for Agentic Search

propositions.controles: compare with a randomly sampled set of queries and a version with a fixed difficulty level
propositions.prediction: The curriculum learning approach is likely to improve the performance of the search agent by 15-25% compared to the randomly sampled queries, and by 5-10% compared to the fixed difficulty level version. However, it may require careful tuning of the curriculum schedule and difficulty level to achieve optimal results.
propositions.texte: Introduce a curriculum learning approach to the agentic search process by gradually challenging the agent with increasingly complex and difficult queries as it improves its performance. The curriculum will be designed to simulate a real-world scenario where the agent is initially given simple queries and gradually given more complex queries as it becomes more capable. This will allow the agent to learn and adapt to more difficult queries and improve its overall performance.
propositions.titre: Curriculum Learning for Agentic Search

propositions.controles: compare with a randomly initialized agent and a version with pre-training on a similar dataset
propositions.prediction: The transfer learning approach is likely to improve the performance of the search agent by 10-20% compared to the randomly initialized agent, and by 5-10% compared to the version with pre-training on a similar dataset. However, it may also introduce domain shift or overfitting issues if not carefully managed.
propositions.texte: Explore the application of transfer learning to agentic search by pre-training a general-purpose agentic search agent on a large dataset of diverse queries and then fine-tuning it on a specific target dataset. This will allow the agent to leverage pre-existing knowledge and improve its performance on the target task. We will investigate the use of different pre-training tasks, architectures, and fine-tuning strategies to identify the most effective approach.
propositions.titre: Transfer Learning for Agentic Search

propositions.controles: compare with a baseline model and a state-of-the-art model
propositions.prediction: The evaluation framework will provide a comprehensive understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of each architecture and training method, while the reliability analysis will help identify potential issues with stability and consistency. Additionally, conduct a reliability analysis to measure the stability and consistency of the results across different runs and hyperparameter settings.
propositions.titre: Performance Evaluation and Reliability Analysis

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Inverse Reward Design for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Design a novel reward function that inverts the process of retrieving web search results to implicitly assign dense and informative rewards to each interaction turn of the search agent. Specifically, we propose to normalize the response times of each rollout and use these normalized times as rewards. This design leverages the fact that most interactions in successful rollouts early on will receive relevant search results quickly, whereas unsuccessful or irrelevant queries yield slower response times due to failed or incongruous web searches.
CONTROLS: Compare against using state-of-the-art GRPO methods with outcome-only rewards and the baseline of no reward (i.e., random exploration)
COST: 100 GPU-hours (assuming small-scale setup with 4 GPUs)
PREDICTION: We anticipate this inverted reward design will maintain accurate search performance while potentially reducing the effect of advantage collapse and improving sample efficiency, but may introduce some reward hacking due to the emergent patterns in response times; some more efficient search strategies do not heavily rely on response times, and thus will not be optimized as effectively.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward-Based Proxy Learning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a proxy learning framework toLTRB the relation between each interaction turn's reward signal and the corresponding components of the search agent's output, such as query terms, retrieved passages, and final answer fusion. We train a task-agnostic model to predict rewards based on these intermediate outputs, then use the predicted rewards as a proxy to optimize the search agent's policy more directly. This approach allows the search agent to receive dense rewards for specific aspects of its reasoning process, effectively credit-assigning productive turns.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effects of using different proxy learning models (e.g., linear regressors, gradient boosted trees, or self-attention networks) and compare against the baseline of using inverse rewards proposed in turn 1; also investigate whether the proxy learns to focus on the right aspects of the search agent's output.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (given the requirements for training multiple proxy learning models)
PREDICTION: By leveraging proxy learning, the search agent should achieve substantial improvements in sample efficiency and generalization to unseen queries; however, this framework may inherit some efficiency limitations if the proxy model is computationally expensive or gets stuck in suboptimal local optima.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 2
TITLE: REVISED Reward-Based Proxy Learning
PROPOSAL: Revise the proxy learning framework to explicitly address the challenge of credit-assignment by incorporating an attention mechanism that selectively focuses on specific components of the search agent's output that are most relevant to reward estimation. This modulated reward proxy learns to prioritize and weigh evidence from various sources (e.g., query terms, retrieved passages, or final answer fusion) and assigns denser, more informative rewards to productive turns. Integration of the attention mechanism requires careful adjustments to the training objectives to prevent mode collapse or biased attention patterns.
CONTROLS: Same as previously described, including comparison against the inverse rewards baseline and investigation of proxy learning model robustness
COST: 150 GPU-hours (new adjustments in training objectives should be investiged)
PREDICTION: By leveraging an attention-based proxy learning framework, the search agent should demonstrate significant improvements in sample efficiency, search accuracy, and the ability to learn diverse strategies for leveraging web search resources. On top of the existing benefits, this framework is expected to be significantly more interpretable and scalable to various search domains compared to other design choices within the set.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 1
TITLE: REVISED Inverse Reward Design for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Revise the inverse reward design by incorporating a deeper understanding of the search process and optimizing the reward proxy to reflect the search agent's epistemic uncertainty and retrieval confidence. Instead of solely relying on response times, we now use a probabilistic mixture model to combine these two variables and predict the agent's true retrieval efficiency. This refined inverse reward design provides a more nuanced and informative reward signal for multi-turn search agents.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the effects of using different types of uncertainty and confidence metrics (e.g., posterior uncertainties of query results or retrieval confidence scores) on search performance
COST: 50 GPU-hours (adjusting the penalty term and inference across the given uncertainty metrics)
PREDICTION: With this refined design, we expect a clearer disentanglement of productive and unproductive turns, leading to higher accuracy and sample efficiency in search and more accurate meta-queries overall; however, excessive sensitivity to specific metrics and lack of robustness under real-world variations in retrieval quality might hinder these advancements.

TITLE: CausalNode Attention for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Develop a novel attention mechanism called CausalNode, designed to select relevant components of the search agent's reasoning trajectory based on their causal influence on the final answer. This attention model leverages a directed acyclic graph (DAG) representation of the search process, where each node represents a turn's output and edges capture causal relationships between turns. By focusing on CausalNode scores, the search agent can adaptively prioritize productive turns and eliminate irrelevant ones.

TITLE: Meta-learned Reflection for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Introduce a meta-learning component to adaptively and dynamically adjust the search agent's reflection strategy based on recent performance and the properties of the query at hand. ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Intrinsic Motivation for Agentic Exploration
PROPOSAL: Introduce an intrinsic motivation mechanism to drive the search agent's exploration and reflection strategy beyond mere extrinsic rewards. We develop a curiosity-based intrinsic reward function that evaluates the search agent's epistemic uncertainty and novelty-seeking behavior within the search space. By promoting more diverse and informed exploration, this intrinsic motivation encourages the search agent to actively engage with the environment and seek novel information.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the intrinsic motivation mechanism against the baseline of using only extrinsic rewards, and evaluate its combination with other reward designs and exploration strategies (e.g., entropy-based exploration or proximal policy optimization)

PREDICTION: We anticipate that the intrinsic motivation mechanism will enhance the search agent's ability to actively explore the search space, adapt to changing task requirements, and engage in more efficient and effective information retrieval; however, excessive novelty-seeking may lead to local minima in performance, requiring careful tuning of the intrinsic reward coefficient.

ACTION: REVISE
NUMBER: 6
TITLE: REVISED Intrinsic Motivation for Agentic Exploration
PROPOSAL: Revise the intrinsic motivation mechanism to incorporate prior knowledge about the query and its required answer. We integrate a knowledge graph-based module that injects contextual knowledge about the query domain and relevant entities into the intrinsic reward function. This contextualized intrinsic reward encourages the search agent to not only seek novelty but also align its exploration with the task requirements and domain-specific knowledge.
CONTROLS: Investigate the effects of using different knowledge graph-based architectures and knowledge graph data sources on the performance of the contextualized intrinsic reward
COST: 80 GPU-hours (modifying the existing implementation to incorporate a knowledge graph-based module)
PREDICTION: With this revised intrinsic motivation mechanism, we expect a more efficient and task-aware exploration strategy, driving the search agent to retrieve more relevant and accurate information. However, the incorporation of prior knowledge may also introduce a risk of over-reliance on domain-specific information, potentially limiting the agent's ability to generalize to new tasks and domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating and Combining Reward Designs for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Develop a systematic evaluation framework to compare and contrast the various reward designs and exploration strategies proposed within this set. We will use a combination of simulated and real-world evaluation settings to assess the performance and robustness of each design in different query domains. Additionally, we will investigate the potential benefits of combining multiple reward designs and exploration strategies to create more effective search agents.
CONTROLS: Evaluate each reward design and exploration strategy against standard benchmarks and performance metrics, and compare their performance across different query domains and environments
COST: 400 GPU-hours (involving extensive testing and evaluation)
PREDICTION: By evaluating and combining the proposed reward designs and exploration strategies, we can identify the most effective approaches for agentic search and develop a better understanding of their potential synergies and limitations. This will enable the creation of more efficient and effective search agents that can adapt to changing task requirements and domain-specific knowledge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Query-Agnostic Volumetric Alignment Model for Sparse Perceptions
PROPOSAL: We propose a query-agnostic volumetric alignment model, termed SpOTT (Sparse Object Transformation Transformer), which utilizes a learned spatial transform to project sparse queries to a canonical volumetric feature space. This novel pre-training framework can learn rich spatial-temporal geometry on unlabeled driving videos and adapt to heterogeneous query-based downstream models for autonomous driving.
CONTROLS: Supervised DEtection TRAnsformer (DETR) for 3D object detection and LiDAR-based occupancy prediction baselines.
COST: Estimated 5000 GPU-hours (approximately 1 month on 8x NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: Expected improvement in 3D object detection and occupancy prediction tasks, with robustness to varying query configurations and sparseties of perception models. Potential failure risks include overly complex transformations leading to overfitting and a dependency on sufficient unlabeled data for robust learning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-Modal P2D-to-P3D Pre-Training and Transfer Learning for SPMs
PROPOSAL: We introduce CrossMVP (Cross-modal Pre-training for 2D-to-3D Scene Understanding), a novel pre-training framework leveraging bi-directional cross-modal interactions between image and point cloud sequences to adapt the dense 2D feature space and+self-supervised learned 3D representations. Through sim-to-real transfer learning, the network transforms and projects the aggregated sparse query features into a learned latent space with 3D semantic information, enabling improved scene understanding and object detection in sparse perception models.
CONTROLS: Baselines on image-based pre-training on DETROPIA (Image-based Pre-training for 3D Detection) and its variants before fine-tuning on SPM downstream tasks.
COST: Estimated 3000 GPU-hours (approximately 2 weeks on 8x NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: CrossMVP is expected to demonstrate improved scene understanding, rich multi-modal representations, and beneficial task-agnostic representations. However, it might be challenging to balance the image-to-pointcloud and pointcloud-to-image modalities, resulting in over- or under-representation of certain aspects.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Cross-Modal P2D-to-P3D Pre-Training and Transfer Learning for SPMs (Revised)
PROPOSAL: We revise CrossMVP by incorporating a feature grafting mechanism between the image encoder and the point cloud encoder, and introduce an auxiliary task to render and predict scene structures with depth information as intermediate supervision signals. This revised approach, named CrossMVP+, allows the model to directly leverage the spatial and temporal context of the scene, adapting the sparse query-based 2D feature space towards a pre-trained, scene-aware 3D representation.
CONTROLS: Baselines on cross-modal pre-training methods without feature grafting and depth prediction, including DETROPIA and its variants.
COST: Estimated 4000 GPU-hours (approximately 2.5 weeks on 8x NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: CrossMVP+ is expected to outperform CrossMVP with improved scene understanding, robustness to varying viewpoint and auxiliary tasks, and robust adaptation to sparse perception models. However, more complex designs might increase instability due to feature grafting and supervision signal misalignment.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Sparse Attention Masking for Efficient Pre-Training of SPMs
PROPOSAL: We propose a learning strategy, termed SamPL (Sparse Attention Masking for Pre-Training Learning), which automatically and differently masks the sparse attention mechanism based on feature relevance and importance during pre-training, thereby enabling efficient adaptation to downstream SPM tasks. Our approach reduces unnecessary attention computation and emphasizes query-specific features for robust scene understanding and object detection.
CONTROLS: Baselines on traditional attention masking methods, such as sparse attention masking using popular pre-trained SPM models in autonomous driving tasks.
COST: Estimated 2000 GPU-hours (approximately 1 week on 8x NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: SamPL is expected to demonstrate significant efficiency improvements, robustness to feature relevance, and improved generalizability to various SPM tasks. However, finding the optimal attention masking strategy and balancing trade-offs between efficiency, performance, and task requirements might challenge the effectiveness of SamPL.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sparse 3D Multi-Modal Prior Learning for Autonomous Driving
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel prior learning strategy, termed 3DGANet (3D Generative Adversarial Network Enhancer), which trains a generator to synthesize realistic 3D driving scenes given a sparse set of queries and combines them with a discriminator that predicts scene structure and semantics from the generated representations. This 3D multi-modal prior knowledge is expected to generalize and improve the learning efficiency and robustness of SPMs in various autonomous driving tasks.
CONTROLS: Baselines on traditional prior learning and generative models, such as prior learning methods and 3D scene generation methods specifically designed for autonomous driving.
COST: Estimated 3500 GPU-hours (approximately 2.25 weeks on 8x NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: 3DGANet is expected to demonstrate outstanding performance and robustness in learning challenging SPM tasks, especially in the presence of sparse and imbalanced data. However, finding the optimal generator-discriminator architecture and training strategy might require careful tuning and hyperparameter exploration.

PROPOSAL: We extend the Adaptive Sparse Attention Masking strategy, SamPL, by incorporating a novel query remapping mechanism, QRM (Query Remapping with Structure and Temporal Awareness). QRM leverages learned structural and temporal dependencies among sparse queries to re-allocate and align their receptive fields, further enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of SamPL for SPM pre-training. Our revised approach, SamPL+, explores new ways of dynamically adjusting the attention masking to better suit the hierarchical and sequential nature of driving scenes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Invariant Representation Learning for Sparse Perception via Graph Registration
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel graph registration framework, termed REGIS (Registration for Graph-Invariant Scene analysis), to learn invariant representations for sparse perception tasks in autonomous driving. REGIS incorporates a series of registration modules that progressively refine the spatial alignment of sparse queries and their surrounding scene structures, enabling the extraction of stable and generalizable features that are robust to viewpoint and pose variations.
CONTROLS: Baselines on traditional viewpoint- and pose-invariant feature extraction methods, such as hand-crafted descriptor matching and GNN-based input transformation.
COST: Estimated 2500 GPU-hours (approximately 1.5 weeks on 8x NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: REGIS is expected to demonstrate improved viewpoint and pose robustness, as well as better transferability across different SPM tasks and driving scenarios. However, the scope of REGIS might be limited to registering sparse queries within a specific scene context, and excessively relying on the graph registration mechanism might lead to overfitting and loss of generality.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: Sparse 3D Multi-Modal Prior Learning for Autonomous Driving (Revised)
PROPOSAL: We extend the Sparse 3D Multi-Modal Prior Learning strategy, 3DGANet, by incorporating a novel multimodal fusion module, MFM (Multimodal Fusion Module), to integrate the strengths of different modalities and reduce the limitations of each individual modality. MFM learns to dynamically weight and combine the contributing modalities to produce a more comprehensive and richer representation of driving scenes, thereby enhancing the robustness and generalizability of 3DGANet for SPM pre-training.
CONTROLS: Comparative ablations and baselines on original 3DGANet, modality-agnostic prior learning, and hand-crafted multimodal fusion methods.
COST: Estimated 4500 GPU-hours (approximately 3 weeks on 8x NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: The revised 3DGANet with MFM is expected to improve the robustness and generalizability of SPM pre-training, with better multimodal fusion and adaptive modality selection, robustness to potential modality-specific limitations, and improved task-agnostic representation capabilities. However, finding the optimal modality weighting scheme and characteristics for MFM might require extensive hyperparameter tuning and careful study of driving scene complexities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty-Aware Pre-Training for Sparse Perceptions with Adversarial Robustness
PROPOSAL: We propose an uncertainty-aware pre-training framework, termed UAP (Uncertainty-Aware Pre-training), to enhance the robustness and reliability of SPMs in real-world driving scenarios. UAP incorporates an adversarial training component that learns to identify and mitigate potential uncertainties in driving scenes, as well as an uncertainty quantification module that estimates and leverages the uncertainty of pre-trained representations for more adaptive and robust SPM adaptation.
CONTROLS: Baselines on traditional pre-training methods, uncertainty-aware training methods (e.g., Bayesian neural networks), and adversarial training methods.
COST: Estimated 3000 GPU-hours (approximately 2 weeks on 8x NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: UAP is expected to significantly enhance the robustness and reliability of SPMs by leveraging uncertainty-aware pre-training and adversarial robustness, with improved performance under real-world driving scenarios, reduced effort required for fine-tuning, and enhanced transferability across different SPM tasks and driving conditions. However, ensuring effective uncertainty estimation and adversarial robustness may require careful tuning and calibration of UAP's components.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multi-Task Pre-Training with Meta-Learning for Sparse Perception in Autonomous Driving
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel multi-task pre-training framework, termed MP-MTL (Multi-Task Pre-training with Meta-Learning), that enables SPMs to learn context-specific and task-independent representations by exploring multiple related tasks and leveraging meta-learning to adapt to new driving scenarios. MP-MTL is designed to be scalable, flexible, and end-to-end trainable, with meta-learners that can efficiently update model parameters and learn from diverse task-specific data sources.
CONTROLS: Baselines on multi-task learning, meta-learning, and transfer learning methods, including popular deep learning architectures for autonomous driving tasks.
COST: Estimated 5000 GPU-hours (approximately 2.5 months on 8x NVIDIA A100 GPUs)
PREDICTION: MP-MTL is expected to demonstrate improved task-adaptation capabilities, robustness, and generalizability of SPMs to real-world driving scenarios, as well as faster learning and convergence rates due to the meta-learning and multi-task pre-training mechanisms. However, finding the optimal meta-learning objective and adapting MP-MTL to a diverse range of driving scenarios, tasks, and environments will be crucial for the success of this proposal.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Scene-Aware Query Pre-Training
PROPOSAL: Pre-train a sparse perception model on unlabeled multi-view driving data by introducing a novel query-aware reconstructor that leverages both 2D and 3D scene representations, enabling the model to learn geometric and spatial-temporal information in a self-supervised manner.
CONTROLS: Compare with existing pre-training methods and models, such as DETR3D, Sparse4D, and the NeRF-based approaches (UniPAD and ViDAR).
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Significant improvement in 3D object detection and semantic occupancy prediction, with the potential to reduce reliance on explicit dense intermediate representations.

This proposal establishes a potential baseline for query-aware pre-training and explores the effectiveness of incorporating 2D and 3D scene representations in the pre-training process.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Scene-Aware Query Pre-Training (Revised)
PROPOSAL: Pre-train a sparse perception model on unlabeled multi-view driving data by introducing a novel query-aware reconstructor that leverages both 2D and 3D scene representations, specifically by sparsifying the supervision signals obtained from NeRF-based rendering using the known geometry, enabling the model to learn geometric and spatial-temporal information in a self-supervised manner.
CONTROLS: (no change) Compare with existing pre-training methods and models, such as DETR3D, Sparse4D, and the NeRF-based approaches (UniPAD and ViDAR).
COST: 120 GPU-hours (additional computational cost for introducing NeRF-based sparsification)
PREDICTION: Improved performance in 3D object detection and semantic occupancy prediction, as the model is able to learn from discriminative geometric information encoded in NeRF-based rendering.

This revised proposal refines the original idea by incorporating the benefits of NeRF-based rendering to further enhance the model's ability to learn geometric and spatial-temporal information.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Transferring Pre-Training to Downstream Models

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Pre-Training Sparse Perception Models with Implicit Contextual Queries
PROPOSAL: Experiment to investigate pre-training sparse perception models using a novel architecture that learns to predict implicit contextual queries from unlabeled multi-view driving data. The model will be based on a sparse query network that incorporates a 3D Gaussian Process (GP) prior to learn the spatial structure of the scene. The GP will be trained to predict the expected distribution of contextual queries given the input images.
CONTROLS: Compare against DiT (a state-of-the-art transformer-based image-to-image translation model) pre-trained on the same dataset as a control, to demonstrate that the learned contextual queries provide meaningful information about the scene.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The pre-trained model will outperform the DiT control by at least 5% on a downstream task such as object detection, demonstrating the effectiveness of the implicit contextual queries in learning a 3D scene representation. However, the approach may fail if the GP prior does not capture the complex spatial relationships between objects in the scene.

Note: DiT is a strong baseline since it can model image-to-image translation, a fundamental task in computer vision, that can be used to learn powerful features for downstream tasks. The experiment will evaluate the extent to which the learned contextual queries are useful for downstream tasks such as object detection.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Revising Pre-Training Sparse Perception Models with Implicit Contextual Queries
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Experiment to investigate pre-training sparse perception models using a novel multi-view transformers architecture that learns to predict implicit contextual queries from unlabeled multi-view driving data. The model will utilize a self-supervised feature learning objective that leverages triplet loss to learn rich spatial and temporal features. The triplet loss will be computed between the input images, their rendered BEVs, and a randomly sampled target view.
CONTROLS: Compare against DETR3D (a state-of-the-art sparse 3D object detector) pre-trained on the same dataset as a control, to demonstrate that the learned contextual queries provide meaningful information about the scene.
COST: 70 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The pre-trained model will outperform the DETR3D control by at least 10% on a downstream task such as object detection, demonstrating the effectiveness of the implicit contextual queries in learning a 3D scene representation. However, the approach may fail if the multi-view transforms do not generalize well to unseen views.

Note: The revised proposal addresses potential issues with the original proposal by incorporating a more robust self-supervised learning objective and a more recent state-of-the-art control.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Revising Pre-Training Sparse Perception Models with Implicit Contextual Queries
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Experiment to investigate pre-training sparse perception models using a novel multi-view transformers architecture that learns to predict implicit contextual queries from unlabeled multi-view driving data. The model will utilize a self-supervised feature learning objective that leverages triplet loss to learn rich spatial and temporal features. The triplet loss will be computed between the input images, their rendered BEVs, and a randomly sampled target view. To improve robustness, the model will also employ view-augmentation techniques and utilize a data augmentation module to learn invariance to diverse environmental conditions.
CONTROLS: Compare against DETR3D (a state-of-the-art sparse 3D object detector) pre-trained on the same dataset as a control, to demonstrate that the learned contextual queries provide meaningful information about the scene. Additionally, compare against a variant of the model trained with more aggressive data augmentation to quantify the effects of data augmentation on the model's performance.
COST: 90 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The pre-trained model will outperform the DETR3D control by at least 12% on a downstream task such as object detection, demonstrating the effectiveness of the implicit contextual queries in learning a 3D scene representation. However, the approach may fail if the view-augmentation techniques do not generalize well to diverse scenes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Query-Based Transfer Learning for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Experiment to investigate the efficacy of query-based transfer learning for sparse perception models. The goal is to develop a framework that enables the transfer of knowledge from a pre-trained sparse perception model to a downstream sparse perception model, leveraging the implicit contextual queries learned during pre-training. To achieve this, we will investigate the use of a query-embeddings module to convert the implicit contextual queries into a compact embedding space, which can be transferred to the downstream model.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that directly fine-tunes the pre-trained model on the downstream task, as well as against a variant that uses a frozen query-embeddings module for transfer learning.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The query-based transfer learning approach will outperform the fine-tuning baseline by at least 5% on a downstream task such as object detection, demonstrating the effectiveness of the query embeddings in facilitating knowledge transfer. However, the approach may fail if the query embeddings do not capture the key features necessary for the downstream task.

Note: This proposal aims to address the challenge of transferring knowledge from pre-trained sparse perception models to downstream models, which is a critical aspect of sparse perception research.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of 3D Scene Geometry on Pre-Training Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Experiment to investigate the impact of 3D scene geometry on the pre-training of sparse perception models. The goal is to quantify the effects of varying levels of scene complexity, occlusion, and viewpoint change on the performance of the pre-trained models. To achieve this, we will create a synthetic dataset with controlled levels of scene complexity and manipulate the viewpoint and occlusion levels within the scenes.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that is pre-trained on a dataset with minimal scene complexity and occlusion.
COST: 80 GPU-hours on a 4-GPU machine
PREDICTION: The pre-trained model will outperform the baseline by at least 15% on a downstream task such as object detection in scenes with high complexity and occlusion, demonstrating the importance of adapting to varying scene geometry during pre-training. However, the approach may fail if the synthetic dataset does not capture the full range of real-world scene complexities.

Note: This proposal aims to investigate how the pre-training datasets and environments affect the performance of sparse perception models. Understanding the impact of scene geometry can help design more effective pre-training strategies for real-world applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Experiment to develop a comprehensive evaluation framework for sparse perception models, incorporating a range of metrics and evaluation protocols that can assess the performance of such models in various scenarios. The framework will be benchmarked on a variety of sparse perception models, including DETR3D, Sparse4D, and OPUS, and will be used to evaluate their performance on tasks such as object detection, semantic segmentation, and 3D reconstruction.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline evaluation framework that focuses only on standard metrics such as mAP and accuracy.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (note: the evaluation framework development can be done on a low-cost machine)
PREDICTION: The comprehensive evaluation framework will reveal significant disparities in the performance of different sparse perception models, demonstrating its effectiveness in identifying strengths and weaknesses of such models. However, the approach may fail if the evaluation framework does not capture the full range of scenarios and tasks relevant to sparse perception.

Note: This proposal aims to develop a standardized evaluation framework for sparse perception models, which is crucial for fair comparison and advancement of the field.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Use of Synthetic Data for Pre-Training Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Experiment to investigate the effectiveness of using synthetic data for pre-training sparse perception models. Specifically, we will create a synthetic dataset using a variety of scene and object generators, and use it to pre-train a sparse perception model. We will then evaluate the performance of the pre-trained model on real-world data and compare it to a model pre-trained on real-world data.
CONTROLS: Compare against a model pre-trained on real-world data and against a model pre-trained on real-world data with data augmentation.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (note: this experiment can be done in parallel with other experiments)
PREDICTION: The model pre-trained on synthetic data will outperform the baseline model pre-trained on real-world data by at least 5% on certain tasks, demonstrating the potential of synthetic data for pre-training sparse perception models. However, the approach may fail if the synthetic data does not capture the full range of real-world scenarios and complexities.

Note: This proposal aims to investigate the use of synthetic data for pre-training sparse perception models, which can potentially reduce the need for large amounts of real-world data and speed up the training process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Role of Edge Computing in Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Experiment to investigate the role of edge computing in sparse perception models, specifically focusing on evaluating the performance of such models in edge computing scenarios. We will use a set of mobile edge computing platforms to deploy the sparse perception models and evaluate their performance on edge devices.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that trains and deploys the sparse perception model in the cloud.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (note: this experiment will require accessing edge computing platforms)
PREDICTION: The sparse perception model will perform within 10% of its cloud-based counterpart when deployed on edge devices, demonstrating the feasibility of edge computing for sparse perception models. However, the approach may fail if the edge devices have limited computational resources or if the communication latency between the edge devices and the cloud is too high.

Note: This proposal aims to investigate the potential of edge computing for sparse perception models, which can enable real-time processing and decision-making at the edge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring Explainability Techniques for Sparse Perception Models
PROPOSAL: Experiment to investigate the use of explainability techniques for sparse perception models, specifically focusing on understanding how the models represent and reason about the input scenes. We will use a combination of attribution methods, such as SHAP and LRP, and visualization techniques, such as heatmaps and feature importance, to analyze the behavior of the sparse perception models.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that does not use any explainability techniques.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The explainability techniques will provide valuable insights into the behavior of the sparse perception models, enabling researchers to identify potential biases and errors in the models. However, the approach may fail if the explainability techniques are not effective in capturing the complex decision-making processes of the sparse perception models.

Note: This proposal aims to investigate the use of explainability techniques for sparse perception models, which is crucial for building trust in AI systems and ensuring that they make fair and unbiased decisions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Efficient and Generalizable Sparse Perception Models: A Meta-Learning Approach
PROPOSAL: Experiment to investigate the use of meta-learning for sparse perception models, specifically focusing on developing a framework that can adapt to new tasks and environments with minimal retraining. We will use a few-shot learning approach and meta-learning algorithms, such as MAML and Reptile, to adapt to new tasks and environments with a few examples.
CONTROLS: Compare against a baseline that uses a traditional deep learning approach and a fixed model architecture.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The meta-learning approach will enable the sparse perception models to adapt to new tasks and environments with minimal retraining, demonstrating its potential for efficient and generalizable sparse perception. However, the approach may fail if the meta-learning algorithm does not effectively capture the underlying relationships between the sparse perception tasks and environments.

Note: This proposal aims to investigate the use of meta-learning for sparse perception models, which can enable efficient and generalizable sparse perception. The meta-learning approach can adapt to new tasks and environments with minimal retraining, making it a promising direction for sparse perception research.

Experiment to develop a comprehensive evaluation framework for sparse perception models, incorporating a range of metrics and evaluation protocols that can assess the performance of such models in various scenarios. The framework will be benchmarked on a variety of sparse perception models, including DETR3D, Sparse4D, and OPUS, and will be used to evaluate their performance on tasks such as object detection, semantic segmentation, and 3D reconstruction.
Controls: Compare against a baseline evaluation framework that focuses only on standard metrics such as mAP and accuracy.

However, the approach may fail if the evaluation framework does not capture the full range of scenarios and tasks relevant to sparse perception.

Note: This proposal aims to develop a standardized evaluation framework for sparse perception models, which is crucial for fair comparison and advancement of the field.

PROPOSAL 5: Investigating the Use of Synthetic Data for Pre-Training Sparse Perception Models
Experiment to investigate the effectiveness of using synthetic data for pre-training sparse perception models. Specifically, we will create a synthetic dataset using a variety of scene and object generators, and use it to pre-train a sparse perception model. We will then evaluate the performance of the pre-trained model on real-world data and compare it to a model pre-trained on real-world data.
Controls: Compare against a model pre-trained on real-world data and against a model pre-trained on real-world data with data augmentation.
Estimated cost: 100 GPU-hours (note: this experiment can be done in parallel with other experiments)
Prediction: The model pre-trained on synthetic data will outperform the baseline model pre-trained on real-world data by at least 5% on certain tasks, demonstrating the potential of synthetic data for pre-training sparse perception models. However, the approach may fail if the synthetic data does not capture the full range of real-world scenarios and complexities.

Note: This proposal aims to investigate the use of synthetic data for pre-training sparse perception models, which can potentially reduce the need for large amounts of real-world data and speed up the training process.

PROPOSAL 6: Analyzing the Role of Edge Computing in Sparse Perception Models
Experiment to investigate the role of edge computing in sparse perception models, specifically focusing on evaluating the performance of such models in edge computing scenarios. We will use a set of mobile edge computing platforms to deploy the sparse perception models and evaluate their performance on edge devices.
Controls: Compare against a baseline that trains and deploys the sparse perception model in the cloud.
Estimated cost: 50 GPU-hours (note: this experiment will require accessing edge computing platforms)
Prediction: The sparse perception model will perform within 10% of its cloud-based counterpart when deployed on edge devices, demonstrating the feasibility of edge computing for sparse perception models. However, the approach may fail if the edge devices have limited computational resources or if the communication latency between the edge devices and the cloud is too high.

Note: This proposal aims to investigate the potential of edge computing for sparse perception models, which can enable real-time processing and decision-making at the edge.

PROPOSAL 7: Exploring Explainability Techniques for Sparse Perception Models
Experiment to investigate the use of explainability techniques for sparse perception models, specifically focusing on understanding how the models represent and reason about the input scenes. We will use a combination of attribution methods, such as SHAP and LRP, and visualization techniques, such as heatmaps and feature importance, to analyze the behavior of the sparse perception models.

Note: This proposal aims to investigate the use of explainability techniques for sparse perception models, which is crucial for building trust in AI systems and ensuring that they make fair and unbiased decisions.

PROPOSAL 8: Towards Efficient and Generalizable Sparse Perception Models: A Meta-Learning Approach
Experiment to investigate the use of meta-learning for sparse perception models, specifically focusing on developing a framework that can adapt to new tasks and environments with minimal retraining. We will use a few-shot learning approach and meta-learning algorithms, such as MAML and Reptile, to adapt to new tasks and environments with a few examples.
