actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Baseline for Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: Experimentally evaluate several pre-trained vision-language models (e.g., GLIP, Grounding DINO) on a real-world object detection dataset (e.g., COCO) without any adaptation to assess their general performance and determine whether the current state-of-the-art object detection models are indeed worthy of adapting.
CONTROLS: Compare performances of GLIP, Grounding DINO, and a state-of-the-art offline domain adaptation method applied to object detection, using metrics like mAP and AP for evaluation; analyze their open-vocabulary capabilities and generalization to test-time adaptation.
COST: 10 GPU-hours (evaluation with 3 models on a moderate-sized object detection dataset)
PREDICTION: We expect that, unlike their offline domain adaptation counterparts, pre-trained vision-language models will show relatively stable performance on object detection tasks without adaptation, showcasing their potential for test-time adaptive object detection.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Baseline for Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
REVISED PROPOSAL: In addition to evaluating the general performance of pre-trained vision-language models on a real-world object detection dataset, also experimentally investigate the effect of full-parameter fine-tuning on their performance and generalization. This will serve as a baseline to understand whether any test-time adaptation method is even necessary, and whether overfitting can be avoided.
CONTROLS: Compare performances of fine-tuned GLIP, Grounding DINO, and their pre-trained counterparts on COCO, while containing overfitting via early stopping or data augmentation; examine the influence of fine-tuning on their open-vocabulary and generalization capabilities.
COST: 20 GPU-hours (evaluation with 3 models on a moderate-sized object detection dataset, plus potentially extensive fine-tuning)
PREDICTION: Fine-tuning may lead to significant improvements on the target dataset, but might also amplify noise, diminishing generalizability, and potentially causing the model to overfit on the target domain, which would indicate a need for effective adaptation methods.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Baseline for Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection
REVISED PROPOSAL: In addition to comparing state-of-the-art offline domain adaptation methods with pre-trained vision-language models, also evaluate their self-learning capabilities on COCO by leveraging pseudo-labeled objects generated from the target data. We explore whether pre-trained models can adapt themselves during testing and whether this adaptation is more efficient and effective compared to offline adaptation methods.
CONTROLS: Compare performances of both state-of-the-art offline domain adaptation methods and pre-trained vision-language models with self-learning capabilities on COCO, ensuring alignment with a confidence threshold for pseudo-label filtering.
COST: 30 GPU-hours (evaluation on COCO, offline domain adaptation, self-learning with pre-trained models, and applying pseudo-label filtering)
PREDICTION: This will allow us to understand the viability of self-learning for test-time adaptive object detection, and whether the dependence on pseudo-labeled objects for adaptation is more significant than the full-parameter fine-tuning requirements for the current pre-trained models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Online Data Filtering for Reliable Pseudo-Label Generation
PROPOSAL: Develop and experimentally evaluate a novel online data filtering method to obtain high-quality pseudo-labels for test-time adaptive object detection. The method uses a combination of uncertainty estimation and cluster-based filtering to address the challenge of inadequate pseudo-labels and unreliable online pseudo-label generation.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed method against traditional filtering approaches (e.g., fixed confidence threshold) on the test data, further evaluating the improvements on data with diverse densities and noise levels; compare a set of standard object detection models adapted online with pseudo-labels filtered using the proposed method against pre-trained counterparts.
COST: 40 GPU-hours (implementation of the online filtering method and its evaluation on a moderate-sized object detection dataset)
PREDICTION: This method should result in more consistent and effective pseudo-label generation for test-time adaptive object detection, particularly in scenarios with diverse densities and noise levels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Test-Time Adaptive Object Detection with Label-Space Expansion
PROPOSAL: Propose and experimentally evaluate a novel label-space expansion technique for test-time adaptive object detection, allowing for addressing open-vocabulary challenges without requiring the pre-trained model to be re-trained. The approach involves learning adapter modules to dynamically expand the label space based on encountered pseudo-labels.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed approach with current TTAOD methods on synthetic/real-world datasets with varying label spaces; evaluate the expansion quality and detection accuracy for scenarios with limited category overlap between source and target domains.
COST: 60 GPU-hours (implementation of the label-space expansion method, its evaluation, and comparison with existing TTAOD methods)
PREDICTION: The effectiveness of label-space expansion will be mostly dependent on pseudo-label quality and expansion capacity, which in turn are influenced by pre-trained model quality, uncertainty estimation, and efficient pseudo-label generation modules, like the one proposed in Proposal 2.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Theoretical Analysis of Test-Time Adaptation for Object Detection
PROPOSAL: Provide a theoretical framework to analyze the asymptotic performance of test-time adaptive object detection methods, focusing on the relationship between model complexity, adaptation iterations, and labeling noise. Derive bounds on the convergence rate of test-time adapted models, considering the statistical properties of test-time adaptation, such as online sequential sampling and pseudo-label updating.
CONTROLS: Simulate scenarios with varying model complexities, adaptation iterations, and noise levels to verify the theoretical bounds and their implications on practical test-time adaptation.
COST: 
PREDICTION: This theoretical analysis will clarify how different methodological choices affect the long-run performance of test-time adaptive object detection, ultimately guiding the development of more efficient and adapted testing strategies. Its difficulty relies on directly quantifying pseudo-labeling reliability and its effect from new data, however with appropriate linearisation approximations considerable theoretical insights can still be extracted.

ACTION: REVISE 4
TITLE: A Theoretical Analysis of Test-Time Adaptation for Object Detection
REVISED PROPOSAL: Focus the theoretical analysis on identifying the sufficient conditions for the convergence of model parameters during test-time adaptation, by considering the averaged reward of all iterations through maximizing entropy with an inequality for measuring bounded numbers based upon adjusting the batch learning rates in hyperparameter space. Assume that the reward of adjusting step-sizes indicates a benefit.
CONTROLS: Leverage cross-validated experiments to verify the proposed sufficiency conditions on a variety of test-time adaptive object detection methods and scenarios, while adjusting their learning rates' effects using the examined popular group's variable sensitivity to maximize learner's found potential parallel-based functioning procedures for processing yet any possibly inaccurate pseudo-labels eventually correctly evaluate them.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learning for Efficient Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Models
PROPOSAL: Explore meta-learning approaches to adapt vision-language models for object detection at test-time, where the model learns to adapt to new categories or distributions more efficiently by learning from a set of meta-training tasks with different adaptation scenarios. This involves developing a meta-training protocol to prepare the model for various test scenarios and fine-tuning it for specific instances.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed meta-learning approach with current state-of-the-art methods for test-time adaptive object detection on COCO, including evaluating model generalization capabilities and transfer learning adaptation outcomes in synthetic/real-world scenarios.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (meta-training protocol implementation, testing on various scenarios, and comparisons)
PREDICTION: Successful meta-learning adaptation will enable object detection models to adapt quickly to diverse target categories or distributions without requiring extensive pre-training or source-domain data, improving the practicability of test-time adaptive object detection in real-world applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Online Pseudo-Label Correction and Inference Scheduling
PROPOSAL: Develop and experimentally evaluate a scheduling-based approach that efficiently corrects pseudo-labels and adapts the detection model concurrently during inference, leveraging the insights gained from the analysis in Proposal 2 and the meta-learning approach in Proposal 5. This involves selecting the optimal scheduling strategy to find a balance between reducing wrong pseudo-labels and increasing model adaptation efficiency.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the proposed approach with various scheduling strategies and baselines, such as using fixed confidence thresholds or ignoring pseudo-labels on COCO, evaluating metrics like adaptability speed, accuracy, and conservation of pre-trained knowledge.
COST: 100 GPU-hours (implementation of scheduling strategy, its evaluation, and comparisons)
PREDICTION: This proposal should improve the adaptability speed and efficiency of test-time adaptive object detection while maintaining or even improving its accuracy and pre-trained knowledge retention by effectively correcting and leveraging pseudo-labels.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Experimental Evaluation on Real-World Object Detection Datasets
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comprehensive experimental evaluation of the proposed test-time adaptive object detection methods and controls on real-world object detection datasets, such as COCO, KITTI, and Cityscapes, to assess their performance, generalizability, and robustness to various domain shifts and artifacts. This will include detailed comparative analyses, failure case studies, and lessons learned.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of proposed methods, controls, and state-of-the-art methods on real-world datasets, considering various metric criteria and structured evaluation protocols, such as precision-recall curves, adaptation speed, and accuracy; analyze cases of success and failure to identify potential pitfalls and areas for improvement.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (comprehensive evaluation on multiple real-world datasets and detailed analyses)
PREDICTION: The results of this evaluation will provide a clear understanding of the strengths and limitations of test-time adaptive object detection methods, allowing for a more informed decision-making process when selecting methods for practical applications.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Towards Robust Vision-Language Detectors at Test Time
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effect of optimizing an adapter in addition to the detector's classification head during test-time adaptation using the standard offline self-training objective with noisy pseudo-labels. This is an ablation to previously proposed methods that train adapters but only update the classification head's parameters online.
CONTROLS: Compare to the standard self-training approach without adapters and to previous adapter-based methods that update only the classification head. Use Grounding DINO as our pre-trained detector and simulate the test-time adaptation process on the PASCAL VOC and COCO datasets.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The adapter optimization might offer comparable performance to previous methods in certain scenarios (e.g., VOC), but still suffer from the high sensitivity to noisy pseudo-labels and degradation of pre-trained knowledge in others (e.g., COCO).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Improving Noisy Pseudo-Labeling through Contrastive Adversarial Learning
PROPOSAL: Modify the self-training objective to leverage a contrastive adversarial loss between positive (correctly pseudo-labeled) and negative (incorrectly pseudo-labeled) pairs of targets and detector outputs. This aims to reduce noise in pseudo-labels by focusing the adaptation process on examples with reliable pseudo-labels.
CONTROLS: Compare to the standard self-training objective with noisy pseudo-labeling and to a baseline with noise-reduced pseudo-labels generated using a standard confidence threshold. Use COCO and Cityscapes as additional real-world testbeds to assess adaptation performance.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed method should reduce the negative impact of noisy pseudo-labels and maintain the pre-trained detector's generalization capability. However, its performance might still degrade when high-quality pseudo-labels are scarce.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Improving Noisy Pseudo-Labeling through Contrastive Adversarial Learning
PROPOSAL: Instead of directly leveraging a contrastive adversarial loss, incorporate a noise-robust scoring function into the self-training objective. This function evaluates the consistency of pseudo-labels within multiple iterations of the adaptation process, and the detector gets updated only when this consistency score exceeds a certain confidence threshold. This aims to further improve the selection of pseudo-labels used during adaptation.
CONTROLS: Original controls remain the same, i.e., compare to the standard self-training objective with noisy pseudo-labeling and to a baseline with noise-reduced pseudo-labels generated using a standard confidence threshold.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised method should continue to reduce the negative impact of noisy pseudo-labels, but potentially better handle scenarios with high-quality pseudo-labels being scarce. However, the increased computational cost may limit its practicality in real-time applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Meta-Learning for Efficient Adaptation in Test-Time Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Encapsulate test-time adaptation into a meta-learning framework, where the pre-trained detector learns to generate optimal adaptation steps (in terms of pseudo-label confidence and updating the detector's classification head) for a new target domain. This is done by treating the detector as a meta-model that updates pseudo-labels and adapts itself based on a given small batch of target data.
CONTROLS: Compare to the standard self-training and contrastive adversarial learning approaches, and evaluate adaptation performance on various datasets, including those with open-set scenarios and image-text pairs from multiple domains.
COST: 2500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This meta-learning framework should improve adaptation performance by providing a more structured way of updating the detector, especially in scenarios with limited target data. However, the computational cost may still pose a challenge for real-time applications.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Target Domain-aware Multi-task Learning for Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: Combine the adaptation process with multi-task learning, where the pre-trained detector is trained to predict not only object classifications but also semantic features related to the target domain (e.g., domain-specific attributes, scene information). This aims to provide the detector with rich contextual information about the target domain, improving its adaptation performance.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of the multi-task learning module on the adaptation process using existing benchmarks, and compare to a baseline where the detector only adapts its classification head.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The integration of target domain-aware multi-task learning should enhance the detector's ability to adapt to target domains with diverse characteristics, particularly when little information is available about the target domain. However, the added complexity could still limit its practicality in some scenarios.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Towards Robust Vision-Language Detectors at Test Time
PROPOSAL: Instead of optimizing an adapter during test-time adaptation, apply the adapter's feature transformation to the pre-trained detector's feature maps during the adaptation process. This modulates the detector's feature space to better match the target domain's distribution, and the optimization is done directly on the detector's classification head.
CONTROLS: Compare to the previous adapter-based approach, and evaluate the impact of using direct feature transformation on adaptation performance.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The revised adapter-based approach should retain the benefits of adapting the detection model's feature space while reducing the sensitivity to noisy pseudo-labels and increasing computational efficiency. However, it might not be as effective in preserving the pre-trained knowledge as previously proposed methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Return of the Source: Analyzing the Impact of Secondary Source Domains on Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether providing access to a secondary source domain during test-time adaptation can improve performance, particularly when the primary source domain has limited diversity. This analysis aims to better understand the limitations of source-free adaptation and provide insights on potential ways to relax the source-free assumption.
CONTROLS: Compare adaptation performance using the primary source domain only, secondary source domain only, and a combination of both source domains. Evaluate on various datasets with diverse characteristics.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Including a secondary source domain may alleviate some adaptation difficulties, especially in scenarios with severe domain shifts, but could also lead to overadaptation and a loss of pre-trained knowledge if not carefully managed. The findings should provide a foundation for future work addressing the limitations of source-free adaptation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Curriculum-based Pseudo-Label Filtering for Adaptive Object Detection
PROPOSAL: Develop a curriculum-based framework to progressively filter pseudo-labels according to their confidence and difficulty (e.g., based on the detector's entropy or pseudo-label accuracy). This enables the detector to focus on the most informative and reliable pseudo-labels, potentially improving adaptability and generalization.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of pseudo-label filtering on adaptation performance, comparing to a baseline without filtering and various existing approaches.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The proposed curriculum-based pseudo-label filtering should significantly improve adaptation performance by focusing the detector's efforts on the most informative pseudo-labels, but may require careful tuning of the filtering criteria to achieve optimal results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Efficient Federated Learning for Test-Time Adaptable Object Detection
PROPOSAL: Propose a federated learning-based approach for test-time adaptable object detection, where multiple client devices or edge devices cooperatively adapt the shared model using their respective test data. This framework can be particularly effective for resource-constrained devices, promoting privacy, and reducing communication overhead.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of federated learning on adaptation performance, comparing to a centralized learning approach and considering various network topologies and client device scenarios.
COST: 1800 GPU-hours (estimated, as actual computational cost may depend on the specific federated learning implementation)
PREDICTION: The proposed federated learning framework should improve the efficiency and scalability of test-time adaptable object detection, making it more suitable for applications requiring global adaptation across multiple devices. However, potential issues with communication overhead and model synchronization may need to be addressed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation and Analysis of Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Detectors
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comprehensive evaluation and analysis of the proposed test-time adaptation methods, including a thorough comparison of their strengths and weaknesses, and an analysis of their potential limitations and biases. This will provide a deeper understanding of the design trade-offs and provide insights for future research directions.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the proposed methods on various benchmark datasets and consider multiple evaluation metrics. Compare the results to existing test-time adaptation methods and provide a detailed analysis of their differences.
COST: 3000 GPU-hours (estimated, as actual computational cost may depend on the extensive evaluation procedure)
PREDICTION: The comprehensive evaluation and analysis will provide a clear understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of test-time adaptation methods for vision-language detectors, enabling the identification of future research directions and the development of more effective test-time adaptation strategies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Online Bootstrapping for Reliable Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel adaptive online bootstrapping strategy that combines the advantages of self-training and pseudo-label filtering. The strategy involves iteratively selecting a subset of confident pseudo-labels and re-training the detector on these selected pseudo-labels, ensuring that the detector stays robust to noisy or missing pseudo-labels. We will implement this strategy on top of the revised meta-learning detector from previous proposal and evaluate its effectiveness on various cross-domain adaptation tasks.
controls: comparisons with the standard meta-learning based detector, Faster R-CNN based TTAOD methods that require source-domain statistics, and the adaptive meta-learning detector without online bootstrapping
Specified cost: 200 GPU-hours
Prediction: The adaptive online bootstrapping strategy will significantly improve the reliability and robustness of the detector in the presence of noisy or missing pseudo-labels, potentially leading to improved accuracy on target domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Foundation Model Pre-Training on Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: We will conduct an in-depth analysis of the influence of foundation model pre-training on the test-time adaptation performance of vision-language detectors. Specifically, we will compare the adaptation results of detectors pre-trained with different vision-language pre-training objectives (e.g., contrastive learning, masked language modeling) and with varying levels of pre-training data. We will evaluate the detectors on a diverse set of cross-domain adaptation tasks and analyze the impact of pre-training on the detector's robustness to domain shifts.
controls: comparisons with detectors pre-trained with standard object detection objectives, and detectors with and without the adaptive online bootstrapping strategy from proposal 2
Specified cost: 250 GPU-hours
Prediction: The analysis will reveal the limitations and strengths of different pre-training objectives and data scales on the test-time adaptation performance, providing valuable insights for the design of future vision-language detectors for TTAOD.

We will train the detector with both the classification loss and an uncertainty estimation loss, and evaluate its performance on a range of metrics that account for both accuracy and uncertainty.
controls: comparisons with detectors without uncertainty estimation, adaptive online bootstrapping strategy from proposal 2, and detectors from proposal 1

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Scalable Complexity Trends in Route Optimization
PROPOSAL: We investigate the influences of model capacity, computation, and solution space size on the accuracy of a neural network designed to solve the Euclidean traveling salesman problem. We use a synthetic dataset with varying problem sizes (10 to 100 cities) and a fixed neural network architecture (a variant of the CapsNet route optimization model). Our performance metric is the average error between the learned routes and the optimal ones.
CONTROLS: We compare our results against a naive baseline (a simple backtracking algorithm) and an ablation of the model's capacity limiting (removing the caps layers).
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours to train and evaluate the models for each problem size.
PREDICTION: We expect to see scalable trends in performance according to the number of cities and model capacity, with diminishing returns as the model approaches the optimal accuracy. However, the actual rate of improvement could vary significantly as the model becomes more computationally expensive.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Impact of Representation Space Dimensions
PROPOSAL: To investigate how the dimensionality of the representation space influences the accuracy of the neural network, we introduce a new variable in the problem and modify the neural network architecture to accommodate it. Specifically, we add a new coordinate system to the problem by introducing virtual cities that are not part of the solution space, but affect the network's decision-making. We observe how the performance change as the number of virtual cities increases.
CONTROLS: We compare our results against an ablation of the new architectural component (removing the virtual cities), and a baseline where we only add noise to the existing coordinates.
COST: Estimated additional 50 GPU-hours to fine-tune the model with the new component.
PREDICTION: We expect to see a positive correlation between the number of virtual cities and improvement in route accuracy, as the model leverages the additional information to learn more efficient routes. However, we may see a tendency for the model to overfit if the number of virtual cities is too high.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: REVISED: Scalable Complexity Trends in Route Optimization
PROPOSAL: We modify the previous experiment to include a synthetic dataset with varying solution space sizes (from 10 to 100 possible routes) and a fixed neural network architecture. We use a direct metric to track the problem's complexity (the number of possible routes) and a fixed performance metric (average error). Our primary goal is to investigate the relationship between model capacity, computation, and the solution space size.
CONTROLS: We keep the original baseline (naive backtracking algorithm) and ablation (removing model capacity limiting).
COST: Estimated additional 50 GPU-hours to re-run the experiment with varying solution space sizes.
PREDICTION: We expect to see a negative correlation between solution space size and accuracy, with diminishing returns as the model approaches the optimal accuracy. We also anticipate that the model's failure to find the optimal solution will be more pronounced for larger solution spaces.

Added complexity to existing experiment in evaluation of model's capacity vs. the problem solution size on route optimization of traveling salesman, in  solution space the intervene the classical dependency measure of Optimality ratio between the # possible solutions present on problem definition.length

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Curse of Dimensionality in Route Optimization
PROPOSAL: We introduce high dimensionality in the representation space by modifying the problem to have multiple coordinates for each city (e.g., x, y, and z coordinates). We investigate how the increase in dimensionality affects the model's ability to find the optimal solution. Specifically, we examine the impact of the curse of dimensionality on the model's performance, as the number of cities increases.
CONTROLS: We compare our results against an ablation of the increased dimensionality (using only 2D coordinates) and a baseline where we use dimensionality reduction (Principal Component Analysis).
COST: Estimated additional 20 GPU-hours to fine-tune the model with the 3D representation.
PREDICTION: We expect to see a decline in model performance as the dimensionality increases, due to the curse of dimensionality. We also anticipate that the model may struggle to find the optimal solution when the number of cities is large. However, we may see some positive effects from using dimensionality reduction techniques.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Computational Efficiency and Solution Space Size
PROPOSAL: We investigate the relationship between computational efficiency and solution space size by varying the number of cities in the problem. We measure computational efficiency as the number of epochs required to reach a certain level of accuracy. We examine how the solution space size affects the computational efficiency of the model, as the number of cities increases.
CONTROLS: We compare our results against a baseline where we use a fixed number of epochs and an ablation of the early stopping criterion.
COST: Estimated additional 50 GPU-hours to re-run the experiment with varying solution space sizes.
PREDICTION: We expect to see an increase in computational efficiency as the solution space size decreases. However, we anticipate that the model may be less efficient when dealing with very large solution spaces, due to the curse of dimensionality and the difficulty of finding good solutions.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Adaptive Sampling and Solution Space Size
PROPOSAL: We investigate the impact of adaptive sampling on the model's performance when dealing with large solution spaces. We implement a sampling strategy that adapts to the model's performance and selects the most promising areas of the solution space. We examine how the adaptive sampling affects the model's ability to find the optimal solution, as the solution space size increases.
CONTROLS: We compare our results against a baseline where we use a fixed sampling strategy and an ablation of the adaptive sampling technique.
COST: Estimated additional 30 GPU-hours to fine-tune the model with the adaptive sampling strategy.
PREDICTION: We expect to see improved performance when using adaptive sampling, especially when dealing with very large solution spaces. However, we anticipate that the model may overfit the sampled data and lose generalizability.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: REVISED: Scalable Complexity Trends in Route Optimization
PROPOSAL: We revise the previous experiment to incorporate the findings from the following experiments and prepare a baseline comparing all previous experiments with there own isolation findings for "Route Optimization of traveling salesman Problem"s analysis overlap. We refine the comparison metrics for evaluation, with a focus on overall performance, efficiency, and sampling strategy effectiveness.
CONTROLS: We retain the previous baselines and ablations, refining the experiment to evaluate the cumulative effect of the proposed strategies.
COST: Estimated additional 50 GPU-hours to refine the experiment and analyze the cumulative effects of the proposed strategies.
PREDICTION: We anticipate seeing reinforcing trends across the individual experiments, indicating that the proposed strategies are complementary and effective in addressing the challenges of the "Route Optimization of traveling salesman Problem".

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Model Capacity and Solution Quality vs. Annotation Reliability
PROPOSAL: We investigate the relationship between model capacity, solution quality, and annotation reliability for the traveling salesman problem. We generate multiple versions of the problem with varying degrees of annotation quality and examine how the model's performance and solution quality change in response to these variations.
CONTROLS: We compare our results against a baseline where we use high-quality annotations and an ablation of the annotator selection process.
COST: Estimated additional 40 GPU-hours to fine-tune the model with varying annotation reliability.
PREDICTION: We expect to see a decrease in model performance and solution quality as annotation reliability decreases. However, we anticipate that the model may be more robust to annotator errors than previously thought, and that the impact of annotation reliability may be more complex than a straightforward trade-off between model capacity and annotation quality.

ACTION: ADD 7
TITLE: Evaluating Overfitting and Generalization in Route Optimization
PROPOSAL: We investigate the extent to which the proposed strategies for addressing the challenges of the traveling salesman problem lead to overfitting and/or generalization issues. We test the robustness of our models to unseen data and evaluate their generalization capabilities by using both synthetic and real-world datasets.
CONTROLS: We compare our results against a baseline where we use a simple model without any special handling for overfitting or generalization.
COST: Estimated additional 60 GPU-hours to fine-tune the model for robustness and generalization.
PREDICTION: We expect to see that some of the strategies for addressing the challenges of the traveling salesman problem lead to overfitting or generalization issues, and that the model's performance on unseen data is affected by the quality of the annotations and the capacity of the model.

ACTION: ADD 8
TITLE: Consolidated Model for Route Optimization
PROPOSAL: We combine the insights from the previous experiments to propose a consolidated model for route optimization that incorporates the key findings on scalability, representation space dimensions, curse of dimensionality, computational efficiency, adaptive sampling, model capacity, and annotator reliability.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the consolidated model against a baseline that uses the state-of-the-art route optimization algorithm.
COST: Estimated additional 80 GPU-hours to fine-tune the consolidated model.
PREDICTION: We expect to see significant improvements in the performance of the consolidated model, especially in terms of robustness, generalization, and adaptation to varying problem sizes and annotation qualities.

propositions.texte: To investigate how the dimensionality of the representation space influences the accuracy of the neural network, we introduce a new variable in the problem and modify the neural network architecture to accommodate it. Specifically, we add a new coordinate system to the problem by introducing virtual cities that are not part of the solution space, but affect the network's decision-making. We observe how the performance change as the number of virtual cities increases.
propositions.titre: Impact of Representation Space Dimensions

propositions.controles: We compare our results against an ablation of the increased dimensionality (using only 2D coordinates) and a baseline where we use dimensionality reduction (Principal Component Analysis).
propositions.cout_texte: Estimated additional 20 GPU-hours to fine-tune the model with the 3D representation.
propositions.prediction: We expect to see a decline in model performance as the dimensionality increases, due to the curse of dimensionality. We also anticipate that the model may struggle to find the optimal solution when the number of cities is large. However, we may see some positive effects from using dimensionality reduction techniques.
propositions.texte: We introduce high dimensionality in the representation space by modifying the problem to have multiple coordinates for each city (e.g., x, y, and z coordinates). We investigate how the increase in dimensionality affects the model's ability to find the optimal solution. Specifically, we examine the impact of the curse of dimensionality on the model's performance, as the number of cities increases.
propositions.titre: Curse of Dimensionality in Route Optimization

propositions.controles: We compare our results against a baseline where we use a fixed number of epochs and an ablation of the early stopping criterion.
propositions.cout_texte: Estimated additional 50 GPU-hours to re-run the experiment with varying solution space sizes.
propositions.prediction: We expect to see an increase in computational efficiency as the solution space size decreases. However, we anticipate that the model may be less efficient when dealing with very large solution spaces, due to the curse of dimensionality and the difficulty of finding good solutions.
propositions.texte: We investigate the relationship between computational efficiency and solution space size by varying the number of cities in the problem. We measure computational efficiency as the number of epochs required to reach a certain level of accuracy. We examine how the solution space size affects the computational efficiency of the model, as the number of cities increases.
propositions.titre: Computational Efficiency and Solution Space Size

propositions.controles: We compare our results against a baseline where we use a fixed sampling strategy and an ablation of the adaptive sampling technique.
propositions.cout_texte: Estimated additional 30 GPU-hours to fine-tune the model with the adaptive sampling strategy.
propositions.prediction: We expect to see improved performance when using adaptive sampling, especially when dealing with very large solution spaces. However, we anticipate that the model may overfit the sampled data and lose generalizability.
propositions.texte: We investigate the impact of adaptive sampling on the model's performance when dealing with large solution spaces. We implement a sampling strategy that adapts to the model's performance and selects the most promising areas of the solution space. We examine how the adaptive sampling affects the model's ability to find the optimal solution, as the solution space size increases.
propositions.titre: Adaptive Sampling and Solution Space Size

propositions.controles: We compare our results against a baseline where we use high-quality annotations and an ablation of the annotator selection process.
propositions.cout_texte: Estimated additional 40 GPU-hours to fine-tune the model with varying annotation reliability.
propositions.prediction: We expect to see a decrease in model performance and solution quality as annotation reliability decreases. However, we anticipate that the model may be more robust to annotator errors than previously thought, and that the impact of annotation reliability may be more complex than a straightforward trade-off between model capacity and annotation quality.
propositions.texte: We investigate the relationship between model capacity, solution quality, and annotation reliability for the traveling salesman problem. We generate multiple versions of the problem with varying degrees of annotation quality and examine how the model's performance and solution quality change in response to these variations.
propositions.titre: Model Capacity and Solution Quality vs. Annotation Reliability

propositions.controles: We compare our results against a baseline where we use a simple model without any special handling for overfitting or generalization.
propositions.cout_texte: Estimated additional 60 GPU-hours to fine-tune the model for robustness and generalization.
propositions.prediction: We expect to see that some of the strategies for addressing the challenges of the traveling salesman problem lead to overfitting or generalization issues, and that the model's performance on unseen data is affected by the quality of the annotations and the capacity of the model.
propositions.texte: We investigate the extent to which the proposed strategies for addressing the challenges of the traveling salesman problem lead to overfitting and/or generalization issues. We test the robustness of our models to unseen data and evaluate their generalization capabilities by using both synthetic and real-world datasets.
propositions.titre: Evaluating Overfitting and Generalization in Route Optimization

propositions.controles: We compare the performance of the consolidated model against a baseline that uses the state-of-the-art route optimization algorithm.
propositions.cout_texte: Estimated additional 80 GPU-hours to fine-tune the consolidated model.
propositions.prediction: We expect to see significant improvements in the performance of the consolidated model, especially in terms of robustness, generalization, and adaptation to varying problem sizes and annotation qualities.
propositions.texte: We combine the insights from the previous experiments to propose a consolidated model for route optimization that incorporates the key findings on scalability, representation space dimensions, curse of dimensionality, computational efficiency, adaptive sampling, model capacity, and annotator reliability.
propositions.titre: Consolidated Model for Route Optimization

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scaling Simulated Euclidean TSP
PROPOSAL: Train a range of artificial neural networks (ANNs) on a synthetic dataset of Euclidean traveling salesman problems (TSPs) with varying sizes (up to 1000 nodes) and solution spaces. Use a fixed capacity model and scale up the TSP instances to observe performance trends. To scale the TSP, create new instances with combinatorially increasing solution spaces and uniformly generated node positions.
CONTROLS: Compare against the Frank-Wolfe algorithm and a random greedy algorithm for TSP. Study the impact of model architecture and activation functions on observed trends.
COST: 10^5 GPU-hours (using a mix of batched training and efficient generation of synthetic data)
PREDICTION: Performance will improve smoothly up to a critical capacity limit, but will not continue to improve as polylogarithmically with increased solution space size, reflecting the curse of dimensionality. Failing predictions: might observe non-smooth dependencies between model complexity and TSP instance complexity due to model sensitivity or optimal solution becoming non-negligible outliers.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Dimensionality Impact
PROPOSAL: Scale the dimensionality of the Euclidean TSP synthetic dataset (and the solution space of the model) to study how performance degrades as the curse of dimensionality sets in. Specifically, compare training times, test accuracy, and the amount of overfitting on TSP instances in dimensions from 2 to 8. For higher dimensions, reduce the TSP instance size to maintain combinatorial solution space growth, allowing us to observe the effects of increasing dimensionality without excessive computational cost.
CONTROLS: Compare against the base case (dim=2) and the results from the first proposal (Scaling Simulated Euclidean TSP). Investigate how different neural network architectures react to the increased dimensionality, and what form of regularization can mitigate these effects.
COST: 5 * 10^4 GPU-hours (using a mix of batched training and dimensionality-reduced TSP instances)
PREDICTION: Performance will degrade significantly with increased dimensionality, with the degree of degradation depending on the model architecture and the type of regularization used. Failing predictions: might find that certain models are able to handle higher dimensions without much performance loss due to bias-variance tradeoffs.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Refine the Dimensionality Study
PROPOSAL: Refine proposal 2 (Analyzing Dimensionality Impact) to also directly challenge the model with adversarially crafted TSP instances in higher dimensions. Instead of using uniformly generated node positions, create TSP instances with specifically designed node configurations that exacerbate the effects of dimensionality. This will allow us to better understand how the model's performance degrades in the presence of carefully crafted "hard" instances. 
CONTROLS: Compare against the uniformly generated node positions (base case) and remain the same as previously established for this proposal.
COST: 1.25 * 10^4 GPU-hours (taking into account the smaller instance size needed for adversarial cases)
PREDICTION: The model will exhibit a significant performance drop in adversarially crafted higher-dimensional TSP instances, revealing limits in the model's ability to generalize. Failing predictions: might not observe a significant performance difference between the uniformly generated and adversarially crafted instances if the model's capacity is sufficient to handle the worst-case scenario.

TITLE: Refine the Dimensionality Study
PROPOSAL: Refine proposal 2 (Analyzing Dimensionality Impact) to also directly challenge the model with adversarially crafted TSP instances in higher dimensions. Instead of using uniformly generated node positions, create TSP instances with specifically designed node configurations that exacerbate the effects of dimensionality. This will allow us to better understand how the model's performance degrades in the presence of carefully crafted "hard" instances.
CONTROLS: Compare against the uniformly generated node positions (base case) and remain the same as previously established for this proposal.
COST: 1.25 * 10^4 GPU-hours (taking into account the smaller instance size needed for adversarial cases)
PREDICTION: The model will exhibit a significant performance drop in adversarially crafted higher-dimensional TSP instances, revealing limits in the model's ability to generalize. Failing predictions: might not observe a significant performance difference between the uniformly generated and adversarially crafted instances if the model's capacity is sufficient to handle the worst-case scenario.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Learning Algorithm Impact
PROPOSAL: Use the same synthetic dataset of Euclidean TSP instances with varying sizes and fixed capacity models to study how different learning algorithms affect the scalability of performance. Specifically, train the models using various optimizers (e.g., Adam, SGD, AdamW) and compare the results. Additionally, experiment with different learning rates, weight decay rates, and batch sizes to see their impact on performance and stability.
CONTROLS: Compare against a set of standard hyperparameters (default learning rate, batch size, etc.) for each optimizer, as well as a baseline of uniform random updates (a form of weakness baseline). Evaluate the impact of each optimizer on the observed scaling laws.
COST: 1.5 * 10^4 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The performance of the model will improve as the learning algorithm is optimized, but the scaling laws will be influenced by the specific choices of hyperparameters. Failing predictions: might find that some optimizers cause a non-smooth performance curve, which could suggest difficulties in scaling the optimization process itself.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying Capacity Limitations
PROPOSAL: Use the existing synthetic dataset of Euclidean TSP instances to quantify the capacity limitations of the fixed-sized models. Specifically, train multiple models with different combinations of capacity (number of layers, number of neurons per layer, etc.) and evaluate their performance on a range of TSP instances. This will allow us to establish a relationship between model capacity and performance on the TSP task.
CONTROLS: Compare against a set of standard model architectures (e.g., fully connected, convolutional) and different capacity combinations. Plot performance curves to illustrate the relationship between capacity and performance.
COST: 2.5 * 10^4 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The performance of the model will improve with increasing capacity, but the rate of improvement will slow down as the capacity approaches the optimal value for the TSP task. Failing predictions: might find that there is a threshold capacity above which performance does not improve further, which could suggest another fundamental limit on model performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing Solution Space and Representation Space Interplay
PROPOSAL: Since the TSP problem inherently couples solution space and representation space, design a weaker coupling between the two by introducing randomized node positions that have no direct geometric relation to the TSP problem instance. Then, train the same models on the TSP problem with this added noise to observe how the performance degrades and whether we can recover some clarity on the fundamental scaling laws not influenced by geometric intuition.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original TSP instances without added node position noise and the results from previous proposals. Investigate how the interplay between solution space and representation space affects the observed scaling laws.
COST: 1.2 * 10^4 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The performance of the model will degrade significantly due to the introduced coupling breaking, and the scaling laws will be influenced by the properties of the representation space rather than the geometric properties of the solution space. Failing predictions: might not observe the expected degradation in performance and could find that the geometric intuition strongly informs the scaling laws even in the presence of added noise.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Investigating Learning Algorithm Impact
PROPOSAL: Refine the third proposal to explore more sophisticated learning algorithms that can potentially reveal underlying mechanisms governing the scaling laws. Specifically, experiment with meta-learning approaches that can adapt to the properties of the TSP problem instance, such as gradient-based meta-learning and model-based meta-learning. Additionally, investigate how the learning algorithm affects the exploration-exploitation tradeoff in the high-dimensional solution space of the TSP.
CONTROLS: Compare against a set of standard learning algorithms (e.g., Adam, SGD) and evaluate the impact of each on the observed scaling laws. Analyze the exploration-exploitation tradeoff by visualizing the model's behavior on a range of TSP instances.
COST: 2.2 * 10^4 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The meta-learning algorithms will exhibit improved performance and scalability on the TSP task, revealing novel insights into the underlying mechanisms governing the scaling laws. Failing predictions: might find that the TSP task does not benefit significantly from meta-learning algorithms, which could suggest limitations in our current understanding of these approaches.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncovering Emergent Scaling Laws
PROPOSAL: Use the insights and results from the previous proposals to investigate the emergence of scaling laws in neural networks for the Euclidean TSP problem. Specifically, design an experiment to analyze how the learned scaling laws generalize across different instances of the problem and to what extent they can be abstracted and applied to related problem settings. Investigate whether the emergent scaling laws can be used to guide the design of more efficient algorithms for TSP and related problems.
CONTROLS: Compare against a set of standard approaches to TSP and evaluate the impact of the learned scaling laws on performance and efficiency. Analyze the generalizability and transferability of the learned scaling laws across different instances of the problem.
COST: 4 * 10^4 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The emergent scaling laws will be found to generalize across different instances of the TSP problem, and will provide valuable insights and guidance for the design of more efficient algorithms for TSP and related problems. Failing predictions: might find that the learned scaling laws are highly instance-specific and do not generalize well, which could suggest limitations in our current understanding of the problem.

ACTION: REVISE 6
TITLE: Uncovering Emergent Scaling Laws
PROPOSAL: Refine the sixth proposal to focus on the theoretical aspects of emergent scaling laws, aiming to establish a rigorous understanding of the underlying mechanisms governing these phenomena. Specifically, formulate a mathematical framework for characterizing the scaling laws and derive a set of theoretical predictions that can be tested against the results from previous proposals.
CONTROLS: Compare the theoretical predictions against the empirical results from the previous proposals, providing a thorough validation of the theoretical framework.
COST: negligible (assuming the framework exists)
PREDICTION: The theoretical framework will successfully capture the essential characteristics of emergent scaling laws in neural networks for the Euclidean TSP problem, providing a unified understanding of the underlying mechanisms governing these phenomena. Failing predictions: might find that the theoretical framework is insufficient or incomplete, requiring further refinements or extensions to capture the full range of scaling behaviors observed in the empirical results.

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Fine-Grained Contrastive Learning for Multilingual Data Selection
PROPOSAL: Implement a fine-grained contrastive learning approach to learn a universal data-quality signal across languages, by creating a multilingual dataset with dual samples: high-quality and low-quality content. We'll combine this with a self-supervised learning framework, where the model learns to distinguish between these two samples and decides which ones to select for pretraining data.
CONTROLS: We'll compare this approach with existing methods, such as FineWeb2-HQ, and apply it on a large-scale multilingual web-crawl dataset, e.g., CC-Web.
COST: 10,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might show higher robustness and generalizability across languages compared to existing methods, and, with proper hyperparameter tuning, could potentially select pretraining data more aligned with the LLM's downstream performance, reducing the risk of bias and over-specialization. However, we might encounter issues with scalability and hyperparameter tuning for very large-scale multilingual datasets.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cross-Lingual Evaluation of Model-Based Data Selection for LLM Pretraining
PROPOSAL: To address the challenge of evaluating and comparing model-based data selection approaches across languages, we propose a novel cross-lingual evaluation framework. This framework will assess how well different data selection methods, including our fine-grained contrastive learning approach, generalize to languages beyond their training language(s). We'll use a set of carefully selected monolingual evaluation datasets from various languages and languages families, and a set of multilingual evaluation metrics (e.g., BLEU scores, ROUGE scores) that are language-independent.
CONTROLS: For comparison, we'll consider existing methods, such as FineWeb2-HQ and DCLM, as well as heuristic and rule-based filters, such as deduplication and domain-aware sampling. We'll also investigate the effect of training a universal data quality rater on a single multilingual dataset vs. a set of individual language datasets.
COST: 5,000 GPU-hours ( additional to the fine-grained contrastive learning proposal)
PREDICTION: By evaluating the cross-lingual generalizability of data selection methods, we might uncover interesting insights on how data quality varies across languages and identify promising strategies for multilingual pretraining. However, we might struggle with selecting an optimal set of evaluation metrics that accurately capture language-agnostic data quality and are sensitive enough to detect subtle differences in data quality between languages.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Cross-Lingual Evaluation of Model-Based Data Selection for LLM Pretraining
PROPOSAL: To enhance the cross-lingual evaluation framework (proposal 2) and make it more comprehensive, we revise it to include an additional experimental component: a multilingual benchmark dataset will be created by combining multiple monolingual benchmark datasets from diverse languages. This combined dataset will serve as a proxy for real-world multilingual data and allow us to compare the performance of different data selection methods in a more diverse and challenging setting. By doing so, we'll gain a deeper understanding of how model-based data selection approaches handle different languages and noise distributions.
CONTROLS: As before, we'll consider existing methods (FineWeb2-HQ, DCLM) and heuristic filters. We'll also investigate the impact of dataset size and bias on the performance of our revised framework.
COST: 5,000 additional GPU-hours (up to 10,000) 
PREDICTION: The revised framework should provide a more robust and comprehensive evaluation of data selection methods across languages and datasets, but we might need to carefully curate and preprocess the combined dataset to ensure it accurately represents real-world multilingual data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: jointly Training a Multilingual Quality Rater and a Downstream Task Model
PROPOSAL: Instead of training a separate data quality rater and pretraining a downstream task model, we will jointly train both models on the selected pretraining data. This will enable the quality rater to learn the desired data quality signal in the presence of the downstream task objectives, which should lead to more robust and informative pretraining data. We'll evaluate different joint training strategies, such as using a multi-task learning framework or meta-learning approaches.
CONTROLS: We'll compare the performance of jointly trained models with the performance of models that use a separately trained quality rater, and with models that use existing data selection methods (FineWeb2-HQ, DCLM). We'll also investigate the impact of varying the priorities of the downstream task and the quality rater during joint training.
COST: 8,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Jointly training a quality rater and a downstream task model may lead to improved downstream task performance by optimizing the quality rater for the specific task requirements, but we might encounter challenges in designing a suitable joint training objective that balances the competing goals of data quality and downstream task performance.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: jointly Training a Multilingual Quality Rater and a Downstream Task Model
PROPOSAL: To further improve the jointly trained model (proposal 3), we will incorporate a decoding objective during the pretraining phase, where the model is asked to generate coherent and relevant text given a prompt. This decoding objective will allow the quality rater to learn a more nuanced understanding of what constitutes high-quality text, and enable the downstream task model to learn more effective text generation and inference strategies.
CONTROLS: We'll compare the performance of jointly trained models with and without the decoding objective, and with the performance of models that use a separately trained quality rater and a pretraining phase without decoding. We'll also investigate the impact of varying the complexity of the prompts and the number of pretraining iterations on the model's performance.
COST: This revision will add 2,000 GPU-hours to the existing estimate of 8,000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: Incorporating a decoding objective during pretraining may lead to significant improvements in downstream task performance by enhancing the model's ability to generate coherent and relevant text, but we might need to carefully design the decoding objective and the pretraining phase to avoid overfitting and ensure that the model maintains its ability to select high-quality text.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Impact of Data Quality on Downstream Task Performance in Low-Resource Languages
PROPOSAL: We will conduct an in-depth analysis of the impact of data quality on downstream task performance in low-resource languages, where the scarcity of high-quality training data can have a significant effect on model performance. We will evaluate the performance of our multilingual quality rater and jointly trained model on a range of downstream tasks in low-resource languages, and investigate the correlation between data quality and model performance.
CONTROLS: We'll compare the performance of our model with existing state-of-the-art models on low-resource languages, and investigate the robustness of our model to variations in data quality. We'll also examine the characteristics of high-quality and low-quality data in low-resource languages, and identify factors that contribute to data quality.
COST: 6,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our analysis may reveal critical insights into the factors that impact data quality in low-resource languages, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in improving downstream task performance in these languages. However, we might encounter challenges in evaluating model performance and data quality in low-resource languages where high-quality evaluation datasets and metrics are scarce.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Multilingual Data Selection for Achieving Linguistic Diversity in Pretraining Corpora
PROPOSAL: We will explore the impact of multilingual data selection on achieving linguistic diversity in pretraining corpora, which is essential for building robust and effective multilingual models. We will evaluate our multilingual quality rater and jointly trained model on a range of metrics that capture linguistic diversity, such as token and part-of-speech diversity, and investigate how our model's selection criteria can be tailored to prioritize linguistic diversity.
CONTROLS: We'll compare the performance of our model with existing state-of-the-art models on linguistic diversity metrics, and investigate the impact of our model's selection criteria on linguistic diversity. We'll also examine the relationship between data quality and linguistic diversity in our model.
COST: 4,000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our analysis may provide insights into the importance of linguistic diversity in pretraining corpora and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving this goal. However, we might need to carefully balance the trade-off between data quality and linguistic diversity in our model's selection criteria.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalability and Efficiency of Multilingual Data Selection for Large-Scale LLM Pretraining
PROPOSAL: We will investigate the scalability and efficiency of our multilingual data selection approach for large-scale LLM pretraining, including the impact of parallelization, distributed training, and model pruning on our approach's performance and cost. We will explore techniques to optimize the processing and selection of large volumes of web-crawled data, and evaluate the effect of these techniques on the quality and diversity of the pretraining corpus.
CONTROLS: We'll compare the performance of our approach with existing state-of-the-art approaches on large-scale LLM pretraining, and investigate the impact of various optimization techniques on our approach's performance and cost.
COST: 8,000 GPU-hours (additional to the existing estimates)
PREDICTION: Our analysis may provide insights into the scalability and efficiency of our multilingual data selection approach and identify techniques that can be employed to optimize its performance and cost for large-scale LLM pretraining, while also allowing for effective balancing of the desired linguistic diversity metrics.

Prediction: By evaluating the cross-lingual generalizability of data selection methods, we might uncover interesting insights on how data quality varies across languages and identify promising strategies for multilingual pretraining. However, we might struggle with selecting an optimal set of evaluation metrics that accurately capture language-agnostic data quality and are sensitive enough to detect subtle differences in data quality between languages.

PROPOSAL 3: jointly Training a Multilingual Quality Rater and a Downstream Task Model
Instead of training a separate data quality rater and pretraining a downstream task model, we will jointly train both models on the selected pretraining data. This will enable the quality rater to learn the desired data quality signal in the presence of the downstream task objectives, which should lead to more robust and informative pretraining data. We'll evaluate different joint training strategies, such as using a multi-task learning framework or meta-learning approaches.
Controls: We'll compare the performance of jointly trained models with the performance of models that use a separately trained quality rater, and with models that use existing data selection methods (FineWeb2-HQ, DCLM). We'll also investigate the impact of varying the priorities of the downstream task and the quality rater during joint training.
Estimated cost: 8,000 GPU-hours
Prediction: Jointly training a quality rater and a downstream task model may lead to improved downstream task performance by optimizing the quality rater for the specific task requirements, but we might encounter challenges in designing a suitable joint training objective that balances the competing goals of data quality and downstream task performance.

PROPOSAL 4: Evaluating the Impact of Data Quality on Downstream Task Performance in Low-Resource Languages
We will conduct an in-depth analysis of the impact of data quality on downstream task performance in low-resource languages, where the scarcity of high-quality training data can have a significant effect on model performance. We will evaluate the performance of our multilingual quality rater and jointly trained model on a range of downstream tasks in low-resource languages, and investigate the correlation between data quality and model performance.
Controls: We'll compare the performance of our model with existing state-of-the-art models on low-resource languages, and investigate the robustness of our model to variations in data quality. We'll also examine the characteristics of high-quality and low-quality data in low-resource languages, and identify factors that contribute to data quality.
Estimated cost: 6,000 GPU-hours
Prediction: Our analysis may reveal critical insights into the factors that impact data quality in low-resource languages, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in improving downstream task performance in these languages. However, we might encounter challenges in evaluating model performance and data quality in low-resource languages where high-quality evaluation datasets and metrics are scarce.

PROPOSAL 5: Multilingual Data Selection for Achieving Linguistic Diversity in Pretraining Corpora
We will explore the impact of multilingual data selection on achieving linguistic diversity in pretraining corpora, which is essential for building robust and effective multilingual models. We will evaluate our multilingual quality rater and jointly trained model on a range of metrics that capture linguistic diversity, such as token and part-of-speech diversity, and investigate how our model's selection criteria can be tailored to prioritize linguistic diversity.
Controls: We'll compare the performance of our model with existing state-of-the-art models on linguistic diversity metrics, and investigate the impact of our model's selection criteria on linguistic diversity. We'll also examine the relationship between data quality and linguistic diversity in our model.
Estimated cost: 4,000 GPU-hours
Prediction: Our analysis may provide insights into the importance of linguistic diversity in pretraining corpora and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving this goal. However, we might need to carefully balance the trade-off between data quality and linguistic diversity in our model's selection criteria.

PROPOSAL 6: Scalability and Efficiency of Multilingual Data Selection for Large-Scale LLM Pretraining
We will investigate the scalability and efficiency of our multilingual data selection approach for large-scale LLM pretraining, including the impact of parallelization, distributed training, and model pruning on our approach's performance and cost. We will explore techniques to optimize the processing and selection of large volumes of web-crawled data, and evaluate the effect of these techniques on the quality and diversity of the pretraining corpus.
Controls: We'll compare the performance of our approach with existing state-of-the-art approaches on large-scale LLM pretraining, and investigate the impact of various optimization techniques on our approach's performance and cost.
Estimated cost: 8,000 GPU-hours (additional to the existing estimates)
Prediction: Our analysis may provide insights into the scalability and efficiency of our multilingual data selection approach and identify techniques that can be employed to optimize its performance and cost for large-scale LLM pretraining, while also allowing for effective balancing of the desired linguistic diversity metrics.
